"What the hell is this crap?" My first impressions of the game; looking at the trailer and screenshots.
I decided to randomly look at a video of this game being explained. Before I knew it I was slightly interested.
My slight interest and curiosity got me to download the free version of this game and give it a good college try. After about an hour I knew this was something special. Something I could play for years if not for once in a while.
You are in control of a tribesmen or women of sorts set to survive in the great iron north. You can customize your starting story which impacts your starting gear and situation respectively. You can also customize where you start and whether the tutorial is active or not. From there is up to you create a marvelous adventure filled with peril, exhaustion, starvation, infection, and whatever else might kill you.
The game mechanics make sense and feel realistic. Chopping a tree down with a knife takes hours unlike using an axe, chasing down a reindeer or badger is unlikely, etc. It’s not perfect but it works.
This game kind of reminds me of a ‘create your own adventure book/board game’. Time progresses as you perform actions and move around the world. This gives you time to think about your next action. Do you try and sneak up on that wild pig or do you chunk this rock on the ground at it? Knowing that if you miss it’s probably going to get away. Should I eat this spoiled food knowing it might make me sick?
Death is permanent so make every choice count!
Every action performed is checked against multiple stats. Reminds me of the old DnD days. Makes the world feel more immersive and the combat feel richer. You want to throw that spear? How fatigued are you? What’s you skill in spears? Are you injured? How far away is the target? I don’t know all the exact stats but I know there is a lot going on in the background for everything you do.
I recommend that you just watch a couple video and try it out for yourself. Download the free version at their website.
If this sounds good to you then you owe it to yourself to give it a good college try like I did.
I will leave you with a brief adventure that I had in the Unreal World…
Alone, cold, and starving I come across a lonely reindeer in the middle of a vast frozen forest. He doesn’t notice me so make a slow approach. As I approach I snap a small branch beneath my foot like an idiot which alerts the reindeer to jump to attention. It’s now or never. I draw and shoot my bow. The shot is steady and accurate but the reindeer is already in motion. The arrow penetrates just below the reindeer’s shoulder. It takes off into the dense woods. I follow. After a short while I start to lose sight of it and I am relying on my tracking ability alone. Tracks and blood keep me focused. As night beings to fall I start to loose site of its trail. It’s getting dark and I am starting to lose hope. My stomach growls and I begin to shiver. The cold is taking a hold of me I am beginning to fail. Then I hear something to my south. A yell of an animal. Do I continue on or follow the sound? I hear the yell again. After losing complete site of the reindeer tracks I decide to follow the sound. After about 10 minutes of travelling south I see it… It’s the reindeer I shot earlier. It nearly doubled backed on me. It’s injured, crippled and fatigued. “You’re mine now!” I draw and fire my bow. I am so fatigued the arrow hits the tree next to it. Again! I draw and shot my bow. The arrow flies true and I hit it straight in the neck; blood rushes out. It slows and after a few steps staggers then passes out. I approach and finish the job.
I take a moment to rest but I am too cold to stay still for too long. Night has fallen and I need to rest. I quickly gather some branches and firewood and make a fire. The warmth of the fire gives me a second wind an I decide to skin the animal and butcher some of its meat. I am so hungry I feast on it raw like a ravenous dog. Its late, taking satisfaction of a good kill I decide to sleep for the night. Unfortunately the fire goes out in the middle of the night and I awake in the early hours of the morning chilled yet again. I hear something approaching... I take a moment to scan my surroundings and notice my reindeer has been feasted upon. What could of done this? A dog? No... A bear. As I turn I see the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ himself. I take a step back and it approaches. I draw my bow and take the shot. My shot is steady and true puncturing the bear in the front of his chest. It’s not enough. It becomes enraged and begins to charge. Before I can react It swipes its massive claw and gashes my arm and chest wide open. I fall back… I reach for my knife... It finishes me off with a mighty blow.
Hugh Glass would of been disappointed...
This is just one of my wonderful adventures. Many more await you in the Unreal World.

So I bought the game thinking I could play through the OP story line as its been over 10 years since I started watching, and I have forgotten parts.
Pros:
They appear to be going through every arc of the story line.
Because OP is so long, this inevitably means they end up with a good number of playable characters.
Cons:
The game is very buggy.  I had to reinstall once just to get past the first loading screen.  The game encounters a fatal error if you are in the menu or are not active for too long.
For whatever reason, I can't adjust the volume on my computer when the game is open.  Neither the keyboard FN keys nor the physical buttons on my laptop will change the volume when the game is open... Just a little wierd and annoying.
Controls are terrible, even on a controller.  You can't even play with just a controller because things like skip scene are exclusively on the keyboard.  Oh, and I can't find any sort of pause button, I have pressed every button on my keyboard and every button on the controller, nothing pauses.
More importantly: The game is ridiculously easy, and ridiculously repetititve.  I can't tell the difference between normal and hard mode, it is too easy.  I have been at low health maybe once, and then I just ran to grab an item from one of the many chests and boom back at full hp to resume fighting.  The bosses have a lot of HP and defense, but they really pose no threat whatsoever, it is just a matter of chasing them down and clicking the same buttons to kill them.  There are ridiculous number of fodder enemies that really don't do much more than get in your way (I don't notice my hp changing when they attack).  So after button mashing your way through 2000+ enemies and pathetic bosses you finish the mission, you are done with it right? Wrong.  You see each boss enemy drops coins when you kill them, and you need specific numbers of specific coins to increase specific stats of each playable character.  Therefore you have to replay the mission several times to get enough coins to get your character strong enough to be able to use a different boss's coin to level (rinse and repeat forever).  So now you have enough coins and are done with the mission? Wrong.  You also need to fill up a "legend" for each mission which involves getting an S rank and fulfilling certain objectivies, which sounds fine until you read the objectives and how to get an S rank.  Certain legends have objectives requiring replay with multiple characters (YAY! I get to play the same mission again).  All missions are ranked on the number of "!", kills, and your time to complete.  What are "!" you ask?  Good question, that isn't explained at all in the game.  When you defeat an opponent with an attack from an ally that you activate at the end of one of your normal attack chains, you get 1 ! point.  Problem is that when you are stronger (or even if you are not), you one hit kill the fodder with your normal attack chain so there is nothing left for your ally to attack.  The solution is to be far away and use a melee attack chain combined with a ranged ally finishing move.  Usually there is only one or two such good combos per character, so you end up spamming the same attack combo trying to 1000+ kill enemies with only the last attack.  Okay now you have an S rank.  Are you done? Of course not!  Each character has a couple of additional power ups you can get by achieving certain objectives or playing certain missions with them.  For example, almost every Straw Hat Pirate gets a power up when you complete the CP9 mission with them, so you are going to be playing that mission again and again.
TL;DR: Game is super repetitive, you need to play the same missions many times, and the game itself is laughably easy.

Ok here is the skinny on Bernie needs love:
Short version:
Fun graphics, decent controls, difficulty that at points will test your ability to not throw things, and severely pixilated boobs: It’s like my childhood all over again!
Long Version:
Graphics:  Ok this is made to look retro, which many users these days mark off for, but it has an oldschool tube-type TV mode you can start which I find kind of awesome. Truly enhances that classic-sitting-five-inches-from-the-tv-with-an-atari feel ( that’s a thing right?).
Game Play: The difficulty curve in this is so sharp it will have you pulling out your hair from time to time, but when you finally succeed in passing the blasted level that has been stumping you… you feel like you accomplished something.  For those unfamiliar with the classic side-scrollers, this is a good thing. You don’t want to feel like it was easy or you wasted your time… you don’t want it impossible or you DID waste your time. Hard but playable is the goal.
Controls/Bugs:  The controls can sometimes feel laggy but its something you learn to compensate for. The only glitch I found was on the boss level if you jump just right as the boss is about to appear you can end up with a frozen character unable to  land or move. All in all they chose to keep this one simple. Back forward and up are all you worry about.
Closing thoughts: I found the game quite challenging. If you are the kind of person who knows how to walk away for a bit before the moment of frustration and keep things fun , you should enjoy playing this.

Now on to the good stuff. This game has a decent length campaign that goes from the beginning of Luffy's journey up through the events of Punk Hazard and covers most of the major battles and events in between. The game also has Dream Mode which allows you to pick any character you've unlocked and fight through numerous islands with different objectives. So between the story, free mode (play the story as any unlocked character), dream mode, and an assload of unlockables this game will keep you busy for quite a while. So if you're a One Piece fan or just love the Warriors games, I'd suggest trying this out...though if you have a vita, PS3, or PS4 I'd suggest grabbing it for one of those systems (PS4 obviously being the best choice).

At first, the game felt a bit overwhelming, with all the logs to read, and it wasn't quite clear on how to progress through the story. Turns out, I have been playing too many video games and have forgotten that to continue a story, you have to turn the page.  By reading each log entry, you are given more of the story and what starts out as a simple, "salvage," mission, turns into something that I became engaged in as a player and as the character I was playing as.  This is one of the few games in which I've genuinely cared about the characters and the story.  Sure, The Walking Dead had plenty of characters I liked, but this game had my face litterally no more than six inches from my screen as I read through the text.  This game had moments in which I laughed out loud, stopped to process what I had just read, go back and re-read text files multiple times, feel shocked, and, believe it or not, disgusted.  I'll admit that I originally got this game for a certain achievement (I think you all know the one) but I eventually became more focused on the story.  I recommend this game to all who enjoy visual novels (albeit, slightly unorthodox) and love a complex story that you really want to know more about.
It's fun to play a 15-30 minutes a day to clear my mind.

I dont want to get politics in the way of this review (as I know there has been some controversy around this games creator).  So I'm going to be as honest about the game as I can, without discrediting the creator.  First things first, I LOVE Digital:  A Love Story.  It was immersive, engaging, and overall a nice game to play.  I liked the characters, I loved the setting, I seriously loved that that game.
Now, Analogue:  A Hate Story on the otherhand...  This "game", takes inspiration from the first, but is more story oriented than gameplay oriented.  Well, let's be honest, there wasnt any real "gameplay" in either itteration.  It's more like an interactive story than anything.  So to be clear, the first one had you doing stuff and actually let you connect the dots in the story.  While this one is a WAY more self explanitory story.  Anyway...  I finished the first game.  But this one couldnt keep my attention.  I found myself getting bored with it, every time I tried to play.  The story wasnt bad, but it just didnt resonate with me.  I felt like the story was becoming a little agressive in the way of the creators politics.  It became almost like I was reading a strongly opinioned blog that had nothing but agression towards the "Patriarchy".   As a man, I kinda started feeling like this story wasnt for me, and was directed towards a "certain" audience (like a fox in a henhouse kinda feel).  And after each story, the caracters kind of pressure you into choosing the "right" answer.  Choose the "Wrong" answer, and things will take an OBVIOUS turn for the worse.
I stopped about 3/4 of the way in, and just lost interest in it entirely to the point where I uninstalled it.
Would I recommend this game?  That depends...  None of my friends would like this kind of game anyway, so I cant say for sure.
So dont let my thumbs down discourage anyone else from buying it.  I just didnt like the story as much as the first one (and the first one was free).
I will say this though.  I praise the graphic artist for such great work on the character models.  They fit wonderfully with the characters personalities.
Story:  Meh/10
Game Play:  Reading/10
Artwork:  School Rumble/10  (This is a good rating :3)
Overall Verdict:  Feminism/10  Would fight patriarchy again.

CI Games - Creators of two typical yet very enjoyable linear FPS games. ALIEN RAGE, and Enemy Front. Alien Rage is a linear shooter taking you down corridors and hallways inside of an alien fuel production facility, the game play is solid the kill point system is good enough and it has merit for a few play throughs.
Enemy Front, the true subject of this review is about the best damn WWII game Ive played. Some people have reported alot of crashes and this game moving slowly. The game for me has crashed about 3 times over the course of 3 play throughs. So I cannot attest to this game being the "worst ever, dont buy this POS! etc etc etc". Enemy Front has some great graphics that puts you into the gritty war torn streets of Poland, and out on the beautiful wheat covered fields of Spain. Enemy Front covers WWII from the view point of the Poland Resistance in Warsaw against the Nazi Regime. This is a very understated part of WWII history and instead of the well over done take on WWII from the stand point of USA, UK, and France alliance.
Aside from the articulate environment is the weapons, they are damn near perfect. The weapons look, feel (scale, load times, mechanical noises), and report just like the WWII models, the level of detail in the weapons enhances the gameplay by offering silenced guns and even the first assault rifle ever mass produced, the MP44 or Sturmgewehr, the report from this gun is awesome while its stopping power can cut through multiple enemies. The focus is primarily Polish, and Germany makes/models but there is a few others namely the Sten and the USA trench shotgun which is a blast - literally.
What I found annoying about Enemy Front is that it comes to a rather quick end, about 8 hours.
Otherwise the sneaking system, and alternate routes provided in the levels make the repeat play through safely different than previous attemps. I enjoyed the hostage system and pestering Nazi guards with inspecting corners and other silly places because of noise distractions (you get the ability to toss stones as a way to sneak around or manuever enemies).
The blood spurting in this game was something akin to japanese samurai slasher films, but the blood is really bright red and had me wondering with all these red barrels, red trucks, red crates, and whole facilities with flashing red lights that I had actually stumbled upon some secret Nazi occult that is addicted to fruit punch. It gushes from their vests, every slow-mo load scene you see Nazi's huddled around trucks and barrels being taken somewhere - their high fructose junkies and they want the rest of the world under their sugar shaking fists! End their transport of these dangerously sweet liquids to the shores of Europa before they infest the rest of the world in a diabetes pandemic - Gawd help us all.
Now back from insanity.... I found the multiplayer dead (as of 08/2016). Nothing, nobody, nada.
Overall, if you like to play the fantastical hero who takes on 100 fruit punch loving Nazi's, doesnt mind a beautifully rendered WWII era backdrop, and plenty of ways to keep the parents, dentists, and organic food loving society saved from rambunctious obese kids and toothless adults - then this game is for you... when it goes on sale of course.

Most of this game is reading through text logs in order to understand what happened on an abandoned ship.  What you find is a deep story that makes you feel for the characters.  It is not a terribly long game; my first run through was under 3 hours, but it is was a worthwhile experience.

At last, a game this year that turns out to be a pleasant surprise. Like many, I had shied away from Enemy Front after reading lukewarm reviews (the same was true of Lords of the Fallen, also a very solid game). But this turned out to be a thoroughly enjoyable experience. Anybody who experience the glory days of Medal of Honor or call of Duty (back when they were WW2 shooters) knows exactly what to expect. Since there aren't really many games in that genre/era being made any more, this one was a welcome addition.
Gameplay felt tight and the graphics are often a real pleasure to behold. At times, the experience felt a little derivative, since this game borrows heavily from others (slow-motion bullet cam, slow-motion door breach, etc.) But this is made up for by other aspects in which the game is quite fresh. For example, the first-person stealth mechanics work really well and make for some tense infiltrations. Thankfully, the game never forces you into stealth, slipping seamlessly back into gung-ho action to the moment you are spotted.
My only slight regret is that the game was over so soon. I certainly feel like I got my money's worth and had a good 6-hour experience, but the Warsaw Uprising and French Resistance movements provide such fertile sources that one could easilly make a compeeling story in a game twice the length.

I admit that I'm a complete stranger to the visual novel genre - I can't even remember what led me to pick up Analogue. I do remember seeing the trailer, and being intrigued by the thought that there was more to this story than there seemed to be.
I wasn't wrong in the least.
While I don't have a solid basis for comparison, I do think that the minimalist style, smooth animations and unobtrusive soundtrack really complement the game. The focus is on the story that your A.I. of choice is telling you, and nothing else...with the possible exception of the A.I. themselves. The differences between *Mute and *Hyun-ae are profound, and only become more so as you spiral down into the mystery of the ship. While ultimately, the story here is *Hyun-ae's, *Mute's perspective provides a counterpoint essential to seeing *Hyun-ae's actions in the right light. When you're reading the story told by both women, captivated by the pieces of the puzzle falling into place, the mood can turn rather intense.
Though there is humor here, too. *Mute is remarkably crass, given her programming, and the levity her sass lends some serious situations is appreciated. *Hyun-ae is playful in her own right: should you befriend her enough, she will display different outfits for you, letting you use the in-game terminal to play a limited form of dress-up.
Speaking of the terminal, that and a Yes/No dialogue wheel will be the principle ways you assert yourself in-game. It's actually a nice mechanic. There are several times where the terminal comes in handy, and it's pretty intuitive to use. I also found the UI - probably due to that minimalist feel - comfortable to pick up.
All told, I couldn't find much wrong with Analogue. It was a wonderful introduction to the visual novel genre, and I plan to pick up it's sequel, Hate Plus. Might look into other visual novels as well, if they're half as good as this one.

Crysis in WW2 sounds like a great idea and, on paper, this game fits that description: same engine, small but semi-open maps, nice graphics and pseudo-realistic shooting (1-2 shot kills etc). In practice everything about the game is a little 'off'. The shooting is some of the blandest, most repetitive and frankly boring I've ever experienced. The expansive maps are almost empty and anyway of little use because the shooting is idiotically easy and the AI very poor. Something about the controls feels strange too though I can't quite put my finger on it. I suspect it's a poor port but it certainly isn't very polished and both movement and aiming don't quite work. It's almost like playing a game with poor hit detection in ♥♥♥♥ing single player. You even get little parts stolen from other shooters but somehow made worse: breeching rooms in slow motion from the modern CoDs, the bullet cam from Sniper Elite and 'defend this barricade against waves of mooks' from every console shooter in the last decade and a ♥♥♥♥ing half.
Also like Crysis you can choose stealth or run and gun but the stealth is incredibly slow, underpowered and clunky. As someone who loves stealth games and always takes the stealthy option when offered I gave up even trying early on and went for the action route.
Another part of the game that feels slightly wrong is the sound. Voices are too loud or too quiet despite the distance they are away from you, for example, and often firing sounds will be out of sync with the gun. This latter issue is most noticeable when you fire single shots on an SMG. Even the graphics, the high point of the game by far, are not without flaws. A fair bit of the lighting is pre-baked (your character doesn't cast a shadow for example) and it's merely good looking without an art direction. It's neither realistic nor stylised with the high contrast and overuse of visual effects hurting the already sub-par shooting and giving you ♥♥♥♥ing eye cancer for no good reason. Both the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ graphics and sound prevent there from being any atmosphere despite the game laying it on pretty heavily at times.
The story is as cookie-cutter as the shooting which is a shame given the somewhat unique parts of WW2 the game visits. Rarely do we see any significant amount of the French resistance and I struggle to think of another game showing Poland at all, resistance or otherwise. Sadly this is spoiled by the cliché characters and ♥♥♥♥ing standard♥♥♥♥♥pull reason for your character to be an American instead of a ♥♥♥♥ing native. In European Assault you were from the OSS. In the Saboteur a racecar mechanic. In this a ♥♥♥♥ing journalist. Granted the story does touch upon the anger some members of the resistance feel at being just another scoop but we've played as the Americans in WW2 enough already.
Finally little annoyances like an inconsistent checkpoint system, constant bugs, death by physics prop and even the occasional ♥♥♥♥ing invincible enemy finish off this shitpile of a game. Bodies and dropped weapons disappear almost the moment you turn around too though that can be fixed by tweaking config files. I couldn't even finish the game because three hours in my save wouldn't load (thanks checkpoint system!) and frankly I didn't feel like restarting so I didn't reach Norway but I seriously doubt the game improves. I can't remember where I even got this game but it appears to have come from a bundle or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ key reseller. Frankly it wouldn't be worth playing if it was free.

Addicting, immersive, and well supported by the Devs and especially the modding community,  Rimworld has been in development for the past five years, and just from playing the "Vanilla version" you can easily see the extensive amount of work that has been put into this game.  But what makes this game easily stand out from all the other "Early Access" survival or management games is the extensive amount of free mods that are available in Steam Workshop ranging from "quality of life" mods (e.g. improved lighting, hauling and stacking, or interface options) to more-or-less expansions of the vanilla game (e.g. psychology, children and pregnancy, an advanced "Glitter Technology" mod, and more).
While I recommend that new players begin by playing the Vanilla version of Rimworld for a few hours to familiarize themselves with the base game, once you've done that then the sky's the limit as far as how far you want to tweak your game.
Wanna get swarmed by disasters and raids?
Wanna build that dream colony where nothing ever goes wrong?
Wanna try out both with one group of colonists (that you can also edfit using the "Careful Prep" mod)?
Between the scenario settings, dev mode, and the hundreds of mods available for this game, you will likely spend as many hours toying around with the different settings as you'll be spending building and managing your colony.
Thirty dollars may sound a little steep for an Early Access game, but if you love playing any kind of management or survival game, then you'll spend more than enough hours in Rimworld to justify the price tag (and considering that there are no paid DLC's or micro-transactions, even more so!).  There is ALOT to learn - and manage - in Rimworld, but if you don't mind doing that, then you won't regret buying this game.

Gameplay in City of Steam is very reminiscent of most action RPGs on the market today. In fact, quite a favorable comparison could be made to Diablo 2 or Torchlight 2 from the standpoint that players work to level up skills to make them more powerful. On first glance, City of Steam's combat system is terrific and it certainly isn't bad by any stretch of the imagination. What is boils down to is that it is uninspiring in ways that the aforementioned games are not. As players level, they are granted skill power-ups in one of three disciplines. Points are allotted according to a player's wishes and combat skills are granted. In the end, it's not that the combat system is poor, it's just so much more button mashing of 1-2-3, rinse repeat.
Players are faced with pretty standard fare and work from a belt of abilities learned over time that increase in damage and effectiveness. I played as a Warder and my character had the typical arcing swings of both a great sword and two one-handed swords. It's pretty cool that players can choose a second weapon set for different skills and ways to fight monsters. Weapons can be changed out on the fly and it's worth having that ranged weapon handy to aggro only the monsters you want to rush out.
Questing is pretty standard fare as well. Head to a quest hub, grab 3-4 quests, head to the instances needed for completion, turn them in and done. Again, it's not unusual, just uninspiring and not as well done as most. The quest givers are not voiced which, depending on your particular style, is either a good or bad thing.
Players can utilize an isometric over the shoulder camera or toggle a free ranging camera on the fly. This is a marvelous touch on behalf of Mechanist, something that most players will like very much. In addition, questing can be directed if a player gets lost simply by clicking on the directional arrow that will automatically take characters to the desired location.
Still in the end, combat gets repetitive very fast. Between the same look and feel of all the instances and mashing the same combination of buttons over and over, it's a rather tiresome affair.

Before I start, I just need to add:
The free version is practically (if not entirely) identical to the Steam version. Even if you're totally enamoured with this game by the looks of the descriptions and reviews, I still urge people to play the free version before grabbing the Steam one. Once you've given it a shot, you can make a much better decision on if you want to drop money on it. I told myself that if I played the free version for longer than eight hours, I'd buy the Steam version even if I never boot it up again. I clocked about ten hours, bought it on Steam, then continued to play it for however long it says I have at the top of this review.
I really love this game. It's deep, but I've never felt truly lost; when you make a character, you can pick to have a goal-orientated quest system that teaches you how to play. This ranges from 'This is how you drink water, you
' to building your own house and trading for animals. Once you've grasped the basics, the game opens up as the survival roguelike it aims to be. If you want to know all the cool mechanics that come with the game, the other positive reviews go into passionate detail about what makes the game great. To avoid clashing with people who have literally hundreds of hours of gametime over me, I'll instead relay something that's unique to me; an in-game story.
Fur is really important in UnReal World. It's valuable, it's useful, and it'll stop you from freezing to death when Snow Hell decides to pay a visit. Unfortunately, being a total newbie at the game, the only hides I can get are from squirrels, hares, and ermines. Not very prestigious. The only big hides I had managed to score was one of a bear and an elk, and that's because they fell into a pit trap I set up and became a sitting duck for my volley of arrows. Basically, I'm a bad hunter.
One day I'm out in the snow in my bear fur clothes, checking my pit traps to see if any more suckers have taken pity on my awful hunting skills. The traps are on the border between a mire and a forest, set up to channel and capture any animals walking from one area to another. This time, I noticed a wolf on the world map standing in the mire, so I zoom in on the action to see what's going on.
Turns out, it's not a wolf. It's a
of them.
At this point of the game, the most dangerous thing I've successfully managed to hunt (that wasn't sitting in a pit and woefully awaiting death) is a fox. All the animals I've come across are basically 'let's see how close I can get before it runs away at the speed of light'. The wolves didn't do that. They decided that I'm up for dinner. They charge at me ("What? Animals
you in this game?!") and suddenly I'm reaching for my bow. I thought I was a goner, but it turns out that shooting an arrow into the shoulder of a charging wolf is a good deterrent (who knew?). It became a game of scoring a single wound on each attacking wolf to scare them and make them flee. I scored a particularly good hit on one wolf, and I chased down its limping self and attacked its head for a kill. Skinned its fur and butchered its meat and fat. Good stuff.
That's when I discovered why wolves were even here in the first place; lying in the middle of the field was a wolf-torn elk. I approached it and checked the hide, and was surprised to see the wolves hadn't mangled it beyond recognition. It was about a quarter of the way through skinning it that I realised the wolves were still around -- just keeping their distance. I decided to grab the skin and forget the butchering, get out while I still could. I didn't need the meat, the fur was the real gold here.
So I walk home with some wolf and elk fur under my arms. The total sum of the furs I had back home came to something like 8lbs; the fur I was carring totalled 30lbs. A good catch! I set the wolf fur down and use its fat from the butchering to tan it. I then set the elk fur down and -- wait! I didn't butcher the elk! I don't have any fat to tan it with! 20lbs of fur was threaning to go rotten on me if I didn't find a solution, and fast.
I dumped the fur in my cold, 'please don't rot on me' cellar and made a return to the elk. Turns out, so had the wolves, and they had regained their courage. Some nasty nips later, I decided my life wasn't worth some fat and fled.
I looked up about the tanning process to try to find alternatives for my elk fur. Turns out, you don't
to use fat. The skinned barks of alder and rowan trees work just as well. Big problem; I lived in a gigantic forest of pine and birch. So begins the race against time to find an alder or rowan tree before my goldmine attracts flies rather than merchants.
So I'm darting around the world map, cursing every pine and birch that I see. That's when I find a herd of reindeer milling around. I decided to try my luck, so I zoomed in and took a less-than-hopeful shot at the nearest one, expecting a total miss and all the reindeer to flee. It hits. Fire off a second arrow before the victim has a chance to run. Second one hits.
Oh crap. So this is what hunting feels like.
The reindeer has been so badly hit, it's practically crawling its way across the floor. I catch up with it and start trying to unload arrows into its head. My aim is so bad that it ends up hitting the shoulder, body, and even one hit on the knee, at which point I reprimanded UnReal World for its poor choice of meme references. It was around the time I decided to equip a javelin and start poking its head that my character falls asleep. Turns out, fighting wolves and lugging fur across a continent really tires a man out. Who knew?
I awoke with the reindeer nowhere in sight. I followed its tracks and found it only a short run away, still desperately trying to crawl its way to freedom. I started poking at its head with the javelin until it dies, skinned it, made sure to grab the fat this time, and recovered the arrows I had fired. The fat of the reindeer was enough to tan its own hide, but not enough to tan the elk's. The hunt for the tree was still on.
I read up on alder and rowan trees, and found out that they mostly grow in and around villages. So I poked my head into the local village and -- sure enough -- sitting in the middle of the field all proud of itself was an alder tree. The villagers were probably weirded out to see a man walk into their village, cry 'YES!' and then begin frantically carving the bark off of one of their trees. I didn't care. Elk fur was back in fashion, baby.
So that's how I went from Small Game Extraordinaire to sleeping in the furs of a wolf, elk, and reindeer, all because I decided to go check my traps for a bit. My bear fur clothes had some nasty wolf bites in them and I had sufffered a few nasty scratches myself, but I could probably line the entirety of my house in fur now. It was about this time I realised that maybe, just maybe, UnReal World is an awesome game and that I'm glad I got it.
Stay safe in the cold North, folks!

I'm recommending this game purely based on what is available now for the price. At this point in development, I feel like there is enough content and quality in the game that justifies the 9.99 price tag and not just a donation to the devs as a gamble on a "possibly could turn out to be a good game". You can play through missions and challenges solo (such as elemination, survival, and the Neurogen Incident) or with 3 other players in co-op. There is also pvp multiplayer and a hunger games style mode called "Wargames" or "Hellweek"(They've changed the name over the last update), which is my personal favorite and a sort of horde mode called "get killed by bots" which is found in the playground menu were you can do things like play around with the game mechanics and explore multiplayer maps. Though we haven't seen the highly anticipated "landsharks", Interstellar Marines still manages to deliver tactical gameplay in a tense and suspenseful atmosphere with the CTR training robots, which serve not only as a place holder or "test" for AI, but as a formidable (and fun to kill) enemy. The latest update introduces a proper introduction mission that introduces the player to the newly polished stealth mechanics. You can now earn CP(currency) in addition to TR(exp points) in order to purchase skins for your armor and weapons (all of whish were community created). This is supposedly their first step towards the more extensive customization planned on ZPS's road-map. Even so, there you already have the ability to add/remove silencers from your gun, as well as switch off/on your weapon mounted flashlight and laser sight. Also updated was a smooth new menu UI.
Alright now this is where the decision to buy IM may get difficult. The state of the development team. Now, its been a long and hard road for Zero Point Software and they've recently hit yet another snag in funding. I advise you to simply do a little reaserch as to their history and what it took to get this far (they have a video on it somewhere and I'll post it when I find it), but I will tell you ZPS is a very commited team and they've never struck me as the type of people that take your money and abandon the project/community (they've had opportunities do things like that, but have remained honest thus far). Yes, they have lost alot of members lately, and I think it's reduced to like 3 ppl mainly, but progress is still being made. As of now, they are acivly trying to find a publisher for support. They still communicate with the community, and updates are still being churned out. Progress has slowed to a crawl, but its still progress.
All in all, regardless of their funding issues and lack of landsharks, I genuinely have fun with the game. For the current price, I do at least recommend placing this game on your radar if you aren't comfortable with purchasing.

I honestly love this game, alone it stands tall and proud with very few things other than nickpicks bothering me.  And I would recommend this game to anyone who likes micro-management games such as Dwarf Fortress.  You have 3 story tellers the first is a slow learning curve.  Second is a learning curve with long periods in between events.  Third is either in a really bad mood and ♥♥♥♥s you over at a random time or is in a great mood and you can go seasons without anything happening at all, per say right off the bat you can have 7 people from the pirates show up and anal♥♥♥♥♥♥you with miniguns, or you can have nothing happen for years and suddenly get an event with 1 dude with a club.
The only things that bother me is the mental and travel and hauling system.  Pyromatics can sometime be happy or content then go on a rampage starting fires everywhere (just out of the home area.)  As well as travelling across the map, your people can't just forage on the move when food gets low or stop and hunt for a few days to get some food to the destination. A very touching story tackling major issues surrounding the Asian culture of women's roles in society and familial and cultural traditions. Taken place aboard a long abandoned spaceship of the past, an intelligence agent stumbles upon this craft in order to retrieve important intelligence, only to be surprised by the things he/she finds inside.
The Good:
• Features more interactivity than standard Japanese VNs
• A neat addition of a "command system" minigame that involves inputting command codes into a computer system which is used to interact with the two heroines and the spaceship itself
• A detailed, emotional, yet disturbing story with realistic characters
• Various viewpoints depending on each heroine
• A cute dress-up game featuring Hyun-ae (one of the heroines)
The Bad:
• A rather bleak UI compiled onto a solid white background
• The email log method of storytelling can become quite confusing & sometimes rather boring
• Little romantic interaction for those who are looking for a heavy romance VN
• An unimpressive OST with a lot of replayed soundtracks
What makes this VN different than others?:
• This is a story about hatred, hardly romance or love. This focal point in itself makees this VN a truly unique reading experience.
• Storytelling through logs of the past. Very little text takes place during real time & 99% of the information you acquire about the heroines is through these logs.
Overall, compared to other VNs, the art and music is rather bleak and character interaction is limited, as most of the text comes from logs of the past. But fortunately, the storytelling is strong enough to evoke emotions of empathy for these heroines through strong character development.

This game is like a retro equivalent of what Watch_Dogs could've been, had it not resorted to being a close GTA clone. Unlike Watch_Dogs however, the puzzle theme of the hacking aspect actually feels integrally present, and indeed the hacking feels totally necessary. The game is relatively short, but it has a charming graphic style and slick mechanics.
Despite the title, in actuality you only need to shoot one person in the game- the game is rendered such that using a gun (a late-game tool) puts you at a stretch for time. This encourages the player to favour fisticuffs (or total stealth) alongside using the hacking mechanics- you are never able to just blitz through a level. The deadliness of the guards helps retain a true need for stealth. This makes the game more satisfying to beat.
Once multiple circuits come into play, the game becomes a lot less straightforward, as one has to decide how to trigger events to incapacitate guards utilising multiple devices. It is exceedingly fun to watch your intricate circuits work to your advantage!
In sum, this game is easily my favourite which I possess on Steam. Yes, the game is short, but equally you have a wealth of user content to keep you playing and thinking. This game is a classic example of "you get what you put into it".  Invest some effort in understanding how things work and in forming relationships with (gasp) other people and it can be richly rewarding with virtually any goal achievable.  Want to hang with pals and be space miners?  Space moguls?  Space pirates?  Or work with large groups of folks to be Sky Mashal or Space Warlord?  All wide open, limited only by your commitment.
Go in hoping to "lone wolf" your way through yet another MMO and you will most likely miss the point and burn out quickly.  PvP is a reality - you can spend your time trying to avoid it, and largely be successful at doing so, but make no mistake that you are still playing PvP, you've just elected to be a herbivore.
All that said, there is lots of room for "crafting" playstyles, and the player market is hands-down the best of any MMO I've tried.  And it IS possible to play this game solo if you are of a particular somewhat-warped mindset (like mine), though its more difficult.

edit: I initially gave this game a negative rating, but as you can see, I'm now 40+ hours into the game, so I've now changed it to positive.
The reason for the initial negative rating is the rather-unfriendly UI. There are a myriad of keyboard commands you need to remember by heart. Using a mouse as input is not an option, everything is done strictly by keyboard. I'm the kind of gamer who likes to sit back and relax in my chair while clicking on my mouse, rather than hunch over the keyboard in an upright position, so I wasn't pleased in the beginning. The dozens of keyboard commands are difficult to remember and will force you to consult the "help" page every so often.
However, if you can tolerate this, Unreal World becomes a beautiful sandbox game. You can do whatever you want, whether it be to become a farmer, hunter, lumberjack, fisherman, bandit, serial killer etc. The main "goal" is to survive winter, which is harsh and deadly, so most of your time will be devoted to hunting and gathering food, and building a suitable shelter for the cold season. How you approach this is up to you.
My main complaint (besides the unfriendly UI) is that the game world can feel lonely at times. At present, you're not able to marry anyone or have kids. You do have the option of hiring adventurers and workers, but they will only stay with you for a short time and then leave. You can't move into a village or improve it. The game makes you feel like you're an outcast with no friends or something. You can almost call it a hermit simulator.
Overall, though, I find the game enjoyable. If you're into survival or roguelikes, UW is a very good choice.

In Estranged Act 1, the starting sequence can be a little confusing, however, that problem is quickly solved as you are thrown from your boat and into the water, though there was no indication that you are a fisherman until later when other characters refer to you as a fisherman.
Story
As said before Estranged Act 1 has you experiencing a ship crash which results in your being stranded on an island. At first, you might not even see this game as scary, much less a zombie game, in fact I had no idea that this was a zombie game at all when i first started playing the game. After meeting a man named John who gives you a gun and sets you on your way, your real goal is unclear. The game progesses in a fasion of your moving forward and finding your way around obstacles until you are knocked out by a long fall and captured. When you awake you are tied to a chair and interrogated, which leads to the game resuming the "move forward" gameplay. This continues until you arrive at Arque Corporation, a company mentioned in the beggining portion of the game. There, you meet a doctor (who you immediately trust?) who wants to find a way to send a message for help off the island. After failing at this task due to a signal disruption coming from the other side of the island you part ways. Afterwards, Arque Corporation is alerted to your presence and you must fight your way out. After escaping, you come to a cabin which leaves you on a very big cliffhanger for Act 2.
Playability
If you are using a control, you might be something of a trailblazer here, as the game gives you no help as far as controls go on a controller. All control hints are made with a computer in mind, which would make sense seeing as this game is on a computer based game store. As you progress through the game you get the hang of the controls which are similar to Half Life 2 (it is a mod of Half Life 2 after all) or, if you are not familiar with it, like other mods of Half Life 2 i.e. No More Room in Hell. The only complaint I have is the fact that you can't aim down the sights, making aiming difficult, and causing an unneccesary loss of bullets as you take multiple shots to down one zombie. But, as with the rest of the controls, aiming gets easier and I saw myself downing zombie with one simple headshot again.
Graphics
As with the controls, graphics are similar to higher quality mods of Half Life 2. I saw improvements in water effects, as well as shadows being darker and displaying a true sense of the absence of light when zombies would run out of it straight towards you. This carries over to lighting effects, with light being essential to the game unless you turn the brightness up, which makes getting the Estranged in the Dark acheivement a challenge. Depth of view effects were a nice touch, though there are small problems with it. One small problem I saw, was how your vision would still be blurred after opening a door, until being quickly adjusted. Again, a small problem, but it can't be overlooked.
Characters
What few notable character there are in this game are boring without having a real backstory to them. Voice acting can sometimes seem unrealistic, as some voices are not getting their desired effect. John for example may have been trying to sound like he was truly affected emotionally by the strange disapearence of his wife and daughter, but instead sounded like he was trying to hold back a laugh. Characters also don't seem to react too much to transpiring events. John again, for example, shoots (a zombie as you later find out) someone in plain view of you. After you go up to him he acts like nothing happened at all, he doesn't try to explain the situation either. I for one would probably not trust someone who just fired a round into someone's head.
Sound Effects
Music play a key role in the beginning of the game, though its fades as you get deeper into it, as music changed when you enter a new room for example. The music definetely does scare you with it's creepy effects, as it made me think that something was just around the corner. Battle music always feels right as well as a kind of chase scene. Gun sounds are farily realistic, as well as splash and breaking glass sound effects.
Replayability
With the challenge of acheivements always present, I could definetely see myself playing the game one or two more times, though anymore would be pushing it. The reason for this is that you come to expect and memorize where zombies are as oppose to when you first play the game through.
Wrap Up
Estranged Act 1 is a perfect example of the thought that games don't have to be made by enormous corporations, or be extremely taxing to your PC to be good. A zombie shooter with touches of horror as well, I would definetely recommend playing through at least once, to get the feel of what it means to be estranged.

Have you ever wondered what being a Finn was like before the invention of alcoholism, anime, severe depression and murdering Russians? Well now, through the magic of computer roleplaying, you can at last find out!
This game is a pretty innovative blend of roguelike and survival simulator that dates back to several decades before the current survival game craze. The presentation and interface are true to that era, and so really shouldn't be a hindrance unless you're a millenial casual babby, in which case I congratulate you on managing to read this far without losing interest and playing with your smartphone, you little♥♥♥♥♥♥
The only area where this doesn't really hold is with certain repeated commands - putting down several fishing nets in succession involves a number of awkward key combinations, and the process of chopping down trees and hauling them to a location (which you WILL need to do if you want a house) will inevitably strain your fingers to the point where you will certainly come to sympathize with your likewise strained and fatigued character.
Besides that, the graphics are charming and effective - the sprites stand out, look good and tell you what you need to know, and the menus are decorated with quaint images of Finnish cosplayers in their natural habitat.
But enough about that nonsense! You want to hear about gameplay! The areas where this game really excels are its depth, realism and immersiveness. You begin play at a season of your choice, either in the wilderness or in a friendly, desolate or hostile settlement, depending on the starting scenario of your choice, equipped with either very little or nothing at all to help you weather the oncoming trials. From that point on, you have just one overarching goal: survive.
This isn't nearly as easy as you might think - not because everything is trying to kill you (in fact, the opposite is more likely to be true), but rather because getting the necessities of life is
. Hunting, for example, requires that you first find prey - which involves a great deal of fruitless wandering and scouring the land for tracks. You might follow a fresh and promising trail to the point where you're only a hair's breadth away from your quarry, only to have it suddenly go cold, prompting profound disappointment. If you do find prey, your problems only multiply, as you then have to make a decision - do you close the distance and risk spooking the game in order to get a better shot? Or take the one you have, and risk missing to the same effect?
Managing risks and resources is in many ways the core of the gameplay. You have to choose not only how to conduct your activities, but which activities to embark on, as each have their associated risks and rewards. A hunt is likely to fail, can be dangerous, and is wont to leave you far from home and exhausted come night time. Fishing is safe, but consumes large amounts of your time and might return nothing at all, or an insufficient catch. There are no sure bets, however, and you'll inevitably have to go all in at some point. Sometimes you'll fail. That's just life.
Likewise, every activity has its associated costs. Not necessarily in resources, but always in your character's time and energy. Building a house will give you a leg up, but chopping down trees and hewing logs is hard work that's sure to leave you with an appetite, and to make it worse, all that time you spent doing that was time you didn't spend acquiring food. Consequently, much of the earlier game is an exercise in building a big enough stockpile to be able to do more time-intensive work without worrying about what you'll eat tomorrow. This is difficult, as the most easily acquired foods (fish and meat) spoil rapidly without some means to preserve them, and even if you do get lucky enough to kill an elk early on, there's no way you can eat all the resultant meat all by yourself before it will spoil.
Still, though, overcoming all of those challenges as they come at you brings on a sense of elation like little else in video games. Sure, half of it might just be dying in the cold and worrying about tomorrow's meals, and sure, the Njerpez will kill your favourite dog, and sure, you might acidentally give your pants away for a handful of peas, but everything becomes worth it when you can sit down and look with pride upon your big house, blooming fields and cellarful of dried meats. It's an extremely immersive game, equal parts harsh and rewarding, and frighteningly easy to get lost in. There's far less cannibalism involved than I remember from the last time I played it, but I would still highly recommend it if you're into deep and immersive sandbox RPGs.

It's hard to explain what EvE Online is. It would probably be easier to explain what it isn't.
It's not a game. Not in the normal sense of the word at least. There are no objectives that it points you towards, no obvious progression, no fail state or even a way to play it "right".
It's just a sci-fi simulation of a galaxy. And it's just there.
What makes it, and the reason why it's been going on for 13 years, are the players. Everything is run by players. Everything is made by players. From the smallest bullet to the biggest conflict in gaming history.
And when every single interaction is human, there are no limits on what can happen. You've probably seen the articles around the web - huge wars involving thousands of players, heists and backstabs carefully prepared over the course of years, revenge stories and so much history that you could fill dozens of books. Nothing is scripted or meant to happen.
EvE is not a game. It's an experience, an alternate universe that lives on its own; you're simply trying to make an impact on it and create your own goals.
But if you want to try it, remember: at the heart of it, EvE is about social connections. Alone, you're nothing. You won't go too far if you try to be a lone wolf.
Take your friends along with you, create a corporation or join one of the many already established ones - it doesn't matter which; but stay together, and be something.

Where do I start? UnReal World has been around and in active development a long time. The very first version was in 1992, which was vastly different from the game we have now. I personally have owned it for 10 years now, and in that time it has just kept getting better and better. I can't even begin to guess how many thousands of hours I've played this game over the years. I come back after every major update to find fresh new features to explore, with the basic meat of the game just as fun as I have always found it.
It's an amazing iron age survival simulation, the best I have played.
You create a character, choosing a tribe - each with their own genetics (affects attributes, height, build), knowledge (skills, auto-identification of certain plants, which rituals you might start with), and starting gear. Then you can select from a variety of starts to get things rolling - like being an escaping slave (good luck getting away from the camp full of your former masters) or an unfortunate hunting trip (will you kill the animal that killed your father, or flee?). You also pick which season to start in - each with their own challenges. From there you can either do the basic missions, which are there to get you acquainted with the game and give you attainable early goals; do the advanced missions, which are a bit more difficult and require more time; or just strike off and do your own thing.
Like any good survival game, you need to provide the basics for your character. You'll need a steady source of food - from hunting, fishing, trapping, foraging, farming, or trading. Just make sure you don't misidentify that mushroom and eat a poisoned one, and don't fall in your own trap pit - especially if you filled it with spikes.
You will also need shelter. Options here are a very basic lean to made from spruce branches, a kota (Finnish tent) made from hides that you can pack up and move with you, or a permanent log cabin. Having a smoke house with a fireplace comes in handy for smoking meat, which is one of the easiest ways to preserve your meat. Cellars are also handy to keep your food fresher longer. Need some help building your cabin? Hire a woodsman to cut some trees down for you, some good food may be all he wants.
And warm clothes are a must for when the temperature drops, so don't forget to skin that stag and tan its fur for a nice warm set of clothes. Or just for trading, a good fur is valuable. Maybe you'll use it to buy a dog to come along as your companion, helping to keep you safe from robbers and dangerous animals - just don't forget to feed it.
The hunting in this game is challenging and fun. Most animals are faster than you, but you have more endurance and you can sneak. Hounding an elk and running it down until it tires out is possible if your character's speed and endurance are decent, as long as you can track it well enough through the woods as it flees to keep on it. Especially if you manage to put an arrow or javelin in it when you first spot it, as a wounded animal runs slower. If you don't have luck actively hunting, you can set traps. From small loop snares all the way up to large lever traps and spiked trap pits, you can set a trap for whatever animal you're trying to hunt. Don't forget to bait them with meat if you're after carnivores.
If hunting isn't your style, you can fish. Fishing rods, clubs, or spears round out the active fishing options. Or get yourself a punt or raft and some nets for passive fishing.
Or be a farmer and supplement your diet with a variety of grown crops - peas, turnips, rye, beans, hemp, and more.
Or you could go straight up vegetarian, eating berries and bread and porridge and farmed vegetables. Just don't expect a vegetarian life to be easy in Iron Age Finland - meat and fish are the best sources of protein around. A balanced diet is easier to manage.
The animal AI in the game makes for some fun scenarios. Here is an example of a hunt I had recently:
I saw an Elk in the distance from the mountain near where I was building my homestead, and decide it's time to stock up on meat before the weather gets too hot for drying (started in Spring, still early enough).
I go hunting for it, and put an arrow in it when I find it - giving it a bleeding wound in the thorax. It runs and I begin the chase, relying on my good tracking skill and endurance to make up for its speed advantage. Soon I notice new tracks intermingled with the Elk. Bear tracks! I continue following the Elk, and the Bear tracks are right there with it all the way.
After a while of tracking I finally find my prey, still carrying my arrow... on the ground partially eaten! Bear tracks lead away to the west. As I already have plenty of meat right in front of me, I left my fellow hunter to his own devices and skinned and butchered the gift he left for me instead of going off after him.
It's little details like this that make this game amazing.

I'll share with you my first experience of this game.
~~~
After making some javelines, getting a basecamps set up and being largely unsuccesful at gaining much food I found myself slowly starving to death with very poor nutrition. I had tried climbing up nearby trees to see if I could spot game anywhere near my vicenity with largly no luck, and then I slipped on one of the branches and banged my head.  It wasn't life threatening but it shook me up enough to not try climbing again, as wounds take a fairly realistic number of in game days to heal.
Suddenly while walking back to my camp as the sun was setting, I spy a caraboo herd.  Not only that it looks like they were looking for a place to bed down for the night!
Perfect!  I can just follow them, and then sneak in close and try to kill one of the caraboo before I die myself!
As they lay sleeping I edged closer, javilen in hand with a tip hardened by the fire I created with the local spruce trees. My target in sight I steady my javilin.
Throw and a hit!  The whole herd wakes up!  It's chaos!  The caraboo I hit was only injured in it's hind leg but it was bleeding so by following the blood and it's tracks it was fairly easy to keep up! It looks like I was saved!
Hours pass and it's now night.  The caraboo stopped bleeding and I can only hope that the tracks that I'm currently following belong to the caraboo that I did indeed injure.
One full day passes and into the night again.  I make a stop by a stream for water and try to hit a nearby squirrel with my javilen in a tree.  I miss and it taunts me, jeering and chittering at me as my head throbs and my stomach grows ever more empty while I retreive my javilen from its resting place in a tree trunk.
I continue following the trail one more full day.  My health is low and I can barely keep the tracks focused.  Suddenly I hear a grunt of a caraboo.
This is it!  I'll finally get that animal! I start to sneak.  I creep closer, and closer, I see the animal and it's injured.  It's the same one!  The gods smile on me!
One, step. Two step, three step.  TWIGSNAP!
The caraboo's head jerks up! I hold my breath hoping it doesn't see me.
Two heartbeats pass and the caraboo bolts!  I must have been upwind!
My heart sinks.
My javilen loose in my hand as I stare at the ground where I"m likely to die.  This place isn't so bad.  It's got a nice breeze, fir trees, a stream...
Wait a minute... it's got a stream!
I take off running in the direction the caraboo bolted!
Sqeezing past ancient firs and by long forgotten boulders I run!  My last ounces of strength leaving me with each step!
I'm able to catch up with the caraboo as it's calmed down and then run at it full speed with the wind at my back!
I may not be faster than this animal.  But I'm smarter.  I am a human.  I'm one of the people.
Expectedly the caraboo bolts!  It's more tired than me and injured worse.
My plan is working.  It's headed straight for the stream!
Once it gets to the banks of the water it dives in trying to evade it's persuer.  I walk up to the bank as the fatigued animal vainly tries to splash around in the water using the last of it's energy.  I then take my aim gripping my javilen with all my might and throw aiming for the neck of the magestic beast!
A hit! Hot blood pours into the water around the caraboo.  It staggers back onto shore, falters, and falls.  It's breathing labored I stand over it.
This animal who is no different than me, whom I have tracked for three days lies at my feet.  The same place I would be had I not caught it.  There is no good or evil here.
There is just life.
Later after a fire is made, roasted caraboo in my belly, and a hide tanning on a nearby fallen log.  I pack the remaining several dozen pounds of roasted meat into my pack.  There was a village not a few days from here that would be willing to trade some useful supplies for this meat.  There my journey will continue.  For I am one of the people.

So, i began playing robocraft maybe in late 2017. and it was fun. i had a lot of great games constructing my bots and going out to fight the enemy teams. at the time, teams were something along the lines of 8V8 or 12V12, I can't remember which exactly. This made for games that were wildly chaotic and fun to play in. plenty of bots to do damage to and score to make.
I gravitated toward a more tanky setup at the beginning, then i became a Medic Bot main. and to this day I still am in robocraft.
However later they reduced the team size to 6V6, which was a step in the wrong direction as this meant there were less enimes to shoot and less that had your back. which resulted in you being lunch for the enemy 9/10 times. The reduced team sizes meant that there were less players to shoot and gain points from Via damage, and less team mates to heal for medics. and if you are a medic, then you'll be hard pressed getting points. because healing give you as many points now, and adding all the requied healing items and Damage items will drain your maximum power pool, which leads to many akward situations where you're facing off against the enemy and run out of energy mid fight.
But, I stopped playing after epic loot.
This is kind of a clique reason to stop playing amongst the Robocraft community but all me to explain why with one word: Payoff.
before epic loot you wrere given a paycheck that represented how much you contributed. and you could get by pretty well with these paychecks. if you had a terrible game where you didn't do much damage or score many points, you would get a paycheck that represented that. but if you had a great game where you were the MVP of the team, you would get a healthy paycheck as a reward. and it got even better if you got a really good game on First Win of The Day, which doubled your funds, and it got EVEN BETTER if you had alot of premium people in the server. It brought the community together somewhat.
Premium was also something i was very close to purchasing before epic loot. as it not only gave me 2X funds, but it gave everyone +5% in their funds. it was aweseome! the people who bought the premium could help everyone in the games they played get a little extra cash.
But all of that went away in Epic Loot.
In epic loot the reward system was changed. instead of gaining straight money you were given crates that could contain a max of 8 items if you had premium, only 4 if you were a F2P. the rewards were RNG based. so your reliable paycheck went from consistant and reliable, to a damn slot machien. now i know you can get money from crates, but it's still in no way consistant. i could be MVP of a winning team, get the Protonioum crate and get♥♥♥♥♥♥loot.
The other thing that is more manipulative is that the loot boxes show what you COULD have gotten if you had premium. so if a legendary drops behind that paywall, you're like a little homeless kid pressing his nose up agaisnt the glass of a candy store. people have suggested the change of simply replacing the 4 pedastals with a single pylon saying "if you had premium you could get 4 extra slots" but freejam have since ignored this request.
Oh and did i mention you can pay micro payments to purchase crates? ya it turned into CS:GO basically in that regard.
The reward system went from gratifying and satisfying, to a microtransactin fueled RNG mess.

This game... this game and its sequel are fantastic. Basically all of Christine Love's work is, but these are just amazing.
I actually like Hate Plus more in some ways and Analogue more in others. So I'm torn as far as which is better, but I can safely say that they were both well worth the effort. I have like 4 hours on this game, but I actually played it through multiple times--I read insanely fast--and can safely say that I'm glad I did so.
Writing: Best part, honestly. Love's writing is able to be expressive and emotional with ease. Characters have their own voices, their own personalities--and with this many characters, you better believe that's a feat. Nothing is over wrought or underwritten. This is an episolatory Visual Novel, and it works.
Graphics stuff: I liked the interface. The console part was the least impressive, and some people might find it rather hard to believe considering the advanced tech--though keep in mind that the ship is only a few hundred years ahead of us in its origin--but its a callback to Love's earlier freeware game, Digital: A Love Story and reminded me a bit of the Amie interface. The two AIs are Animu waifu material. No way around that. The art is good quality, though, and their expressions are both endearing and rather genuinely funny. Mute's a bit more expressive, but that fits the character.
Music: It's good! However, it's far from amazing. Digital: A Love Story's soundtrack was PERFECT and I want it rather badly--Analogue and Hate Plus's is decent and I wouldn't mind paying a few bucks for it. There were a lot of good chances to use music to set scenes that were passed up.
All in all? 10/10. Yes, it's not perfect, but a 10 isn't for perfection. It's for games that leave me either thirsty for more ad infinitum or games that after I play them I turn the computer off, stumble into bed, and think lots of big, scary thoughts. This game and its sequel do both.
Try it. It's only $10.
(Also, if you're still unsure, try Digital: A Love Story and "Don't Take it Personal, Babe, it just ain't your story" which are both free and by the same person.)

To start it off:
If you want a story of tragedy, time-skips, mystery, love, and hate in a Visual Novel with a lot of story reading, this is the game.
Why I recommend you get it:
I'm normally not the type to read story or backgrounds in a Visual Novels unless they hook me in with a good intro. The intro didn't have a really strong one but since I was livestreaming it, I continued on. When you learn the first mystery, I got hooked and reeled.
Eventually, you'll learn of what happens to a whole colony in a spaceship that went missing for 600 years, inhabitants missing and the only witnesses are computer AI's.
Gameplay is like Phoenix Wright where you read some stories, ask the AI's about the stories that seem questionable (or spam like the original Phoenix Games), and they'll reveal more diaries and logs from the inhabitants.
Eventually, you'll learn what happened to them, why, and how you decide the fate of the AI's in the end. It's not a story of love. It's a hate story, a story where you find the AI's cute, but in the end, it's just to cover up a cruel past.
Hope you guys do enjoy it. ^^

A fun casual MMO.
Pros
Easy to learn:  If you have played any MMOs the control set up is pretty intuitive.
Light Specs:  Plays well on older computers and laptops
Attractive: Partitcularly considering that the light specs
Auto movement:  Use standard movement or pick an option from a road sign to auto walk to the next destination or quest.
You start with a mount: a steam bike that gets upgraded as you play, the first two to three upgrades come very quickly.
Tons of content that gets unlocked as you play, item customization is particularly cool.
Mining, Fishing, Myth Tablets, Transmutation, and a Pac-Man style mini-game.
Vanquish, Auto Battle, and Training Modes:
-
Vanquish: allows you to repeat a quest in vanquish mode this starts a timer and when it is done you simply grab the rewards
Auto Battle: a "botting" option for battle, you can walk in to a battle and hit this button.  Note: it just spams your abilites, so it works best when you are not worried about using up health/mana potions.  You play more efficently if you are at your keyboard, but it is nice to have a button to press while you pay the pizza guy or grab a coffee.
Training: allows you to afk grind for experience, it gives you an amount of XP every 30 seconds of AFK time, up to 6 hours.
_
Cons:
Pay to Win:  You can buy advantages in the cash shop, this is not too much of an issue for PvE, but I could understand how it could kill PvP.
The human races let you play any caucasian you want (WTF?), character models have fairly limited customization.
Bottom Line:

I just finished Estranged: Act I and it was a great ride. I don't play many mods so I'm speaking from inexperience but this was far more enjoyable than many retail games I've played. The atmosphere was as good as the Steam page led me to expect, despite the opening scene underwhelming me as far as production value goes. It got better as the game went on. The sense of isolation and discovery are perfect. Gameplay is quite solid with good use of the physics engine. I'm a huge fan of Source.
Pacing is impressive as I never had a strong sense of what was coming, how far through the game I was or what the scale of the experience would be. Games get very tiresome when the narrative feels too plotted and thankfully that was far from the case here for me.
Very early on I turned off the HUD in an attempt to remove the control prompts (Press E to move objects etc) because they were guiding me to the solution before I had a chance to think about it for myself. I played the whole game with no HUD even though I was sadly unable to turn off the prompts. That my biggest criticism of this game is the lack of that option should say a lot.
I'll be picking up Act II without hesitation if it can be had for any less than $5. Any more than that and I'll be looking at reviews first, just because I'm criminally cheap. My whole playthrough is on my YouTube channel josephbilling if you want to check it out.
I just added up the duration of the videos and it only totals 3 hours which seems shockingly low for the experience I had. I guess it's compact, though it certainly didn't feel like I was being rushed through it. In this case I would have to say quality has comprehensively defeated quantity.

PROS

Basically everything you want from a fighting game, this game has. Now to talk about story mode, this mode is almost 80% cutscenes that are all moderately long, if you have been keeping up with the anime, i advise you to skip the cutscenes which will then amount to the story mode nothing more than reliving the battles in the anime. For newcomers, the story will start off at a weird spot even with the prologue and may take time for them to catch up.
CONS
-Almost unplayable multiplayer
-Hard to play without proper controller?(not keyboard)
This where we talk about the multiplayer, although some people seem to have no issues, i personally have major issues with this part as the game pauses every few seconds to keep in sync and causes matches to be way too laggy for proper enjoyment
CONCLUSION
I recommend this game only for hardcore naruto fans or that of the fighting game genre, from my experience you can expect mostly a story mode and a mode to test and hone your skills by fighting AI. The story mode will be pretty bland for naruto fans who already watched all of the episodes prior and they should just skip most of the cutscenes(yes, like i mentioned before, the cutscenes are hella long) I ended up beating the story mode within 4-5hrs skipping cutscenes. The story mode is also super easy with almost no real challenge until the last few levels and what path you take. There is no real tutorial so you will have to figure out most of it through trial and error. Also talking about controller issues, it is not UNPLAYABLE with a keyboard as i beat the game on one, just make sure you know your buttons on the controller settings and remap to make things more comfortable because the default settings make it almost unplayable. FYI there are no real graphical settings besides resolution, aspect ratio, windowed mode, and vsync, so keep that in mind if u have a lower spec PC. ALL IN ALL, this game really does make you feel epic and super skilled if you can pull off the long combos, a definite buy for hardcore naruto/fighting game fans. If not, you should get this game while its on sale but you should hold off if its full price.

First off, I am not reviewing Dead Island itself with this review. I am focusing on the fact that this is a Definitive Edition. Personally I love the Dead Island Franchise (what Techland worked on at least), however that is beside the point. This is reviewing the \"Definitive\" aspect of this game. With that being said...
If you enjoyed Dead Island, definitely get the Definitive Edition. If you\'ve thought about getting Dead Island and haven\'t gotten around to it, the Definitive Edition is worth picking up. If you like Zombie games, well, I think you know what comes next.
Dead Island Definitive Edition runs smooth as hell, and looks just as good (compared to the original that is). The enviornment is a lot prettier, the combat is more fluid, the game itself is deeply immersive. It feels like I\'m playing Dead Island for the first time again. I haven\'t run into any problems so far. It\'s everything Dead Island is, but better, as should a Definitive Edition be.
I have played roughly 2 hours of the game as of writing this review, and I feel like I have played enough to get a feel so far, and truly say this game is worth getting.
IN COMPARISON TO THE ORIGINAL:
Graphics - Amazing, definitely improved.
Gameplay - Smoother and more immersive
Loadtimes - For me, almost non-existant. I have seen a loading screen for a total of 1 second during my 2 hours of gameplay (I am NOT exaggerating)
Audio - As of right now, the audio range seems to be a little off. It\'s hardly noticable, but I hear zombies that are pretty far away very clearly, and it keeps me on edge.
Navigation - I haven\'t tried mouse and keyboard with Definitive Edition yet, but it works extremely well with a controller.
Online - Have not tried yet, will try to edit when I do
Overall Dead Island Definitive Edition is a fantastic improvement from the original. If you were on the fence about getting this, I\'d say go ahead and get it, especially if you have the loyalty discount (85% off both Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide, making both $3.00 each).
