TL;DR: The story, and perhaps more importantly the
, are both excellent, which are absolutely critical for the genre. Good soundtrack, excellent attention to minor details. I only wish the game itself was longer.
I've decided to write this review
playing the expansion, Hate Plus, so that that experience wouldn't color my impressions of this game.
No synopsis, that would just be repetitive, not to mention rude. Play the demo. After decades of exposure, I've lost a lot of interest in the manga style, but I tried the game anyway and was oddly drawn to it in a way that is difficult to relate. Perhaps not being Japanese played a role in getting me to give it a shot, I'm not sure. The music is good, but there are not many pieces in the soundtrack. That stuff said, let's just focus on what sets this game apart.
The game itself is one part first-person narrative from the perspectives of many people within the setting, you know, 'before the incident', and one part interaction with one of the two main, interactive characters. If you were to add a repetitive action game in the middle, you'd end up with a far better written and more mature .hack game. I was thankful for the silent protagonist role, having a pre-written stand-in to take on 'your' feelings and beliefs can be very immersion breaking.
The place where this game really excels is in the 'little things'. I'll not spoil what those little things are, but they make the characters that you
interact with feel a lot more believable and 'alive'. Clever use of game devices give the illusion that the interface is natural, which adds a lot to immersion. While some parts are extremely blunt (borderline shocking, considering the context), I felt the story and presentation overall had an alluring subtlety and mystery to it that is strangely devoid in most game stories and, well, from most books, music, and television shows as well.
My main complaint with the game is that it is short. While I don't believe in dragging things out for the sake of length, and there is certainly enough there to get the story across with the degree of completeness that I would consider necessary, I felt that the brevity left an empty feeling. A, 'But, wait, I like these characters! It's over already...?' feeling. It's actually a bit ironic. Loneliness as an underlying theme makes much of the hurried feeling in the dialog quite forgivable (even endearing), but again, there's still an abruptness to it that feels disheartening.
Regarding the style and themes of the game, this is by no means a critique of the writing, which is excellent. But, without looking, I easily pegged
from just the story. For those who know, that is probably not too surprising, but I felt it was worth mentioning. The writing is highly indicative of that person's personal tendancies, experiences, and perspective, which do give it a richness that may otherwise be lacking. I would be very interested in seeing the author involved in collaborative projects (in part because the loneliness is just falling off the plate...).
The author appears to go to great lengths to give a feeling of neutrality overall, aside from the innate societal problems related to the mysterious transition back to the Confucian culture and Chinese writing system of the Joseon era. By the way, if you're on the fence about trying this game, it would be
to you to watch the excellent Korean television shows Dae Jang Geum and/or Tree With Deep Roots (both extremely relevant, for different reasons), though I'm sure other Korean 'period dramas' set in the Joseon era would help spark your interest and understanding.
But, finally, the most important part of the game is the storytelling. In the end, the story itself is not as horribly complex as its made out to be as you go through it, but the way everything is revealed, piece by piece, has you drawing conclusions and asking questions that, of course, you cannot voice, but still feel more immersive and palpable than if you were to quietly come about them while reading the story as a plain narrative text. Having the characters play as guide and co-discoverer with you give a feeling of 'togetherness' that is traditionally difficult for games and books to thrust upon their users.
In closing, I can't wait any longer to play Hate Plus, and I hope to see more material from this game's author in the same vein.

Being honest, the first minutes I played Analogue: A Hate Story I thought it was a boring game with little to no things I could interact with. After having a look at all the good reviews it had here on Steam, I decided I would give it another chance. And that's exactly what I did. It's not your usual game (if you could call it that), and probably not your typical visual novel either, but it narrates a very interesting story, which surely won't leave you unmoved. Some tips, just so you start with the right foot when playing the game, or if you are thinking about buying it:
- Do you enjoy reading and books in general? This is definitely important, because 99% of the game is just reading. I'd recommend that you start playing whenever you don't feel like smashing enemies and just having a quiet, relaxing evening.
- Do not pay too much attention to the family trees. There are way too many characters which only appear mentioned once, So yeah, try not to feel overwhelmed: there are only a few characters you should really focus on.
- Do some detective work! The story is original and very compelling. Even if I thought both of the game's AIs were way too cartoonish for my taste, it's pretty easy to understand them as characters and be moved by their reasons and actions, as well as by all those different stories that take place in the logs of the korean ship where everything took place. It's not really neccessary to think too much about what happens next in the story as you play through it, (you are told about everything at one point or another)  but be sure to use your logic and common sense and you'll be surprised when you find out what really happened in the story  way before you even get to read it.
Definitely a very original and compelling game/story/book. It'll keep you entertained for a few hours, as well as its story will probably stay in your thoughts for a few days more. Btw, I loved the Ender ending. :-)
Ps for the devs: One AI per core? Why can't I disable one of the AIs and enable the other one, if both are in the same core? C'mon! It only makes sense, and that way you would be able to get one of the achievements without breaking the 4th wall. Hopefully it isn't too late to ask for an update? :P

Day of Defeat: Source is an awesome first person shooter inspired by WWII. There are classes, two gamemodes, achievements, and maps!
Choose to be a rifleman, assault class, support class, sniper, machine gunner, or rocketeer. Riflemen are capable of using their semi-automatic M1 Garand (U.S. Soldier RIfle) to take down enemies from long distances and with two hits while the german variant has a bolt action one that does more damage. Assaults can smoke enemy positions and charge in there to destroy the enemy team. The support class is for covering fire and is pretty versatile. Has a medium damage and ranged weapon with two frag grenades/potato grenades. Snipers are self-explanatory. They have a sniper rifle for shooting people at long distances. Machine gunners are more of a defensive class. They can place a machine gun while prone or on a sandbag and mow down an entire team although they're vulnerable. Rocketeers are for picking off key targets most likely machine gunners and snipers and have rocket launchers. They also come with sidearms. The U.S. Army rocketeer has a quick firing M1 Carbine while the German rocketeer has a close quarters C96 machine pistol.
There are two gamemodes for you to play. You have territorial control and detonation. Territorial control is a gamemode where you capture flags around the area. There are usually 5 flags with each team holding 2 and one middle flag uncapped. This is the typical, main gamemode in Day of Defeat: Source. Detonation involves detonating explosives at an opposing checkpoint and sometimes uses an offense vs. defense setup.
It's not the easy game to just pick up and be good at, but it's a fun game.

I'm not much of a writer, so I apologize for not being very eloquent.
I've never written a steam review before, but I have enjoyed this game so much for so long before it came to steam, that I felt like I had to add to any positive press it was receiving here.  I've never seen a developer who worked closer with his community and with greater humility than Sami does.  This is a true labor of love that you'll also really enjoy playing.  It's built to be what we all want it to be, and I have no doubt that it will continue moving closer to a perfect version of itself going forward, as it has since I started playing it.  This is not a game that will stop seeing updates now that it's released.  If you play Unreal World and really dive into what it has to offer, you'll get to come along on a ride that lasts for years.
I'm an RPG nerd, and I currently play in a tabletop game where my character has somehow survived many brushes with death in a harsh wilderness.  I built my character's background by remembering every death i've had in Unreal World as 'Another time I almost died'.  This game builds real stories that you remember and cherish when they have ended.
I sincerely believe there isn't a more valuable 10 dollar purchase on Steam.

Yes, my hours played on the game are pretty much non-existant. I've been playing this game like crazy for the past few days though. I saw the game in my discovery queue and thought it looked interesting. I'm a bit of a cheapskate though and I've been burned by so many games in the past that I didn't want to jump right on it. As I'm reading through the comments, I see mention that you can download and play the game from the developer's website. So I gave it a shot. At first I was a bit overwhelmed but after looking over a couple guides, I started figuring it out a bit.
So I've been playing a bunch for the last couple days and I'm really loving the game. At this point, I decided that I was going to buy this game and support the developer. This isn't some big company. It's a small indie thing and this guy has a huge set of cojones making his game available for free while also selling it on Stream. That shows confidence in your work. It IS that good. It's worth buying even though I could play it for free. I've already talked it up to a couple friends and they're going to try it out as well. Get the word of mouth going on this one.
So actually talking about the game itself. The graphics aren't anything to speak of but they don't need to be. This isn't a splashing graphical game for the Xbox crowd. This is an old school game but it's got depth that the old school games couldn't pull off. You start the world as a Nordic person back in the Iron Age. In most of the scenarios (there are many you can choose from) you start off alone. Usually you've got some basic supplies and a day or two worth of food. From here you've got to find food, build shelter, and stay alive! I've been starting in the summer. My goal has been to build a cabin before the winter hits. That's not an easy task. It's not like other survival games where it's simplified. Building takes lots of time and effort. Fishing, hunting, and trapping are difficult! It's easy to get lost in this game for hours.
Highly reccommended!

Oh how long I had waited to get this game... The anticipation.... The excitement... The total disappointment.
Ok, seriously... On how many "Strategy" games do you have 0 control over your units? Sure, you can tell a location to send all, some or a particular type of unit to go somewhere, but that's where your control ends. You cannot develop tactics on which unit should attack what, you cannot tell a certain number of units within a group (going to or coming from somewhere for example) to go to a separate location (you have to either recall the units or wait unit they reach their destination). This lack of control, while it may seem not so important at first, is where this game fails imo. Most of the time, your units end up being shredded because they focused their attack on the wrong unit or structure (i.e. defences).
Oh, and the voice acting... Oh God, the voice acting... It's so monotonous, it sounds like a computer is doing it. No life, no feel, no reality... If they did hire people to do the voice acting, they either paid so little that the actors wanted to punish the devs by their poor performance, or they hired total amatuers for it. None of the voices sounded like they were in character: they were just reading off the script. Oh, and the script was either changed later on or the actors decided to go as they please because the subs (that appear automatically btw) are different than what they actually say (about 40 percent of the time).
The only good things I can say are that the soundtracks were not so bad actually, and the graphics are appealing...
All in all, not recommended. Unless you like being frustrated by games...

- Good and fun FPS. But has a "slowish" pace in comparison to BRLD2 and BRLD:PS
- Well writen with fun characters.
- Co-Op for up to 4 players with an extra couple of maps designed for duels between friends.
- If you played BRLD2 first like myself you will have a lot of "Oh! So that's why _____ happened in the sequel" moments.
- 1 "serious" DLC (General Knoxx) that requires lots of traveling.
- 2 funny DLC (Dr. Ned's and Claptrap's) with several new enemies and cool maps to explore .
- 1 arena type DLC (Moxxi's Underdome) with a ton of challenges and randomized battles.
- Raid Bosses for those that are looking for a challenge after beating the game.
tl;dr: Fun and balanced FPS

Having played this off and on since release, I must sadly recommend you pass this one up as it is now.
For years Hero Siege was pretty awesome. It was a simplistic, easy to pick up and put down twinstick wave-based hack and slash sort of thing. RPG elements were pretty light but still present and important. You picked a class, beat things up, got experience and relics, picked skills, and when you died you started over with your XP in tact but your progress and relics gone. I liked it.
At some point the devs decided they wanted to make it a deeper more Diablo-like experience and introduced waypoints, a town, gear, rebalanced skills, and while I appreciate their attempt to add depth to the game, it just simply killed it. I'd pay for access to the original HS again.
So what's wrong? First there's way too much stuff going on for a twinstick frantic game. Items drop every few seconds but since the game is built with a gamepad in mind, your interface for comparing and equpping gear is clumsy and slow. Leveling up is the same way, with skills and attribute selection. On top of that you have runes to equip, a hireling to manage, town trips to sell stuff, etc. Each one of these "features" feels like it detracts from the main purpose of the game: beating things up.
Especially frustrating on that note is the fact that for your first 30 levels, none of the above seems like it matters. It'll take you minutes to kill bosses, and they'll one-shot you. Maps are littered haphazardly with monster spawns, most of which are guarded by at least one champion or legend monster that will, also, take you minutes to defeat. Gone is the wave system from the Hero Siege of old; instead you have to hope you can chip out a foothold on a map chock full of enemies that are damage sponges, before you're surrounded and killed.
Your reward for clearing a map is another almost exactly the same map with the exact same enemies. This was okay in the original HS when a map lasted a few minutes. It's painful and tedious in the new HS where you can literally take 20 minutes to clear a map and down its boss.
I level capped many heroes in the OG game. This? I struggle to clear the first 3 maps. Unless something changes, save your money. It pains me to say that.

It's a Koei WARRIORS game people, so if you're not used to them i'll give you a quick rundown because in their template they're pretty much all the same :
* You pick a character between those available and get dumped on a battlefield
* You have a small army and some allies and they have a bigger army full of commanders
* Beat the guys the stage tells you to beat and you win
* Mind the enemy commanders: they're the ones you should be trying to defeat, the foot soldiers are just there to be cannon fodder and add to your bodycount.
* Sometimes the stages have different objectives, like "do X before Y flees" or "escort some random person to a specific spot on the map". Some are easy to do, others like timed missons might be a litte more complicated.
* It's not hard to play, alternate between weak and strong attacks, mow down legions of enemies and feel like a major badass.
* You'll be a one man army regardless of who you pick, but do not expect the same of your AI companions, they'll often fail to solve stuff by themselves and might get in trouble from time to time, getting their butts kicked by commanders or foot soldiers who gang up on them.
*  The same can be said of your foot soldiers who make a huge amount of effort to be almost useless in battle, if some commander or hero unit land in a important base that your army is holding, and there's no companions other than soldiers there, do not leave them unattended.
* Bosses aren't too difficult, just mind their attack patterns and you'll do fine.
* The music is always great: SAMURAI WARRIORS likes techno, DYNASTY WARRIORS is into metal, this game loves rock, metal and jazz and will make you love it too.
* Some battles turn into real slugfests where you can't actually tell what the whazoop is going on: because the objectives change, new people might arrive in the battlefield, another army might come to the party and get into a scuffle with you and the other army you were already fighting with or the lead commander from the  opposing army might withdraw from combat and leave someone else in charge,  they even might go desperate and attempt some stupid strategy. Anything can happen really.
*  After clearing  the story mode once you'll usually have new characters to play and upgrade, and a lot of stupid extra modes to spend time with them.

Review contains spoilers
This game really suffers from what I assume is lack of money and company interest in the game vs the other projects Telltale had running at the time (The Game of Thrones game and the Minecraft Story Mode game). It could have really benefited from a longer development time and maybe the addition of more episodes instead of the standard five.
The writing towards the end felt very rushed. If you're playing Rhys like a good guy who loves his new Pandoran friends and can't stand Jack, then the ending probably feels like it plays out just fine. Telltale no doubt had this route as their ideal player path. But it's a choice game and so not all players went this route and you need to keep that in mind when designing your game. The merging of the paths feels like an OOC character shift in the fifth episode if you're not playing Rhys in this ideal path. He becomes good-guy Rhys no matter how you’ve played him. Fiona on the other hand is the pivot character, so baring a few things her character stays mostly consistent throughout and isn’t as affected by the path merge.
I played Rhys like the corporate scumbag that he is at heart. He wants to be the boss and, if the Eridium mine deal Vaughn mentions in episode one is anything to go by, isn't afraid to do some dubious♥♥♥♥♥♥to get there. It's his dream to be CEO (just like Handsome Jack) and I wanted to give it to him. So I played him nice to the Pandoran crew, but ultimately driven for personal gain and trusted Jack. The scene in episode four when Rhys can choose to rule Hyperion and it's announced over the loudspeaker is one of my fave moments because he's just so damn happy. I wish I could leave him in that scene forever. Seriously, play it that way and look at his face. It's precious.
This all goes out the window though when the writers decide Jack is an idiot who thinks it's a good idea to betray and kill Rhys. Jack's character is driven by betrayal, and reacts negatively when betrayed by people he's learned to trust. Borderlands the Pre-Sequel tells us as much. He's also smart, and knows that any copy made of himself would not in a million years agree to being anything but Number One. So an army of Jack's wouldn't work. You'd just have a death match for Jack superiority. But I digress. If you've trusted him through the whole game why in the world would he all of a sudden turn around and betray Rhys? To betray someone who is putting all their trust in him without being betrayed first isn’t how his character works. And it makes zero sense for him to even try and use Rhys as a skin suit when he could just upload himself into the robot as it is like Loader Bot does later on. There is literally zero need for the endoskeleton conflict other than poor writing as a way to get Rhys off Helios and get the gang back together. There are tons of fans who've come up with much more cleaver alternatives that would stay more true to Jack's character while still getting the gang back together on Pandora and not breaking character for either path.
The way they bring the paths together with Fiona is a little strange as well. She’s upset about the vault key deal, that she set up, and blames it for her life going to♥♥♥♥♥♥ That makes zero sense for either path and feels out of place.
One thing that Telltale games have always done that grates me the wrong way is that they have a character or several characters that they just assume you're going to be buddy-buddy with. And if you like that character than it's totally chill and you'll have a great time. But if you don't, then the railroad train you're on seems very very obvious. Kenny from The Walking Dead was my first experience with this. In TFTBL this is not so much a character as it is a romance.
I absolutely HATE the romance option in this game. And it’s because it’s not so much an option as it is a continuous nudge. A lot of players liked this addition if the end slides are anything to go by, but if you're like me and didn't, then the constant nudging, the forced "hey pick the flower for the pretty girl" scene and related scenes from the Atlas dome, and Rhys getting flustered over Sasha in episode five without player input had me rolling my eyes hardcore.
It feels especially off-putting when you consider the game is in the Borderlands universe; a universe known for being pretty inclusive for non-straight identities. To have another option in addition to Sasha, maybe Vaughn for example since the two have history, then the romance addition wouldn’t have been so grating. It would feel like a proper choice.
Just let me be gay in your games, Telltale, it's not that hard.
Despite how I feel about episode five's writing it contains what I think is one of the best scenes Telltale has ever made. The scene where you confront Jack in the wreckage of Helios and have to dismember yourself to save your life is both beautiful and horrifying in a way that left me speechless. Body horror is one of those things that usually squicks me out, but the way it's handled in this scene was perfect and really shows that, despite being portrayed as a wimp most of the game, Rhys is much stronger than he looks and I really liked that. Whichever cinematic artist was in charge of that scene deserves a raise.
The art style for the Borderlands game plays very well with Telltale's comic book look and I like the new character and set designs. The engine is showing its age, though, especially during action sequences.
So in conclusion despite my many problems with the game, it's a fun game with enjoyable characters and more engaging choices than I’ve seen in previous Telltale games. It’s earned a spot on my personal fave games and I loved it so much I bought it on both the PC and PS4. It’s worth both your time and your money. Would definitely recommend.

A long time ago, the developers for this game took a wrong turn in the development for this game. It has since turned into a pay to win, grindy hellhole, a mere shell of its former self. I can see why people who didn't play back then like this game as it is now, but if they would have played it back then, they would never accept playing it in its current state. The new (or rather not so new by most standards but new for anyone who used to play back when the game was actually enjoyable) methods for getting stuff in-game, all the paywalls, and the horrific balance issues are not exactly helping the game get better.
It is my opinion that the developers should care less about trying to squeeze as much money out of this game as they possibly can, but instead focusing on making a product that is enjoyable for players, both for those who have countless hours to sink into games, and those who don't have the time to send a hundred hours just to get enough stuff to make anything.
Things like returning to the old battle reward system, or making the game more balanced would be a small step in the right direction, but it most likely never going to happen, because quite frankly the developers are too busy bathing in the money they are getting from this to actually care what the older community from back in early access thinks.

This is a curious visual novel. It's one of those stories that you can't really express in words to give it justice, so you have to experience it for yourself to really understand what's going on here.
The general gist of the story is that a colonization vessel, which was sent more than 900 years in the past, has been found derelict in space with everyone on board having been myseriously killed several centuries before. There are two AIs aboard this ship that have context as to what happened, but the true story is in the logs that the last generation aboard the ship had kept. You're only given a very small amount of logs to begin with, but you will eventually find the entire truth as you show your AI friends what logs you are more interested in hearing about. They will also give their own context and thoughts to drive home what happened aboard the Mugunghwa.
Overall, it's a story about how a majorly regressed society with its own major problems can cause its own demise by not being able to look past its own norms. It's a very tragic story, one which you know was diseased in the beginning and only furthered by the fact that it's a guarantee that none of them will survive the encounter.
As for the two AIs, I really liked the default AI (*Hyun-Ae)'s route. Without spoiling anything, her emotions and thoughts feel real and the situation she's in really adds to the experience. *Mute wasn't quite as strong; while her opinions were definitely understandable, she never had the same type of draw that *Hyun-Ae did.
This VN is also not afraid to show a girl on girl love affair between a noble and a peasant in a society where women are expected to fully devote their lives to their husbands. Normally this would be fanservicey nonsense, but it really adds to the setting to have something like this within the game. Applause to Love for this.

Although not at all innovative in its mechanics or story, Enemy Front is a bit of a black sheep in the ocean of first person shooters. Not only does it take place during World War II, which is a contrast to the contemporary and futuristic settings that are currently trendy, it also focuses on the equally fascinating yet not as famous resistance movements of WW2 – as opposed to the well-known exploits of American, British, and Soviet armies that have many times been explored in older war shooters. Here we take on the role of fictional American war correspondent Robert Hawkins, who infiltrates Nazi-controlled Europe at first in search of exciting news to print, but is then moved by the stories of ordinary people risking their lives to rise up against the Hitlerite regime  and joins their struggles in France, Norway, Germany, and Poland.
Most of the game is set during the Warsaw Uprising of 1944, the largest military operation of resistance against the Third Reich, with various missions in between taking place earlier and in other countries as Hawkins recalls: his time with the French Résistance, taking part in the Norwegian heavy water sabotage operations, and impairing a V2 rocket factory alongside an antifascist German agent. It is wonderful to see the gaming industry finally give some recognition to the armed acts of civilians against the Nazis, but Enemy Front falls short of its potential to tell a more powerful story. Its one-man-army protagonist can blast through waves of German troops with ease; even though the plot does on a few occasions slow down to show the more sombre moments of Polish civilians trying to deal with the war – it even touches upon the topic of mass executions – the game for the most part sticks with the bombastic themes of an action blockbuster.
One thing that can’t be denied however is the beauty of Enemy Front’s environments. Yes, the foliage and character faces look dated, there are some low resolution textures here and there too, but the amount of detail put into creating the picturesque communes and châteaux of France, the snowy mountainous surroundings of Vemork, the rural forested areas of Germany, and of course the haunting magnificence of a once glorious Warsaw gradually bombed to utter ruin by the Luftwaffe is stunning. Moreover, many of these areas are quite faithful recreations of real locations in wartime Warsaw (Holy Cross Church, the PAST building, Copernicus’ monument, the Varsovian sewers, etc.). Sadly, there are some historical inaccuracies when it comes to other visual details, such as the anachronistic appearance of a StG 44/MP 43 in 1940, which is 3 years before it actually entered service.
The gameplay at first seems to be fairly unremarkable, clearly modelled after modern military shooters, but Enemy Front eventually shows its cards and you realise that it has more up its sleeve than the boring singleplayer campaigns of much of its competition. Although mostly linear in design, some of the levels here are actually surprisingly open-ended with larger zones and multiple possible approaches, along with secondary objectives and collectibles. There is even a basic stealth system in place with shooting out lights, quiet knife kills, carrying dead bodies to hide them, and so on. The sniping mechanics previously tested in CI Games’ other series “Sniper: Ghost Warrior” are immensely fun to use here. It also helps that the core gunplay works well and is satisfying thanks to blood gusts and nice sound effects. Enemy Front’s score is great as well, yet the soundtrack used in combat gets slightly repetitive even in this 8 hour campaign.
Perhaps Enemy Front’s biggest flaw is its instability. Even though it is significantly better than it used to be at launch, I still had to restart from a checkpoint on 2 occasions because of glitches that stopped me from progressing further. I came across some floating corpses, enemies clipping through objects, and other such minor annoyances too. These problems didn’t occur all of the time, but they were too frequent for the fairly short experience that this game is. This and some oddities in otherwise competent enemy AI give away the fact that Enemy Front clearly didn’t have the benefit of the same budget as a typical AAA production in the West. Nevertheless, when it comes to the overall quality of the product, this is perhaps CI Games’ finest creation yet – finally stepping out of mediocrity as a genuinely decent game, even if somewhat rough around the edges and at times awkward (e.g. the HUD is oversized and intrusive).
In the end, I would recommend this to anyone looking for something thematically fresh in the war FPS genre – especially so if you are into partisan history. Enemy Front feels like a heartfelt tribute from its Varsovian studio to the men and women who took part in the Warsaw Uprising. As a game it is far from anything ground-breaking or revolutionary, its Eastern European production values clearly lag behind that of Activision and EA’s FPS offerings and so its set pieces are also less impressive, but the gameplay is actually more varied and engaging than most of the recent CoD or Medal of Honor titles. On the other hand, its online multiplayer can't truly compete with either of those franchises, probably due to the fact that its development was outsourced to a different company. Regardless, it can be fun for a while, if you manage to find any active servers.
Here are some tweaks to make the game even more pleasant to play: skip all the intro splash screens by going to <Local Disk>\Program Files\Steam\SteamApps\common\Enemy Front\Game2\_FastLoad\ and deleting "IntroMovies.pak"; increase the FOV by finding "system.cfg" in the installation directory, editing it and changing both "cl_fov=" and "r_DrawNearFov=" to 59 (this is a vertical FOV number, so it should equate to 90 for horizontal FOV). To make enemy corpses and guns stay on the map forever change values for "g_enableWeaponUtilization" and "g_enableDeadBodyUtilization" from 1 to 0. Finally, again in the same file, change "g_show_crosshair=" from 1 to 0 if you want to play without the crosshair. It might seem weird that all of this can't be changed through the in-game options menu, but this is a problem that has unfortunately become the norm for most multiplatform FPS games on the PC.

This game has an interesting concept behind it: it's a RISK-like game, where each player gets some starting territory in the map and the goal is to conquer all of them, by occupying empty territory, or invading the territory from other players. You can also fortify your territory, and train more troops to defend it. It's turn-based, obviously, and the twist it has is that at the beginning of each turn, you get to "bid" for one of DaVinci's inventions, which are special cards that can grant bonuses to your units.
Like I said, it's an interesting concept, but I think it falls short. The game has a tutorial, but it barely explains the rules, it just tells you stuff like "select a territory", or "here you can see how many points you have". It never goes into detail as to what you should do in order to achieve victory, only telling you things like "occupy land" and "get points". I messed around in several of the maps, and I could never figure out how the AI was getting more points than me. Not to mention that some of the cards are special "works of art" that can grant you victory points; what the game forgets to tell you, however, is that you must activate them first; having them doesn't do anything.
I think this game would have been a lot better having MP. It's based on a board game, after all, and board games tend to be a lot more fun when you play against other people.

TLDR – Oil Rush is a graphics intensive version of what I would call a “virus game” similar to the Galcon series. Technically it’s real time strategy, but it’s all about moving your troops between map “nodes,” protecting your own while capturing your enemy’s when his troops are away. The game maker took a simple gameplay concept and prettied it up with modern graphics and a campaign story.   7.5/10
The game takes place after global warming has flooded the Earth and left humanity living on ships and small floating towns in the middle of the ocean. The most precious commodity is now oil, used not only for keeping the navy ships moving but for producing electricity and other necessities. You play a young navy commander named Kevin who is fresh out of school and ready to kick raider♥♥♥♥♥to protect your people (and grab oil supplies while you’re at it).
Game play is simple in Oil Rush. You usually start with a factory that automatically builds units until a limit is reached. You can send these units to any other “node” such as another factory or oil derrick. If the node belongs to an enemy a fight breaks out and whoever has more units will win and gain/keep control of the node. You cannot send your units into the middle of nowhere, they can only be sent to another node. And since the max limit of units is pretty small, the action is pretty fast paced (it’s hard to build up a massive army and crush the enemy because they’ll probably have the same size army as you). The more factories you control, the higher your unit limit is, so if you strike fast and capture factories early you’ll probably win the round.
There are a number different types of factories since every factory can only build a single type of unit. Additionally, there’s a tower defense element to the game because your factories can be “upgraded” to have automated defense bunkers to back up whatever units are there to defend. If your factory is heavily defended with bunkers you can feel safer sending all your troops out to attack. Oil derricks function as nodes on the map (you can send troops to them) but they cannot be defended with bunkers and they only produce oil, which is kind of like mana for your special powers. The special powers aren’t especially awesome but they can turn the tide if you have almost enough units to conquer an enemy node.
Pros:
+Simple gameplay where you’re really limited in what you can do. Don’t go in thinking it’s a real time strategy game like Starcraft, this game is all about capturing and holding map nodes.
+The graphics are very good for an indie game. My video card fan was spun up the whole time.
+Unlike the Galcon games that I’ve played, Oil rush has an actual story campaign. You follow Kevin’s progress through hardships and an increasing number of enemy factions.
Cons:
-The simple gameplay may turn some people off. As you progress in the campaign you get access to a lot more units and more special powers, but the core gameplay remains the same.  Capture and hold as many factories as you can until you reach your unit max, then send them to attack an enemy node.
-The gameplay may be simple (moving troops around), but the game itself can be extremely difficult. Even on easy mode, some of the campaign missions are against overwhelming numbers of enemies.
Overall, if you like virus type games you should enjoy Oil Rush. It’s like playing Tic Tac Toe with high end graphics on a bigger board. A simple concept framed with modern technology.

I've had this game a long time, picked it up maybe two weeks after it came out.  When I first played it it was a great little bullet hell rpg, with waves of enemies followed by bosses, and endgame bosses at the end of each 5 stage zone.  You could get mind blowingly, game-breakingly powerful and just blow through stuff, and there was a lot of development that needed to be done because content was limited, but there was great potential and I was greatly looking forward to updates and DLC.  Fast forward a few years and I see this little game on my list and I think "Yeah!  I loved that game!  I bet it's awesome now with new content!"
Oh.  Dear.
Now there are no waves of enemies.  Just a dump of mobs littered around the map.  All relics vanish upon death.  The balance of bosses is unreasonable and ridiculous (I'm looking at you, Grim Reaper) and skipping all the trash levels before the one you want to get to means missing out on a dozen relics and enjoying some of the fun benefits those can give you.
Honestly?  It feels like someone on the dev team played a good chunk of Binding of Isaac, saw the success that game was hauling in, and tried to incorporate it into their game.  The problem is that this isn't Binding of Isaac and it's not supposed to be Binding of Isaac.
If BoI had bosses which would one shot me if I didn't find a single safe space in the room amid a cluster of bullet hell crap, I wouldn't play it either.
As it is, I've ragequit this one too many times.  It's coming off my hard drive.  You should've stuck to your guns, guys.  You had a great game.

In a day and age of countless rehashes and of saturation, comes a game that grabs you and 20 hours later you're hungry, thirsty and your bottom is sore from sitting.
Rimworld has the elements of base building intertwined with resource gathering and there's also an RPG element in there (You have a major say in how colonists develop their skills).
You fight the hostile environment, you fight fire, wild animals and violent invaders which want your resources and will kill your colonists for it. You research, you learn from mistakes and you build a better base, an ever expanding base for which there are no rules - your own imagination is the limit, and you have absolute freedom in organizing and optimizing your structures for efficiency, hazardness or sometimes, hilarity.
It's unique in the sense that micromanagement tends to get tedious in base building games - not here: Micro managing and tweaking, and adjusting and changing is half the fun, especially since by the time you have changed something, there's another crisis in some other part of your base.
You will find yourself abusing the time speeding feature, then alternating between paused and normal speed for hours on end.
If you like base building games (don't know why, but Outpost comes to mind), then you should definetely check this one out.
It is keeping me glued to the PC for hours on end, sometimes playing through an epic adventure for days on end.
I give it a solid 9/10.

Well … where to start? How about the positives. The graphics are nice to look at and the main campaigns story was competent enough to keep me somewhat interesting, but that’s about it. The game is ridiculously easy (even on Hard) and I found myself only dying because I was making dumb decisions like running directly into machine gun fire. I also died due to the game a lot, it wouldn’t always let me throw back grenades and it wouldn’t always allow me to stop using an HMG (or similar thing), causing me to explode and get shot to death respectively. The AI is rather stupid … you could just sit around a corner and wait for the enemies to come into view (though I chose not to do that) and it’s rather unfortunate that it turns out that way as the environments feel like they’re designed for huge open firefights that just never happen. Then there’s the stealth mechanics that just don’t really work and feel cumbersome, I just rarely used them because it wasn’t fun trying to be stealthy and was laboriously slow and tedious. It’s also rather buggy. Friendly and enemy AI getting stuck and freezing, shots not always registering that they hit you/the enemy, random teleportation of the player (happened twice for seemingly no reason), and plenty of crashes during the loading screens. Lastly, it's fairly short and the ending is rather abrupt, only took me about 6 hours and I don't think I can justify purchasing it at full price. I will say that if you're interesting in the more unique setting of the game (half being the Warsaw Uprising, half being ... other stuff) then maybe get it discounted or in a bundle. I'm going to say not recommended for this one, but take it as being closer to neutral than to negative.

For anyone who is skeptical of an early access game, I don't blame you as I too have been burned by them. So this is one of the very few early access games I don't mind reccomending to people as I know they won't get burned like other many early access products.
For anyone who like colony managment games or wants to try to get into them I'd highly reccomend this game.

Five tribe members share a complete lack of survival skills in an extremely hostile steppe. An ancient road streches across the vast seas of sand and rock from east to west, or was it west to east? it's hard to tell in the blistering 50 degree heat ( 122F). The stream that spills lazily into the encampment is nearly evaporating faster than it's replenished. The Gods command the tribe to dig into the crags for respite from the hot sun, but disaster strikes.
Ancient dangers!
the Gods realized that nothing could continue, and thus began the age of war for the tribe, short-lived as it was... As Gumba, the spiritual leader of the tribe broke open the final retainers of hell, chaos erupted. Cannons, Miniguns, grenades, raids, and psychic shock all hit at once. thus ended the short lives of the Steppe clan, as raiders carried away the last of the tribe's gear.
----------------------------------------------------
in all seriousness, this game is so open to chaos at every turn it's hard to keep track of the micromanagement necessary to keep one colonist from snapping and murdering the rest; or even to keep ancient threats away (no super spoilers here). I personally love the challenge the game throws at me, and intend to continue playing for a very very long (and unique!) time.

This game is BAD. DO NOT BUY! And if you got it from a humblebundle along with other games u wanted, DO NOT INSTALL.
This game pretends to be a casual RTS. However, the campaign, even on easiest, is challenging enough to bring problems in the game very obvious.
You cannot give commands to individual units. You cannot focus fire. This means you will often see 2 low health units fighting 2 different enemies and die and will not be able to do anything about it.
Once you give a "move to platform" command to a set of units (the only command you can give), you cannot tell them to change destination on route! You can ask them to go back to the original platform, that's it! They will be making their way to a faraway platform, and there will be a platform under attack RIGHT NEXT to them, and they will be unable to help! You cannot tell them to defend the platform under attack until they reach either the destination or the source, THIS IS WHERE YOU THROW YOUR PC OUT OF THE WINDOW. Clicked the wrong platform by mistake and realized it too late? Cool, you just lost an important objective while your units go on a pleasure cruise and you cannot stop them.
Often there will be a repair vehicle, who wont be repairing your damaged units because they are both orbiting the same platform, while not under attack, at the same speed. Thus they never come close enough to each other for the repair unit to heal the damaged unit. There is no way to command the damage unit to get close to the repair vessel.
If you are like me who likes to finish games, specially RTS ones, STAY AWAY! This game is trying to be casual but is not casual enough to give you a pleasant experience. It just brings out your rage and frustrations with its very obvious shortcomings. Obviously the game was not playtested enough. Games will NOT feel satisfying. The plot of the campaign is cheesy and stereotypical anyways.

Well, they certainly got it backwards.  Seems they released the HD version with better graphics and gameplay first, then released the original version a few years later.
This version has weird frame drops and graphical glitches, low-res NPC textures, cheap blood effects and trippy lighting issues.  It also has bugs that weren't in the original, worse physics and broken hitboxes that can get you stuck in a room because you don't fit through the door on the way out.  Plus when you're not sprinting, you handle like both of your legs are broken and can't seem to walk straight without an extreme input lag.
Do yourself a favor and buy the real HD version; the one that came out years ago.
EDIT: So since everybody else seems to worship the damn thing, I figured I'd keep playing a while longer to see if it gets any better aaaand, no.  It actually gets worse.
The screwy hitboxes aren't limited to doors, you'll get stuck inside of boulders just by brushing against them.  Enemies will also get stuck on boulders and will actually fall through the map... when they don't just die for no reason.  The cancerous Motion Blur just won't turn off even if you turn it off in the options, and the entire screen becomes a blurry mess whenever you start sprinting.  And speaking of sprinting, if you sprint too long your character will literally start looking at the world through rose-tinted lenses.  Finally, the "enhanced" navigation system will tell you to go through walls, and point to the goal in a straight line ignoring everything inbetween... I hope you're good at swimming.
Game is complete and absolute garbage, avoid it at all costs and just get the original.

is half Binding of Isaac, half Diablo, but either of those is a better buy.
+ Lite puzzles

+- Circle strafe to the end of time

- Can't enter buildings

- Equipment doesn't show on character

I remember doing a project back when I was in High school on the Warsaw Uprising. There are many things in the game that were true, from the 1939 invasion to the uprising 85% of the city was destroyed by January 1945, and the uprising lasted 63 days and the game ends on the 62nd day of the uprising. I also met a survivor of the uprising and he told me that it was the most horrific experience he went through and he was just 19 years old when he joined the Polish Resistance. He even told me that he prayed that something like that never has to happen again and that USA does not have to go through what he and the rest of the people of Poland went through back then. If you want a good World War 2 Story based on a true events of the resistance then I encourage you to play this game.

#Note: The game has been free for a long time, and is still free, over at the official website unrealworld.fi .
UnReal World is a procedurally generated top down rogue-like survival game set in a low-fantasy yet realistic version of iron age Finland, and because of this, the game is HARD, especially for new players. if you don't survive more than a week, remember that "losing is fun".
Luckily, for new players, the developers (A two-man group) have added two tutorials in order to help new players (one simpler, more focused on survival, one on more advanced mechanics).
As a rogue-like, the game has a skill system for rating your abilities in everything from timbercraft and construction to fishing and swimming. The base of these stats are dependent on your characters chosen tribe and their physical scores, randomly generated as you create your character. Your skills are then improved as you practice using them.
The game was first released in 1992, and it shows, in some ways. The UI can definitely be improved in some areas, among other things, but the devs are constantly improving the game and it is possible these issues are fixed later on. As an example of the overall attention to detail from the developer, The latest update (the first version released on Steam) added improved winter mechanics, making snow and ice thicker and thinner as winter comes and goes and adding the possibility of breaking the ice, adding another highly plausible way of dying during winter. Something else that has been in the game for some time is one of (if not THE most) advanced animal AI that isn't just randomly walking around, like other games.
In summary, it's a highly competent survival game, and the Steam version is currently just a way to pay the devs for the amazing amount of work they have done. If you feel like playing the game, go to their website and try the free non-Steam version first before buying it here.

Be me, on Memorial Day.
Really hungry, breakfast time, but I'm a few miles from home without a car.
See a Denny's, with a special promotion: "Veterans Eat Free".
Hatch an idea.
Enter the Denny's, asked to be seated with the WWII vets. Skeptical glances, but I act like I'm supposed to be there.
"Oh, so where'd YOU fight, kid?" One old dude asks, trying to prove to the confused waiter that I am NOT supposed to be here. (I was born in '95)
Having played this game, and Red Orchestra/Rising Storm, I prepare a tale.
"I fought in the battle of Iwo Jima."
Old dude raises an eyebrow.
"What a surprise! I did, too. What division?"
Glance at his pin. 3rd Marine Division.
"The 3rd Marine Division."
He laughs.
"Kid, that was MY division."
I nod.
He looks angered.
"That's not funny, kid. I watched many good friends of mine die out there."
I match his anger.
"Yeah? Me too! I remember by midday I'd seen thirteen boys not older than nineteen shot dead by those dirty Japs! I held my best friend while he bled out from a bayonet wound, then bludgeoned the wounded Jap who'd killed him to death with the butt of my rifle!"
His jaw drops.
"W-Wait... Franklin? Franklin Earl Rosenbaum?" (I look fairly Jewish.)
I nodded. "How did you-"
Tears start welling in the old dude's eyes.
"It's me, Frank! It's Tyler Prescott!"
I pretend to recognize him.
"Tyler! Oh my God!"
He hugs me. The server is still staring at us, dumbfounded.
I turn to him.
"Can we get some waffles over here?"
We eat and tell war stories. I recount Rising Storm missions I've done, and he nods along. A few other vets come over and chat with us, and I spin some tales of herosim from DoD. Soon, I'm surrounded by a million old veterans who think they know me.
I eat my waffles.
"How'd you stay so young, Frank?"
I point to the waffles with my fork.
"Three waffles, every morning. I don't look a day older than when I fought back in 1944!"
They all laugh. After a few more waffles and some laughs, I leave.
I bump into a veteran coming in. He looks like me. In fact, he's got an old photo of himself that looks nearly identical to me.
"Hi! Sorry, sir."
The old dude smiles.
"Please, call me Frank."
I nod politely, get outside, and run for my life.
11/10 would steal waffles on a national holiday again.

Magnifico tried to reinvent Risk with the addition of some twists, but in the end it failed by turning a strategy game into something where skill has absolutely no place next to pure luck.
I don’t like to form opinions on board games after such a short time of game play, but going through four of the five difficulty levels and all four maps of Magnifico, I have to say, playing one or two games really exhaust everything this board game offers.
The basic premise is a variation of Risk and Catan: 3-4 players fight over a map divided into several territories, gathering army and fortifying home cities along the way. On top of the usual infantry, the players can use tanks that do massive damage, and planes that can bypass fortification defences. All three unit types can be upgraded with the use of cards that are acquired on pre-turn auctions.
In theory, it all sounds great, but in practise this is not a strategy game but a game of chance. Everything is random from territory values to battles: infantry can just fall down and die from nothing, and a malfunctioning tank can instantly wipe out an army regardless of its size.
The cards are chosen randomly, and being lucky enough to have a winning bid on, for example the one that can sacrifice an infantry to reduce city defences to nothing, can pretty much win the game by itself.
Maybe if there would be multiplayer, it could salvage the game, because the computer either never attacks and gathers victory points behind safe walls, or gangs up on the player and steamrolls them. It’s just not fun to play Magnifico, because it is either boring or frustrating.

This is a very fun puzzle/platformer with a unique system that takes scoping out a situation before hand, then enacting the plan once you're ready. I find the main character funny, the story passable, but I only wish the game was a bit longer as far as the narrative goes. The story is linear, you can choose a slightly different ending, but you'll end up playing all the missions eventually. I very much like the way you restart after you die, because you can pick three sepearate times in the past to go back to and try again, or pick a manual save. There's a level editor, which enhances the replayability, but it isn't 100% accessebile to the player. Their are upgrades, but they feel more neccessary than helpful. It just feels you need to upgrade to pass the game.
Pros:
-Good save system
-NIce atmosphere
-Fun blend of puzzle and platforming
-A sense of humor
-Level Editor
Cons:
-Short and not enough replayability
-Needs a more interesting narritive
-Level Editor is a bit clunky
-Upgrades are not all that useful
Overall, I recommend you give this game a shot. I think you would be pleasantly surprised. If it's on sale, get it. If not, research the game a little more and see if you are sold.

This game is quite pretty with very nice graphics. Unfortunately, the graphics and building defensive turrets around the bases is all the main screen is used for. Gameplay itself is pretty much restricted to moving units from one base to another via the mini-map. All you can do is select 25%, 50%, or 100% of a base's units or select individual kinds of units rather than individual units themselves, limiting your tactical options. No sending sentries or guards in the middle of a channel. Additionally, each base only constructs one kind of unit. If you lose the one base that makes the cheap anti-unit guys, you are SOL. And no constructing your own bases either, you're stuck with the ones already on the map.
One of the biggest irritations is that units don't engage enemy units en-route unless they sail right on top of the unit, and even then they don't chase them. So a massive enemy force can sail right by your front-line bases with only a couple shots exchanged. So much for a defensive line.
The story is amusing if only because of its ridiculousness. Definitely not worth playing it for.
In the end, the game is just a grind of sending units forward, watching them die, building more units, sending them forward, and then back to retake a base, then forward again. Much better RTSs out there. (Also, for those saying it includes TD elements, sure if a couple pot shots as the enemy drives by counts as defense...)

And I played this during the Halloween event, with special quests that give absolutely insane XP bonuses for low level characters (as in jumping you 10-20 levels per), it becomes a lesson in frustration. This is a short free game made using Valve's Source engine. Now, before you jump claiming that it'll look outdated, let me assure you that, even though the Source engine isn't the most modern out there, this game still manages to make it shine. The environments are very well designed, and the atmosphere of the game is intriguing.
As for gameplay itself, it differs drastically from gameplay traditionally associated to the Source engine. There's no weapon inventory, for a start, meaning that you'll have to decide which weapon to take with you. Even then, the amount of weapons available is rather small. Another thing is the lack of armor; here you'll find yourself only with a health bar. As far as the enemies go, they're quick to die, but that doesn't mean this game is easy, as, just like the enemies, you can die quite easily. They're also quick to spot you, which means you'll be running for cover in several ocasions.
Still, this isn't a game of killing and killing. Plenty of times you'll find yourself exploring the environment, at your own pace.
All in all, this is a pretty solid game, in my opinion. Atmospheric enough to be an exploration game, and with enough fights to make it more engaging.

There is so much to say about Unreal World, but first I want to start off by saying that this is not a game that everyone will enjoy. Go check out the game on their website for free:

I won't go into details of what you can do because basically there are SO many things you can do and everything necessary is there to survive. + A game that allows players to use their imagination
+ Awesome Developers (Thanks Sami and Erkka)
+ In Depth Combat System
+ In Depth Injury System from cuts/bruises, to diseases and so much more
+ Accurate Historical Items and Folklore
+ Easily Moddable
+ High Replayability
-Roguelike Graphics: This is a con for some players used to modern graphics (Latest Update Improved them and mods help)
-Slight learning curve with keys (but is easily fluid once you get used to it)

-Pictures are somewhat corny but overall they do well (personal taste and easily moddable and mods help)
Overall, this is the TRUE survival game. I have over 400 hours of Rust and have played just about every survival game out there, but Unreal World just keeps pulling me back in for its in depth system of how we humans are adapted to survive in the impossible. This game allows me to use my imagination and do what I cannot do in my daily life.

Gunpoint weaves an interesting storyline and fun, simple but challenging gameplay together. It is a 2D platformer that adds a lot of great features that make the gameplay easier and more interesting. There are optional challenges during missions that serve to make easy missions harder. There is a great respawn mechanic that allows you to pick up play 2-10 seconds before you died, meaning lots of boring trekking from the last save point is removed. The crosslink system allows you to get through levels in any number of inventive ways, and really makes speedrunning far more creative. The music is, like many indie games, fantastic and very well suited to the game's vibe; I keep listening to it over and over at work (go "Five Floor Goodbye"!). The gameplay rewards lateral thinking, good planning, and some precise timing. Like many stealth games you can go for every conceivable approach e.g. kill every guard; knock out dangerous guards, touch nobody and leave no trace, etc. This definitely adds to replayability, and allows people to challenge themselves to go all Solid Snake on the guards (I'm afraid there's no cardboard boxes in game).
The storyline is very good, you'll find yourself trying to solve the case yourself with the information people give you, you'll find yourself actively wondering whether to trust some people or whether they have their own agendas, you'll find yourself invested in the fates of those people who help you through the game, and you'll find yourself deciding whether to dispense your own justice, or leave it to the state. Analogue: A Hate Story
Lets cut straight to the chase.
- Gameplay -
The basic gameplay outside of the standard visual novel parts consists of using the ships main system, which is sort of like coding but actually fun, and searching through the ships various documents, trying to uncover the story behind the mysterious ship you've set out to explore. The actual visual novel elements are solid, giving you plenty of room to make different choices which heavily affect your relations with the ships two main AI's- Hyun-ae, and Mute.
- Characters -
This might fall short, considering there are only three actual characters in the game, including yourself. However, I found the ships two AI's to be both unique and well written, each in their own way. I can't say much for Mute herself, as I went with Hyun-ae's route, however the limited dialogue I had with her was... Well, certainly interesting. As for Hyun-ae, she happens to be my favorite part of the game, being extremely likable and interesting right from the start.
- Story -
The story is sort of in the backround, but no less involving and important. As I mentioned before, you uncover most of it through the ships various documents, and through talking with both the ships AI's. It seems to be a take on a post-apocalyptic (sort of?) take on japanese culture mixed with a lot of science fiction elements. Confusing, right? Nonetheless, it tells a surprisingly human and very thought provoking story, on morales, cultures, and general humanity as a whole.
- Final thoughts -
Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game, dispite it being a bit short (about four hours, but I'm a fast reader), it tells a compelling story, has some great characters, and is overall a generally good experience. Definately would recommend.

The weirdest game I was not playing. Even though I was playing it.
Like spectating a really bored gamer playing a boring game.
To understand what I mean, you need to know that the game features two vital functions:
Auto-run to get to quest locations, and auto-combat which will spam all your skills it can and glug any potions you need for either Health or Mana. (called 'Steam' in this game)
And that's all you need to know. If you're not fighting or moving, click the quest marker and your character will go there. Upon which they'll then end up fighting if that is required, which is automatised as well. And in general, the game's enemies are simple enough that, all you would have to do anyway is spam your skills. That's all there is to it.
The 'selling point' for this game is that it's a mere 50mb. A nice premise, but there are flashgames out there that take less than 1mb and are tremendously more fun than this. Again, there is no reason to not play this game on auto-mode because in 95% of the time, it is the most efficient way. Not to mention that potions are stupidly cheap to buy in mass ammount, and auto-combat includes auto-looting.
In fact, whenever you pick up gear that is a straight upgrade to what's equipped, it will prompt you to equip it. Have skillpoints or stat points to spend? The game will remind you of this and offer a convenient 'automatic' button that'll spend these in the amount best suited to your class.
Everything in this game is designed to remove any thought process from you. You choose a class, choose a race with a handful of variations, have a VERY basic array of options to change your hair (the face is stuck with the one of the 'race presets' you picked) aaaaand... that's it. Press quest marker to continue.
There are games out there that make tremendous usage with little space. They draw you in, even if their style happens to be 8-bit. And then there's games that use very little space, and have absolutely nothing to show for that feat. City of Steam just doesn't bring anything worthwhile to the table.
Don't get me wrong, it doesn't do anything particularly horribly bad. If anything, what the game does is simply somewhat sub-par, beneath the commonly accepted standard across the board. This game just enables you to turn it into a lazy man's game, a detriment to an already unimpressive title.
Honestly, this shouldn't be on PC. This should just be on iOS and Android and it would flourish like crazy. games that size are not uncommon and it wouldn't be impossible to translate the controls.
Maybe it already is on mobile devices, but I'm having a mighty hard time finding it.
I would really just say... don't bother with it unless you've got absolutely nothing else to do and you want to spend that free time on something that won't enrage you.
But neither will it really engage you.

Time for a long essay about this game because that's just how awesome this is.
NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM 3 Full Burst is a game based on the manga/anime franchise Naruto (obviously). Since this is the 3rd game, it starts the story in the middle so if you haven't played the other games (I haven't) but you have read/watched the entire series, it's all good. This game just goes on the story from the part right before the Great Ninja War. If you are a Naruto fan, this is a guaranteed "You'll like this" game for you.
The game is a 3D style fighting game and you go can either go through the story to fight the battles that happened in the manga in the game. The one thing I like about this is that everytime a battle starts, it starts on the normal difficultly, but if you are having trouble with that battle and lost over three times, the difficultly gets lowered. I really liked that, caused me not to get stuck on certain battles.
The cutscenes are animated 3D models, and that is pretty amazing how they made them look beautiful with models, at the same level as RWBY, which is probably the best 3D animation(anime?) ever. The characters and voices were great (I think they used the same ones from the anime) and matched the story of Naruto overall.
There is one section of the game where you can play as Naruto's pregant mom and that part really cracked me up. Another thing is that everytime you buy ramen from the ramen guy in town, all your health and chakra gets restored. THE RAMEN IS MAGIC!!!!
This game is supposed to be on XBOX controllers but the PC version is also great, but has some problems. There are glitches in the game. Sometimes theres one battle that just causes the game to crash, or one specific move that will cause the game to crash. This is one of the reasons why I never actually completed the entire story within the game. One of the last battles during the Great Ninja War would keep crashing, so I gave up. (I already know what happens anyway)
I suppose one of the things I didn't like was the spread of save points. Some save points would be placed 2 minutes of each other while others are 2 hours from each other. That was one of the cons of this game since I can't play games in a marathon and I don't think I am the only one.
Overall, this game has its ups and downs but is a great game. It's also pretty long and hopefully you will enjoy it as much as I do. Thanks for reading this long essay. ^-^

Make no mistake, this is a board game for PC. It feels like Risk with a twist, but I find Magnifico a lot more appealing since I don't particularly like Risk.
It has a good tutorial and the rules are always one click away. There are several strategies you can deploy to win the game, but you will always have to use all available mechanics. You need money to get stuff and troops to defend your territories, and technology to gain extra points and upgrade your economy.
Scoring is according to "the more" you have. More lands, more castles, more upgraded castles and more tech cards. On your turn you may move troops, invade empty lands, attack enemies, build castles or siege weapons, and activate upgrades. The actions are limited by number of uses and the amount of gold available. Controlled lands supply fixed troops and/or gold every turn. The map is generated randomly at the beginning of the game. A land may either produce 30 gold and 0 troops, or 10 gold and 2 troops every turn, for example. Siege weapons ("tanks" and "planes") allow you to counter tech cards and fortifications.
It is a simple game to pick up but still manages to deliver a bit of a challenge and get you engaged. I actually find it very relaxing.
The only downside, and single reason I don't recommend it to everyone, is that it has no multiplayer for some reason. It feels nonsensical since it is a board game adaptation, but still, if you have no friends or just want to fiddle around a better Risk like, without delving into the pits of Hearts of Iron and the likes of grand strategy in terms of world conquering, this is a simple and interesting game.
While completely different in mechanics, I'd say that if you enjoyed other boardgame adaptations like Ticket to Ride or Smallworld 2 (not Talisman, that game is a chore) in the sense of slow paced casual fun, you might also like this.

Please read the following to get a decent perspective of the game before buying.
Pros:
- Very smooth, sleek design. Graphics are very nice.
- Simple controls yet very immersive and very to understand.
- Extremely immersive in nearly every aspect (Massive +).
- Being stealthly is very rewarding (Mentally and in the game).
- CO-OP is slightly more fun than single player.
- Not the hardest game to run, but will require a decent PC.
- Guns feel very nice and play better than i thought they would.
- A.I is very smart, even on easy difficulty.
- Devs seem to be more active than other communitys which is good.
- Potentially great story.
+ And a few more that i forgot xD
Cons:
- Reloading while in cover is broken. The animation dosn't work correctly.
- Hardly anyone online to play with, even the devs know. "people will be on for you to play with, it is usually during the evenings in North America and Europe."
- When on some hard difficultys the A.I is a little too smart. They one shot very often.
- Sandbox is sometimes broken. You fall striaght through the floor and never return which results in restarting the map.
- A.I needs to be more... 'Workable'. Once you've been spotted, you're done for. The A.I, when aware you're around, totally ruine the immersion, i mean completely!
- No checkpoints! This might be deliberate but holy crap is it fustrating. You play through a long missions then you make a wrong move, guess what? You're back at the start. Same goes for CO-OP. When you join they could be across the map and you're at the spawn.
- Story is terrible. You start on the tutorial which is great fun, then... wait what? You're running around in some random facility. Story has been thrown out the window completely. Wrost thing is that the story has great potential.
I would recommend that you buy this game. even though there are more cons than pros, because i think that if the devs stay active and keep updating then this will be something. This game has great potential, i believe, and i would like to see a more active community on it.  A few tweaks here and there and some updates mainly on the story then this game will have more pros than cons.

Well... UnReal World... Where do I start? I started playing  it back in december of 2014 and since then, I am hooked! the graffics may not be the best (the new ones look great, dont get me wrong) but who needs graphics when you have such an emersive, rich game that can take you to places you always wished you could go! For me, what got me into this game at first was curiosity, but I had a feeling I would like it, and oh boy do I! You start off with a multitude of scenarios, wich can greatly challenge you or make life easier for your character. And if you're into challenges, make up your own! with a multitude of skills to learn and master. But skills in UnReal World aren't like skyrim or Unturned, its a pore realistic approach where the more you practice, the better you get IE, you want to raise your cooking skill, cook stuff! But what you can cook doesnt depend on your cooking skill, the taste depends on your skill. For crafting skills, there's obviously no taste, quality is the factor. All and all, the game itself is HUGE, not in size itself, but in its potential for your mind to create more of the game. right now, I've started a new character for the steam release, but before that, I played with a character for a WHOLE 9 MONTHS... IRL. and I didn't get bored once. I have to admit I got my fair share of near death experiences, which is scary since the game is PERMADEATH. Oh and by the way, if you haven't already deducted, I LOVE this game and I would like to say thanks to SAMI MAARANEN.

I'm just going to start this review by letting potential buyers know that I've put several hundred hours into the free version of this game. I'm twenty-four years old so this game has been "In-Dev" my entire existence and it shows through in some good and bad ways*. When I saw UnReal World on Steam my jaw dropped, I loaded $25 onto my wallet, and bought it immediately. No regrets.
I'm going to do a light Pros & Cons to sum the why of it up.
Pros:
+ Deep game mechanics.
+ Actually a survival game. (Unlike Rust/The Forest/ and others that make the claim)
+ High Replayability.
+ Immersive Lore.
+ Progressive skills.
+ Massive crafting system.
+ Extensive Medical system.
+ Many mods made by the community and refined over time.
+ Easy to create your own mods. Google the resources you need and the system is easy to learn.
Cons:
-- Mixture of Traditional & Digitized sprites for graphics.
-- Complex context menus required for maneveuring through the game.
- Basic/dated sound effects.
Neutral (Because this could be a plus for some, a negative for others.)
* +/- Overall a dated old-school look and feel.
+/- A slight lack of "end-game" content, but reaching the end-game takes plenty of time and new updates are planned to rectify this.  A few of the planned updates are: family management, village ceremonies, and more. This is all detailed on the development page.
+/- End game content  by 3rd party developers. I think that a game's merit shouldn't be based off the content created by the community, but while you're waiting on new updates things like the Shaman mod can give you your fix of additional content. It adds many "rituals" that feel lore-friendly and allow you to delve into spiritual magic and ultimately align yourself with light or darkness.
+/- It is lacking in music overall, but the new title screen music is promising.
Due to the time when the project was initially started the game has been stuck in the past as far as graphics, sound, and the general presentation goes.
The skin isn't beautiful, but the meat is sturdy and supple. [It must be a Kaumo.]
For those who aren't deterred by the time investment it takes to learn this game it is worthwhile and has more to come.
You can check out the developer's plans over on the website under the Development tab.
Protips for those who intend to buy it/already have:
(I'll update this as I think of more.)
! Use the mouse wheel to zoom in/out. This is very useful for hunting.
! The help menu is your friend. Even for seasoned veterans.
! Dogs are man's best friends for a reason. They make hunting much easier.
! Humans used to use a method called "Persistence Hunting" to hunt down big game. The short of it is you use your incredible endurance to run an animal down and track it until it collapses from exhaustion then shower it with arrows or beat it to death in its sleep. How metal is that?
! Try to spawn close to the Driikiläiset people (Cyan on the map, toggle culture colors on) so that you can trade with their massive amounts of shops if you find a village. You'll do quite well for yourself by peddling your crafts to them for various supplies.
! Trap fences can be difficult to get the hang of, but making a house relatively near one can help guarantee your cellar stays stocked throughout the winter.
! When starving and tracking down an animal have ranged weaponry.
You miss 100% of the shots you don't take -Lebron James on hunting, maybe.
!!! Don't give up. Every death is a chance to learn or try something different although it is frustrating to lose your progress. If you really don't want to lose out on it (and this is often frowned upon, but your own choice) then you pull up task manager (Control + Alt + Delete) and end the URW.exe process before going through the menu that deletes your character/progress. Everything that happened up to your death will be the same when you reload the game. You lose out on the experience, but it is your purchase and decision.
