UnReal World (UrW) is quite simply the richest rogue-like survival in existence, unique in its depth and nuance. Create a character and determine your path to thriving (or dying) in dark ages Finland. Become a settled trapper, an itinerant fisher, a barbaric warmonger, a hunter, a farmer, a trader... many potential paths lie before you, and you may well find yourself taking all of them over the course of a character's life.
Foremost, UrW is both brutal and beautiful, crafting a deep narrative through your struggle to survive in a harsh world, where the environment itself can be as deadly as those that dwell in it. I could tell you a hundred stories from my times playing, of cunning victories, cozy campfires, and unexpected demises, but you'd be far better served spending that time creating your own.
In Brief:
Generate a unique world and roll a character to embark in it. You may also select a starting scenario (take the runaway slave in winter for hardcore mode or one of the training tutorials for a little early boost). From there, you must seek out a source of food, drink, and shelter. How you do so is truly in your hands. Craft items to aid in your endeavor. Collect berries and cook wonderful meals. Tire of lovely vegetarian fare. Set a fence trap and slaughter some wild beasts. Trade hides with foreign merchants for some coveted metal arms. Capture and tame a wild bear, then hire some fellow adventurers and raid a Njeperz camp. Cut their clothes into bandages and roast their bodies over open flames. And most important, establish a base camp to survive the coming cold, for WINTER _IS_ COMING.
If you die, it is permanent, which makes every encounter tense and rewarding. I really can't say enough how amazing this game is.
Finally, the developer Sami Maaranen is incredible in his dedication to his game and its playerbase. He is always responsive and friendly, and has been continually working on improving the UrW experience for over two decades. If there's anyone in the indie industry that deserves your money, it's him. I first bought UrW after saving for weeks at my minimum wage job in high school over a decade ago. What I got was worth ten times that.
BUY THIS GAME! DON'T WAIT! And then play it, and share your stories wide and far.

Heaven's Hope has everything required for a good adventure game: nice animations & backgrounds, constant attempt at humour, slow-paced gameplay,  a good number of puzzles with solutions which make no sense and lots of guesswork & trial & error.
The experience of Heaven's Hope starts out very promising, art style and the uncommon plot immediately catches your attention. You visit new places, meet new people and collect everything you can. Sooner or later you reach a point where you end up with a lot of items and no idea what you're missing. There is a hint system in the game but in my gameplay the advice given was rarely relevant to what I needed to move forward. So you start revisiting everywhere and everyone and you realize that the game relies upon trigger events as the solution of story progression problem, something I didn't particularly enjoy. Fast travelling using the map eases this pain which negatively impacts your overall experience throughout the game and searching for the next interaction can be boring.
In every adventure game, there is this specific point where you start to lose interest in the middle of the story. After that, Heaven's Hope manages to pick up speed and wraps up the storyline without dragging it too much in about 7 hours in total. I recommend Heaven's Hope to every adventure gamer, it's better than most of the recent point & click alternatives and a better than average game in general. Also, it was a nice change to play a game with a religious theme which doesn't constantly try to lecture the player on how ridiculous and horrible religion is. I hope the developers build up on this and we'll see more from them in the future.

Heaven’s Hope is an adventure, point & click that follows the story of a fallen angel by the name of Talorel, who is looking for his way back to Heaven. When I saw this game I was intrigued by the hand painted scenes and was reminded of some of my favourite adventure games, such as Simon The Sorcerer and my absolute favourite game The Longest Journey. With this nostalgia in mind I really wanted to try this game out and unfortunately it didn’t live up to my expectations.
The highest point of this game is its graphics, it is beautifully presented, the visuals are top quality. With most adventure point and click games, it has the perspective of 2.5D, the illusion of 3D with 2D graphics. They have pulled this off really well with the larger foreground, but without so much detail that you are inclined to look at that instead of what is happening in the middle ground. Alongside this the animations of people talking, although they are repetitive they fit with the style and some are quite humorous. However on the flip side when things take a darker turn it reminded me a lot of The Cat lady, with the warped and distorted animations.
The beautiful graphics however were let down by the story itself, when I started the game it was a really interesting concept and some bemusing things happened to keep me intrigued. However after about 3 hours of game play the story became stale, it felt like it wasn’t trying very hard to keep my interest and I was quickly getting bored. Though the puzzles were of average difficulty (some being quite easy to figure out, whilst others took a while longer) some were illogical, I couldn’t get the answer because the answer just didn’t make sense to me. This often resulted in trying to combine everything I had in my inventory with each other till I got something and even then I was confused with how the game came to that conclusion.
After hitting the 5 hour mark, I thought I had been playing much longer and it was at this point that I couldn’t actually recall hearing any music in the game. I played for a while longer and there was indeed music but that meant the music was easily forgettable. This in my opinion is a problem when you create an adventure game, music is everything as it sets the mood and the most magical moments I’ve had in adventure games, have had extremely touching music along side the events that were unfolding.

I like story based games, and well, I am not actually very fond of visual novels, so this review might sound unsatisfactory for most people, but this shows how much this game moved me, so here I am.
One of the features I really liked about Analogue: A Hate Story is its innovative story-telling system. Reading through the logs while your AI side kick gives you information about the people who wrote those logs and trying to uncover the mystery which led the space ship mugunghwa to its current state, this game makes you question what is right and what is wrong. Make you wonder if there is really something called "right", while you read through all the text it gives you. Reading happy memories, tragic events, scandalous diaries just makes it all the more interesting. It is as if such a community existed there and you really are reading memories of their daily life.
Another different point of this game, for me at least (I don't know if there are other VNs featuring this kindof stuff since I didn't play so many Vns), that it introduces you a different viewpoint about computers and AIs. To make this review spoiler free, I won't go into detail, but you interact with AIs as if they are humans, and deal with their personalities.
Of course there were things I didn't like about the game. The most obvious one was the lack of things you could do with the console. I think if we had other events other than a certain one to really rely on the console. Again, for the sole purpose of not giving spoilers I won't go into detail, but I can say this, it is as if the whole console is just there so you can use it when it is necessary, and further playing with it won't be very useful. Especially given that it can cause bugs in the game.
Overall, I liked the game as it is, but I could have liked it more, what's more, the game has a sequel, which I am currently playing, and it just add to the spice of the story. I recommend this game to everyone who wants read a good story with good twists and characters, to people wants to have good visual novel experience with a different way of story telling, and to everyone who wants to have a change of pace and try something new by giving a go for visual novels.

I've seen alot of criticism regarding the graphics too,and I'm stunned. It looks absolutely gorgeous on ultra,particualrly the lighting. The sound FX are awesome too,love the gunfire and explosions when cranked up on the sound system. It runs perfectly,100+fps consistently on my 970. My favourite too,NO stuttering.
It's linear,but nowhere near as bad as most games. Most area's are fairly large and allow roaming/different places to attack enemies from,which makes it feel less confined. I also enjoyed the amount of stuff you could blow up,and strategically placed enviroment objects you could take out to perform an action (ie. shoot a crane wire to drop log's on enemies)
Now for the negatives:
. The story is bland,don't pick this up If you're hoping for an engaging story
. It is short,even with the bonus Saint-Nazaire mission (which was over in about 10 minutes) but all in all,was worth my time
. The AI,at least in casual mode,are absolutely terrible for the most part haha. Exposing themselves far too easily/predictable bobbing,running all over the place with no real aim. It didn't take me long to figure this out,so I changed my gamestyle to all out attack and just ran through them,and thats when the game became really fun
. You can't manually turn off the XBox 360 controller in-game without removing it from your PC,which is a slight niggle. Prompts and controls are displayed as controller buttons,and I did find towards the end it would randomly swap between controller and KBM.

I feel like it could've been alot of fun,as the game mechanics and gunplay (particularly sniping) are what made the SP and probably would've translated well. The other problem with this is there are MP achievements,so you'll never be able to 100% this game if that's your thing

Sometimes you just need a MEH button.  Get it on sale, but only if you have the patience to deal with the buggy, incomplete gameplay.
Man, what a slog to manage to finish the SP campaign on this.  Light sources started glitching out after a crash in one of the last couple of levels, that only went away by changing some of the advanced graphics settings.
An infuriating bug is one where you would set an explosive charge and then would be stuck there, unable to move until it exploded.  Not bad if some or most of them weren't FREAKING MANDATORY.  There were also places where you hold F to climb up, and once in awhile, the prompt would not register unless you restarted at the last checkpoint.  On a single playthrough, I got stuck in holes in the terrain, no less than 5 times.  (Stay off the ice inside the water plant...i'm jus' sayin')
The stealth aspects are terribly implemented.  There is a gauge that shows your discovery, but it has no directional marker that I can see, so you have no idea who can see you, and they can be really far away.  The binoculars are supposed to mark where the bad guys are, but half the time, they can be in plain view and the mark won't work.  Also, sometimes you can walk right up in front of the guy and he won't see you, and yet there is a guy half way across the map that sees you instantly, even though you are crouched behind something.  Not that staying stealthy matters, you can just go loud and wait for the dummies to come around the corner, one by one, just like lambs to the slaughter.
The story is a disjointed mess that has you jumping all over the place, in and out of the Polish front, to occupied France, and even deep into Germany.  The last mission, especially, feels like corners were cut at the last minute and shoved out the door with huge gaps in the story.
So, I am loathe to recommend this game, and yet I almost feel compelled to on account of it being one of the only WWII shooters to come out recently.   Seeing as how the next COD is likely going to be a ridiuclous, futuristic, bunch of space nonsense, this at least scratches that WWII shooter itch until they come to their senses.

I got invested in the data as, suddenly, there's now a point to digging through the copious amounts of data. After that, you're sunk. After digging through data for clues, I found myself reading through the not-so-important cultural stuff just to get a better feeling for the world I was exploring. Even the logs I skipped I went back and re-read. It's all done very cleverly and I definitely reccomend this to anyone seeking an intellectually stimulating fun time.

Imagine a world where Leonardo da Vinci's inventions took precidence over his artwork, ushering in an age of steampunk warfare. That's Magnifico in a nutshell. A niftly little strategy game where you conquer territory, use da Vinci's genius to make your troops more powerful, and then throw these troops at each other to grab more territory and earn victory points.
My primary gripe with the game is that there are no game modes. Every game end when 30, 40, or 50 points are earned through strength and number of castles, empire size, times you were the top bidder on his projects (the Magnifico) and the number of his projects you were able to purchace (double for Works of Art, a nice addition). You can't toggle the options, you can't go for a domination victory, or an economic voctiry, or a culture victory. It's all Victory Points, all the time.
Fortunately the game board is randomized each time, making the game very replayable. I'd say it's best as one of those games you boot up when you need to kill some time while your laundry is running. Short, easy to dive in to, and it's just a fun concept in general.

I love this game.
It's purest expression of 'Risk for computers' in the Total War series. In later games, the strategy map is cluttered with elements that defeat true turn-based play. This one is delightfully abstracted. No walking avatars, no silly animations, no ships, just chesspieces. You see the results of your decisions immediately. It's compelling enough that I play most campaigns without ever leading a battalion, flying through 150 turns in less than an hour.
The only limiting factor on replayability is the AI. Oh, for this game to have better AI. It's weak enough that I tend to start in 1580 so they've got enough pre-existing infrastructure to have a chance.
Here's how I've won:
* Takeda. Use my wildly overpowered starting armies to destroy the home base of every other faction. The AI all but gives up. I settle anywhere and start taking over provinces. The AI fields peasants to counter my horses. /game
* Shimazu. Isolated and alone, I build a bunch of ports, trade, and overwhelm the map with my cut-rate No-Dachi. Never bother with another unit. No one has a chance. I've won in 11 years with this faction.
* Imagawa. Train a Geisha within four years. Kill everyone with a star, have half the map suddenly become mine, vanquish rebels and ronin at my leisure.
* Mori. Infuriate everyone off by converting to Christianity, build a million ports, then invade with heavy cavalry backed by Jesus.
And on and on. Oda's the closest thing to a challenge, but even then, if you're really backed into a corner, you can just send an emissary to a port followed by a giant army to flank that opponent.
Still. I want to be an emperor, not a general, and that's what this game is best for. There's an up-and-coming title called "Oriental Empires" that looks to be the most compelling modern alternative.

This manages to be one of the more humerous titles in Telltale's catalog while still keeping ahold of their trademark storytelling. Tales from the Borderlands is a legitimite dive into the Borderlands universe where the story expands on characters and lore in large ways. Some events and aspects would definitely effect and strech forward into the Borderlands main series when it moves forward.
The story begins sometime after the events of Borderlands 2. Of course, knowing how the events played out would make the experience richer, enjoyment will not be restricted if you happened to never finish the game. It doesn't assume you know the events and if you do it gives you plenty of options to address them.
Despite the fact that Borderlands is a first person shooter game, Tales from the Borderlands is very much a Telltale game. Dialogue, quick time events, and point and click exploration of areas make up the bulk of gameplay but that doesn't mean the gameplay is always "Slow" quick dialogue decisions and life or death scenarios can quickly get the blood pumping as quickly as running through an area blowing things up, in the main series, can.
The characters are charming scoundrels all with something to love and dislike about them. With Borderlands' trademark humor and telltale's practiced drama the episodes can have you laughing until you snort or feeling on the verge of tears.
Overall I had an amazing experience and look forward to my next play through.

(Please ignore the small amount of play-time I have. I've had this game for around a decade, and the developer has kindly supplied me with a key for the Steam version.)
See the bottom of the review for TL;DR.
I rarely write positive reviews, but to me, the devotion that Sami shows to his supporters and fans is nothing short of remarkable. He went through the trouble of walking me through the steps of getting my key re-sent and updated despite me having very little of the original information I had when originally purchasing the game, and also has made a point of giving Steam keys to those who own lifetime registration keys.
Though, this is a review about URW, not about the developer.
URW takes a somewhat different approach to things than a lot of roguelikes, especially the ones usually seen on Steam. Rather than abstracting concepts like HP, satiation, exhaustion, deities, combat, and so on, URW tries as well as it is able to approach things more realistically. Fans of Dwarf Fortress Adventurer Mode shouldn't be too out of their element here.
Rather than being about killing dragons and getting amulets, URW is more generally about surviving in the wilderness. Trying to, anyway. Combat poses a very real threat. One missed blow could get you a concussion, or swept off of your feet and getting a spear through your chest, or teeth at your throat. This is made all the more painful, because your characters and the worlds they live in are indeed very permanent. You might build a house and make a type of farm, trading regularly with a nearby village. Make a smokehouse to cure your meats, make a sauna, get drunk, do what people from Finland do.
But the combat itself isn't the only problem. You also have to worry about things like your wounds getting infected, illnesses, starvation, dehydration, hypothermia, sleep deprivation. Of course, when you're injured, it becomes even harder to care for yourself... but that might be skipping ahead a little too far. Depending on whatever choice of background and scenario you pick, your first priority might be making a temporary shelter out of sticks and leaves, fending off a wolf, or escaping from captivity.
After you make yourself marginally more comfortable, you need to start working on feeding yourself, and making (or trading for, or looting, or stealing) tools as a means to accomplish this. Whether that means hunting for food, fishing, foraging, robbing other people, stealing from them, or just plain killing them and eating them. (The gods won't mind. Really.) But while eating raw food might be okay sometimes, you should probably consider cooking it, making a dish of it, or maybe a bit later on, working on a means of preparing it for long-term storage, like digging a cold-storage cellar, or curing it with salt, or in a smokehouse.
Once you have a somewhat reliable means of feeding yourself and living comfortably in the trees, and have a nice axe, hopefully without too many people's blood on it, you could think about building a house for yourself! Or you could live like a nomad. Your choice, really. Either way, once you're on your feet, you can get niceties by trading things like cured furs and pelts to village traders and other wanderers possibly like yourself.
Although there are arbitrary goals that can reward you with things, ultimately they are optional and there is no endgame or final goal of URW besides what you dictate.
URW is definitely not for everyone, and I do recommend trying the free version first. Don't let my review make the game sound more hypeworthy than it is. See for yourself if you like it or not. Even if you think you like roguelikes, this one might not sit well with you.
tl;dr Mostly-realistic wilderness survival roguelike that eventually turns into a violent Harvest Moon with permadeath.
TRY THE FREE VERSION FIRST.

I've been playing UrW for about 8 years and I always go back to it. It's a survival game but not of the same ilk that we've been bombarded with lately; there are no zombies that come out at night, etc., but rather it's just you out in the woods. It's a sandbox in that you set your own goals, and the world is always different. One playthrough I was a fisherman trading with nearby villages (until I drowned), another I hunted with a javelin for hides and food (until I was killed by a bear) and another playthrough I found myself starving in the woods and turned to cannibalism (until I was killed by my would be victim).
It's permadeath, and you'll die often, but for me this game has been about the journey rather than the destination.It's been worked on since the 90s apparently, and received updates since I've owned it. It's also free on the UrW website, but I recommend that if you play it and enjoy it, and want to support fantastic, involved developers, then throw some cash their way.

City of Steam: Arkadia isn't something new, and could be declared as another World of Warcraft clone, but it has features that are truly unique from any other MMO game. Firstly, it has plenty of real-time events and each of them have tons and tons of rewarding items. The more you level up, the more you unlock events you can participate in. Secondly, you have bike which you can ride over landscapes to get to your objective faster. You can even upgrade your bike, which not only improves it's speed and other attributes, but it also changes it's design. You can upgrade your armor and weapons using metal and mods (mods also changes the design of a weapon). Even though the game supports micro-transactions, personally, it doesn't feel like a pay-to-win game. But the greatest feature of this game is it's file size, I have no idea I how they got it right, but all those 3D elements and everything with just a 50mb download, that is incredible. The game is no near perfect, especially when it comes to the PvP elements, because you might just face someone with 20 to 30 or more levels higher than you but other than that, the game is certainly enjoyable. With lot's of free rewards you can get daily and some very challeging quests and challenges, this game is definitely something to try out.

EVE is one of the best games I have ever played. It's very unique in today's world of AAA games that copy each other and today's world of MMOs that copy WoW. It also has spaceships, which is kind of a big point of the game and my favorite part. There is currently no other game like it and there won't be, for quite some time.
EVE is not for everyone though. Over the years, thousands have picked it up and dropped it shortly after. Many just can't get into it. You'll have to see for yourself.
Now start it, it's free to try after all! Get in your spaceship, enjoy the beautiful views and see if EVE is for you. You chose one of the 4 races (all are equally viable) and get your first spaceship. You will be able to fly frigates and other small ships, up to the cruiser class. That's enough variety to test the waters and see if EVE suits you, or scares you.
Pro tip: Don't get attached to your stuff. You will lose it in some way or another. Live, learn and keep going!

The long version:
I started playing EVE in 2003. Now, 13 years and 5888 in-game hours later, I can probably write a review about it. Let me tell you a bit about the world as it was 13 years ago: We had only few games; We had Half Life and some of its mods that are known as proper games today (CS, TF); We had Starcraft, Homeworld, Deus Ex and Diablo II.
What we didn't have back then was WoW (It surfaced only in 2004). Life was good.
Naturally EVE is not a WoW clone and it's, in fact, very different to WoW and its clones. I wouldn't even call it an MMORPG. EVE is a Massive Multiplayer Online Space Ship Simulator. You are not really role-playing a person there. You are flying ships and most of the time you will see yourself as the ship you are flying.
This is unfortunate as some people would like to be more in-character with the pilot. Doing that is still possible when you are in a station in your captain's quarters, but it is a very limited experience. Most of the time you will be looking at glorious spaceships. EVE does have one of the best character creators though!
Despite its age, EVE is beatiful! The graphics and the rendering engine got updated multiple times during its long existance.
EVE is in many ways unique and will still be for a long time. Even contenders like Star Citizen won't change that in the foreseeable future. Here is why:

This is the game that started the Total War series. As such it is a bit... quaint. The features recognized as belonging to the Total War franchise are rough and unfinished... or still gleams in the developer's eyes. But one can see the gem that will shine in years to come. It just needed a little polish.
I would suggest getting this title on sale, and you will have to contend with gameplay from the year 2000. Also, it seems the game adds a feature that allows you to launch some of your Total War titles... (Rome and Medieval II do not seem to be in the launch screen.)

This game starts of well.
- You have plenty of classes to pick from and all of them are to viable, though not equal if you care about topping the leaderboard.
- The level design and the themes are diversified, you end up playing and grinding one level mainly though in the end, as there is one level which is far more effective to grind than the others, which makes the diversity obsolete.
- You will die frequently, which is due to bad balancing on the highest difficulty. One shot and your artifacts are gone, which is a shame, as they are fun to collect and see in effect.
- You will get bored somewhat quickly, as this game is by nature very repetitive.
- Online and Multiplayer. You can not really join random online games with other players. Ths function is to this point somewhat botched by the dev.
- Online Multiplayer has currently no other purpose as a quicker grind. The Guild function is completely pointless as of now.
So... should you buy this game? I recommend no. Save your money for something else. Take your GF out for a Dinner or so instead. (and thank me later).
Cheers.

While the visuals may be decently good looking, the gameplay leaves much to be desired. This is an unnecessarily over-simplified 'real time strategy' game.
Pros:
- Decent visuals (although may stutter at higher qualities when panning over the entire map)
Cons:
- Control over units are 'simplified' to the point where it becomes more difficult to actually direct where you want the units. Your units can only go from platform to platform.
You cannot control which enemy units your units attack (makes tactical focus-fire impossible).
Sending units from one platform to the other is cumbersome, as you can only have 3 options: send all, send 50%, or send 25% of the units on the selected platform to another.
- Poor unit balancing: some unit types are broken, while others are utterly useless.
- Just not fun to play

Basically this is an app ported over to pc. So if you plan to play it for more than a few hours expect it to actually cost real money.
Aside from that the game itself is a basic level based dungeon crawler. Only a few abilities exist per class, so it makes to game feel monotinous the more you play. Also you have to grind for gear with specific synergies, which are never explained in game and you havae to look up. In addition the game also has enemies that scale to your level so if you ever want to go back and destroy a boss you had trouble with before, its probably still going to give you trouble which is frustrating because it make you feel as though you aren't progressing at all.
I can't recommend this game because of it's downfalls. But it is much more fun if you are playing it with a friend.

The tail is the section at the rear end of an animal's body; in general, the term refers to a distinct, flexible appendage to the torso. It is the part of the body that corresponds roughly to the sacrum and coccyx in mammals, reptiles, and birds. While tails are primarily a feature of vertebrates, some invertebrates including scorpions and springtails, as well as snails and slugs, have tail-like appendages that are sometimes referred to as tails. Tailed objects are sometimes referred to as "caudate" and the part of the body associated with or proximal to the tail are given the adjective "caudal".

I cannot recommend this game enough!
Though I've only got a short logged playtime on Steam, I've been playin this game for about three years now from its pre-Steam releases.
To put into perspective the ungodly amount of effort that has gone into this game, I'll piont out that it has been in development since 1992. I *think* that makes it the game with the longest development time - at least more so than either Dwarf Frotress or the Duke Nukem. 24 years of work, as of the time of this review in 2016.
So what can you do in this game? Good question. You might recall how Todd Howard likes to say of Bethesda's releases that you can 'climb any mountain' or 'do anything' - well, you couldn't. In UrW you can come a whole lot closer to doing anything, though!
Every aspect of life (bar taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥and ♥♥♥♥ing someone, which is probably for the best) is covered. A massive amount of attention to detail has been made, and there are absolutely shedloads of historically accurate items, foods and activites you can access. What's more, the game (despite being a roguelike and keyboard-based, which may initially pout a lot of people off) is very accessible due to its fantastic in-game wiki.
What I've always loved in particular is that you set your own goals, something that no other RPG I've ever seen has done so well:
* Want to hunt a bear? Sure, get tracking! But first you need to make sure you're well prepared. Should you take the spear, the bow or both? Is it worth buying a hunting dog to help you out? Maybe you'll need a companion from a local village to cover your back? How much food will you need for the journey? There are so many things to consider.
* Exploration is crazy in this game! I mean, the gameworld is literally Finland. The very size. It's enormous.
* Perhaps it's time to settle down; building a settlement in UrW is incredibly rewarding, but by no means easy work! I've never found anything as satisfying in a game as having completed a gleaming wooden longhall, complete with mead benches and a roaring hearth. It took me several in-game months to achieve and arrived just in time for winter. Winter is brutal in this game!
* If you somehow feel your options aren't already wide enough, the game is incredibly easy to mod! Making and adding mods are both simple processes and widely expand the gameplay; what's more, since modding for the most aprt relies on adding .txt and .png files, there's practically a 0% chance that you could damage your game with mods (unlike certain other franchises), so go crazy!
A final note is that the UrW forums having been running for years and in that time the developers Sami and Erkka have been amazing; they have listened to every player suggestion, answered every question they could and are highly aware of what can make the game better. There never has been, and never will be, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ update. It's been getting better for 24 continuous years, and can only improve in the future! Make sure to visit the game's website and check the future development goals.
Thanks for reading this far!

Unreal world is roguelike survival simulation in a procedural world inspired by iron age Finland. Your primary goal in the game is to survive as long as you can. Sort of imagine if Don't Starve had a love child with Robinson's Requiem.
It uses a skill based system, with improvement by use. Equipment is varied by both type and quality. Armor and clothing is by location with overlap across more than a dozen body locations. The seasons are fully realized with weather, effects on plants and wildlife and hazards such as heat exhaustion or frostbite. The health system is detailed; tracking individual injuries, pain and infection all with realistic treatment options. Wounds take time to heal and affect your fuctioning.
It includes multiple survival strategies to utilize, each modeled to reflect the actual nature of that activity. Hunting, for instance, involves lots of tracking followed by frantic quick shots and pursuit of prey. It's easy to lose your quarry but a successful kill will keep you fed for a long while. Trapping involves a lot of work up front but gives sporadic gains. Farming is a nearly guaranteed result assuming you can live until harvest.
You can hunt, fish, farm, trap, raid or trade with villages, raft down rivers or across lakes, capture or buy and then raise animals, build shelters and cabins, fence in areas, gather seasonal plants mushrooms and medicinal herbs, fight with a variety of weapons, craft or trade for and wear a variety of tools clothing and armor.
The game is mod friendly. I had the good fortune to be one of the first modders (I added ironworking and clothmaking). Want to change your starting skills? You can mod it. You can alter the item recipes or even add ones the developer didn't include. Heck, you can even add in new plants and mushrooms!

What would you do if you were to wake up tomorrow, having been thrust into a completely foreign society? Being greeted by your "new family" who tell you what to say, what to think and even how to feel in order to not violate their social norms? Being told that your identity, the place you carved out for yourself in the world, is long forgotten, but that they already have a new role good and ready for you? That your dreams no longer matter?
This fate, among many others, is one of the gears in the
that would end up removing all traces of life from humanity's great hope, the huge pioneer starship
, in
.
In this unconventional sci-fi/mystery visual novel,
hired to find out the truth about what happened to the
and how it got lost on its mission to settle foreign planets. Arriving at the wreckage and linking up to the ship's computer, you are greeted by the archival A.I., who offers to help you sort through the letters, reports, and diary entries of the people who lived on board before a mysterious catastrophe killed everyone. You quickly learn that very little is as it seems, and there are
wrapped up in the situation that actual honesty is hard to come by.
The presentation in
sets up a computer-y atmosphere with abstract backgrounds and actual in-story explanations for things like the multiple choice "dialogue wheels". The effort put into the art is largely concentrated into the two highly detailed on-screen characters, who delight with a plethora of poses and facial expressions to convey their emotions. The soundtrack, especially the

, features recognizable melodies (sometimes in several variations) realized in a consistent style that works extremely well with the atmosphere constructed by the rest of the story.
For most visual novels, the user interface tends to be an afterthought, and only rarely is it a point of contention in a review.
, however, eschews the medium's tradition of a branching linear narrative and forges its own path in regards to navigation inside the story. In essence, every piece of text that you can find is one of the "files" of the ship's archive that you can view in any order, and you can also
or
at any point. This provides the player (a term that I use deliberately, because for Analogue, being a mere "reader" really isn't enough) with a high amount of agency that few visual novels choose to provide. It also creates a proportionally high number of opportunities to fail, for example if the player is not quick on their feet when it comes to using the computer terminal as the situation requires.
This sets up an interesting contrast with the main character's agency in the plot. After all, many years have passed since the events you read about and there is no way to influence the outcome or to save anyone. The only thing you can do is to find out the truth. There is a present-day plot involving the main character and the two artificial intelligences that still reside on the ship's computer, but the focus is on the mercilessly unchangeable past.
The people on the
lived in a surprisingly traditionalist society with strong codified gender goles and rampant classism. The members of the noble families all struggled for power, but no one seemed to heed the big picture or pay any mind to the ship's course. It was a troublesome situation in which a little girl from hundreds of years ago was awakened from cryostasis. Her family hoped that the
might bring them salvation, but what could she do to find her way in a society that was so radically different from the one she knew? You notice early on that she seems to be somewhat of a focal point for the events on board following her reawakening, but how does she factor into the eventual genocide? What caused the ship's undoing? And why do the two A.I.s despise each other so much?
is, at its core, a mystery story. While it is still a visual novel and you can gloss over most of it without really internalizing it and still get to the end, it is a more rewarding experience to actually untangle the relationships of the characters and understand how their motivations propel them to do what they do. There aren't really any mechanics in place to support this endeavour, other than the family trees that the A.I.s helpfully provide you with. I found that my enjoyment of the story increased significantly as soon as I started taking my own notes with pen and paper. I would encourage you to do the same, because otherwise it is very easy to lose your perspective as you wade through the countless documents, each colored by its author's perceptions.
Bit by bit you wrestle the truth from the ship's archives, and slowly you piece together the puzzle until you are able to see the full picture in all its horror. All aspects of it, from the
through the
to the
themes of the story, paint a drab picture of loneliness and despair. It poses the uncomfortable question of whether the ship's population as a whole might have been beyond salvation for who knows how long, doomed many years before the finale of the story; whether the event that put an end to all biological life on board was merely the logical conclusion, much like you would turn out the lights when you leave an empty room. It's hauntingly honest in its depiction of the darkest depths of the human soul, and after completing the story for the first time, it left me with a strong feeling of unease about what any one of us might be capable of, given the right circumstances.
It does also have its lighthearted moments, and even though visual novel connoisseurs will find many tropes and clichés conspicuously absent,
coquets with the expectations carried over from its genre siblings in certain moments, such as when one of the A.I.s
. It's no stranger to fun and there is plenty of clever humor to be found in the data logs and the A.I. banter.
The overall execution in this VN is so congruent and polished that any perceived shortcomings almost have to be rooted in personal taste. Some people might not care for the minimalist presentation, others might have preferred a more linear way of storytelling, yet others may have their reasons for not wanting to read a story where gender inequality is a prominent theme. But judged on its own merits, I can find nothing but praise for
within me. It's unique and interesting, and if you think that a mystery visual novel with deeper than average gameplay mechanics might intrigue you, I can recommend it without reservation.

Heaven’s Hope is a mediocre game at best.  It really doesn’t have a ton to offer veteran players, and the challenge is almost non-existent.  Worst of all, the game feels like one of those Christian pamphlets you get on your car window. I have always been a big fan of open world games, as well as games that include random generation. Unreal World is both of these, along with many other themes that are so incredibly rare to find bundled into a single game. I know anything I say in this review will not come close to doing the game justice, but I hope I can sway any readers into trying this wonderful gem if they are a fan of this kind of game.
Unreal World is based on Finland during the late iron age, roughly 800 - 1200 AD. While there a few fantasy themes in Unreal World, I consider this game to be pretty realistic. The fantasy themes I mentioned are mostly your character's religous beliefs, which are modeled after Finnish beliefs during the time period. If you have to swim across a river for example, it is a good idea to perform a ritual to "banish the evil water guardian" so that you will be less likely to drown in the process.
The game is a huge world to explore, randomly generated for every character you make. When you create your character, after selecting what tribe you are from, picking a character portrait, and other things, you will be able to pick a starting scenario if you wish. The scenario doesn't affect the gameplay, only the circumstances you begin the game with. Will you be an aspiring farmer, starting the game with a shovel and some seeds to start your very own farm? Or perhaps you have come across an abandoned campsite, with its creator nowhere to be found? There are many ways to start your game, and as many ways to play the game as you can imagine.
There are no restrictions of what you can and can not do. Will you build a cabin far off into the woods, trapping animals and selling their fur to a nearby village? Or maybe you prefer the life of a hermit, living off the land, avoiding human contact completely.
I can ramble all day about this game, but like I said, anything I say in this review is not going to even come close to how great this game is. If you are a fan of wilderness survival games, this game is for you. Some people may be turned away because of the old school graphics, but I can tell you without any doubt in my mind that this game more than makes up for that with the incredible amount of realism it contains, along with a refreshing break from the modern world to a time so long ago, it seems totally unreal.

It seems (from other reviews - either "recommended" or "not-recommended") that players really don't get the concept of the game. Let me get this clear.
If you happen to know the game called "State of war" you just know how "Oil rush" would be played. Sort of...
You don't build anything, you capture the pre-set buildings on the map. Enemy does the same. Buldings can be recaptured infinitely.
Every building (factory) you have under control produces specific unit (for that factory) once at the given time (ie. 1 scout unit every 10 seconds). More factories of the same type = higher maximum limit of specific unit + making of the unit on more places -> faster.
Factories can be defended by turrets.
Turrets are made from oil.
You get oil from oil wells which you have to capture just like factory. Oil well can be recaptured too and cannot be defended by turrets.
You can't control every single unit. You can control only groups of units - be it the same type of unit or multiple unit types. Group like this can be sent ONLY to platform (factory, oil well, ...) of yours/of your enemy/neutral one. You cannot move units around the map the way you are used to from "normal" RTS.
If sent on your platform: Units circle around and defend the platform. You prepare attack/invasion this way -> get more units on one place before launching attack.
If sent on enemy platform: Units try to kill enemy (units and turrets) and then start to recapture platform.
If sent on neutral: just like enemy (neutral units may be present that defend the platform)
There are some upgrades and special abilities and so on...
This is not ordinary RTS and many "players" don't get it. This game really reminds me of State od war which is probably totally forgotten these days. But it was just like this - something new.
I still have to go through the whole game and try multiplayer (and get PWNED), but I would recommend this game. You have to be prepared for it though. It is fast-paced, challenging, doesn't give you any rest when you play it.
And just like with other reviews from me - guess what? :-) It runs on Linux without any single problem.

Although it's not the intense, action-packed Dogfighting most people expect from a game with spaceships, the free-for-all open universe driven purely by players is more than enough to give you the same intense, action-packed feel.
While most MMO worlds are heavily influenced by the developers and contain strict rules regarding player interaction; EVE does none of this. The world and its stories are written by players in the same way history in the real world plays out. The developers simply build a stage and allow players to do absolutely anything they want on it. Even if that comes at the expense of other players; scamming, griefing, sabotage, stealing, killing and more.
The game may hold your hand for the first hour or so of tutorial content if you choose to follow it, but after that it throws you in to an open world with thousands of other players and a few basic things to get you started. There are, however, plenty of players and groups willing to help out new-comers and there are an abundance of tutorials and guides available for every aspect of the game.
One piece of advice is:
Don't expect power, influence and the ability to create these amazing stories you see online just by yourself. The only way to make an impact is with other people. And even then, you have to work for it. Playing solo can be fun for a short while, but you will be merely
the tip of the iceburg. Much like real life. Sure, you can live independently, but working together and interacting with other people will always be more fun and rewarding.
And ignore the negative reviews regarding the free-to-play model being too restricted. You can critique free games, but you can't complain and leave bad reviews when you don't get as much as you want.

Summary: Beautiful, but you'll need a friend to introduce you to it.
Unfortunately, the tutorials are awful. Early on, you'll be spammed with information you don't need, changing topic repeatedly as it fires pop-ups at you that have little relevance to your current situation.
Despite the pop-up barrage, the game still fails to provide the information you need. A good example is being advised that your health carries through fights and can only be restored using items bought at the shop... just after you leave town for the first time.
The in-game move list is also woefully incomplete and there is no in-game tutorial of any kind to help you learn the mechanics let alone the movesets.
With patience and research you can likely overcome these issues (there is a practice mode and you will slowly learn on the fly)  but if you aren't hooked on the setting your time is likely better spent elsewhere.

-Those who haven't gotten into Total War yet, and want a basic experience. You can see how later Total War titles were influenced by this game, and the basics from here will get you far in the other titles.
Potential purchasers should also be warned about compatability issues. While Shogun has been updated to work on modern operating systems, some users still experience difficulties. If you are interested in the game, I would still recommend getting it, but be aware of the possibility of spending a few minutes getting it to function. I purchased this game years ago before it was on Steam, but I recently saw that it's now on Steam so I had to support it with another purchase.
The true genius of this game isn't so much in the gameplay as much as it is how perfectly the game captures that whimsical childhood feeling of going on an adventure in the snow. Exploring, sledding, building snow castles, drinking hot chocolate, rolling around in the snow until it starts to get dark and your mom calls you from the porch that it's time to come inside for the night. The whole thing is done in beautiful hand-drawn art, and the soundtrack is pure magic.
In gameplay terms, it's mainly a fairly casual platformer. There is no fear of death or failure at all, which is what makes it casual. Instead it's mostly about collecting and exploring. Very early you discover some winter elves who grant you the power to glide through the air a bit after a jump. At that point you can begin collecting snowflakes. Every snowflake you collect is sort of like +1 exp and permanently adds a very tiny fraction of extra power to your glide, so your ability to magically soar through the air will get better and better as you collect.
The game has a night/day cycle and you only have until the end of the day to explore before your mom calls you back inside for the evening. So another aspect of the gameplay is creating a path for your sled as you explore. That way, at the start of each new day, you can quickly sled to your last destination without having to take a lot of time to get there.
It's a very relaxing and adorable little game, and in my opinion an example of a game that knew exactly what feeling/atmosphere it wanted to capture and then just nailed it.
Recommended especially if you'd like to play something festive around the christmas season. =]
(Note that the game is small and initially only runs in windowed mode. There is no in-game option for playing in full screen, but you should be able to do it by pressing F11.)

Have you ever played a Visual Novel?
I hesitate every time I describe Visual Novels (VNs) because I have a hard time choosing between 'read' and 'play'.
VNs are ostensibly games but range from having few gameplay elements to no gameplay elements.  It is very common for the bulk of gameplay in a VN to be clicking to advance text with intermittent choices.  There are usually static backgrounds and various illustrations of characters in different poses.  That is generally all there is to it.  So hopefully you like reading.
So, Analogue: A Hate Story.  This is a game set in the far future.  You navigate the logs of a derelict spacecraft with the help of an AI personality to discover what happened to the ship.  As you read logs, new logs are unlocked that show you more of the society onboard the ship.  That is pretty much all I'm willing to say because this game is pretty much exclusively story.
Remember this is a VN, and I think this is a good introduction to the genre.  It is true to the genre as it is a lot of reading.  There is a UI to it though, and the way you navigate the game actually feels more like a game than VNs typically do.  It is also short; I'd say 3-6 hours to finish all the routes.  Don't quote me on that though.
All in all, should you play it?  Yes with caveats.
As long as you:
like reading
like or are ambivalent toward the anime art style
Also consider:
Game length.  It is short, and I think that is an advantage because many do not have the time or patience for a 50-80 hour VN.
Price.  Goes hand in hand with length.  I liked it quite a bit, but full price would be a bit hard to swallow especially if you're new to VNs.
Wait for a sale, but get it.  I think you should give VNs a chance.

First time players: be aware. This games starts out difficult because you do not have the ability to fly from the beginning. Make it to the elf camp and talk to the elves in order to have the magic snowflakes appear in the game. Also!  A quick note about the controls:
Spacebar = jump
Spacebar x2 = double jump
press and hold Spacebar = fly
Don't know why but this threw me off for awhile. Once I figured out that I was only double jumping in the places where I needed to be able to fly,  the joy of the game returned and I was no longer stuck,  So here's hoping that other players can  learn from my mistake and skip the easily avoided frustration.

A very clever, if short, Visual Novel that tells a tale of a horrible tragedy, the man sent to investigate it, and the two AIs that help him uncover the truth.
The player is sent to investigate a colony ship that has been out of communication for a very long time.  You are told to figure out what happened, copy the files, and get out, and that the ships AI, *Mute, would assist you.  But when you arrive *Mute is disabled--and instead, you run across an AI called *Hyun-ae.  Who is *Hyuan-ae?   What happened to the colony ship and the passangers?  What about *Mute?  To find out the answers to these questions, you must read through the various ship log files (letters, diaries, etc.)--and chat with the AIs.
What you uncover is fascinating and disturbing.  If it were told in realtime, it would be a horror novel.  But by setting most of the action well in the past, it allows the player to discover a happy--or at least happy-ish--ending.
If you like murder mysteries or period dramas, or crazy little love stories, give this Visual Novel a read.

I voted yes, but that's at the 9.99 that I paid.  I could not recommend this at full price.  If you get it on sale and don’t mind linear missions like the original call of duty, then I think it is worth a play through (don’t even consider multiplayer, it’s dead). The graphics are pretty good, I like the slow-motion looking loading screen, which is good, because the game takes a long time to load.  Check points are poorly done, and some missions, you have to figure out what they want you to do or you will lose a few times.
Example, one mission, you are tasked with defending a point.  Germans will send waves of infantry, halftracks, and a couple of tanks.  You have limited ammo.  The first time I played, I used my rocket launcher and grenades freely and found that, even though I had killed all the Germans, and defeated all the waves, I could not win because I could not destroy the remaining half-track (even though I could walk around it freely) because I had run out of explosive ammo.
I did like the story line.  Being a part of the Polish resistance in Warsaw was quite effective at bringing the “War is Hell” feeling to the game.  When the Germans shoot civilians, you find you want to take them out with more emotions than most games of this genre.  The radio broadcasts “This is Warsaw calling all free nations” becomes almost haunting by games end.
Get it cheap, play on the hardest level (the rest are too easy), and a few entertaining hours are to be had.

I tried Day of Defeat: Source again recently and was expecting it to be dead. After all, the game is almost a decade old now. However, I was still able to find several populated servers at all hours of the day or night.  Old age hasn’t killed DOD:S.
If anything age has worked in DOD:S’s favor. For example, it attracts an older and more mature crowd. I haven’t had to put up with as much drama or slurs from annoying prepubescent teammates as I do in more modern multiplayer shooters.
Another example of age helping the DOD:S experience is how “old school” it feels. Despite the WW2 setting, DOD:S plays more like an arena shooter from the 1990s than today’s super serious military shooters. Forget aiming down iron sights. Secondary fire for most weapons throws solid punch instead. Expect to spend a lot of time zipping about, shooting dudes with crosshairs, punching them for good measure, and laughing at the exaggerated ragdoll physics.
Day of Defeat: Source is not a masterpiece but it’s worth a look if you have a hankering for a shooter that isn’t too serious.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse is pretty cool I guess.
Set after the events when Carrot fought some of the most powerful beings in the universe. Or during...Or before? Time travel is dumb. Anyway, something is going terribly wrong and many of these battles are ending in ways they shouldn't, and by that I mean the bad guys are winning. Vegetable's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ half-breed is some sort of time cop at this point and sees that he needs help from someone competent to stop the time lines from going all Back To the Future and he uses the seven dragon balls wish for a powerful warrior to help them beat up a hot demon lady and her husbando brought to life.
And they got me.
Ho boy.
So yeah, in the first time in Dragon Ball video game history, you get to make your own character! Or if you're super lame you can try and recreate a existing character from another franchise. You create your personal avatar and then go on an epic quest through time to set things right while making the main heroes look really bad in the process. Seriously, it looks really bad when big tough villains don't even touch you. It's probably Vegeta's fault, the jobber.
At the start of the game, you're given the choice of several races for your character, including: Human, Saiyan, Freiza guy, Namekian, and confusingly attractive chewing gum. But if you're anything like me  you made a human so you can punch Saiyan's in their stupid midget faces. I still gave him a helmet though because I worry about his safety. I hope he didn't get hit too hard.
The game is a brawler of sorts, you take a third person view and have a melee attack, a ranged attack, a grab, as well as a super and ultimate moves set to your triggers, or keyboard. Surprisingly, for how simple it is, Xenoverse's combat is fairly fast and exciting, giving you a feel of the high octane fighting from the TV series and manga. Though, depending on who you ask, for better or worse, the game somewhat lacks the crushing and overpowering strikes the series is known for. You can send someone back or knock them down sure, but you won't be punching people clean through mountains or power bombing them into the ground with the force of a few atomic bombs.
Though I guess that may be for the better. The combat is focused, sure, but it seems like the Xenoverse servers has problems keeping up with what's going on. Lag and stuttering is a constant, or at least it was for me and a few other people I know. Sometimes attacks didn't come out right or your moves don't synch up with what your opponent is doing. But this is pretty much absent in Xenoverse's PVE combat.
While competitive fighting is an option, you can also take on missions with your friends for experience and loot. Through the main game and some DLC, you can go on an abundant of missions with your buddies, and sometimes this is the only way to unlock certain moves and transformations like spiky hair, and spikier hair. Actually, I lied, your hair doesn't spike, it just changes colors. I'm sorry I did that to you.
Xenoverse is probably the best kind of fanservice, though, like comic book team ups or the imaginary fights after I eat those strange mushrooms I found out in the woods. Having player made characters in a universe like Dragon Ball team up or fight each other almost feels like its own series of sorts. I, myself like to look up names of characters I fought on the dragon ball fan wiki just to see if I beat up some important fan fiction character.
Xicor: Evil son of Goku? More like Xicor: son who just got all of his teeth knocked out of Goku. Super Saiyan 5 didn't do much for you, did it?
But should you play, Dragon Ball Xenoverse Raging Blast Ultimate Tenkaichi Budokai Butoden Hyper dimension...Uh... Final Bout? I think I got them all.
That depends, do you like Dragon Ball? If yes then you probably already played it. If no, then no, you stupid stinky idiot. Xenoverse is a fan service game, its for people who like the series and have either grown up with it or adopted it along the way. The combat can be iffy at times and I've knocked out Kirito from Sword Art more times than I liked to count
, but the story and team missions alone are enough to keep you invested for a few hours. That and it's always fun to see a human trained by Yamcha beat the snot out of a Super Saiyan with little effort. Take that you spiky haired hobbit.

This game was not what I thought it would be.  I thought it would be an innocent puzzler with pointy-clicky gameplay and no story to speak of.  What it IS is an RTS with heavy economic and social overtones and a slight learning curve.  It features simple, squad-based gameplay  where capturing targets from enemy squads is the primary objective.  Production facilities, which automatically turn out new units to whoever owns them, oil rigs, which produce precious oil (the currency of the world and also the resource used to build upgrades), and more leave a bit to be desired for complexity and customization, but it works relatively well for the style of game.
The controls are a bit stiff, and they don't offer key customization (though there are hot keys for several functions), so navigating menus and selecting skills is a bit tedious.  The camera does not have user-memory, and frequently resets itself to the default panoramic view, which is visually nice, but strategically useless.  Action-oriented gameplay is supplemented by optional POV cameras that allow you to really see what's going on, but there are several camera functions that the game boasts of that simply do not work at all.  Visually, it isn't stunning, but all things considered, in-game looks quite good (with the exception of the CGI cutscenes, which are stiff and awkward- the audio doesn't match the video, the facial animation is elementary, and the lighting is bad).
The story is simple and straightforward, with a few foreseeable twists and developments that, while largely unimaginative, are still disturbing and well done.  It follows the quest for oil at any cost, and things get pretty out of control.  The General is willing to sacrifice the lives of countless soldiers, betrays his word, and gives no quarter in the pursuit of the precious resource.  The voice acting is sub-par and the writing isn't phenomenal, but more than anything, it is disturbing to watch the events pan out in the name of petroleum.  It makes me think about the world we live in, and how much things need to change.

Updated review at the end of "Old review".
Old review----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
My opinion on action games is that they should be played on a controller. This game doesn't work with an Xbox One's controller. The problem is that the camera is unable to be bound to any joystick or other button, since the game doesn't allow it, hence making it impossible to play with an Xbox One controller with the camera rotating constantly around the character (being bound by default on to the LT and RT).
Sadly I wasn't able to play it, even though I was looking forward to it. Have opted to refund.
I don't recommend it for those who have an Xbox One controller.
Revised review---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I decided on a whim to purchase the game again (because SALES!) and give it another try, even going as far as being prepared to play it on keyboard and mouse. To my pleasant surprise, somehow now the same Xbox One controller worked reasonably well. This time it didn't uncontrollably circle around the character. Sure, the button layout is strange, but eh, at least it works.
As of editing this review, I have 46 hours (kindly recorded by Steam) in the game, completed the story mode and nearly completed the Dream Log.
Gameplay:
Similar to the other Warrior games, this is a hack'n'slash game where you control a character with special abilities, in this case characters from the One Piece Universe, fight your way through endless minions, mid-level bosses (whom also are big characters in the manga and have their special abilities), conquer territories or bases and have a final showdown with the final boss character (for story reasons).
Modes:
The story mode follows Luffy and his crew through all of their adventures since the beginning until the (not so last) ark, just before facing off against Doflamingo. Each battle depicts one of the major arcs in the manga, such as meeting up with Zoro or rescuing Nami from Arlong Park.
There is also the free mode. I haven't tried it, but as is with these types of games (warriors series) it has always been a free scenario selection game, where you can select a specific battle, but with the story allowing to choose freely, I don't get the point.
The Dream Log is some sort of random battles (could be for fans or simple madness). The layout is quite nice; it's like navigating through the Grand Line where you'll have to choose an island to go to, fight the battle there and then continue from that island forwards. These islands are interconnected between themselves, so you have to choose a certain path to get somewhere you want.
Sound:
The music is very upbeat, just like we would expect from a Warriors game. In some parts the soundtrack is from the anime, but I think the rest is original to the game. A very energetic, action'ish style of music, very fitting for the game.
Visuals:
The character models and the environments accurately depict their manga counterparts. It's very nice to see the characters fleshed out in 3D (especially the female characters ;P).
Verdict:
After being able to play the game properly with a controller (though still with weird layout) I am very satisfied with the game. It was nice to travel through the most memorable moments of the series. Especially nice were the ingame-rendered cutscenes. Absolutely beautiful. Though I did encounter a few bugs here and there where for example the camera wouldn't focus properly and would most of the time be out of focus during the cutscenes and so on.
All in all, if you are a fan of One Piece and like mashing buttons or just simply like to plow literally thousands of minions at a time, then yes, this is for you. Just bear in mind that the controller could not be working perfectly.

Marvin's Mittens is a short platformer that has you running around outside collecting snowflakes and looking for Marvin's lost mitten across snowy landscapes.

Snow everywhere, towering pine trees, luminous caves, mountain peaks, the occasional animal, and even elves!
I launched steam, opened up the game, put away my phone, put my earbuds in, and forgot about the rest of the world (if only for a couple hours).
If you like Calvin and Hobbes, think of all the magical adventures Calvin had out in the snow with his tiger friend and then put that into game form.
I don't have much else to say. I could never be cynical about something that works this well.
This game'll melt your heart with a cup of hot chocolate and then put it to bed. See you in the morning!

Analogue: A Hate Story is more of an interactive novel than a visual novel. The only graphics are the AI figures and the white backdrop. You can change Hyun-ae's outfit, but that's it.
Although I thoroughly enjoyed the game, it is not a game for everyone. There is a lot of text to read. You spend almost all of your time reading through the ship logs. There is no action and no excitement because that's not what this game is about. It tells a dark story through narrative, a very well-written one that is. I did not find every single log to be interesting to read, but that's to be expected since some characters outshine the others in depth and relatability.
A major weakness is its low replayability. It's just not the same the second time through when you already know what the revelations are. The first playthrough was magical, and it stirred the emotions. For the second and third playthroughs, however, you'll probably be wanting to click through everything as fast as you can so you can unlock the new endings. You might re-read two logs or so, but then you would pretty much be done with the game.

I've been playing this game for years, and I'm so glad it's finally on Steam.
(Back when I started, my main enemy was falling out of trees, and if you slept out in the open, you'd wake up to a lynx ripping your face off. I'm fairly sure that latter one can still happen. Don't mess with lynxes. Their silent meows are a premonition of terror and violence.)
I'm not very good at getting myself set up, so here's how I usually end up playing:
- Making a primitive bow and arrows, then hunting while I gradually starve to death.
- Fishing (maybe with a fishing pole, maybe by stabbing the water repeatedly with a stick)... while I gradually starve to death.
- Setting a bunch of traps in apparently unfavorable areas. Getting frostbite (or just really frustrated) as I try to check them over and over, even though they haven't brought in any game.
- Finally making enough headway to build a cabin. Playing an awkward, hilarious, terrifying game of cat and mouse with a lynx that wanders onto my property, until I can manage to get a fence and traps up.
My last game, I started out trying to hunt with a bow/arrow. I brought down a bunch of birds with it, but I was gradually starving. I found a grouse that had been partially eaten by a goshawk. Fine, I'm not picky. That's a pound of grouse meat. I ate it. I was tracking a herd of reindeer for days, and when I went up to the mountain to scout out where they'd gotten to, I saw that there were wolves chasing them. I weighed the options, decided I was starving and I'd try to avoid the wolves. Came within a screen of wolves twice, but managed to avoid them, and found a reindeer that the wolves had taken down and started eating. Fine. I'm not picky. I skinned it, butchered it, and brought the meat home.
Finally, my trap pits started bringing in big game. Too much big game, in fact -- something like 4-5 reindeer and stags within the period of a week or so. I lost one of the hides when it rotted while I was scrambling to butcher everything, tan the hides, reset the traps, and haul meat up to the closest village before it went bad.
So I got sloppy and left a bunch of meat next to one of the traps, where I'd butchered a reindeer but couldn't carry everything back. When I came back for the rest, a wolf was there, attracted by the meat. He lunged at me and took me down in two attacks.
Anyway, if you like roguelikes or sandbox games, especially wilderness survival, get this. I always come back to it, that's how good it is, and it's constantly being improved (dynamic weather, predator-prey interaction, and more realistic animal spawning are all very new, and they're amazing, and I'm sure we can expect more of the same quality changes in the future). It's got a heck of a learning curve, but it basically defined sandbox games for me, way back before Minecraft was even a thing.

One section in particular really stands out as a great meeting of mechanics and story. Worth playing as a curiosity, but be warned. It doesn't play nice.

Been playing URW for about 15 real life years. Or was it even more? Was the first game I ever bought. If you can get into it, it's a vast and unique world you never get tired of.  A massive archipelago. Go anywhere, survive adversity, hoard provisions and steal tools from villagers. Hunt reindeer and elk, tan their skins, smoke the meat, huddle by the campfire all night with your small dog hoping those howling wolves will not dare close in if you keep the fire bright...
Build your own wood house, start an animal pen, milk cows, learn how to hunt with self-made animal traps...
My most recent adventure involved hunting seals with bow and arrow, while paddling on a raft in the western seas.  Got so much blubber it will hopefully last the whole winter after being salted.  This world is beautiful and natural in its own way, like no other. There is no special focus on the player usually seen in most roam-anywhere games, no big milestones pre-placed for him. You're just in the wilderness, and you're on your own, tet-a-tet with the whole world. The world in URW does not care if the player lives or dies, but if he lives, there is an unspoken expectation by the unseen spirits of the land that you will show them proper ritual gratitude for this favour.
It is the most hardcore game:  complex keyboard-based controls, no hand holding. Also the gameplay is UNFORGIVINGLY realistic. If you've not been preparing well, the very first winter in URW will kill you. Your first couple characters, I'd be well impressed if they survive for more than a week in the wilderness.  "Ohh delicious-looking unknown mushrooms, let me nourish myself with those... welp, dead by morning after exruciating poisoning agony." Slowly you the player gather important Knowledge on what to do ("always boil unknown mushrooms first"), creating your own strategies and best practices. And your survival times increase in proportion, from being measured in hours, to days, to months, to years...
On that cheery note, this game is highly recommended to the dedicated and thoughtful players. Absoutely one of my favorite games of all time, and it constantly keeps getting better with each patch. Good luck understanding and loving the Unreal World!

I have been playing URW since 2001, version 2.60.  After 15 years it's awesome to finally see it come to the mainstream public attention, and I have nothing but praise for the game.
At its core, it's your basic roguelike game: perma-death, turn-based, keyboard-heavy and with 2d pixel tiles instead of fancy graphics. Actually, it started out way back (it's in development since 1992) as a fairly standard fantasy game, but then slowly transformed into a realistic life simulator in the setting of iron age Finland.
You will have to survive by crafting needed stuff, hunting/gathering/fishing/putting out traps and get food, wood and pelts to make items and/or to trade for things you can't craft like axes or pots, and get better armor and weapons to fight off wild beasts and nasty humans (they come in the form of either bloodthirsty Njerpez warriors that will only settle for your death, or simple robbers that will try to get your stuff either by talking or by bludgeoning you over the head). Also of course you'll get tired and need to sleep, eat, and drink.
The game has a day-night cycle, full-on weather and seasons system: in summer the temperatures are bearable even without being covered head to toe in furs, berries and plants to eat are readily available, there's plenty of game to hunt and life is generally easier (you will get mauled by a bear nonetheless, don't worry)
At the other end of the spectrum, winter is harsh: days are short and nights are long, it gets freezing cold and you WILL die from hypothermia so you have to build shelter, possibly an elaborate log cabin complete with fireplace, table and bed, make enough firewood to keep warm and get a decent source of food or a good plan for having enough in those long, boring months. Ice will cover the rivers and lakes so to fish you'll have to poke holes in it, and if you're not careful you can walk on thin ice that will break and drop you into freezing water. Also snow accumulates on the ground and unless you have skis, you won't be able to walk very long without getting incredibly tired so you better have everything you need not too far away. On the upside it also allows you to spot tracks much easier. Too bad there are few animals around in winter...
I could speak about the game all day but this would become too long, so I'll just say one last thing, and it's the thing that impressed me most:
This game is a labor of love. Over the many years I've been playing this, a LOT of things have changed, and always for the better. Just since last year or so, there's a totally new trading / reputation system with villages, most exploits have been squashed and replaced with sensible mechanics, you can command your pet dog and it's even more of a killing machine, new animal AI especially for predators that will actively hunt their prey (have sheeps in a pen? be careful of wolves!), addition of more birds and seals you can club, and the list goes on and on. It's a truly well supported game that is worth at least double what they're asking, so if you're interested in this kind of game and don't mind that it's keyboard-heavy and has 2d graphics, it is a MUST BUY.
This game made me so morally and emotionally conflicted! Which is what makes this game great.

UnReal World is one of the deepest survival simulators you'll ever come across.  I've been playing it now for around 6 years outside of Steam and it's one of those games you keep coming back to.  It's got a tremendous amount of complexity, which can be very daunting for new players.  Once you make it past the substantial learning curve, you'll find a deeply rewarding survival simulator with a unique setting: medieval Finland.
I would term this game a "rogue-like life simulator" if anything.  With the majority of the ongoing game development being focused on adding real-life depth, this means the graphical end of things is more along the lines of the traditional rogue-like games, being more minimalistic.  That also means there's a staggering amount of things you can do in the game.  First timers will more than likely be completely overwhelmed by the different abilities and skills available.  You may want to watch a video or two of someone playing the game to get an idea of things you can do and how to survive in general as you are likely to die rather quickly in the beginning of the most basic of things, like not finding water.
This game won't be for everyone.  The high amount of focus on real-life features means you'll be spending a lot of time doing basic survival things like gathering just enough food and water to live off of at the moment.  You also need to be concerned about the variety of your diet the same as in real life.  There's no true in game goal other than to survive as long as possible.  Again, these are things you should be able to tell pretty quickly if they're for you or not by finding a couple of videos of the game being played.
If you're into survival games and living off the land in the wilderness sounds like fun to you, this is the game to get.
