This game absolutely blew my mind. I was already a fan of both Telltale and Borderlands, so when I first heard about this game I was more than a little excited. I eagerly awaited for all episodes to be released, and then finished them rather rapidly in succession. What a ride!
This game offers a very similar way of play to the other Telltale series games such as The Walking Dead, however this particular game has a lot more mechanics and action sequences then we saw in the aformentioned title, and all of which are interesting and very well made. Decisions feel rewarding, a lot of cool and unexpected things happen, with the typical Borderlands humor being both prominent and, in some cases, matured.
We also get to learn more about some familiar characters from the Borderlands series, and the newly introduced characters are both fitting and strong on their own. The story is interesting and engaging, you always want to know what happens next, and I had much difficulty limiting myself to one episode at a time. I always wanted to jump straight into the next episode, but at the same time I wanted to savor the awesome experience I was having.
That being said, being a heavily story-driven and linear game, there is little replay value unless you want to really explore all dialogue and see what the many optional choices would have led to. How the end scenes play out is highly dependant on your choices along the way, but it takes a good ~10 hours or so to get there, so you might be better off looking the different variations up on youtube, due to the linearity. (After beating it yourself, of course!)
All in all, I highly recommend this game, well worth its money even for a single playthrough.

First time I heard about this game was when Mr. TotalBiscuit posted his "WTF Is..." video about
and thought it looked decent, but I said to myself that I'd NEVER buy it for full price. Years later, end of 2015, I bought it for ~€3 and I'm glad that I waited. Not saying that it's a bad game, but it has its flaws.
In both movies and games, you've seen and heard most of the stories from World War 2, right? Normandy, St. Petersburg, London, Paris, Berlin, Japan, Africa... you name it. But in this game, the developers chose a quite different route when it comes to the story.
You're playing as the american journalist Robert Hawkins, he's telling the story of his journey to Warsaw and how he came to help the people of the city in the uprising against the nazis. You get to help out the resistance fighters in the snowy mountains in Norway, you help a german SOE (Special Operations Executive) agent to free prisoners from a POW camp and you help a french man and his polish allies to escape death.
It is actually quite nice to be in other, mainly untouched, parts of the world in a WW2 game. Kudos!
It's nice to look at, after all, it is powered by the Cry Engine. But it is not very well optimised. I had to lower the settings to medium overall to even be near 60FPS at places, otherwise it would be somewhere between 20-40FPS - especially when a lot of things are exploding. Not really optimal.
Other than that, I didn't find that many things to complain about. One or two guns stuck through a wall, but that happens in almost every game, so I can't really complain about that. If anything I could complain about how grainy the cutscenes before and after missions were. They were really bad. It would be better if they would just create the cutscenes within the engine itself - like they do in the first "cutscene" in the extra mission - "Saint-Nazaire".
Nothing to really say about this. This is probably the worst part of the game, besides the multiplayer. The explosions doesn't sound good, the weapons sound decent, the voice acting is on par at best. But I did like the background music at places, so I guess it has that going for it.
So, the main meat of the game. What is a game without gameplay?
? I don't know. But this game is pretty fast paced, but you can choose to be stealthy if you'd like to. I tried it once or twice but it seems like the enemies will always find a way to see you.
Sometimes I would die for no explainable reason but I guess I was too aggressive or something like that. Shooting nazis are always just as fun, especially when the environments are so varied and the missions are rather short (there are 16 in total and I completed them all on medium in just above five hours - including the extra mission).
This game has gotten A LOT of bad reviews here on Steam, but I don't think it deserves it... not all the way at least. I mean, for the price I paid (~€3), it's not a terrible game. Sure, it's kind of short and the extra mission I got when buying the game didn't really deserve a special place in the main menu (mostly considering it was only ONE mission which took about 10 minutes to complete and didn't really bring anything new to the story of the main campaign). But at least it's FUN and that is the most important thing about a game - the ability to entertain the player. So I do recommend it, IF you're able to find it cheap.

Now for everyone else, Dead Island is a somewhat underrated little co-op, FPS/ARPG hybrid. Think melee-centric Borderlands with zombies and you get the idea. You'll be questing, looting and levelling one of four characters across three sprawling areas of tropical Banoi. Dead Island is a solid example of first person melee combat, it still holds up despite being superseded by Dying Light.
Whilst the focus of the game is on four player co-op, solo play is viable and equally enjoyable. The sun soaked beach resort and city streets become a lot more sinister on your own and the games atmosphere really shines.
You've probably heard some terrible things about it, but Dead Island is often criticised for what it isn't, rather than praised for what it is. If the Borderlands style of looting and questing appeals to you, you could do a lot worse for a lot more money.

I often feel like hipster about certain things in life. One such things are WW2 FPS games. While everyone yells and screams on the internet that we have enough of those, I've on the other hand been dreaming about HD remaster of MOH – Allied Assault on Frostbite engine or some new COD returning to Europe’s battlegrounds of 1940’s. Buying this game, after reading all the reviews , I thought that it shouldn’t be that bad, but it really is...
You are playing as Robert Hawkins, an american journalist, who covers different resistance's actions in Nazi occupied Europe. Story mainly takes place in Warsaw, during city’s uprising against German army, however trough some flashbacks game will take you to the various locations around Europe like France or Norway. So in the terms of different levels, game has some variety to offer in it's 7-9 hours campaign. You’ll be fighting in the streets of Warsaw, snowy mountains of Norway, french countryside and so on. Story isn’t anything original and breath taking, its quite boring and filled with cliches, but we don’t play these games for story, right ?
This tittle also has multiplayer with some modes like Death-match and Team Death-match in it, but it’s practically dead, I could find server to play maybe 3 times, and it didn’t last more than one round.
For me the game runs fine, I had almost constant 60 FPS and game crushed once trough my play trough. HOWEVER, this title is quite populated with bugs and glitches, nothing really game breaking, but it takes you out of experience quite often. They may vary from something like it’s sometimes hard to define what is true light source in the level, sound sometimes has this weird glitch when you can’t detect from which side its coming and if the source is in some place or out in the open, and the list just continuous.
Enemy Front runs on CRYENGINE, so it looks pretty good, but nothing amazing, something like 7/10, however the game is really bright and colorful, not brown and grey like most WW2 shooters out there, and it truly shows, I really enjoyed walking around some levels especially in the french country side. One thing I really liked was the music, and how it changes from whats going on in the game, also loading screens are pretty cool, but they are rendered in really low resolution, something like 360p as well as the cut-scenes and  another thing that ruins cut-scenes is lip-sinking, it’s mostly of, maybe its design for polish language or something, but it doesn’t work well with the English at all.
Last thing I didn’t cover is the game-play, and well it’s mixed bag, since the game runs on CRYENGINE, it barrows something from Crysis games, like focusing more on stealth, marking enemies with binoculars and so on, however stealth is a bit broken in this game, sometimes it works quite good and at the other times it’s just a mess, but since AI soldiers are quite stupid, you can give-up on stealth all-together and you’ll be just fine, only in this way, the game will become more boring. One thing I Liked about game, that it introduces some new weapons from polish army like “Lightning” – the polish sub-machine gun or WZ.28, and some other new weapons, which I didn’t see in WW2 games. The sniping mechanic in the game is just weird, it’s a “Sniper Elite V2” rip-off and just doesn’t fit in such game.
So to sum it up, game has some cool ideas and design choices, but execution at the times is just awful, game also has annoying bugs and glitches, boring story, half-broken game-play and almost none-existing multiplayer. I would only recommend this title for 5 euros or less, and if you are WW2 junkie like me, who needs some fresh stuff to kill Nazis with. For everyone else - just avoid this title.

At first I was led to believe this may be another minimalistic horror game of the Amnesia or even Dear Esther-esque variety, and I'll confess I was slightly disappointed when I was given a gun quite early in proceedings...leading to the realisation this was "just another" Half Life 2 mod.
But oh, what a mod! While it inevitably shares a degree of the look and locations of ANY first-person shooter you care to mention (sewers, a warehouse, etc), it maintains a consistently "watery" thematic throughout, and a firm emphasis on atmosphere and storytelling over, say, extreme difficulty and loads of different weapons and enemies and all that other (often extraneous) nonsense.
Look, it's short, it's focused, it's fairly linear, but above all, it's FRICKING FREE. And even if the subsequent Acts turn out NOT to be free, I'll happily part with a small amount of cash to see what happens next...especially in light of the enigmatic cliff-hanger of an ending we're given, and all the other unanswered questions we're left to ponder, such as: why are there so many WOMEN in the island's sinister military-style operation? And what's with all the "infected" dudes wearing Star Trek uniforms? Was the island host to a nerd convention just before the mysterious events occurred?!
Looking forward to some juicy answers to these questions and more in Act II..!

Imagine any grid turn-based strategy game, but forcefully made into an real time strategy game. This is what Oil Rush attempts to do.
Combat consist of moving units from one node to another. You can not redirect your units to another node if they have already been issued an order. You can however, cancel an order, but they can not be issued another order until they return to the node they came from.
All unit production are automated, you can not tell any single structure to stop building. So, you are more or less forcefully fed units that does not go over your maximum unit supply limit.
The campaign story is composed of predictable plot, with bland characters, and filled with stereotypes.
The whole game just screams turn-based for me, rather than a real time strategy game. There aren't too many moments were you have to react to immediately, and very few micro-management of units or actions. You can't tell a weak unit to retreat, you can't tell a repair ship to prioritize repair, you're more less just hoping the AI will do its job. Most of the time I'm just positioning my units to just either ride the momentum of an assault, or just allotting the units between defense locations as I see the enemy units slowly crawl across the ocean.
If you do like this game, I would suggest playing Eufloria instead. The controls there is much more refined.

One Piece Pirate Warriors 3 is the first installment of the Pirate Warriors series to come to Steam, with the previous entries being exclusive to Sony consoles. It's especially interesting due to the fact that prior to this title there had been  no One Piece games officially brought to PC.
The game follows the story of the anime series from the very beginning all the way up to the point at which it was currently ongoing at the time of the game's release. Cutscenes are done in an interesting way, with some being fully animated in-engine, some are full-motion video, and a lot of them are just two characters standing almost statically with their lips faffing about for a bit...not a fan of those ones, they seem a bit lazy to me.
The game has an impressive roster of characters with all the playable ones being characters that were prevalent for a part of the series. The amount of content here is actually quite impressive as well with 2 full campaigns to play through, those being the main story, which I previously mentioned, and the Dream Log, which has you going from island to island to take part in a plethora of battles as a character of your choice. Together these could take around 30 hours to complete at least.
Replay value is also heavily present here as you can level up characters by partaking in more and more battles, receiving coins that feature different characters which are used to raise a character's stats, and with 37 playable characters to level up here, this game will keep players busy for quite some time.
Being a Koei Tecmo port however, it does have some issues in regards to porting, although thankfully performance is not one of them, with the game running at very consistent 60 FPS. It does however look worse than the PS4 version due to this port being based on the PS3 version, albeit looking slightly better than that version due to slightly higher resolution textures.
Compared to the PS4 version though, the textures look worse, colours appear more washed out and faded and the game has a rougher look to here than it does on PS4. It's far from a deal-breaker for me, but I'd keep this in mind.
The PC version also lacks the online co-op available in the PS4 version for whatever reason which is most definitely disappointing. Local co-op is still an option but since I have no friends nearby(
) I would of have really appreciated the inclusion of online coop...again not a deal-breaker but disappointing nonetheless.
So I might seem like I'm disappointed with this game so far due to the issues present in the port but the fact that remains is that this is a game where you can just kick a**holes around and break-dance pirates to death as some blonde dude in a tuxedo...I mean what else should I need to say to sell you on this game?
It's just as over the top and ridiculous as the Warriors series always has been and I love this game for that, it's just rare to find a game in this day and age that lets you go so f**king crazy with combos and special attacks that are are absolutely stupefying in the best possible sense. And with so many characters and combos to unlock and pull off, what's not to love?

Somewhere inbetween love gone wrong, opportunities missed, bad grades and relationships fading, you gradually lost pieces of your heart and the small bits of innocent belief that a better world could be. But your angina decay went so slowly you could not be aware at the time.
Time. You had all the time in the world. Time to find any solution to any mind or heartache presented to you. Time to waste. Time to enjoy.
Now you know how precious time is. But even more, you are painfully aware of how precious any pipe-dream solution to get those bits and pieces back are. Because you are still looking for them and your body cells have long since started to decompose more rapidly than they renew, and your hair is thinning and graying like it's a race to the finish line.
Today you live among hipster d0uchebags hating on anything older than an hour of existence, pathetic script kiddies on your lawn leaving snarky internet comments, sold-out parents with their fake smiles and monster mortgage - everyone pretending to enjoy life after their precious childhood were whisked away. And however faint your hope, you still struggle with the idea that somewhere there has to be a key, a door, or even the tiniest of glimpse back to those wonderful years. And you would again, for a brief moment, enjoy a full, red heart behind your dusty, weathered rib cage.
This game, then, is my gift to you. It's for all the snowmen and snow castles in life that you wanted to build, but never could because of lack of talent or not winning the gene lottery. It's for the sled rides that didn't have a deadline connected with them, only the sheer joy of feeling the wind in your hair as you lost your mittens and scarf, going so fast down the hill your parents would have a heart attack if they saw it. And nothing could rival the biggest, burning smile that stemmed from your soul and materialized in full between your ears.
It's for your kids, to enjoy something else than generic Zombie Killer Survivalz, Call of Modern Warfare Crapsh|t Ultimate Edition 3, or FIFA Overpaid License Lawyer Edition. It's pure and simple in the most beautiful form. It's for you to take a sneak peak at and play after the kids have gone to bed and you no longer have to pretend to be an adult. It's for you to link back to a better time. It's for all your hopes and dreams that went away so easily, and were beyond your grasp for the longest time.
Marvin's Mittens will grab your wrinkled hand, and inch by snowy inch carry you through what you initially thought would be some hand drawn images, but turning out to be as close to a Winter Holiday with Calvin and Hobbes that you will ever be so lucky to get. Go and play in the snow. Lose a mitten or two along with your worries. It will mend your silly, tired heart and make you smile - for real this time.

Interstellar Marines is an old school tactical FPS games in a wonderful dark SCI-FI world with a realistic combat system.
It's still Early Access and a small Team's working on but since the beginning i enjoyed more than 350 hours of gameplay.
You can play 2 big maps in Singleplayer or 4-Player Coop: Starcrown Aerospace (infiltrate a fortress on a planet) and the Neurogen Incident (big cargo environment and science labs in space).
3 types of Challenges: Survival, Elimination or Escape you can play alone or in Coop.
And the PVP mode Deadlock with a few maps for example Dynacore, Stronghold and Evacuation where you have to take points and hold'em as team. A round end's, after your team took all points or eliminated the whole opposing team. Every week there are community gatherings for EU and US where you can play with Dev's and IM-Progamer from different clans, to have a nice talk in the chat or in teamspeak. At christmas they add a funny Terminator PVP mode where one player is totally overpowered with a special-damage weapon and armour so you have to take the T-IM101 down as team or you die several times :)
And the great Wargame (Hellweek) PVP Arena within 8 completely different maps (on the moon surface, in the jungle, mountains, wetlands, industrial environment and more) where you have to fight against bots and other players, collect weapons and ammo, points and marked air drops. You can play alone or teamup with other players in wargames, but after one hour the team or the first four player with the highest points will win and the round is over ,then you have to wait a few minutes until the next wargame-arena event starts. The enemys in Interstellar Marines are two kind of robots, a runner (weapon: fist) and a gunner. But there will come more, i wait hard for the alien race: the landsharks. Your equipment: 3 different weapons: SMG, AR and a pistol all with flashlight, laser and silencer (pistol without silencer) and skins for your suit and weapons, i hope a shotgun and something like a knife will come too also more types of enemys and a few animals in the environment would be perfect for the atmosphere i guess (jumpscares). But what i really love in IM ... the atmosphere, the day/night cyclus and changing weather, exhaustion system... unique. The price is definitely worth it.
If i have one word for Interstellar marines: Intense.

I can't recommend it for everyone, because of the large learning curve and non-standard controls (I made sure the last laptop I bought had a number pad specifically for this game). The mouse is rarely, if ever, used; instead, nearly every action has a hotkey or two.  However, If you are willing to put time and effort into learning about the game and don't mind playing through trial and error, Unreal World provides a unique survival game experience.

RimWorld is one of the most complete packages I've gotten in a game purchase in a long time (I only just added it to Steam, but I've played several hundred hours via the direct download since alpha 9). Are there nitpicks? Sure. RimWorld is simultaneously the most polished Alpha-level early access game I've ever seen, as in good enough to have been full-released a couple years ago, and in desperate need of a concentrated consistency and balance pass to ensure all of these brilliantly detailed little features and items make sense together. I don't think that should stop you from buying and enjoying this game, especially because the vibrant and active (and reasonably well-supported by the developer) modding community is so quick to provide solutions on the few occasions that the base game does come up short.

Not only that, but both the company that owns the anti-cheat and Aeria sent me only two replies to my support ticket, one of which was useless, and the other was essentially saying "**** you."
In order to actually be able to play the game for more than two minutes, for those that also had this error, you have to exit Steam (it's a third party program, can't launch the game on Steam using Steam), close your antivirus, Teamspeak, everything. Then you have to launch the game from the executable called "NWZLauncher.exe," located in your ...\Steam\steamapps\common\ava folder.
TL;DR Verdict: Do not install, but don't necessarily uninstall. Great game, terrible customer service. Game can't be run with any other programs running, including Steam and antivirus.

Approx a year or so ago, Rbocraft used to be strange, confusing, and the program would constantly flag up as a trojan to my AV. I never had the opportunity to really enjoy what it used to be.
I took a dive in more recently as I've been having the itch for something tho unleash creativity in, and I arrived just before the Body Builder Update.
I have to say that this game has an interesting way of balancing out fairness between designs. The more you try to focus on a larger body for more life or trying to add in more components or weapons -the less energy is available to buff your unit's attack -thus glass cannons can exist but inversely they have no real defenses and can not typically risk the investments on mobility support to really avoid everything. Bigger guns tend to have a lot of health and pack a punch, but are bigger targets, can cause tipping issues on glass cannon builds, and are typically easy prey to the railguns. Thus, big guns on tanks can be difficult vs having several types of smaller scale weapons and some support units. The selection of mobility types each have certain advantages and disadvantages as well. The max mixture of guns and support units are 5, and there is a 2000 CPU or energy limt which all parts a mech is build from fill; Going over 2K CPU means that the build can only be used in custom matches -and I'm not sure how many players even bother with the custom games.
In game, people rarely talk, outside of GG at the end of a match. There are those who complain in Battle Arena, which is a casual point capture based game type. There are some who for whatever reason dip out of matches and lose out on the fact that you still can gain EXP to rank up and even lesser quality item drop crates and then there is of course those taking the battles too seriously and whine because the match up system can not infer skill on a build and can only balance based on the CPU, Mobility type(s), weaponry, and support units equiped to builds.
It is worth a try.

Warning. This is a game that has been in development since the 1990's. Its graphic appearance and mechanics also draw their lineage to this hazy age of nostalgia, gameplay experimentation and one-man development operations.
Now that this warning is out of the way, listen closely. UnReal World is as close as you can get to a realistic depiction of a sparsely populated iron age sandbox game. You will grow hungry as your fishing nets stay empty, game eludes your arrows and spears and trap fences stay empty. You will become desperate in your pleas for the forest spirits so they'd take pity on your starving and cold form that struggles to hang onto life in the cold forest. You will curse that handaxe you lost in the mire and think of the piles of as direly needed equipment you'll have to give away, so the village tradesman will grant you a new axe.
This game is a roguelike, but you'll only find cold and dark in the pitiful caves in this game. It will punish you, until you learn how to play it. Then, when you sauna is lit, the walls are filled with drying meat, the fur and leather piles grow in your hut and the cellar is full of potatoes and salt, you will sit back and enjoy rewards of your hard-learned and earned labours, some pissy Njerpez will stumble on your farm and score a lucky hit on your forehead with an axe he probably found where you lost it, sending your head and save game flying into the horizon.
Such is life, as the Finnish proverb goes. Enough life-like that it was used as educational tool in 1999.

As a fan of Christine Love's work (Digital: A Love Story, Don't Take it Personally, Babe) I appreciate the unique themes she tackles, especially concerning that of technology. Analogue: A Hate Story doesn't disappoint- it touches on many mature themes such as sexism, homosexuality, and more. It also paints a unique picture of an ancient fuedal-like society aboard a sci-fi space station, meshing the old with the new. The writing is spot-on and makes for a great read.
That is, if you like reading- this is a really simple sort of novel in that there is little to no scenery change, and only a decent amount of interaction. Additionally the user interface is not the easiest to get used to, mainly the command console- you will very likely at some point seek a guide for the command you'd like to use for a certain section. Otherwise the UI is fine, if plain- take a look at the screenshots, as it's what the entire game looks like.
Aside from those very minor gripes, if you get this game you're in for some great and thoughtful reading. It's a great story, and will take more than one playthrough to really understand and see everything.

I haven't played many visual novels, only two in fact, but I really enjoyed this one. Looking past its very typical anime presentation, there is a really intriguing story and compelling mechanics. There are a couple of cringey fan service moments, and there is a bit of silly romance in there with the AI you spend a lot of the game interacting with, but for the most part you will be trawling through archives of diaries and letters on an abandoned space station, filled with family fueds and intrigue, and you will eventually learn what happened to the station and the people on it. Because you're reading through people's very personal writings, you get a very intimate perspective on the whole story that works wonderfully to make the long dead characters come to life again.
If you're interested in playing games with good stories, I would recommend trying this out, and it's very accessible for people who haven't played visual novels before.

Last game I was required to play and now review as part of my deal with Alex.
I am ashamed to admit that I actually enjoyed this one. No real cliches here, not really weeb♥♥♥♥♥♥ just tells a good story and happens to be an anime game.
Because the story is actually good, I'll warn that spoilers follow.
It is a visual novel, just told using interesting mechanics, and player choices are abundant, so I'm okay with it.
Epistolary novel -- story told through series of documents, letters, and text entries. A narrative is made clear by reading accounts given by other people of events. Also uses the unreliable narrator mechanic, the persons giving you information and exposition withhold information and hint at things to be discovered later. I like both of these things.
Your character is an investigator or mercenary of sorts investigating a ship that was lost contact with thousands of years ago. It was apparantly a ship holding an entire society meant to establish the first colony in another star system. AI on ship *Hyun-ae greets character. Many documents, letters, and diary entries detailing life on the ship before everyone died give the player a sense of what was going on.
The story revolves around the character 'The Pale Bride' which is mostly a tragedy. A young girl, the 'Pale Bride', of 13 on the ship was put in cryogenic stasis b/c she was dying and they figured those in the future would have better medicine on the ship.
Stasis pod is shattered, she awakens to a deeply backwards society resembling ancient China, Japan, or Korea, one of those. Complete with emperors, family dynasties, and deep misogyny, the new society does not at all have the means to heal her, and rather intends to have her married off to the 'emperor'.
The character protests at first and maintains her own free will, but is slowly degraded and controlled. The girl's real name was apparantly Hyun-ae, the name of the supposed AI on the ship.
The last diary entry revealed details the girl refusing to be married to the emperor, only to have her tongue cut out by her adopted father for speaking against a man. Her description of the scene is rather disturbing and you'll quickly come to be horrified by and hate the society she's awoken to.
Everyone on the ship has been dead for 600 years apparantly. The security AI on the ship, *Mute, entirely accepts the backwards beliefs of the ship's culture, but reveals things to the player about what happened to the ship. Primarily, she reveals that *Hyun-ae is responsible for everyone's death.
When questioned, Hyun-ae will reveal a diary entry where she had become a submissive, dehumanized wife of the emperor, having almost entirely forgotten her past identity and sense of self. During a visit to her adopted family, her 'father' says how happy he is with her, as she used to be so protesting and angry, but that she's really surprised them all and become a success.
Upon hearing this, she suddenly remembered all that had happened, how she had lost herself, her identity, and now that her adopted father was actually praising her for how she had become dehumanized and made into an object, she wanted nothing more than to kill him.
She could not bring herself to stab him with the knife she held. The player will recall an earlier entry where it is detailed to 'The Pale Bride'/Hyun-ae that the password to the emperor's shipcomputer is her birth name, as a sign of appreciation. This is willingly revealed to her b/c it is assumed that women couldn't ever use a computer. Using this, she accesses the computer and disables the ship's life support and downloads her consciousness onto the ship through some sci-fi absurdity.
Of course, there are many other details and sub-stories, but that is the gist of it. There are five endings allowed for the player depending on their choices. The easiest is to simply gain the password to the computer, download the ship's files, and leave the AIs behind. The four other endings require a more thorough search and understanding of the narrative.
I started the game not expecting it, but I must admit that the game is dark/disturbing, tells good stories, is not plagued by awful cliches, has good music, requires player agency and choice, and has multiple ways to complete it.
I recommend this game.

Although Valve has irreversibly ruined what was once a great game with novel ideas since buying Day of Defeat from the original developers, the game still maintains some level of entertainment. I have no idea how much it costs because I've always owned this game - maybe 10 dollars now? - but it's still worth it. Unfortunately, there aren't any other WW2 first person shooters anymore. I highly doubt anyone plays CoD WaW anymore and Heroes and Generals is...meh. Unless people are still playing Enemy Front.
I don't know about everyone else, but basically my entire time spent playing DoD source is  similar to the life of a heroin addict. I spend all my time when I play trying to relive the glorious moments possible in the original DoD, when you could set up an MG and literally slaughter SO MANY people on the other team before you got killed - if you got killed. Unfortunately, source engine has eliminated that ability because of lighting and because of how overly accurate all guns are, but that is my quest.
To go into further detail:
DoD, before Valve bought it, had paratrooper maps. Paratrooper maps were CS like 1-spawn only objective-based rounds, with paratroopers - obviously. So you had excellent maps like hedgerow, and you got FG42s, and the greasegun, as well as the K43 and M1 Carbine. Valve got rid of all of that. They got rid of the British team entirely, and with them the Enfield, Bren, Sten, Webley, and their grenades. In addition, they also got rid of the Bar bipod, and the MG34. This variety is what made the game so awesome from 2000 until it was bought.
One of the most absurdly ridiculous things in the game is that Valve put in RPGs, and they were there for a now non-existent purpose, yet the class and weapons remain in the game. The RPG class is just ridiculous - Allies get M1 Carbine with only 3 mags, Axis gets an automatic C96 with a stock. Both of them very good  guns in the game, especially C96. Then they can drop their RPGs and get a primary. Those classes were originally put in the game for objectve maps where you actually had to destroy building parts or other objectives with them . The modern game literally has none of those maps, yet, you can still use the class. And it's completely ridiculous - I say this as someone who likes playing that class - because you can literally run around and rocket people in the face. Snipe people with rockets.
Even if you get the original DoD on Steam, you're not going to find that experience. Maybe you can find some private servers of beta DoD, if you are willing to try to look at 17 year old graphics. Nonetheless, the game is irreparably broken, and Valve hasn't done a mother ♥♥♥♥ing thing to it in literally 10 years. Over10 years. They have literally never made an actual content update. The ONE thing they ever updated was the patch that introduced film grain to spectator mode and made a few other spectator adjustments. Every single gun is royally broken, overpowered, overaccurate, over-recoiled, and the hitboxes are supremely broken. The netcode, as well, is ungodly bad. It's embarrassing that this blemish exists while other Source games are so solid like Left 4 Dead or Insurgency.
If you want a WW2 game that isn't complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I suggest playing Red Orchestra 2.

Okay I don't really leave reviews but this game gets an exception. It has one of the best stories I have experinced in gaming in years. If you are on the fence buy it don't let the low metacritic score scare you because it isn't really fair. Short answer get it but if you want a more in depthe review look Below.
In-depth review minor spoilers
Don't worry like I said only minor spoilers. In this game you play an intersteller investigator assigned to investigate the wreck of a multi-generation colony ship sent out by Korea in the 24th century. What makes the game interesting is what you find as you dig through the ships logs and your interaction with the ships two AI's *Hyun-ae and *Mute (the * denotes they are AI's.) Basiclly, at some point in the ship's past all computer data was wiped and the captain declared himself emperor and institued a feudal secioty that like one would expect is sexist, classist, homophobic etc. But the story isn't about the formation of that culture (that's the topic of the sequel Hate Plus.) The story is about how that civilization ended as told through the eyes of the people living at the time
Where the AI's come in is that both AI's have opposing views on the morality of the secioty *Hyun-ae the first AI you encounter is critical of the ships culture where *Mute is a defender of it. As you would expect this makes you like *Hyun-ae better than *Mute since *Mute is basiclly a woman defending Sexism. But the funny thing is as the story unfolds and certain plot twists are revealed *Hyun-ae becomes less likable and *Mute becomes more likable leaving you feeling conflicted about both.
Now the Bad. more minor spoilers
My biggest beef with this game is it forces you to choose the ending half-way through the game. I get what the developer was trying to do you are supposed make a snap judgement as to which AI is right, before you have all the information. That would be Okay but I don't feel like it is well executed since it easy to pick the choice you don't want (in my first playthrough I wanted to side with *Hyun-ae but got stuck with *Mute) and after that choice you cannot switch AI's again for the rest of the game. So save at when your log enteries hit 50% complete.
Issue 2 i have is that the "perfect" ending requires you to do large amounts of metagaming the only way you can get it without help takes at least 2 or 3 playthroughs (depending on who you side with playthrough 1) and I do mean at least that number in reality you could play the game a dozen times and not find the perfect ending.
All in all I give the game an 8.5 out of 10.

This is a side-on puzzle game in which you use super-powered trousers and a 'hacking' interface to infiltrate a selection of buildings, extract the information you want, then get the hell out of there; usually through comically jumping through a window and faceplanting the concrete outside.
Both the movement and hacking have been done in an extremely intuitive way, which encourages you to experiment with the environment with your limited toolset to achieve your goal - jumping through glass into a guard and knocking them uncouncious with classic batman-esque sound effects; wiring a switch to a door, slamming it into guards to incapacitate them, hotwiring a plug socket and a siren so that all the guards sprint to the room you want and are promptly electrocuted into unconciousness - it's all extremely satisfying, and the reward of discovering an ability that hasn't been explicitly outlined is tangible.
This summary may make the game sound violent, but any violence in the game is dealt with in a comic, non-gratuitous way; also offering the option to complete every mission non-violently if you so choose (both options are equally viable and as rewarding).
The end of each mission gives you a rating for 'violence', 'witnesses', 'noise', and 'time' - each affecting you overal A-F grade - giving those gamers who enjoy things like speedruns and perfect executions something to aim for; while this really helps the replayability of the campaign alone, the majority of this game's replayability comes from the Steam Workshop - where people have used the game's level-creator to create a huge selection of missions to sink your teeth into.
My only complaint about this game would be the campaign length but, as this is more than made up for by the Workshop, it's nowhere near a dealbreaker and I thoroughly recommend this to anyone looking for an engaging puzzle game that can be picked up and put down as needed.  Top marks.

Gunpoint is a 2d stealth/puzzle game. You can rewire devices in the level to do certain things, such as rewiring a light switch so that instead of turning out the lights, it opens a door into a guard, knocking him out. There are a ton of devices that all do different things when triggered and you can wire almost any combination of triggers/devices together. Your character is also very mobile: you can crawl up walls and hang from the ceiling, and you can superjump with a pair of robolegs your character buys in the opening cutscene. Levels also have a couple of collectibles, in the form of laptops that you can hack to read emails from the game's characters. The characters are really well written, and the dialog is pretty funny. The characters will also give optional goals at the start of levels if you want more of a challenge.
And if you want to spend more than a couple of hours on the game, you had
better go for every one of those challenges and collectibles, because this game is short as HELL. I took my time and meandered about the levels, reset them a few times, and I still beat the whole game in like 3 hours. There's a level editor with workshop integration, but a game shouldn't have to rely on user generated content to last for more than one short sitting.
In short;
PROS: solid gameplay with interesting mechanics, well written characters, funny dialog
CONS: short as hell, can easily be beaten in a few hours

If you are at all a fan of strategy games, feudal Japan, or games that require thought, you will proabably enjoy this game, at least to an extent.
Shogun: Total War is the first game in the very expansive swath of Total War games,
I found out about this game after recently playing Civ 1991, which I also enjoyed.
This game will make you care about each individual Daimyo. You'll be upset when Takeda sends a ninja at you and fails while you're allied. You'll scream at your monitor when Hojo attacks you while allied even though you were leaving him alone and he has no chance of success.
In short, the game is split into two phases, the Strategy Map, and the Battle Phase.
During the Strategy Map, you move units around, train units, and create buildings. When two or more non affliated units meet, they battle.
In the Battle Phase, the units are at your command in real time to do battle.
If you don't wish to read any more, stop here at this Tl;dr:
This game is decent. Buy it if you are even remotely interested in the themes this game portrays, or are a big fan of the Total War series or strategy wargames in general.
Onto the specifics:
Graphics:
They hold up today, especially when played in the highest reso you can muster. They aren't flashy, and they aren't sexy, but they get the job done. The only time I had gripes with the graphics specifically is when there were 2k+ units on the field at once and I couldn't tell which unit was which from my aerial view.
Gameplay:
A mixed bag. The Planning Phase is alright. It could totally be far more informative, as you'll oftentimes be overwhelmed with information about who is doing what, and you may forget what your providences are currently up to. Moving units en masse is VERY clunky, and is one of the reasons why I haven't put more time into the game.
The Battle Phase is fun, however. There is very little which can mimic the rush of adrenaline you get when you send a 1k man squad, including your Daimyo, over a bloody river in order to take that one strategic advantage you need to wipe Shimazu off the map.
However, with the exception of the Mongols and the Mori, and even the Mori to an extent, the clans are too similar because you always end up running Geisha, Heavy Calvary, and Kensei anyways. Surround 4-5 Kensei with a few units of Calvary and Heavy Calvary and every army you attack will invariably rout. While this is going on, send your 2-3 Geisha after every Daimyo you see, and you win. This works even on Very Hard. This makes pretty much every clan the same, and destroys diplomacy and stealth because the Emissary is garbage when compared to your Geisha, and the CPU usually offer alliances anyways. The Ninja take like 3-4 Emissary kills before they can even dream of reliably taking out a worthy General, and if at any point he fails, bam, everyone knows you're a sneaky ♥♥♥♥♥ using Ninja. Geisha however, don't die when they fail, and there is nothing anyone can really do about it besides throw another Geisha at yours, or hope and pray their higher leveled Ninja can stop her. This is the second reason why I haven't put more time into this game, some of the gameplay mechanics are too broken, which renders large swathes of the game pointless. The same happened in Civ 1991. Why struggle to maintain an economy or a republic or a democracy when you can just have one or two far off settlers which constantly buy and sell barracks in a despot that sheds blood on every turn? I am no Sun Tzu, and I didn't look these strategies up for either of these games, so I'm sure others have figured this out before me.
Sound:
Mostly positive. The Muskets are nice to listen to, the screams and shouts of various units are nice, background music is non intrusive. The "Yo-hoh-ho, yo-hoh!" actually really gets you in the mood during the Battle Phase. The archer sounds are paltry, however, and the voice acting is abysmal.
Multiplayer:
Non existant.
While this isn't technically true, there are LAN battles, that is just it, only LAN BATTLES. The full campaign is not playable in any form in multiplayer, which, in my opinon, makes none of the battles have any weight.
Entertainment Potential and Replayability:
For casual players who don't wish to always run the best strategy, and just wish to watch or passively intervene in thousand man battles, this game is required reading, and will last for a long time. However, once you grasp the mechanics of the game and then realise some of the glaring flaws, the game becomes too easy, and loses most of its challenge. That combined with the very slow and clunky movement of units in the Planning Phase make subsequent playthroughs boring and sometimes even irritating.
Overall, I'd give this game somewhere around a 6.5-7.0. I like it, yes, but can't exactly reccomend it to anyone due to its glaring flaws.
Keep a look out for my other reviews. <3

I love Interstellar Marines!!!
It's currently a game in progress but totally worth getting right now.
Several types of game play:
Playground
Single player
Co-op
Multiplayer
Hell Week
Maps:
Maps are dynamic, anamorphic and dirty unlike other FPS games.
In Breif:
Dynamic elements:
Ever changing light and weather conditions. These change at random intervals and the associated sounds increase the realizm of the moment. One moment a gentle breeze and sunny skies, the darkness rolls in with hard wind and driving rain, a short while later... Darkness falls and silence... A flashlight or walking could give you away...
Anamorphic elements:
Most other FPS maps are quite static with maybe a door or a window to break to achieve an objective. In ISM many maps physically change often causing you to reroute to achieve an objective. Matched with everchanging environmental variables this is quite engaging.
Dirty elements:
I love the fact that the physical ripples of water motion can give away a creeping enemy. You hide in long blades of tall grass or have ferns providing disguising you for an unaware opponent.
Tracking a target that runs into a bush and still nailing him; but they run behind a tree and you miss... A missed shot can give you away. Sometimes you're in a combination bushes grass and trees, you might be spotted and shot at. They might hit or miss depending on that coverage. It's harder to hit what you can't clearly see...
This provides a better sense of realism than other POP FPS games with maps that have clear sightlines in all directions and no cover.
Currently there are 3 guns:
Pistol with ironsight
Submachine gun with dot sight x2 zoom
Battle rifle with ACOG x4 zoom
All are equipped with Flashlights Suppressors and Lazers.
Each have different fire rates, damages and accuracies.
Fresh free content on an almost monthly basis with huge updates quarterly to semi annually.
The Dev's:
ISM Devs are all approachable and easy to talk to.
There's an event every Monday/Tuesday where the dev's join into a public game and interact directly with the players. Don't miss out! They even have a teamspeak channel for all to speak freely.
I'll most more as ISM evolves. Don't pass up on this great game!
THE SHORTER BREIF REVIEW:
This is the best game you never played!
The maps are dirty and anamorphic with dynamic weather conditions.
The Dirty:
You can actually hide in the environment. Stratiegic use of camoflauge and environmental terrain is fantastic; actually blending in to your surroundings!
Anamorphic:
The terrain constantly changes. You have to change your thinking on the fly to achieve objectives.  This is unheard of in  any other game ever played!
Dynamic:
The weather variables add a unique element to play. One monent its sunny and calm making you easily heard as you run; next its stormy and raining which maskes your running but also makes it harder to hear and spot enemey movements. then it's almost pitch black. Do you wisk using your tactical flashlight and give away your position or do you fumble in the dark hoping to catch an enemy off guard?
Extras:
There are single, co-op and multiplayer missions with adjustable difficulties on the single and co-op missions. also there is the scavanger hellweek.
Hellweek is meant to mimic the real world marines final rite of passage. 9 different servers all interconnected with up to 64 players each! It lives up to the name!
This game is in development and the dev team is working hard to release patches that are hassle free; they are doing an excellent job!
Be part of this great legacy!

tl;dr: Current recommendation: avoid it like the plague
One step forward, several steps back.  Dropping the wave system is a great change; all the other crap they added in, not so much. There are so many annoyances in the game now:
Ring of flies takes longer to dodge than clearing an entire map does; it's faster to just leave the game and start a new one.  It also applies whether you instakill the boss or not; isn't that FUN?
The overhauled act bosses are super gimmicky.  Not hard to deal with, just annoying gimmicks that drag out the fight, and can oneshot, because reasons.  Get the grim reaper to 1hp?  Nope, he's not dying anytime soon.  Prepare to be teleported into the middle of easily dodgable skulls that take longer to dodge than it does to actually bring the boss down to 1hp; hope you weren't in the middle of a movement skill when you got teleported or you'll finish the movement after the teleport and probably smash right into a skull.  Yay. GREAT DESIGN...not.
Boss and mini-boss death animations still take ages and they can still start new attacks during it; terrible design that doesn't look like it'll change anytime soon.
Level scaling everywhere; I really don't see the point in this.  Right now, you level up and you essentially get weaker; enemy health and damage scales dramatically.  Have fun slogging through massive hp bloat if you don't have mythic weapons/gear.  In the process of grinding while leveling, you get weaker relative to the enemies for every run where you don't get an upgrade because you have leveled up; sounds like a great recipe for FUN, doesn't it?  The game used to have a feeling of progression throughout the leveling process; that's gone and leveling is a poor experience because of it.
Have a full set of mythic gear at low levels, ending up with +40 or more to all your skills?  Have fun trying to manage your mana.  To be fair, they've said that a "fix" is incoming for this.  Their "fixes" in the past tend to not work, so I'm not holding my breath; many times, I lost gear/relics to bugs in their save system that were "fixed" both before and after the supposed fixes.    Play on PanicNet at your own risk.

A brief story of Bone of the Owl-tribe:
I'm stumbling through the woods when I find an abandoned camp. The camp has pretty much everything I need except water so I take off looking for water. I must have been wandering snowblind and dehydrated because when I snap out of my stupor I'm standing in the middle of a frozen lake. I learn this just in time to fall through the ice.
I am finally able to get out of the water and back on to the ice, so I then start crawling for the shore. I get to the shore and I realize "hey, I can make a hole in the ice and drink the water". As I am raising my axe to punch the hole, some tribesman I do not know walks up and politely informs me that I will donate all my stuff to him. I tell him to go to hell and as bad as I just wanted a drink of that cool water, I turn the axe on the interloper who then whistles for his friend (up to this point I though that his use of the words "us" and "we" was just an eccentricity...like the royal "We").
With an axe in one hand and a knife in the other I am getting the better of this upstart worm of a thief, but I can see his friend has come out of the treeline with a huge - what I can only describe as a "pole". I guess it was supposed to be a staff but no normal man would wield this giant piece of wood as a staff. I get back to the business at hand and I have finally killed the thief who started this whole affair.  When I look up again the other thief has closed the distance and brains me with this monstrous tree that he has carried with him. I black out.
The next thing I know, I am waking up in an unfamiliar part of the forest (sans axe and knife) and twice as thirsty as before. I crawl for what seems like days when I see a village...

Unreal World is an incredible example of what Roguelikes can be. In solid, continuous development since 1992, URW has no end in sight, with Enormous Elk (developers Sami and Erkka) continuing their work in bringing Iron Age Totally-Not-Finland to life.
URW is the epitome of survival games, yet predates the current craze by literally decades. It's realistic, it's tough, it's unforgiving, and extremely rewarding to play. There is a lot of depth and complexity to explore, and you can live your (probably short) life as a fisherman, hunter, trader, hermit, cannibal, raider... whatever strikes your fancy.
Roguelike mechanics, charming tileset graphics, and harsh survival interweaved with a touch of mysticism and the spirit of nature (which is simulated in great detail, from plants to animals to weather and seasons). Playing URW is simultaneously zen, and at times stressful (when you fall from a tree and break all your limbs and freeze to death, or almost anything to do with bears).
Highly recommended, and sold for a pittance. If you have doubts, check out the developers' website for the free version. If you find yourself enjoying the game, pitch in on Steam to support it years to come. This is a true labour of love, and with all things going well, will see years and years of improvements ahead.

I've been playing this game for years and it just keeps getting better and better with every iteration.  It's nice to see it up on steam where it will get more exposure and bring a great deal of enjoyment to many others who discover it.
It is a rich single-player world where you will have to survive.  No, not one wave after another of enemies, but the harsh realities of living in a land where even the weather can be your enemy.  Yes, there are some (NPC) people whom you might have to fight with, but many more whom you will trade with and develop a relationship for mutual survival.  You pick a spot to make your cabin.  Cut the trees to make the logs.  Fish.  Hunt.  Plant.  Make your tools or trade for them with nearby villagers.  Stock up on foods, make warm clothing and much, much more... and maybe,  just maybe, you'll survive the cold, dark winter.
I enjoy the turn-based aspect of this game, allowing me to go at my own pace.  Graphics are tiled top-down and not spectacular, but with each iteration of the game, they get better and better.  This latest version the graphics (particularly the lighting) add a lot to immersion.   It doesn't really matter though, because you soon get lost in the details and become immersed in the world no matter what.  How much snow fell while you were sleeping, do I need to use my skis?  Has it been cold enough to go out on the ice?  The edges of the lake are solid, but is the middle safe enough to walk on?  Did I hear a Elk in the distance to my left?  I better check my trap lines.  I wonder if the village I discovered earlier last week has some better spears to trade for.  There were  rumors of a bear in the area and it's hide would make nice warm clothing for cold winter days.... and on it goes.
Modding is easy and enjoyable, especially with this new version, allowing you to tweak many things or make completely new ones.  The creators of the game are also responsive to the community and very friendly.
I don't really have anything negative to say. It might take a little time to get used to the key commands, but the help file is easily accessible after hitting the ESC key.  The game does what it's suppose to and just gets better and more detailed with every iteration.  It's turn-based, survival, wilderness simulation that makes for a great afternoon or evening of play.  I'd say try it out, the price is very reasonable.

Gunpoint is a 2d stealth/puzzle game. You can rewire devices in the level to do certain things, such as rewiring a light switch so that instead of turning out the lights, it opens a door into a guard, knocking him out. There are a ton of devices that all do different things when triggered and you can wire almost any combination of triggers/devices together. Your character is also very mobile: you can crawl up walls and hang from the ceiling, and you can superjump with a pair of robolegs your character buys in the opening cutscene. Levels also have a couple of collectibles, in the form of laptops that you can hack to read emails from the game's characters. The characters are really well written, and the dialog is pretty funny. The characters will also give optional goals at the start of levels if you want more of a challenge.
And if you want to spend more than a couple of hours on the game, you had
better go for every one of those challenges and collectibles, because this game is short as HELL. I took my time and meandered about the levels, reset them a few times, and I still beat the whole game in like 3 hours. There's a level editor with workshop integration, but a game shouldn't have to rely on user generated content to last for more than one short sitting.
In short;
PROS: solid gameplay with interesting mechanics, well written characters, funny dialog
CONS: short as hell, can easily be beaten in a few hours

Analogue: A Hate Story is an excellent visual novel.  The story is excellent and enticing, and the characters (despite there only being two you can interact with) are deep and interesting.  As far as replay value goes, it's a good game to replay a couple times in order to get all content; but once you've 100%-ed it, you may want to move on to another game.
If you're not familiar with visual novels, they are a genre of video games that rely heavily on reading text, and primarily offer binary choices as the only method of affecting the game.  Analogue is unique in this genre because the player gets the story through reading diary entries and correspondences between people from hundreds of years ago, rather than by interacting with other characters.  In addition, the player isn't limited to infrequent binary decisions: they also can affect the game by showing any of the logs to either one of two AI characters, and they will read and react to whatever its contents are.  There's also other ways to interact with the game, but going into detail about them would spoil the fun of discovering how to interact with the game.
If you're on the edge of buying or not buying Analogue: A Hate Story, I would definitely recommend getting it.  It is plenty of fun, has a fantastic story, and by the time you're through, you'll probably feel quite strongly for one (or both) of the characters.

Very early first impressions after playing just a few turns. Very easy to play, much less complex than Panzer Corps. Manual tells you nothing, there's no tutorial. There are hints in Frontline: Road to Moscow before you start a battle, which basically tell you how the game works, but not in this game. Instead you get a pop up occasionally explaining things. Not very obvious how things work at first but I'm picking it up quickly. No fog of war, so you can see where all the enemy units are. Definitely seems to be a "wargame lite" designed for casual play, but strategy is still needed. There are several combat mechanics and special abilities that aren't obvious at first. These need to be explained better. I've already had several units wiped out. Well it is D-Day after all...
Game is not very polished. Starts in a window (press Alt+Enter to fill screen), no resolution options (although it's running fine in 2560x1080), graphics are pretty but not very sharp. Found a couple of bugs already, landed some units and they've retained the landing craft icons (so I'm now moving and attacking inland with landing craft). Also the frame rate is insanely high (up to a totally unnecessary 1000 FPS) which was straining my graphics card, but I fixed that by running Bandicam in the background to cap the framerate to 30FPS. I've reported these bugs. Knowing Slitherine they'll be fixed. Warhammer Armageddon had the same frame rate problem and they've fixed that in the latest patch I think.
Early conclusion: Pretty looking turn based wargame. Quick and easy to play (but with a certain hidden depth that isn't obvious), would suit casual players who don't want too much detail. A few bugs at the moment, but no doubt they'll be fixed. It's no Panzer Corps, but it would be unfair to expect too much at this price point. It seems like a fair price for what you get.
Update: I've been playing this for a little while now, on and off, and I'm getting to like it more and more. It's really quite enjoyable. I haven't encountered any major bugs yet, and the landing craft icons disappeared after reloading.
Another Update: Airstrikes are definitely overpowered, in the sense that you can do as many as you like, you're only limited by the points you have to spend. But I have a ridiculous number of points, so I can do as many as I want each turn. It's making the game way too easy, I can just bomb everything to oblivion and I don't need to attack with my ground units at all. In fact I've been purposely not using it just to give myself a bit of a challenge. This really needs to be addressed. Just like there's a limit on how many units you can buy, there should be a limit on how many airstrikes you're allowed each turn. Having maybe 3 or 5 airstrikes max each turn would solve this problem.
Also, nearing the end of the first scenario, it locked up. It's done this several times before but it usually only lasts a short while then you can continue. This time I was unable to continue and lost all my progress. Obviously this should be fixed too (I'm using Win 7 64 bit), but as a safeguard, an autosave at the beginning of each turn would be nice.
At the moment, you can deal with these issues by imposing a voluntary air attack limit on yourself each turn, and saving (save and quit) each turn, just in case of an unrecoverable lockup, even though it's a bit of a hassle to reload each turn.
I still recommend this game, but it's more of a cautious recommendation now, on the assumption that these problems will be fixed. You might want to avoid rushing into a purchase until they are.

What is Enemy Front all about? I've only got 1.2 hours on my play time, i've actually played more as I played a copy on a different account for some time, but not much more. With that said, it's still true I haven't played the game much. I only really play it when i'm in a very specific mood for a WW2 FPS, and that isn't too often. Enemy Front has a cool idea for a setting, the Warsaw uprising and rebellion during Nazi occupation, but it frankly doesn't do much to flesh out this potentially excellent setting. That's about the biggest problem with Enemy Front, nearly all of it's good ideas aren't well excecuted or are just barely good enough to be passable. Missions typically play out with a fairly decent stealth system that is plagued by bad AI and bugs. It also has a good selection of pain-stakingly detailed WW2 weapons, one of the things Enemy Front does really well. You'll sneak around, steathily dispatching Nazis, until things go south. At that point the gunplay comes to the forefront and it's a very mixed bag. So, with that said, here are the pros and cons.
Enemy front isn't entirely awful. In some regards its terrible, but in some aspects it's quite well done. The stealth focused missions give a nice feeling of freedom, and the guns do feel very good to use when things go south. However, the gunplay is hindered by the poor AI and killing enemies in this game with guns just doesn't feel very satisfying. Enemies just kind of slump over in a rather unexciting way, often bugging out or glitch through scenery. It just doesn't feel right. But this is the pros, not the cons. There's a very good selection of guns and they are very detailed and have good sound effects. Actually, the sound design in general is fairly solid. Besides the voice acting, this game has quality sound. The graphics are by no means spectacular, but they are generally solid. The WW2 setting is recreated well and feels authentic. The level's are fairly well designed from what i've played and are fairly open for exploration and for stealth gameplay. The stealth system works mostly as expected and is rather satisfying at times. If not for the bad AI, this stealth system could possible carry the game, but with all the previously mentioned problems it holds the system back.
- Good stealth system
- Authentic WW2 weapons and a good selection of them
- Decent graphical fidelity and decent performance
- Solid sound design in all regards but the voice acting
- Solid level design with lots of stealth and exploration
- Interesting setting
- Authentic WW2 levels
The cons list is roughly even with the pros, which is essentially what makes up Enemy Front as a whole. It's a 50/50 experience with about half good and half bad on the whole. The voice acting is pretty bad, not attrocious, but not good enough to carry the weight of this story and setting. The Warsaw uprising makes for a great story, but this game relatively squanders it and doesn't make much use of it. As a result, this game doesn't feel much different than a typical WW2 FPS. The only thing setting it apart is its stealth system, but sadly the terrible AI detracts from the system in a major way. The AI often stands in the open or doesn't properly use cover in most cases. In addition to that, there are numerous glitches, far too many for even a small time release such as this. The combat feels rather unsatisfying as a result of the bad AI, glitches, and just general lack of a visceral feeling to the gunplay. Stealth runs can often be blown by seemingly nothing and other times the AI can be so stupid that it'll ignore you shooting a friend in the head, acting as if nothing has happened. When the stealth system works properly it can be satisfying, but this is pretty uncommon for it to fire on all cylinders.
- Bad voice acting
- Little mission variety
- Terrible AI
- Unsatisfying gunplay
- Too many glitches and bugs
- Lackluster, boring story
Enemy Front is just one big mixed bag. It has serious ups and downs and squanders a lot of it's best aspects. Between the broken AI and glitchy nature of the game, its rare to see the game at it's best, with everything working like it should. When the game actually goes as it should, it can be a pretty solid WW2 shooter. But sadly, that's really the best the game can be is merely solid. Even at it's high points, its nothing more than a decent, mostly generic WW2 FPS. Is it worth buying? At full price, I'd say no, definitely not. At a discounted price? I'd say yeah, but at least half off or more. I think I payed $15 for this game or $10 and frankly I expected better, but I'd say I got what I payed for. If you love WW2 like me, and you've been Jonesing for a return of WW2 shooters, then you just may find something to like in this game. Otherwise, if you're just a lover of shooters or just looking for a fun game, i'd say look elsewhere as this game is only going to really appeal to a specific group of people.
Enemy Front is a good idea for a WW2 shooter, but it's sadly a squandered idea and most of its best mechanics are ruined by other bad or broken mechanics that interfere with the few good systems in this game.

I still have the big, red, cardboard box this game originally came in. I remember playing a demo of it on an old PC Zone demo CD. Good times, good times.
The game runs great on newer systems, now. You can run it in your native resolution without a problem. I've experienced no glitches or bugs, apart from a strange sound glitch which cuts off the voice acting in the throne room.
The game is still as fun as I remember it. It's not a complex game. The diplomacy amounts to sending emissaries to forge alliances and nothing more. The only goal is to build up resources and then use said resources to recruit armies in order to conquer Japan. That's it. It's simple, but a lot of fun. I also love to cheesy cinematics - characters actually looking at, and talking to, you; it's also one of the main things I loved about the old C&C games.
I will say that I am speaking from nostalgia. I love this game still, because I loved it well over a decade or so ago. You may find it hard to get into if you're coming from newer TW games.
If you can overlook its simplistic design, then I highly recommend giving it a go.

tl;dr: Current recommendation: avoid it like the plague
One step forward, several steps back.  Dropping the wave system is a great change; all the other crap they added in, not so much. There are so many annoyances in the game now:
Ring of flies takes longer to dodge than clearing an entire map does; it's faster to just leave the game and start a new one.  It also applies whether you instakill the boss or not; isn't that FUN?
The overhauled act bosses are super gimmicky.  Not hard to deal with, just annoying gimmicks that drag out the fight, and can oneshot, because reasons.  Get the grim reaper to 1hp?  Nope, he's not dying anytime soon.  Prepare to be teleported into the middle of easily dodgable skulls that take longer to dodge than it does to actually bring the boss down to 1hp; hope you weren't in the middle of a movement skill when you got teleported or you'll finish the movement after the teleport and probably smash right into a skull.  Yay. GREAT DESIGN...not.
Boss and mini-boss death animations still take ages and they can still start new attacks during it; terrible design that doesn't look like it'll change anytime soon.
Level scaling everywhere; I really don't see the point in this.  Right now, you level up and you essentially get weaker; enemy health and damage scales dramatically.  Have fun slogging through massive hp bloat if you don't have mythic weapons/gear.  In the process of grinding while leveling, you get weaker relative to the enemies for every run where you don't get an upgrade because you have leveled up; sounds like a great recipe for FUN, doesn't it?  The game used to have a feeling of progression throughout the leveling process; that's gone and leveling is a poor experience because of it.
Have a full set of mythic gear at low levels, ending up with +40 or more to all your skills?  Have fun trying to manage your mana.  To be fair, they've said that a "fix" is incoming for this.  Their "fixes" in the past tend to not work, so I'm not holding my breath; many times, I lost gear/relics to bugs in their save system that were "fixed" both before and after the supposed fixes.    Play on PanicNet at your own risk.

I've been playing Unreal World for a few years now, and for as impenetrable as it might look in some of the screenshots, it is actually one of the most understandable and playable roguelikes I've experienced.  It provides a real sense of accomplishment as well.
The first time I finally killed a large animal was as exciting as anything I've experienced in a game.  I had to sit back and just enjoy the accomplishment for several minutes.  When I made the mistake of building a fire too close to my log cabin that I had spent months (in game) and hours (in real life) building, and watched it burn down, I felt a real sense of loss, but also that I had learned something, and was ready to jump back in and try again.  The game's depth and pacing are, in my opinion, what set up these moments.
If you enjoy the survival genre, you owe it to yourself to give this a try.
An additional note: the development cycle for this game has been great over the years.  The developers (all two of them) keep the community informed and are constantly making improvements to the game.

This game is about the cutest thing I've ever seen.  If you have children between 6 to 8 years old, this is a perfect platformer for them to get started on.  The graphics, atmosphere, music, and the little bit of writing and dialog that there are, all add up to make a great child's game.
There are no bad guys to defeat, no pits of spikes to traverse and no health bar or damage from falling from too high: simply the wonder of discovery as Marvin wanders out of his backyard in search of his stolen mitten.  Along the way, he meets magical elves who aid in his quest.  Marvin occasionally spies small animals, and if he moves slowly, he can whip out his sketchbook and draw a picture of them.
After about ten or fifteen minutes of playing, Mom calls Marvin back to the house for bed at which point she hums a short lullaby and gives the opportunity to save progress and quit.
The only con is that the last couple of levels, or screens, have one or two really difficult spots for small kids to handle.  It will probably require an adult or older sibling to get the child to the very end and discover who stole Marvin's mitten.  But the simple and heartwarming ending is well worth the effort.

I've played various versions of UnReal World over the past 12+ years, including dozens of hours on this latest version which is being released on Steam. It's got a lot of attributes of a rogue-like: turn-based movement, permanent death, lots of stuff to discover, lots of stuff to craft. Somewhere in its development, more than 10 years ago, it strayed from the path of being a fantasy game to being a simulation of iron-age Finland.
The combat system is straight-forward, but unforgiving. The character has skills for various weapons; combat results are based on attacker and defender results; damage is allocated to hit locations after accounting for armor. Positioning matters: getting behind an opponent allows unblocked attacks. Injuries matter: serious blows to the legs can lame or cripple a creature, a hard blow to the head or even torso can stun. Combat can be drawn out or over quickly, depending on the hidden rng and positioning, so new players are advised to tread carefully at first. Or, you can accept that it's a rogue-like, and just get killed and restart.
If your character can survive or avoid combats, time will pass. You'll have to keep your character fed or starvation penalties will mount. You'll have to think about water, and warmth, and shelter. And eventually, maybe before your character is fully prepared, winter will arrive. In the UnReal World, winter changes the game. For about five game-months you need to stay warm and stay fed. Every day will be short. Every night will be long. The leading cause of death in winter might be boredom; the cabin fever and the routine of safe survival becomes too much and the player takes a character out to adventure in the great white north, into the teeth of a blizzard. Some of them make it back to their cabins. Having said that, with good fur clothes and ski equipment, a character can do a lot of hunting and trapping through the winter, or timberwork, or any number of other tasks.
I think my characters have died every way possible in this game. I'll let you discover the various ways, and head off myself for further adventures. Enjoy!
