PLEASE NOTE: I've only played through the first 2 and a half levels at the time of this review. This game is amazing! It's controls are simple, but what it lacks in complexity with controls, it more than makes up for with complexity in gameplay, much like the old style of video games this gem is based off of. Basically, the first level starts out relativley simple, getting you used to the cloaking and stealth aspects of the game. It forces you to learn what traps do what and how to avoid them by a bit of trial and error. I find this system MUCH better than outright telling you or forcing you through a tutorial, because it lets the player feel like they figured it out themselves and earned it. With regards to death or getting, the game is very generous, but in the right ways. Each time you get to a checkpoint, a nice little beep happens. There are checkpoints every one or two screens or so, so death won't set you back to far. Worried it sounds a bit too easy? It's not! This game is so generous with checkpoints because each area is very challenging. I've only played on normal mode so far and it's very difficult, but there's a harder difficulty as well. Pretty much, this game forces you to figure out how to get through a room's traps and guards, then use quick reflexes and timing to get through; it's a beautiful blend of puzzle solving and skill. Gameplay-wise I find this game to be nearly perfect (something VERY rare for me to say!). Now that I've shared my thoughts on the most important aspect, I'll move on to the more aesthetic parts of the game. The soundtrack is amazing! Definitley pick it up if you enjoy the music in the trailer. The graphics are very stylized to look like an old DOS game or something, and the virtual screen is curved to simulate the curve of an old monitor. The graphics are beautiful in their own way, and add some mystique to the game (perfect for a spy game!). The cutscenes, music, and sound effects work together very well to set a mysterious atmosphere. I have next to no complaints (again VERY rare for me to say). As someone who enjoys old NES games and a good challenge, I wholeheartedly reccomend this game.

Master Spy is a fantastic stealth-platformer. It's an difficult, yet rewarding experience that involves you having to work out how to get through a room and then having to execute on that plan without being caught. The enemies/obstacles individually feature some basic, yet very readable behaviors which is important in a stealth game. Those enemies/obstacles are combined and tied together wonderfully to with the level design to bring out some really intense and awesome moments.
On top of all of that is some great pixel art and music. Both of these tie together very well to bring out an awesome 80's action movie/NES aesthetic. This game also features cutscenes which are wonderfully reminiscent of Ninja Gaiden and help drive that aesthetic home.
I very much recommend this game to everyone, but especially to anyone who enjoys platformers, stealth action games, or anyone who likes the idea of MGS1's arcadey stealth being transformed into a platformer and painted over with a coat of 80's action/NES aesthetics.

Disclaimer: If you are a sim racing fan, do NOT buy this title. If you are a console gamer that is looking to branch out towards sim racing then DO buy this game.
What I mean by the above paragraph is that this game is not even close to good enough for a sim racing fan. The amount of modding and configuration changes needed just to make this halfway decent isn't worth the trouble since there are plenty of better games out there right out of the box.
However, for people who are used to racing games on consoles or using handheld controllers then this is a good experience to be had for someone getting their first wheel and looking to try something different.
The core concepts are there so someone with their first wheel can learn to drive before moving on to a proper sim racing title later on.
The car selection is decent for this type of game. The track selection though is weak and the licensed tracks are actually incredibly inaccurate. This came as a huge surprise to me since some of the developers for this game started out working with a different developer that built proper racing sims so you would think they would have known something was off.
In conclusion:
Sim racing fans? Pass
New to racing games? Give it a try

Analogue is a pure visual novel, has little gameplay, and is a much more passive experience than Digital: A Love Story (which is free and I humbly suggest you play first).  Despite its multiple endings, Analogue is much more straigthforward than Digital; you should not be at a loss for what to do more than once or twice.  Also, the dialogue choices rarely matter beyond a given conversation.  I didn't see this as a problem as it adds much needed interaction with the characters, but it may conflict with your expectations.
The game is passive but not unengaging.  At the very least, the documented narratives should unsettle you but it is balanced with a decidedly less depressing and more interactive overarching story.  That being said, some story arcs are less interesting than others.
I realize this kind of game doesn't appeal to everyone, but if it interests you I doubt it will disappoint.

Yes, the development has been slow. Yet, it has been ongoing.
What do I love about this game? Mainly the vision of where it's going. God, would I love to see this game finished!
The current state of the game is decent.
There's some great multiplayer action, with a dynamic twist to the levels (lighting changes, heights change, soundscapes change). There are some co-op  missions with a story, and some other co-op game-modes you could just jump into and play some. And ofcourse, there's Hell Week. Hell Week is a sandbox consisting of 9 maps, where you compete against other players. At first, I wasn't too sure about this game-mode, as it could take ages for something to happen. But since the addition of teaming up, AI-controlled CTR's patrolling the maps and the Supply Drops it's getting a lot more fun.
The atmosphere works great as well. The Neurogen Incident is particulary tense and scary at times.
We just need the development to go faster, and there's only one way of doing it: supporting Zero Point Software as much as we can, by providing feedback, money (so they could hire extra people) and patience.

Tales from the Borderlands is a pretty bad game with a decent story.
The highlight here is clearly the story and the characters. The game does a pretty good job of advancing the Borderlands storyline and is much better written than anything in the main series. The two lead characters are both pretty interesting, especially Fiona. The game also makes a great use of the existing characters from earlier Borderlands games. Out of the supporting cast, Sasha was really the only one I didn't really care for.
Too bad that on the gameplay front the game is much less impressive. The gameplay is your usual Telltale fare, heavy on QTEs, light on any kind of compelling gameplay. The game tries to offer bit more action than is usual for Telltale, but it is very clearly the engine is simply not built to properly support this.

I don't normally like anime and I don't generally go for visual novels so I am hardly this games target audience. That is assuming there is a target audience, but as a person who craves new and different experiences in video games I would whole heartedly recommend Analogue.
To label Analogue as a visual novel isn't exactly fair.  It's something between that a kind of puzzle game. You're tasked with recovering the logs of a derelict spaceship and to do this you have to interact with two different AI programs each with their own perspective on the events that lead to the population of the ship being wiped out.
The game's creator does a nice job of playing to and eventually subverting the kinds of tropes you expect from a game like this. The quality of the writing is strong though occasional use of certain modern colloquialisms seem out of place and slightly jarring.  The one question that was most puzzling to me, namely why a futuristic bunch of intergalactic travelers would adopt the culture and esthetics of feudal Korea, remained unanswered, but whatever.
If  you're looking for something different, and I usually am, then play this. It's interesting and often emotionally engaging.

A very well crafted and stylish twitch platformer.  The game combines vanilla platformer gameplay with a core mechanic of stealth/avoidance, which rewards precision and forethought.  As the game progresses, new obstacles and mechanics are added at a very steady pace - just as you've started to get the hang of one death-trap, it throws a new one (or two) into the mix.  By the later stages of the game, you'll have to navigate some truly terrifying areas that want to chop you up in just about every way imaginable - but the levels are cleverly designed and follow a clear logical pattern.  You'll find that, as with most spy movies, if you move fearlessly and don't hesitate, the right moment will often present itself - you will always have just the right amount of time to jump away from that tiger, and find just the right window to slide between two guards, and have just the right timing to land on a spike trap as it disarms.
That's what it's about - evading certain death by the skin of your teeth and living to spy another day.  It's a really gratifying challenge, and it's accompanied by beautiful cut-scenes and music that give the game tons of style and charisma.  After beating the game, I'm really interested in revisiting the levels to find any extras and see if I can cut down on my times.

Let me begin by stating that you are better off playing Digital: A Love Story before you play this game. You can play it and understand it, but it would be better for you to play that before you play this, at least to get the gist of what Christine Love is about with her writing. But anyway, here's my review of the game, trying to prevent any spoilers to the best of my abilities:
SUMMARY:
The time is... Very far into the future. After the horrific events of "Digital: A Love Story" that took place in the alternate future of 1982, we are introduced to the idea that a machine that the government created had a slight knowledge constrainment complex. The computer decided to split its components to learn the most about the one thing that it could not comprehend: Human emotion. Therefore, the one thing the computer tried to emulate was humans; some capable of something the computer, affectionately named "Mother" by the seperate constructs, had not been prior: Love.
Much later in time, humanity has developed brilliant technologies: one of them being the fact that you can travel through space with Light Speed and beyond, with several colonies set up around the galaxy. However, the thing is, colonies had to be set up the hard way years before: Generation Vessels. A Generation Vessel is a huge vessel capable of containing an entire society for literally generations while they head for the next planet to colonize. However, there's a problem. When society is contained in such a way that leaves the beurocrats, the power-hungry and the overall morons to run the ship, eventually people forget things. Things that might be important. For instance, why you're even floating in space to begin with. And so the sad tale of the Mugunghwa begins with, ironically, it becoming lost in space for years.
This is where you come in. As a freelance worker, you get a job from the Museum after the Mugunghwa suddenly appears out of nowhere, completely derelict. As you enter the console and try to log in, you realize you can't obtain the files you require to complete the mission without help. Good thing there's an AI in charge of the ship named *Hyun-ae who's more than willing to help you find the password... Or maybe a little more, especially since there's a discrepency: an AI named *Mute is supposed to be in charge of the ship, not *Hyun-ae, and the fact that a recurring character by the name of "The Pale Bride" keeps appearing in the log documents... What link does she have with what happened to the Mugunghwa?
STORYTELLING:
I would like to point out that the storytelling in this game is fantastic. It's perfectly paced, however you need to take one thing into consideration: The logs that appear are not in chronological order, until others are unlocked. Speaking of which, how you answer questions reveal different logs for you to read, as well as the different logs you show *Hyun-ae, the different logs you would recieve if you showed the same to *Mute. Aside from the jumbled chronology, it's really well done, and I commend Christine Love highly for it.
Plus, when you actually get to spend some time talking to the AI themselves, I found myself wishing that I could actually be speaking to them, Cortana style. (Actually, if someone blends the Cleverbot program with this thing, that would be awesome) They are rather life-like, and that's fantastic. It made me care about the characters, and that is really awesome, especially for a game.
GAMEPLAY:
Ah yes, this is something that shouldn't really even be an element in Visual Novels, should it? Kind of goes against what the Visual Novel thing actually is. But in this, I must say, when you have to step in and make big decisions -- and there are several, and some will make you sweat -- you really have to think about them. There is some actual gameplay in there, so it isn't a glorified clicking or space bar simulator, or anything, though the "gameplay" is really just a console you have to wrestle with. There was one point when the game... Well, I will abstain from the details, but I felt legitimately relieved, intelligent and glad I love Sci-Fi afterward. It's awesome, and it is one of the things that makes this game awesome.
SOUND:
There are no voice actors, much unlike Steins;Gate, Chaos;Head or most other Visual Novels, which means the only real sounds are the generic button sounds and the soundtrack. Now, the generic button sounds are actually quite good, and I quite enjoy the sound that plays when you show a log to the AI. But the real thing that I enjoy about the sound is the music. The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic, and I highly reccommend you buy the Soundtrack with it. It's really well made, and it conveys what is happening perfectly. It's very atmospheric, and I quite enjoy it.
REPLAY VALUE:
There is no linear plot. It has something of seven different endings, meaning you are going to get a bucketload of replay value in this. Plus, there are tons of achievements and tons of logs for you to unlock!
OVERALL:
What can I say? You can dress *Hyun-ae in a lab coat and she makes a Steins;Gate reference. You can't go wrong with this game. However, if you do not like Visual Novels, I might play Digital: A Love Story first.

It is *hard* though, you're going to lose a lot and have to learn from your mistakes.
Great music too (just listen to the trailer). Very authentic sounding retro sound effects.
Backgrounds are lovely and apparently all are hand-pixeled, the cinematics are really neat too. It feels like the cinematics were really pulled from the glory days of pixely adventure games, rather than being retro for retro's sake. Everything feels very lovingly crafted.

So I really wanted this game for months, but the price was too steep for me.  When it went down temporarily in November, I jumped on the chance to buy it.  Now that I have had a few months to play it, here is what I think.
I don't really care for the whole argument about shading, brightness, or any of that.  But there are some drawbacks with the graphics.  First of all, most of the common "cannon fodder" enemies have their heads moving away from their bodies.  I mean it is really easy to see that the heads are simply not attached and are weaving away from the bodies.  I thought that was kind of annoying.  To add to this, you will often see their weapons floating right next to them rather than being held.  On the plus side, it kind of makes you feel like you are killing a bunch of Jedi or Sith, just pretend those weapons are being held by the Force.  However, part of these faults can also be found on major characters like Kuro, Aokiji, Usopp, and Ivankov but with these guys the problem is the hair.  With Kuro you may find his hair floating a few inches away from his head, making it seem like he is bald.  After a few moments of laughing it became a little annoying.  As for the others, the dynamics between their head and their hair is annoying in that the hair will often move independently and block your view of the character's faces.  It may not seem like much for some, but I was really aggravated by that.
I absolutely adore the gameplay.  It is fun, objectives will change which will keep you on your toes, and the interactions between major characters can be very enjoyable.  Sometimes the objectives will not be that clear, but you can just wing it and figure it out along the way.  The gameplay can be hard at first but if you have too much difficulty, go to Dream Log and level your characters up.  The downside is that eventually as you level your characters up, the gameplay becomes really easy even in the Hard difficulty.  If you ever want a REAL challenge, then try the Nightmare Log.  Now THAT is a challenge.
Dream Log I found to be an absolute gem.  It is a great way to unlock characters, level up, and get rare coins to further improve your characters.  And all of the island missions have themes that border on weird to absolutely hilarious.  For example, one mission is Men vs Women.  I was on the side of the men, and who was on my side?  Akainu, Blackbeard, and a bunch of other male pirates with Akainu saying we have to win for Justice.  There was just something about that whole thing that had me cracking up.  Keep in mind that on all of these missions, the characters who appear will be completely randomized.  The only things you can choose are who to play as, which side to select if the option is available, which costume to use, and how to strengthen your character.
For the main story, there are two options.  The main one is where you play any arc in the story with a handful of characters that coincide with the arc from the anime/manga.  The other option is the Free Log in which you can play any arc you want but the difference is you can play as any character you have unlocked.  Do you want to storm Impel Down as Akainu or Whitebeard?  In the Free Log you can do that.  Also, each arc has a percentage rating of how well you complete the requirements in said arc.  The more of the requirements that you complete, the better your percentage rating, and as such the better rewards you will get upon completion.  Some of these rewards are rare coins that you cannot get anywhere else that can help to boost your characters' stats, give them a new special, or give them a new costume.  You will find that if you want all of the rewards, or maybe are just a perfectionist, there is a LOT of replay value because the game will reward you if you strive for an S-class rating in everything.  And do not worry, unlike some games you will not be penalized for taking damage, healing yourself, or performing a bunch of specials.  You are evaluated on other criteria that I will not divulge.
The tutorial I found to be very disappointing.  While they try to be helpful, they are often unclear and when they tell you which keys will do what, they use symbols instead of the actual keys to tell you.  For example, they use one symbol that looks like a pink shooting star and tell you what it will do.  Problem is, I don't know about you but I do not have a pink shooting star on my computer.  So you have to go into the options menu to figure things out on what symbols stand for what keys.  It is annoying but after awhile it becomes second nature and you can pull of pretty cool moves really easily.  The lack of clarity is also clear for several optional events in the game, so you will probably find yourself going online to help get some clarity as to what needs to be done and how.
There are a lot of characters to choose from, and I love this.  I love having options and you will more than likely find a few of your favorites are available to play.  However, you will also find a bunch of characters you cannot play and yet are still in the game as allies or enemies.  Fortunately, that does not stop you from being able to perform cool specials with them.  Unlike a bunch of other games, you will find that each character is unique.  They do not do the same punch, kick, grapple thing that you will find every character doing in some games.  Each character has their own unique actions and abilities that makes each play through feel completely new and special.  Now there is one playable character that I will list as both a pro and a con (Unnamed because it's a spoiler).  The con is that they have not appeared to fight in the series yet, so we know very little of what they can do.  As such, I feel like the developers jumped into this character too soon.  The pro though is that they are an absolute blast to play.  Their specials are also awesome and coincidentally have the coolest names.
As for DLC, it is for some but not for others.  I bought the two packs on Steam for extra Dream Log missions and costumes and I adore them.  I will be honest though, I care more for the costumes than the missions and trust me, I love the costumes.  There is an extra set of costumes not on Steam but you can just go to the Bandai Namco site, become a member for free, and you can download the extra set for free.  Also, other than just adding some very nice aesthetics, the costumes themselves also offer new abilities.  Equip your character with their New World costume, and they will have access to their New World abilities.  Keep in mind though, even if you have those new abilities, if your character is not at a high enough level then you will still struggle on even the easier missions.
So in conclusion here is what I think:
Cons:
- Graphics need improving.  They look nice but there is a serious problem when it interferes with the characters.
- Gamplay does get a bit repetitive after a while
-Even on hard, can still be a little too easy.
- Tutorial is terrible
- Some of the optional mission events, like Treasure Events are not clear so you will have to go online to figure them out.
-  The game finished before the Dressrosa Arc was finished in the manga, as such the game and the manga will differ on the arc.
Pros:
- Very fun gameplay
- The game gives some very good incentives to getting 100% or S-Class on missions and Dream Log.  As such, a lot of replay value.
- Large selection of characters.  You will almost be guaranteed to find one of your favorites to be playable.
- Costumes, while adding a great deal to aesthetics, also affect gamplay.  New World Costumes grant that character the ability to use their New World abilities.
While there are a lot of cons, if you can get past these then I highly recommend that you buy the game.  It is truly a blast.  While I do believe it is worth the current price of $49.99, I would still recommend waiting for it to go down.

The repopulation has greatly improved since the 10.2 patch which did a wipe and merged the servers. The game itself is amazing and one of the most complex MMO's to date. It has a very complex craftingsystem and it is almost impossible to make everything yourself, but you can if you really want to. If I'd had to compare it to something it would be to SWG, but instead of lots of professions there are lots and lots of skills. From entertainer and storyletter to one of many crafting professions. You can not only improve your profession skill but even specialize in making a certain item or killing a certain enemy, in that way it surpasses even SWG in complexity. You can also recieve NPC missions and select which you want to recieve so you can do combat missions, non-combat missions, trade missions, diplomatic missions and more.
There are a few downsides, this is not a AAA MMO and it shows. The graphics are mediocre and the playerbase is a lot smaller. There is however an activa playerbase and the GM's are also very helpful and respond fast. While the current game is great there are still stability issues, it can crash on loading a new map or sometimes even at random after a few hours. The crashes aren't so frequent that it becomes unplayable though.
There are daily hotfixes and the game is being worked on with some major changes to the map incoming. I really believe this game is an underappreciated gem and deserves more attention. It is complex and doesn't hold your hand so you will spend some time reading what you need to get what. You can also place workorders to let people work for you to get what you need. There is no limit to what you can learn, but because there is so much to learn it pays to specialize. If you are looking for the average MMO that holds your hand, this is the wrong place but if you enjoy complex gameplay this is the game for you. I can't wait for the actual release.

Allowign the player to choose what style of character Conway is what really makes this game special. The player gets 3 basic choices of personality: stoic, crazy, and not-giving-a♥♥♥♥♥♥ All 3 are wonderful, and this alone would make me recommend this game, but when you add on the exceptionally fun gameplay, Gunpoint stands above many other puzzle-platformers of its ilk.

Portal by Pixar. It's not on the same level as Portal but it does it's own thing and makes it work. The levels are heavily physics-based mechanical challenges rather than the "this should logically be impossible find the loophole" puzzles that Portal sets up, and the game is unapologetic about this. The main reason I approve of this choice is the "slow" dimension, which is basically "remember those ridiculous Quicksilves scenes in the recent xmen movie? Here's a game of that". The ridiculous spectacle of what this game has you do makes it memorable to me.
That said, the game is very much "style over substance". It's got the Pixar aesthetic, the wacky physics puzzles on a crazy scale, and that's basically it. There isn't much story to speak of, or much sense of progression until you hit a new third of the game. If you want to live out the aforementioned Quicksilves scenes and aren't hung up on the above flaws, give this a shot.

Going into Quantum Conundrum i expected a Portal like expierence but with different dimensions to toggle, especially because Portal's former lead designer "Kim Swift" worked on this game. And yes, there are some similarities like going from room to room to solve "puzzles" and a narrator making dumb but often funny jokes. But sadly the puzzles aren't as great.... I expected brain twisting and greatly designed puzzles. But what we got are puzzle like environments based more on momentum and physics than actually solving diffecult puzzles. This however is fun and original aswell, it creates a good balance between solving puzzles and platforming.
Now i really enjoyed my time with Quantum Conundrum. The game has great cartoony graphics and the mad scientist voiced by "John de Lancie" is quite funny sometimes. And even though the game is rather short, this actually benefits the game in my opinion. For me the length was perfect, around the point it all got a bit repetitive the end was near. Something else Quantum Conundrum does really well is create a original and great universe. Everything is made really well, and just fits. Unfortunately the ending is rushed and just not satisfying in anyway.... And although the game has a great balance between puzzles and physics, timing certain actions can get frustrating at times.
I still recommend this game to any puzzle fan out there. It's a fun and challenging puzzle platformer with a well made atmoshpere. The game will take you around 4 to 6 hours to finish. However there are alot of collectables and achievements to get if you would like to get the game on 100%.

On a nostalgia level, this game delivers--the gameplay, graphics and sound are dead-on.  The controls are more crisp than any NES/SEGA platformer, and the lack of hardware limitations means the backgrounds are absolutely beautiful.
From a storytelling level, this game is also a near masterpiece--the so-contrived-its-almost-dada dialogue pairs perfectly well with the over-the-top plot, and the vector cutscenes tie the whole affair together beautifully--everything works together perfectly here.
From a level design standpoint, Master Spy has a spelunky-style education system, where the game introduces new hazards and problems then encourages you to solve them via repeated death.  Unlike spelunky Master Spy has mid-scene checkpoints, meaning the game avoids some of the frustration problems you might get with Spelunky-like games.
This game is a fantastic example of mechanics, aesthetic and narrative all working together to produce a fantastic gaming experience.  10/10.

I don't have much experience with this type of game. I have played a few like it but most were free online games that were not very good. Picked this game up on a steam sale and it has gotten me interested in this genre. The gameplay is pretty much reading through letters and journal entries,  trying to understand what caused the death of the ships inhabitants. The best part of the game to me would be the two A.I. programs, the soundtrack, and the way you interact with the game.
The game introduces you to the two A.I.s and they are fun to be with. Sure they play up to some stereotypes and some people will get upset that the choices you make with them basically boil down to being nice or being rude with no gray area. I like this because if the relationships in the game were as complicated as real life then it would be frustrating. The two A.I.s are fun enough to listien to and interact with. I did not find a single time that I found myself wishing that they would shut up (though to be fair I only went through the game once and so have limited experince with one of the A.I.s.) The tedium of reading letters and journal entries are broken up by showing the letters to the A.I.s and getting their view of it which can be radically different depending who you show it to. This fleshes out the story while allowing you to get to know the A.I.
The soundtrack of the game is fun to listen to. It re-enforces the space theme of the game and changes at some of the more important parts. I can't say much more about the soundtrack since I am a pleb with little knowledge of music. All I can say is that I love music from video games that I can listen to in the backround and this serves that purpose. It is a soundtrack that I do plan on buying.
Finally I enjoy the way that you interact in the game. You start the game at a computer terminal, typing in commands. The rest of the game is spent going through screens, reading journals and interacting much the same way you would if it was actually your computer. I have not played a lot of games that used this set up so it may just be the novelty speaking but I felt less disconnected from the game than other games I have played in the similar vein (again, a very small pool.) The computer interface is used very effectively about half-way through the game in a way that was loads of fun.
Overall I really enjoyed this game. Is it worth 10$? I can't answer that because I bought it for less and am new to the genre and don't know the average cost of these games. I enjoyed it and if you can get it on a steam sell I would suggest you do. I had fun and there is some replay value with the multiple endings. So to me it was worth it and I might pick up the sequel at full price with the soundtrack.

So far Master Spy has been recommended by all 18 to review before me. Why toss my hat in at this point? Because this game deserves it. The release was too recent to call it a hidden gem, but it's definitely a gem that deserves more positive reviews.
Chances are if you've navigated to this page you have some interest in this type of game. If so, I have only one thing to ask before wholeheartedly recommending this game. Are you very put off by having to die many times in the process of learning and then pulling off heavily execution-intensive plans? If not, get this game. Everything about the game works extremely well, particularly the soundtrack and controls - both important in such a rigorous platformer. It is true what others have said: Master Spy is frustrating because of how demanding it is, but almost never unfair.
It took me probably a little long to beat Novice Mode at 5.7 hours, as I kept grinding through levels even when my execution was slacking badly, but there are harder modes and a little extra content already revealed to me so far. If you're worried about playtime, I will definitely be playing more of this game, and even at this point I would definitely say it is worth $10.

No C6 ZR1 :( What a shame. I'll be comparing this to Gran Turismo 5 because IMO its basically Gran Turismo with Porsches and a much smaller selection of cars (no Ferraris).
Pros:
- One thing I really like about this game is when you switch to 3rd Person, Hood-cam, or bumper cam, it doesn't do what Gran Turismo does and gives you the games default tach and speedo. Instead it gives you your car's factory tach and speedo.
- When you buy and mod a car, if you sell it back, you get all your money back hence why I flip my cars very often and the sole reason why I don't have a permanent fleet. Applies to cars that have "Work" done to it. I personally think its a great thing :P

- Don't have a racing wheel, gearbox, or pedals. But Gamepad #28 allows you to use clutch :D
- Compared to Gran Turismo at least, this game has slightly more freedom when it comes to tuning in most aspects. If you get "Work" done to your car or you have a Tier 4, you can adjust aerodynamic bits and pieces in much greater detail than GT. Brake Cooling Ducts is an example.
- Compared to Gran Turismo, cosmetic customization (paint, vinyl, decal) is better IMO. Aero kits....slightly better, not much of a selection and its a full kit, you can't select individual pieces to slap on like GT. Wheel selection a lot better.
-THE SOUNDS! MMMMMMM DAT V10 THO. No seriously the engine sounds are pretty nice. Way better compared to Gran Turismo....not even worth comparing. Its on a whole other level. If you play a lot of other NFS games, you can definitely tell they use the same sounds. But thats one thing I like about NFS games, the engine sounds are on point for the most part. Never been disappointed by the engine sounds in a NFS title from the ones I've played that is...which isn't many (Rivals was my first, MW2012, SHIFT, SHIFT 2, Hot Pursuit, mobile NFSMW).
Cons:
- As one of the reviews pointed out, not all the cars can get "Work" done to them so you can't get the S13 to like Tier 3-4 or whatever. but I don't really care since I flip cars every 30 minutes.
- I do dislike the aerodynamics upgrade section (just upgrades in general) and how when you go up in tiers, you get less body kits. For example, Tier 1 you get Stage 1-3 body kits, cockpit upgrades, and weight reduction, and just overall upgrades. Tier 2 however, you only get Stage 2 and 3, Tier 3 is only Tier 3. Tier 4 gets nothing. I get that its not Gran Turismo where you can make your Corvette ZR1 or Ford GT have 830+hp with a top speed of 240+mph (can confirm my C6Z and Ford GT in GT5 has hit speeds over 240+) but at the very least give us more than just one stage of aero upgrades, and cockpit upgrades since both of these are cosmetic (bodykits improve braking according to the game). I don't want my C6Z to have a giant wing and full race kit. What if I want something simple like a Supervettes ZR6X kit? What if all I want is a tiny lip spoiler and a front splitter? Nah you get a full race-kit instead. Not a super big deal I guess, it does limit tuning IMO.
- One thing I liked about Gran Turismo was the power limiter when you tuned your cars. Sadly that is not a tuning option here. I'd say there is a little more freedom in tuning compared to Gran Turismo but they don't have engine tuning which is....not a big deal I guess? I'd like to limit the power outputfrom my monster Vette so I don't roast my tires in 2nd.
- Cosmetic thing but on the Veyron at least, the rear wing/spoiler doesn't pop up at 150mph (or whatever speed its suppose to activate). Not that I've noticed at least. Seems like the car(s) that have automated wings don't actually use them.
- Never been on any of these tracks IRL but I don't think some of these sections are THAT bumpy. Like VERY bumpy. You hit that invisible bump in the road and you'll bounce to the damn moon while also losing all the positions and dropping every single position in existence.
- When you go off track, you can reset your car back on the track, I'm not sure if its because of my control layout or game balance, but when you do this, your car stalls and takes forever to start up again (not always the case but it happens), valuable time wasted trying to get the car moving again.
- This is most likely on my end but sometimes when you downshift, I do heel-toe downshifts, but a lot of times when i flick the joystick to downshift and blip the gas, the gas gets blipped, but the the gear change never happened/registered completely. You'll see your character model reach for the shifter but you don't change gears. Sometimes I need to drop a few gears and you guessed it, didn't downshift at all. Could be my controller, could be the game, its a thing and I'm putting it out there.
Conclusion: I personally quite enjoy the game, its not too complicated, Great car selection IMO. SOME of the cons can be ignored/overlooked. The bumpy sections....you'll want to rip your hair out when you're first but the magic bump or oil slick causes you to go off track.

Even as someone who isn't normally a fan of, nor an expert at, stealth platformers, this is a great game in my eyes. The mechanics are unique, but not so convoluted that you lose track of what does what; the controls are simply "move, jump, and crouch to cloak", and the obstacles are fairly easy to comprehend the point of even without tripping them. Simple, but effective. And of course, the retro-style graphics, sounds, and music make for a great throwback to the old days; the plot, however, is in no way "old", as it manages to keep you intrigued the whole way through. However, I shall avoid elaborating on that so as to avoid spoilers.
The goal in each room is to collect the key cards to unlock the elevator at the end, and then get into the elevator. You must avoid guards, cameras, motion detectors, guard dogs, and plenty of other interesting obstacles and traps that almost become absurd (spinning sawblades and sleeping tigers? Someone apparently decided to spend their promotion paycheck on security advancements). A simple goal, but difficult to pull off without quite becoming frustrating. You need
timing, reflexes, and a keen eye; much more interesting than the usual "crawl around and hide behind walls" that seems to plague a lot of stealth games these days.
I haven't beaten this game, but I can safely say that it will provide a very nice challenge even to those of you who consider yourselves particularly good at stealth platformers. Definitely worth the money and then some.

Eve is one of the most amazing games I've ever played. Its single shard universe, player driven economy and risk-reward gameplay mark it out as something quite special. There is not much else currently like it, and its PVP is what has kept me playing regularly since I first started playing four years ago. I've sunk many, many hours into it, though they don't show up here since I've not launched it through steam until it's recent switch to f2p. I can't stress enough how much I have enjoyed the PVP in this game over the years.
It might sound like a glowing reccomendation at this point, but it's important to clarify that what's kept me so hooked for so long has always been the player driven content, fueled by the interactions and conflicts that are possible due to the sandboxy nature of Eve. When it comes to content created directly by the developers themselves, well lets just say that aspect is very poor. The underlying game has changed very little since I've been here, and many so called improvements such as interface redesigns have been for the worse. They are obsessed with upgrading the graphics at the expense of stability, (I'd have been happier with annual graphics overhauls) and they are also obsessed with fixing bugs to the exclusion of almost everything else, especially new content. New content comes in drips and drabs with most so called expansions being awash with nothing but bug fixes. And, with so little content released, the chances are whatever they do add in any particular exansion will be irrelevant to you personally. In the entire 4 year period I played the game they added barely 2 new ships that fitted my playstyle to where I could use them day in day out.
I can't honestly recommend it because of how little new content has been added to the game, and also how mind-numbingly boring all the PVE is. If I'm paying a monthly subscription to "play" a game I expect there to be some compelling content that makes me want to "play", and none of the PVE content in Eve is compelling enough to want to play for its own sake. After a couple of years in Eve the optimal playstyle is to log on for PVP and play other games the rest of the time.This led me to question why the developers even deserve my subscription money. After a lot of soul searching, the conclusion I reached is that they don't! Having had 13 years to come up with fun PVE I doubt that they are going to magically find their inspiration now. With the introduction of the cash shop it's in their best interest to maintain things the way thay are since this encourages players to purchase PLEX rather than spend their time making ISK through playing the game.
I know from the comments that there are those who will read this and lack the experience in Eve to fully grasp what I'm saying. So let me attempt to clarify. I have access to highclass wormholes, incursions, and I have a good industrial setup, I have no problems making ISK if I need to. My issue with Eve is that none of the PVE in the game is compelling enough to play for the enjoyment of the activity alone. Eventually the activity is done for the isk alone. Hence grindy.
Why am I paying to play a game I don't play? The compelling reason to play Eve is the player interaction, and that player interaction is not a resource that CCP have a monopoly on. I had just as much fun in Ultima Online back in the day. Any sandbox will do. I'm not paying £10 a month for a game where the developers think a ship and some bugfixes is an "expansion", nor do I think anybody else should settle either. So, while I've had a good run, I have decided to look for an alternative that has both old-school full-loot PVP, and PVE that is engaging enough to be worth doing for its own sake.
Some have asked in the comments, if I love the game so much, how can I not reccommend it? Eve's biggest problem is its business model, it was created when subscription was the only viable option in town, and only a brand new game can overcome those problems. There are three other large full loot MMOs currently in development since the world is getting bored of WoW clones.
Eve has taught me that the subscription model is dead. CCP has very little incentive to add new content, and that's exactly what's happened. Newer games that use a Buy to pay model are where I personally feel the future is in, since customers can buy once and play with no restrictions, developers are incentivised to add new content since selling new content is how they make their money, and customers only need to pay for the content that interests them. I know there will be challenges adapting buy to play to work in the context of a full-loot pvp mmo, but I think someone somewhere will manage it. And I am content to wait.
Due to the old fashioned business model, CCP got complacent. So little content has been added to Eve over the years that I could actually be happy playing as an alpha full time. Alpha encompases the ships that I already spend 99% of my time in, despite having 80 million skillpoints. But why would I bother when I could play something else which offers at least the promise of new content.
Regardless of my lack of overall recommendation, if you love PVP, crafting, or trading, then you owe it to yourself to try it anyway and make up your own mind.

There are just not enough detective/sluth games out there. Not enough games make you feel like that underground vigilante, trying to manipulate the intrigue between competeting factions. Even less games allow you to be a clever spy tinkering with your electronic environment to outsmart guards and enemy spies. It's hard to fine that "Yes!" feeling when an intricate plan goes perfectly according to plan, leaving no witness and no casualties. There's just a certain smug satisfaction you get from watching guard try to turn a light back on, only to be opening doors or turning other lights off elsewhere. It's a certain satisfaction you can only really get out of Gunpoint right now.
I'll make this somewhat brief. You should buy Gunpoint. It's an incredibly clever and fun game with lots of funny and well written dialog along with fantastic stealth gameplay. There are multiple-ish ways around each level depending on what upgrades you've gone for, and there are multiple storylines you can follow, although they don't ultimately effect the final ending. It is an incredibly polished and thought-out game, and you should play it.
Although, you might want to wait for a sale. If there is a problem with Gunpoint, it's that it's way, way to short. Took only a little more than two hours to beat, and while there is some incentive to replay levels for a better rating or follow different contracts, there isn't much incentive to spend that much time with the game after beating it. There is a workshop, but it's fairly limited. There are a few good maps, but a lot of them are just boring or broken, and there's rarely something new uploaded. So, if you're the type that needs to maximize bang for your buck, $10 for 2 hours of gameplay might be too steep a price, and you might want to wait for the sale.
But at some point, you should buy and play this game. Simply put, it's fantastic.

The game is really amazing. Couldn't afford it when it was sub-based, but thanks to that brilliant move on the part of CCP now I can. I think EVE would be probably my first MMO that I'll pay in for anything at all, that's how I'm in love with this game. Started yesterday, barely scratched the surface, but love it already. Well, while there are limitations to Alpha clones (free accounts), there are, the fact that you can buy premium status (Omega Clone) just for in-game currency (i.e. if you put enough work or find some rich sponsor, for free) fixes that problem. Obviously it takes time to get enough ISK to buy PLEX (item that when used gives you 30 day of premium/omega status) unless you're a beggar or get lucky with drop, but in other MMOs that have some kind of "premium" status, you can't even do that.
I really recommend anyone trying it out, if it's not your cup of your favorite beverage, that's okay. But since it costs literally nothing to try, why the hell not?

So Alone in the Dark. The series that inspired Resident Evil. Never really got into them. And I'd heard about this game for years and how terrible it is, but like always, I was like "how bad can it possibly be?" I mean, it was published by Atari and it ain't no crapass indie turdfest with its head shoved up its♥♥♥♥♥ Luckily, I am one of the few who can get this to run on Win7+, if the reviews on steam are any indication because it was a really halfassed port of a console game in the first place.
Anyway, this game is amazing. It's a perfect storm of completely insane design decisions (tank controls in a game from 2008, mind boggling control scheme, "press x to blink" mechanic (???), among others that i'll get to later) that combine into a sort of weird fever dream of impressive stupidity that made me laugh almost the entire time I was playing.
You start the game drugged and you have to press x to stop the screen from blurring, but it blurs so quickly you have to basically spam x, which means your screen is black 75% of the first five minutes of play, and some dude leads you up to the roof in order to execute you.♥♥♥♥♥♥goes south, and the first major part of the game is Tomb Raidering and fire fighting your way through an exploding building. Yes, fire fighting.
You have to switch back and forth between first and third person in order to use items, and both modes control completely differently. When in first person mode, it controls like a standard FPS, but when you switch to third, it switches to static camera tank controls like in the original survival horror games. No biggie, I thought, I'll just use first person mode the whole time. But you can't do that, and it just jarringly shifts you out of it without warning when it doesn't want you to use it. I died about five times in one of the first areas because of this sudden shift and the resulting change in controls.
The game is also super proud of its destructible environment mechanic so you spend a lot of time trying to smash through doors with a fire extinguisher. Unfortunately, the dude swings the thing in such a wide, awkward arc that you almost always slam the fire extinguisher into the wall next to the door. I figured out that the best way to do this is to face perpendicular to the door and kind of wiggle the fire extinguisher around until the door decides to swing open. It's ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic.
The first time you encounter an enemy, you run out of bullets almost immediately since it IS a survival horror game, and you spend the rest of the fight running around trying to find chairs to smash over her head. I finally found a lamp that i used to awkwardly pummel her into submission. Then I kicked her corpse into the rapidly spreading fire. And by kicked, i mean awkwardly shuffled around behind it until it triggered the next scripted event.
I stopped because it crashed, but this♥♥♥♥♥♥is a wild wild ride and I've never played such a spectacularly stupid (but entertainingly so) trainwreck in my life.

2015, I was looking for a really good game. I didn't know anything Dragon Ball, and I think I played one Dragon Ball Tenkaichi Budokai game on my ps2 a long time ago.
I came across Dragon Ball Xenoverse on Steam after realizing that the last Dragon Ball game I played was actually pretty fun.
I was anxious to buy this, so I watched some gameplay videos on Youtube. The game looked exactly like what I expected, and when I finally bought it and went into the game, it was out of this world. It was my favourite. I began watching the first Dragon Ball whilst playing Xenoverse's story mode, then Z, then GT, now Super. It feels like I've known Dragon Ball all my life, and I am now sitting at 1,700+ hours on Dragon Ball Xenoverse.
This is a game you can relax on the first few hours of playing, create your own character, do the whole story, unlock everything, max your level, do all the Parallel Quests, make all the maximum wishes to Shenron, learn the basics, and then get serious and dedicate to online PvP. Learn all the combat tricks, the mechanics, and surpass everyone. This is what Xenoverse is about.
You don't only get stronger with leveling. No, that's just the beginning. You get stronger with every new trick you learn, and I'm not just talking about the moves, I'm talking about how you can use them, combine them, find other uses for them. And you can never truly learn everything. There is so much to master, so much to test on dumb AI and then take into battle vs players.
Even with Xenoverse 2 coming out, this will always be a game I will revisit and play, because I just don't care. I love it.
And you should too, and if you don't, get it with Xenoverse 2. You can transfer your character from Xenoverse 1 to 2 later. We can all play them both as one masterpiece of a Dragon Ball game!
Give yourself an experience worth every penny it costs, even if you don't know what Dragon Ball is, because I didn't either.

I bought this game off the sales bin.That was  the best move, considering that the game is good but at the same time, rather rough around the edges.
The graphichs are great, with nice & colorful outdoor scenery predominenlty.Sound effects were generally okay,with the note that some of them are recycled from older CI titles.
The problem lies with the gameplay, rather uneven at some points, making the game progress a chore, not an enjoyful experience.While you get some interesting weapons, and levels, the game never gives you or itself, the chance to fully utilise them.The problem is that the entire game world is based on the engine of Crysis (CI made everything to advertise that) which by itself is a free-roaming, sandbox type of game.
EF is more scripted and moves in rails, and that contradicts with the mechanics of the engine.This in turn creates some weird outcomes, such as the enemy spotting your position accurately (even on open areas), when you use silenced weapons on one occasion, but hardly taking notice that their fellow soldier was killed, even if they stand next to them on other.
On other cases, the game might require you to do a specific task, -such as destroying a tank- but gives you just one antitank weapon to use, with one shot.If you miss, well, reload the level.
It's like writing a program in perfectly good code (which compiles great), but the programs' logic has flaws. Would I recommend this game?Yes, but not at full price.

i went into Tales from the borderlands without really knowing what to expect, and i gotta say this: i was not dissapointed with what it turned out to be. at first, i was worried that it was just a money grabber but boy, was i wrong.
pros:
- the main cast are all very well written and relatable, which is always extra nice in a game like this.
- the voice cast is phenomenal with big names like Troy Baker, Laura Bailey and Patrick Warburton, but Dameon Clarke as Handsome Jack really takes the cake for the best performance in this game.
- the humor from the original games really gets to shine through here, and it's as marvelous as ever.
- the relationship between Rhys, Vaughn, Fiona and Sasha is very interesting to witness (and be able to influence) since it's people from two extremely different cultures getting to know each other.
-you actually feel like you're influencing the story and the relationship between characters, unlike in some other familiar games.
-unlike the walking dead, it doesn't feel like TellTale is trying too hard to rip your heart out from the very first episode, barely even knowing the characters. They give you time to really care about these guys before stepping on your emotions.
- there are bad puns and refrences to other games. perfect.
- not a single moment feels like it's too stretched out, and it didn't feel like they were running out of time either. it's very well balanced.
- Loader bot is a pro in himself, but you knew that already.
- the music is amazing and each episode has it's own perfectly fitting track.
- the stunning cinematopraphy in the opening credits for each episode blows my mind every time.
Cons:
-the action scenes can be very confusing or frustrating because of awkward camera angles and/or editing
-TellTale and action scenes are not very good friends, so the animation can at times look akward or weird during those scenes.
- SPOILERS: in the last episode, Helios crashes. it's an Emotional moment, sure, but i think it was a huge waste of good space station and of borderlands history to let it go down like that
- SPOILERS: it is never explained how Athena gets out of her imprisonment, which they made out to be a HUGE deal, but this just made it feel irrelevant.
-broken money system. when you, as Fiona, steal money from a dead bandit, it at times does not go to your wallet and it just... dissapears?
tales from the borderlands is among the best game i've ver had the pleasure of playing, and i think it's a shame that it's so overshaddowed by games like the walking dead and the wolf among us. it's worth the price, and i wish for more people to get the amazing experience it is to follow Rhys and Fiona's take on the same story about trust, teamwork, survival and betrayal.

In my experience, Analogue: A Hate Story was a hard sell. There was that stubborn wait until it was on sale because I doubted it would be any fun at first glance. Now that I have experienced the story, my objective is to find and buy everything else in this series. The entertainment value is surprisingly high, considering this is little more than an interactive choose-your-own-adventure novel at first glance. Going without tips or hints was a challenge, and earning each ending so far has made each new secret unlocked feel like a big and well-earned reward. This is a genre I typically avoid, but I'm thinking I might just be addicted to it at this point. This isn't the sort of game for everyone, and some of the dialogue is unexpectedly irreverent, but this will remain a personal favorite of mine and a fun replay once a year at least.

"A.V.A is a very good game. I like it, it has good gameplay, and it's fun." Is something a child would say. I for one would say the game is on average.
-=Gameplay=-
This game has a veriaty of game modes, my favorite being senario, some include; Team Deathmatch, Anihilation, and many others. If you've played Combat Arms, you might like this. It still has the same rediculous recoil pattern, but the game has a less pay to win element. It influences teamwork and strategy and plays a bit like Battlefield. It has a simple 3 class system; Pointman, Assault, and Sniper. Pointman is out in the front with an SMG or shotgun, Assault is in the middle holding a rifle or MG to take down enemie in medium and short ranges, and Sniper, you would guess, takes people down from afar.
-=Weapons=-
Most weapons you have to pay with real world money to purchase, but earning ingame money is fast and easy. Even though there is a slight pay to win thing going on, ingame purchased items can just as easily kill other players as real world purchased items, not to mention the fact that you can rent most real world puchased items with ingame cash. All weapons have a insane recoil patten, as I said befor, but theres are easily obtainable attachments that can dull the recoil down. There are weapons that can be purchased for an unlimited amount of time but, they must be repaired over time. One last thing, there are lots of rewards for leveling up so you don't have to spend a lot of money.
-=Graphical Display=-
I cannot say much about it's graphics because I run it on low, but they look decent to my eyes.
-=Over All Score=-
I'd give the game a -6/10-

Getting one thing out of the way: calling this a stealth game, in my opinion, is a bit of a stretch. Sure, under the hood stealth is avoidance and timing so the line is blurred. But this one definitely belongs alongside super meat boy and other high precision platformers rather than stealth titles. But don't let this turn you off on the game, it's really fun to play.
The comparison to super meat boy is a good one. It learns from it. Repetition is good when it doesn't waste our time. So you die and instantly respawn. And you will die. A lot. In one chapter I died more than 400 times. We have a wide spectrum of mechanics to keep the game fresh, the invisibility cloak makes you invisible and slower, some enemies move back and forth, some only move when you have your back to them, others instantly jump at you independent of cloak etc. You learn as you go.
My main criticism is that these levels are quite big. This kind of gameplay of high precision, difficult, repetitive, works better with short levels. There is a checkpoint system in the game but I don't find it nearly generous enough. And it is awkward to say the least. It saves when you 'pick' a file object. So naturally it disappears after you pick it up. Then you start asking yourself 'should I have picked this up after doing something else?' then you discover that there is a super hard section ahead and you picked the file (saved) before a less tough one, so every time you respawn you have to redo the less hard section first. You could reset the level and pick up the checkpoints in a better order but that requires replaying some of the level, which can be quite the pain.
I'm still playing the game, cursing and yelling as I go, but I always return to it. It's very compelling! Worth buying.

Word Count: 59,000 words
Setting: Set thousands year into the future, a pre-FTL colony ship from the 2000's, the Mugunghwa has been found.  As it's disappearance is an unsolved mystery of history, you are assigned to retrieve from the derelict any and all logs that might reveal what happened to the ship.
Remote accessing the direlect's central computer, you meet two AI who help you navigate the logs, left behind by the long deceased crew.
Gameplay: Like you would expect from a NV, the game is HEAVILY text-based.  The opening has you interfacing with a really basic computer interface (the override terminal), where you have to type out the commands; for example "enable_ai [name]."
From there, the game proceeds to a slick, minimalistic interface.  The currently active AI stands to left, and on the right are buttons to talk to the AI, access the log documents, and return to the override terminal.  (It also contains recently read messages and the "Exit" and "Options" buttons on the bottom right).
Dialogue with the AI is handled through "chat bubbles," while your responses are limited to two choices (typical of a "yes or no" or "agree or disagree" variety).  The majority of the game, however, is spent reading the logs, letter, diary entries, ect, of the crew.  Only a few of these logs are initially available.  But you have the ability to show these logs to the AI's, to which they will give a response, often unlocking related material.
Another thing of note is that during conversations with the AI, *Hyun-ae in particular, the "chat bubble" will often proceed to fill up with text, only to have the "bubble" suddenly flicker, part of the text gone to replaced by something different.
My overall views on the interface is that it does it's job.  It's clever, minimalist,and streamlined, allowing you to focus on the story itself.
Story aka the part when the review really begins
While being set far, far into the future, the story is actually about history.  To be more specific, it is about the the civilisation of the crew which, having been separated from any outside influences for hundreds of years, have adapted a Joseon Dynasty-like society.  (It should also be noted that all the crew are descendants of Korea)
The story can be divided into two what I like to call "arcs," (the correct terminology might be "path,"  but I feel the word "arc" better expresses how I viewed them), the *Hyun-ae Arc and the *Mute Arc.  Each arc is the sum total of the logs that particular AI provide and the input they give concerning those logs.
*Hyun-ae Arc:   What I consider to be the primary arc, this Arc focuses on the Pale Bride and the Kim family, to which she belonged.  To be blunt, I didn't really enjoy this arc all this much.  It relies heavily on culture shock and plot twists, to shock the player into having the desired emotions of disgust, sorrow, and empathy, and to communicate the ideas and thoughts behind the arc.   Unfortunately, I already have had a general knowledge of this type of culture, and I found myself able to predict the major plot twists well in advance.  As a result, I never felt any shock (although I will give the story credit for momentarily making my sick to my stomach when I realized what the last plot twist was).
This problem compounds with the issue that the arc really has only one character, the Pale Bride.  Almost all the logs in the arc are there only because they mention the Pale Bride (or were written by her), and the arc's AI, *Hyun-ae, only really humanizes the Pale Bride, only giving generalist descriptions of the other characters involved.  That is fine, that's what this arc is about, the Pale Bride and her alone.  But the problem is, to truly enjoy the arc, you need to sympathize with the Pale Bride.  But the only way the story makes you sympathise with the character is via shock, once again bringing us to the issue stated above.
Overall without that all important shock factor, this arc felt try dry and uninspiring.  It is, however, very detailed and realistic in its presentation of the ship's society, and it proves to be a fairly interesting experience (it caused me to lose a night's sleep, in fact).
*Mute Arc:  This arc focuses on the Smith family, and *Mute's relationship with them.  In contrast to the *Hyun-ae Arc, this arc focuses on humanization of its characters, something it pulls of wonderfully.  As a close friend of the Smith family, much of *Mute's dialogue focus on trying to get the player to better understand the members of the Smith, to not only see the bad in them, but also see the good.  Via *Mute's feedback, each life.  They were all flawed; many of them did horrible things; but it also made you realize that they weren't necessarily people.  It made you better understand the circumstances that accompanied their actions, their feelings, their motives.  It is this humanization that made me love this arc.
Summary & Recommendation: A slick, streamlined interface; a story with a highly detailed society based on an actual society in our past; a "primary" arc that relies heavily on a shock factor, without which the arc is uninspiring (but still fairly interesting); and a secondary "arc" that does a great job of humanizing it's character, of presenting characters that are deeply flawed but not necessarily bad people.
Analogue: A Hate Story is a fascinating and entertaining experience.  If you are looking for a good story, this VN comes with my full recommendation.

i went into Tales from the borderlands without really knowing what to expect, and i gotta say this: i was not dissapointed with what it turned out to be. at first, i was worried that it was just a money grabber but boy, was i wrong.
pros:
- the main cast are all very well written and relatable, which is always extra nice in a game like this.
- the voice cast is phenomenal with big names like Troy Baker, Laura Bailey and Patrick Warburton, but Dameon Clarke as Handsome Jack really takes the cake for the best performance in this game.
- the humor from the original games really gets to shine through here, and it's as marvelous as ever.
- the relationship between Rhys, Vaughn, Fiona and Sasha is very interesting to witness (and be able to influence) since it's people from two extremely different cultures getting to know each other.
-you actually feel like you're influencing the story and the relationship between characters, unlike in some other familiar games.
-unlike the walking dead, it doesn't feel like TellTale is trying too hard to rip your heart out from the very first episode, barely even knowing the characters. They give you time to really care about these guys before stepping on your emotions.
- there are bad puns and refrences to other games. perfect.
- not a single moment feels like it's too stretched out, and it didn't feel like they were running out of time either. it's very well balanced.
- Loader bot is a pro in himself, but you knew that already.
- the music is amazing and each episode has it's own perfectly fitting track.
- the stunning cinematopraphy in the opening credits for each episode blows my mind every time.
Cons:
-the action scenes can be very confusing or frustrating because of awkward camera angles and/or editing
-TellTale and action scenes are not very good friends, so the animation can at times look akward or weird during those scenes.
- SPOILERS: in the last episode, Helios crashes. it's an Emotional moment, sure, but i think it was a huge waste of good space station and of borderlands history to let it go down like that
- SPOILERS: it is never explained how Athena gets out of her imprisonment, which they made out to be a HUGE deal, but this just made it feel irrelevant.
-broken money system. when you, as Fiona, steal money from a dead bandit, it at times does not go to your wallet and it just... dissapears?
tales from the borderlands is among the best game i've ver had the pleasure of playing, and i think it's a shame that it's so overshaddowed by games like the walking dead and the wolf among us. it's worth the price, and i wish for more people to get the amazing experience it is to follow Rhys and Fiona's take on the same story about trust, teamwork, survival and betrayal.

Personal opinion:
Borderlands is an ok game as far as I'm concerned. If you're a diehard fan of the Borderlands series, then why don't you have it already? If you are looking for a good entry into the series, I'd recommend to start with Borderlands 2. Sure, there are some characters in Borderlands 2 that you would know a little bit more about if you played the first one, and some areas would be cool to go back to, but the second part is just way better rounded out and honestly, the narrative is not what makes you want to play a Borderlands game. Borderlands hasn't aged all that well, and it's not even all that old. If you can get it cheap, grab yourself a friend and play it, otherwise, there's not much harm in skipping this one. It's not bad, but it's not too great either, especially when there are two newer Borderlands games to choose from.

Here are some things that happened when I tried playing Alone in the Dark (2008)
First things first – accessing the Display menu inevitably crashes the game unless you do a lot of resolution fiddling. I just left it alone, and played the game without subtitles, which I don’t generally do.
You wake up as three guys with machine guns threaten you and some old guy. The old guy is led to the elevator, while you are to be taken past him, to the roof, to be executed.
You’ve just suffered a concussion, so you have to keep pressing a button to blink your eyes so that the screen does not dissolve into a blur. This is not the least bit annoying.
Your captor insists on you never turning to see him, eventually threatening to shoot you. I managed to turn around just as he did so, and it’s because he’s holding an uzi gangster-style, which looks hella uncomfortable.
As you go up to the roof, the walls open rip open to display some supernatural nastiness. Your captor freaks out, but not enough to actually do anything.
The uzi-wielder shoves you against the wall and opens the door to the roof.  The darkness was waiting for just that moment to rip open the walls and devour him. This naturally causes the floor to collapses, dumping you in an unlit abandoned corridor.
The corridor leads to a mirror. You walk up to it and scream “my god…who the hell am I?” Then you punch the mirror and shatter it.
At this point you've gotten over your concussion, and the blinking mechanic is abandoned.
You eventually make your way to the elevator roof, just as the old guy and his captors step in. The older one has to tell their captive – called Paddington – that Paddington is the only one who can manipulate “the stone”.  If he won’t, his suffering will be… legendary.
“About time”, says the younger one (referring to the fact that you’ve had time to walk to the roof, get a guy eaten and walk back before the elevator arrived), and then the darkness eats him. The elevator collapses, taking Paddington and the old guy with it, and you jump off.
“To climb up (when on a ledge) SPACE” the game tells me. A moment later its prompt just goes “^” displaying an arrow as I face a ladder. It’s Space again, by the way.
At this point the game keeps telling me to arrow things. It’s alternately E and Space.
I unfurl a fire hydrant hose (?) into the elevator shaft and use it to rappel down. The elevator shaft starts to explode and burn down.
I’m told to use Space to jump past obstacles, and die three times trying to move past a grate getting electrified by a loose wire. At this point the game remembers to tell me that I should use my body to move obstacles aside. The wire no longer a problem, the fire opens a hole in the wall, which I jump into.
I grab a fire extinguisher and am told to spray the flames away. The controls don’t work. I redefine them in the options menu, and they still don’t work. Grabbing the extinguisher puts you in third person mode, and apparently you need to be in first person mode to spray the extinguisher, rather than use it as a melee weapon.
Thankfully, the flames have died down on their own, without the need to spray them.
I’m told to break down the door using the extinguisher. I can’t melee in first-person view, and random third person swings just won’t hit the door.
There’s a flaming gap in the floor. As Edward drops his extinguisher and obligingly dangles on the edge of the gap, I’m told that I can’t jump with melee items equipped.
As Edward pulls himself up from the gap, he faces the camera. Whether I hit forward or back (though I haven’t tried first person view) he simply slides back to dangle over the flames. Eventually the damage kills him.

This game has multiple classes, special graphic style and many secondary quests with pretty good main story.
1. Story
It is not complicated one but it keeps you going. It will definitely take you some time to get to the end of it. The big finale was pretty insteresting eventhough the last fight was very easy, although the boss looked cool. The main story has some twists, but nothing that surprising. It also had some awesome voiceovers, especially the robots :)
2. Graphic
Borderlands has definitely its own graphic style and even I played this game many years late, I still had no problems with the graphic quality. I had to get used to the style, but never had some major issues.
3. Gameplay
Alright. This one gets a little bit tricky. Some guns on some enemies acted weird and eventhough I hit 100% headshot, I didn't kill the enemy. The guns are pretty fun and it's nice that you have many options and can hold up to 4 guns at the same time. Also some other gears to put on later stage. Eventhough there is the car system and port system, there is going to be a lot of running. You can't go everywhere in your cart and shoot everything easy with it which I really liked because that would be just dumb. The gameplay itself could get sometimes repetetive and even intense because even with really good weapons and headshots it took a lot to kill the enemy and if there was more of them, well, then it was not pleasant. You get respawn though, but it cost you money. The money it cost is calculated on how much money you own at the moment which was nice. Also if you die you actually don't die right away and you get a chance to kill enemy which pops "second wind", basicly resurecting you on spot which was very handy. Although there was some weird things with some guns I enjoyed the gun play and the special class skill was also pretty cool.
4. Final words
Finishing this game took some time and I got sometimes a little bit bored, but it kept me going. Only thing what bothered me was that I had to clear some areas over and over again and a lot of running didn't help either. Nice touch is that you some enemies have different weak spots so you just dont go headshot everything. Story was decent and gameplay was enjoyable enough.

I've spent most of my time with this game outside of Steam, and it's quite possibly my favorite racing game of all time. Up there with Most Wanted and GT3. Quite an unique mix of arcade and simulation, meaning the driving is precise and requires skill and thinking, but at the same time it's also very dramatic in both how it feels and it's presentation.
What I hate though is the inability to make whichever car you want competitive. I finished Most Wanted with the Punto I bought at the start, and fully upgraded it was just as fast as the most expensive cars in the game. Which is not realistic, let's face it, but games don't have to be. Shift doesn't have that, not by a long shot, and towards the end of the game you'll have to switch to more expensive cars, on top of which you'll have to ignore all cars that for whatever reason can't be WORKS-converted. All cars below tier 4 that don't have WORKS available become obsolete very fast, which is stupid. I'd love to finish the game with one of my favorite cars, but they just can't keep up.
Still though, a great racing game. Fun, thrilling and well worth what little it costs these days.

First to review a game, so nervous ;-;
I streamed a full walkthrough of this on Twitch and this is what I have to say:
If you are looking for challenging precision platformer, with high quality pixel art backgrounds, fitting music, engaging retro-style cinematic cutscenes - this game is for you.
The game itself is really simple, you play as Master Spy, who can only jump(+double jump roll, which is important move) and clock/decloak to solve all your platformer needs. Every level consists of 1 or more screen where you have to find keycard/s to unlock the exit to the next level. Be warned, levels quickly become from easy to really hard and each new level tries to add a new mechanic to the enemies or environment. Cutscenes in this game will probably inspire you to play more and more to uncover what's going to be next in the game. And speaking of cutscenes, I strongly suggest look for 8 very well hidden secret areas in the game which also unlock even MORE cutscenes to the main plot.
Not gonna spoil much, but consider engaging gameplay experience.
If you played games like Super Meat Boy, Boshy or any other action precision platformers, you will find this game quite similiar to your likings.
The only minor complaints I have is that game doesn't have at the moment configurable Audio, only disable everything. No sliders for music or SFX. So Windows Mixer is the only thing you can do besides using your hardware's sliders.
No reconfigurable buttons and instead of classic PC platforming scheme of Z and X, game uses X and C buttons, "C" for "Cloak". Expect at first to missclicks a lot to Z when you want to jump, which will fail for you, if you are used to classic Z/X controls. Alternatively, you can use Controller.
P.S. Press T while you are in game's level :P
