This review is long, and worthwhile to read BEFORE downloading the game, please read it all.
INTRO
Before writing this review, I'm going to give you a quick backstory on my whole experience with the game.
I orgininally played this game from from 2009 (when this first came out) and all the way until 2012 (until Aeria Games bought out IJJI games, the orginal owner). I did get back on during the Aeria Games ownership (see below). I had spent over $3,000 between 4 different accounts over the whole period of 3 years.
BACKSTORY
Alliance of Valiant Arms (AVA) came out in early 2009, creating critical fame that all free MMOs need to survive. The publisher, IJJI games had bought the licensing from Red Duck USA (a Korean affilate of Red Duck).
The game recieved great reviews following the release with frequent events and updates (Weapons, maps, gamemodes and AI missions).
After 2010 the game started to bottom out, some people blame this on lack of content, some blame it on the lack of players. This game had a great ESports community on the Korean version, even had professional teams on the North American version.
In July 2012 IJJI had gone bankrup (some people dispute this) and sold the whole company and rights to Aeria Games (subsidary of a German media company)
In early 2017 the North American publishing company En Masse bought rights from Aeria Games, aquiring the full game rights to publish in early 2017. En Masse is a subsidiary company to Bluehole Inc.
ISSUES AND DOWNFALL
When the game first released under IJJI there where serveral issues with people that caused their charactors to be deleted, and store purchases would not work in the ingame premium weapons and armor market. Some causing complete desync to the servers.
Soon after IJJI had recieved complaints, they fixed and put patches out and resolved all of the connectivity issues, even assigning NA, EU and a south american server, making great progress.
Around 2011 IJJI reported that there where issues funding the game, around the same time, sales and account creations haulted, instead of immediately quitting, IJJI put out more content, bringing back players and creating more revenue.
The game was going smoothly, until 2012. IJJI did not renew their contract with the game creator Red Duck, and then sold the rights to Aeria Games, which inturn published the game.
The reason regarding the under-the-table sale is still mostly unknown. When this was realized, a majority of players quit the game. Knowing that Aeria Games will destroy the game IJJI worked so hard to create.
This caused a major snowball effect, mainly the pro scene being torn apart and forgotten. This is where the game completely went down hill.
The first mistake and loss was the account transfers, Aeria Games and IJJI partnered together to try to create a seamless transition. The transition worked for a majority of players, but it was Aeria Game'ses response to players that caused major termoil between the games GMs and players.
The majority of problems stemed from the people who had worked hard for their accounts, creating forum posts for help, but recieved little to no help from the staff.

This game is an interesting concept for a puzzle game. You are a kid going to his uncle's (who is a
narcisist scientist) when something happens causing a lock-down on the house. Your uncle has a mild loss of short term memory, and can't figure out where he is so he asks you to go restore power to remove the lock-down. In the process you get access to the IDS device that he was working on that allows you to shift between dimensions (More on that soon).
The story isn't complicated, but it gets the job done and gets you going where you need to be. The dialogue along the way is cheesy, but in a good way (Though if you are not a fan of cheesy humor, I would suggest muting the voices).
The gameplay itself is quite interesting. You gradually unlock 4 (well, 5 if you count the base dimension) dimensions that allow you to modify physics. These are Fluffy (Or, light weight), Heavy (Heavy weight), Slow down (Everything moves at a near crawl, even lasers), and Reverse Gravity. You, personally never are altered (The idea is despite the fact you are going through the rifts, you personally remain physical to your dimension). Now, these mechanics lead to some interesting relationships between objects: A steel Safe becomes able to be carried while in fluffy, You can toss a table in fluffy then quickly change to Slow and hop onto the platform (That normally would be going fast) as a platform across a gap. A cardboard box can be used as a heavy weight using Heavy. Or with Reverse you can have something utilize the bottom of a conveyor belt to be carried along (or quickly switch to keep it floating). It's not as though you just unlock them all as you go along: Each room has certain dimensions availble (though they can be changed via what batteries you find in the puzzle), so they give you a general direction on how to solve it, and leave it to you to figure out how to use your tools to reach the exit.
It is worth noting this concept shines in one level in particular: You choose one and only one of the 4 and have to solve the room from there, and based on which one you start with changes the entire solution.
That said, the puzzle aspect partially comes from how well you can execute it as well (You can only "Table Surf" if you are good enough, after all) so if you are looking for a pure puzzle game, you aren't getting that. That does not make this a fun title though.
There are also a lot of neat little features, such as how paintings and such change based on the dimension (Example is a painting of a grandmother where in fluffy her hair is insane, where in slow there is a grim reaper standing behind her). Another is that during death or loading screens you get some hilarious dialogue (Things you will never experience because you died #93487: The Zombie Apocalypse (Though this may be for the best)). There are also little knick-knacks in each level that you can hunt for, given a neat sense of exploration, even if all it does is add little dolls in the main lobby.
That all said, there are a few issues. One annoying one is the give-away hints. Your uncle will give you a hint on how to beat the chamber after a while of being in. It's a neat idea, help stumped players get through, but often times he says it after what seems 1 failed attempt (not counting deaths), which means if you don't get a puzzle right first try (whether or not you get the solution) he's gonna chime in and basically become Navi (There is one puzzle where you clearly have to go up, and he constantly goes "You need to get higher.") If the hints were so dead give-away (Almost shouting "HERE IS THE SOLUTION") or he didn't just tell you within moments of entering the room this wouldn't be an issue, but together it can be a bit annoying.
Another is some questionable hit detection. Numerous times I've been standing on a ledge where suddenly I just get booted off, or I hit a ceiling that still appears numerous feet away. It can cause some annoying and at times frustrating deaths.
The game itself is also rather short, unfortunately. Though it could be positive because that also means it doesn't over stay it's welcome.
On a side note I have seen this game compared to Portal. While it has a Portal feel to it, it's not going to quite get rid of that itch, though it will help satisfy it.
Overall, a really fun puzzle game and definitely worth getting if you are looking for an enjoyable game.

I understand what this game is as a 'hack and slash' with a top down perspective. There are many others like it, however from reading other reviews I can understand why this game is well recieved. You can ignore this review being "negative", it's not to dissuade you from purchasing the game, rather my experience with the game was poor. In fact I think most of the positive reviews show this game in a much better light, but I would like to share my difficulties with the game and some things I was not found with. I believe this was not a game that can be played cooperatively in the way that each person is actively helping another, outside of just resurrecting someone.
My main concern with Hero Siege is the multiplayer. This game looks like it has a good enough experience for a single-player runs as a roguelike and there's a bit of competitive spirit to it. The problem with Hero Siege at least for myself is the connection on the official servers. It can be good at times and then all of the sudden start to become choppy. The only reason for playing this game, was to play as a group of four with communication. Once the connection is choppy it becomes hard to tell apart even with the map. Then there were maps where the connection was absolutely perfect and the game runs fast as it should be. The only problem being that it throws off everything as you were playing at a different speed beforehand (noticeable within dungeons and such).
The equipment in the game is very varied with many different statistics that you have to be balancing. However the inventory UI can be very difficult to navigate. The menus may be very easy once you've gotten used to pushing F and G to open and close between the menus, but I wish it could've been more accessible. In comparison to other games with equipment that needs to be regularly changed, you could use your mouse to hover over equipment to see their stats. Instead Hero Siege requires you to inspect every single item. The game tries to make it simple and clear-cut with arrows up and down for the main stats such as health, armor and attack, but these items have more important attributes such as a secondary effect or boosting skills. Being able to inspect items by having your cursor go through them would just be a nice convenience, but I can understand why people are okay with the method that Hero Siege has gone with.There is a list of relics that can be obtained throughout various runs of the game. However you can only see what relics you have with the press of the ESC button (bringing up the menu). The game does not tell you what the relics would do, another inconvenience as you should supposedly know, by reading the text when you pick it up (which is usually just a line or two) and/or you should just look it up on the wikia. The game could have been more convenient if it allowed for a description of the item's effect if you could hover your mouse over it.
I was talking about the cooperation in the game and while you can lure monsters away from teammates, it's more effective to just spam long ranged attacks from a distance. With focused firepower you are able to overpower enemies even on the harder difficulties that you decide to play on. There are effects such as slowing down enemies and inflicting damage over time but it's much easier to just do as much damage as possible. This limits the use of weapons from close range (especially in lag-sensitive situations, where you believe that you can back up and be safe from an enemies close ranged attack as well as swing at the same time, however with the connection you manage to take damage otherwise, and if you were a long ranged character you wouldn't have to suffer with that, but another problem - ranged attacks from enemies not showing up properly). However long ranged characters have the obvious advantage, especially with how slow some attacks are done.
This is not of any fault to the game but I still find it absurd that if a player can level so quickly when pushed to a high enough difficulty. Unfortunately progression was made too quickly at one point making it impossible to cast skills with the current gear and it forces you to go back to other difficulties to find gear, which in a cooperative environment is damaging in terms of feeling progression. If one of your teammates starts falling behind in gear, but never manages to find other gear while you're progressing at a much quicker pace (ie: EXP% gain increase) then it lead to a discouraging experience. For some reason I was gaining EXP while I was dead, when another team member was not and he was dead as well. I'm not sure if this was the result of gear with a specific effect or not, but it lead to gaining so much more levels than everyone else and it didn't feel fair in terms of progression as a team. There are portals to different levels and acts for each one, but it just felt...uninspired. None of the levels, albeit I've only played very little, stood out to me and if you were to turn off the background altogether I may not have even noticed. The traps can be varied, push puzzles and enemy spawns as well, but it just didn't stick out to me. Even from looking at screenshots there hasn't been one that caught my attention and drive to actually reach that level.
There were bugs that showed the levels of our teammates being different than what they were (AND different for each person what they were showing) the consistency of that hurt gauging our progress. There were multiple instances of players crashing for the server and we were forced to quit to make a new room. I was also extremely disappointed when I learned that certain characters/classes were locked off and required purchasing even though the game should be in our possession, making it feel like part of the game was sealed off, and we weren't willing to pay for it. In addition to convience while there are exit timers and wave timers, which are important for random multiplayer lobbies (so you have a fair chance of picking up items, etc.)
I've played a fair share of top down perspective games and a number of hack and slashes, this one is actually okay. It's just that in my experience with this game as a "cooperative game" was not a positive one. I would not recommend it for the multiplayer experience, but this game to pass time with for mindless grinding I can definitely see it being really strong. Speaking for myself, that when as a team, If a boss was defeated or a wave was completed, it felt hollow as a victory as a group.
It's free, what have you got to lose?

Depending on the map, failing an objective may be game over, or may result in a new objective.  The currency you earn is used to unlock music/pictures/videos, which seemed a little lacking?  The only other purpose I've found for currency is to use it to level up characters; using the currency you can level up any character, up to your highest level character, so if all you do is play luffy, then you can level up your others up to w/e level he is.
The characters all feel very unique, and each time I think, "this is going to be my favorite," I come across someone new.  Usually when I play dynasty warriors the emphasis is on the weapon type or continually hacking and slashing.  The button smashing is definitely still in this game, but it just feels like the skills/combos are longer and have more satisfaction to using them.
Other than a few characters having some odd shading here or there(some look burned or oily?), I enjoy the graphics.
So far I have only encountered one bug, which is the mini-map randomly zooming in or vanishing.  The only way to bring it back is to open the menu and then close the menu, presto, the mini-map returns. While, not a bug, there is from time to time a tremendous frames drop, I know this is kind of expected though.
Game is fun, Amazing Story.

This is a wonderful game if you're into games with the overall "attitude" of ArmA. It is slow, tactical, and deliberate. It has a very fun cooperative mode (as of writing it has only 2 coop maps, but I gladly keep going back).
Pros:
- Nice graphics. It's not Far Cry 4, but I didn't want a gyrocopter anyways.
- Small details on the maps make it feel more realistic. Flashlight effect is nice.
- Combat is deliberate and deadly. You will die repeatedly if you're not careful.
- Atmospheric. You get the very real tension of moving through a power relay, being hunted by robots in the darkness.
Cons:
- A little bit buggy still.
- Doesn't update very often.
- Can't host your own servers.
- Menus are a little clunky. Ish.
Overall a hit. If you like solid team-based shooters with fun, atmospheric objectives this is for you.

A great visual novel based game, Loved every second of it. I've had limited experience with visual novel games, most of them stemming from well known titles such as Fate/Stay Night and Clannad as the likes. But lets get on with the review.
Story: Lets start here, since visual novel's main draw is the story.. The game starts off as you playing as a space engineer recieving a distress signal. Upon reaching the ship, you reach the mainframe and start looking at the logs, unsuspectingly coming across an A.I. From there, you find out what happened to the ship and its crew. The story was fantastic, and gives very interesting in-sight into how women were treated in earlier centuries, as well as ancient korean traditions. The characters you read and meet upon have their quirky personalities you will come to deal with, and they done great work on them as well.
Graphics: Great hand-drawn korean style artwork. It lacks the luster of triple A visual novel games, but the artwork isn't the main focus, but the story. Don't expect Gainax level artwork, but its still pretty good.
Gameplay: To many budding visual novel gamers, the type of user interface is quite different. Menu's and selecting options can be a real challenge intially, but once you get a hang of things it's really not that bad. And of course, reading is the gameplay here, and read you shall. In-game, you will read and read upon logs in which you find out what happened to the crew, there are also moments where you make choices that will determine the outcome of the end. There are also few sequences where you do some activites which is a interesting change of pace. Overall, pretty solid for a visual novel.
Replayablity: Of course there is replayability, mostly in which you start over and see what would happen if you were to take a different route. So expect at least 2-3 times playthrough to do everything in this game.
Final notes: I personally loved it, and recommend to any budding or current enthusiast of visual novel games, or otakus. Hehe

Pretty straightforward choice. Do you like visual novels, darkness and nitty-gritty or futuristic settings? Then yes, this game is for you and you will almost certainly find enjoyment in it, I can say for a certainty that I did, and this isn't my first time around the visual novel block. It holds itself together well, has a fairly decent story pacing and the mood is quite pretty, in its somberness. Allow me to emphasize, it is a dark game, if you have trouble with the idea of exploring some rather dark elements and events, then this is not a game for you. If for some reason you have do not like visual novels, then I actually wonder why you’re even reading this review, this game is not for you, nor will you find it enjoyable. I won’t spoil anything, but the game has several endings and is worth at least three playthroughs to get all of the information and story, along with the separate endings.
In short, if you like dark visual novels with some minor dating-sim elements, buy it, you will not regret it. If you don’t like visual novels, reading or dark events, then this is not a game for you. I recommend it glowingly, it is a fine game, especially for the price.

The opportunity for a real and good game is there.
But no, the entire interface consists of reading something, and then clicking a big button to get more bits to read. Total failure.
There is one timed event, but the characters tell you explicitly what to do and there is NO actual challenge or possibility of failure.

Alone In The Dark was a promising game when it first came out in 2008; it had a great storyline and some cool game mechanics that involved playing with fire (which is awesome) but the main problem it had back then that still holds true now, unfortunately, is the control itself. The game uses fixed camera angles where the player controls Edward Carnby like a tank and the game mechanics as a whole feels stiff and outdated. It's as if the developer tries to emulate the controls from the original Alone In The Dark and bring it to the next-gen and although it sounds like a cool idea on paper but in reality - it's not.
The supporting characters are mediocre as well with an annoying female partner named Sarah and an uninspiring antagonist named Crowley. Everything about them is boring and they just don't provide any sense of motivation into the story. It reminds you of that abysmal movie adaptation by Uwe Boll, which was originally supposed to coincide with the game but thankfully, it didn't happen.
Despite its flaws, Alone In The Dark is still fun to play. If you get pass the fact of its stiff controls and awful driving sequence (good luck trying to finish the earthquake scene on your first playthrough), you'll learn that the soundtrack is outstanding and the weapon manipulation is really intuitive. It's incredibly satisfying to blow up stuff with a fire-induced gun and home-made explosives. It's just too bad the publisher has not released any patches to fix these problems until now. But then again, it's Atari; what do you expect?
For me, I appreciate Alone In The Dark for what it is so I give it a thumbs up for an ambitious attempt. If you really want to experience the game in its entirety, I suggest getting the PlayStation 3 version that addresses all the gameplay issues found in the PC and Xbox 360. If you don't have any consoles at all, then you're stuck with the PC version. Either get it when it's on sale or don't get it at all. Your choice.

This game does something that i must say i really appreciate it for, and that being that it gives the world of Pandora a story focused game.
The lore of the borderlands games is rich in good story concepts and ideas, something that they sadly never use alot in the borderlands games since they focus mostly on gameplay rather than story, but that's where this game fits perfectly in. Adding a long and interesting story arc to the franchise.
One thing i did notice with the game was it's surprisingly clunky animations, it has that old kind of animation style where you can see that it's been hand animated (quite poorly) because it's all choppy. And for a company like TellTale you thought they'd put more detail into their games since just simple animations is much of their whole game.
Another thing i noticed was the humor. While this game has the look of a borderlands game, it most certainly didn't have the feel of the Gearbox games
but what i mean is that the game is very story heavy (which i'm not against) but it actually toss very little jokes and references into the mix, something that has more or less become a theme in the new borderlands games, so it was more about telling an actual story than it was re-creating something the main games did.
Much like other Telltale games though the game is at least enjoyable on the first playthrough, so wherther or not the game varies alot don't really matter. I mean look at The Walking Dead, that game is praised even if the choices you make have little to no impact.
I'd say this game is worth a buy if you like the borderlands games and would like to see something more story directed. It took me about 12 hours to finish the game 100% so it will still give you a fair bit of play-time to complete.

The game that started the popular survival horror genre returns better than ever! Players control Edward Carnby, the main character from the original Alone in the Dark, on a thrilling journey through a dark and terrifying re-creation of New York's Central Park where Carnby must discover the truth behind a dark conspiracy.
With inspiration from the presentation style of popular action TV dramas, Alone in the Dark will be split into a number of distinct episodes. With approximately 30-40 minutes of gameplay comprising each episode, the structure of Alone in the Dark pulls you into world that delivers a fiercely gripping and terrifying experience. Each time the player launches a saved game, the episode will begin with a video summary of the previous episode to quickly re-immerse the player in the story and removing the need to remember where they were or what they were doing. Every episode will close with a nail-biting cliff-hanger ending to rattle players' nerves, and if the player is leaving the game a video teaser of the next episode will play to leave them wanting more.
Alone in the Dark will provide a complete next-generation, action packed experience within a highly detailed, free roaming environment, featuring a mixture of real-time physics and full environmental interaction. The game will mark a new beginning for the Alone in the Dark series.

Tangledeep is a deep and rewarding roguelike, with visual and audio themes reminiscent of the Mana series of RPGs and a mix-and-match class/ability system similar to Final Fantasy 5 or Final Fantasy Tactics. Other systems, such as the ability to raise monsters or to power up items by going into them and completing extra dungeon levels, are also incorporated into the game.
Essentially, it's a mixture of concepts from Legend of Mana, Final Fantasy, Disgaea, and Shiren the Wanderer (or Dungeons of Dredmor)!
However, it never feels particularly derivative - instead, this mixture of features from many JRPG franchises comes off as a logical progression of the genre, a fusion of ideas that have worked well separately into a set of systems that work even better together.
I couldn't recommend this game more, and it's only going to get better in the future - it feels more or less like a complete game now, but the developers have a lot more planned for inclusion.

I first played the original Need for Speeds in the mid-1990's and lots has changed for the better.
After being too busy for gaming for many years and overlooking racing games I got DIRT, WRC, Grid, MxGP, Mx ATV, Pure, Nail'd, Insane, Track Mania,  N4S Hot Persuit & Shift and a few other racing games the past few years.. All those mentioned being good (except Grid 1 I don't care for, too touchy).
For N4S Shift it is original or different from the others mentioned in that it is not a SIM but not pure arcade either (most racers noted fit into one or the other category), it fits a good balance between pick up quick fun (without needing to get all into it with a steering wheel) with realistic elements like heavy braking and not always going full throttle.  No music, just roaring engines too, a good change up for N4S. TONS of upgrades, tracks and type of race events to mix it up so you can get 25-50+ hours if you wanted.
SHIFT probably is not the best hybrid (some sim some arcade elements) racer on the market (haven't tried The Crew or many others that may fit that profiel) since its a few years old too, but its a good racer for a reasonable price.  Since i ride motorcycles, hoping for a better biker games in the future, hint EA!

I downloaded this game for the Black Rose Spy item, and I love the knife. But the game is not so good. Terrible, matter of fact.
The first thing I noticed was that the game opens in a small tab, and can't go full screen. The naming and customization features are very limited, offering only a few pre-set faces and room for a short character name (not even enough room for the common username length.) You are then allowed to join a community server match.
Now for the gameplay, which was far from impressive. The point of each match seems to be to "kill each other for twenty minutes," gameplay that lacks originality and is boring and repetitive. At least "Call of Duty" has a point. The gameplay has a really clunky feel to it, with seemingly incomplete firing animations and game models.
The graphics aren't the best around, and have blocky texture models and whatnot. That's all I have to say about those, though.
"Alliance of Valliant Arms," in conclusion, is an overall very bad game, and unless you're looking to recieve a cool Spy knife for "Team Fortress 2," I would not recommend it at all.

A physics puzzle-platformer with ties to the Portal series both in theme and production (it was directed by Kim Swift, who worked as lead designer on Portal) and though the puzzles in QC are (subjectively) better than Portal's, it lacks any of the latter's charm or personality.
The level design is templated similarly to Portal, with the main character (here a 12-year old boy) moving from room to room in a massive mansion repurposed into a research facility (that is, a mansion repurposed to look like Aperature) with the hero's amnesiac mad scientist uncle playing the part of GLaDOS, instructing him (ie, the main character) through the facility espousing hints, quips, and barbs.  Instead of a portal gun, though, the player hops between different dimensions, which results in slowing time, making things heavier or lighter, and reverse gravity to solve puzzles.
And though the puzzles themselves are masterfully made, creating situations that are intellectually satisfying while remaining simple enough to avoid frustration and utilizing each of the dimensions, the mark that QC missed, mainly, is atmosphere: the uncle (voiced by John de Lancie) is utterly unlikeable (it feels as though they wanted him to be both endearingly eccentric and abrasively intellectual that they missed the mark on both counts) and that the levels, after a while, became very same-y.  I got the feeling that the game was made by an engineer, with a token world built around the levels.
All in all, I'd give it a B
If you like physics puzzles (they really are very good) and first person platforming, but can make concessions for world- and story-building, and have already played Portal, then this is a game for you.

Not many people might like this or even read this review, but i will write down my thoughts.
In this game, you play as edward carnby, who wakes up to an amnesia, and try to identify yourself and the events going on around you. After a very nice introduction to yourself you will find yourself in the horror that shadows the whole world and you will try to solve mysteries with some allies.
Short review:
This is my favorite game. Very nice ambiance, exciting story, strong characters, thrilling survival and good looking visuals for its time, 2008. There are few glitches of the game but i think i can tolerate them. Resource and inventory management is crucial to survive. Music is fantastic. Controls are complicated but it creates variety of actions in gameplay. A very depressing open world game with a relatively big map for its own time. The story may not be much appealing or interesting for everyone but i think survival is enough to keep you playing.
Long review:
- Alone in the dark is a horror game. But the horror is not cliche jumsp scares or chasing. This is an openworld game with a very depressing and shivering environment. And conviniently the game takes place in the night :)
- The rpg element of this game is edward carnby. He is trying to remember his past while also trying to run away from bad guys and creatures around him. The story of edward carnby is not only about his memories. It is also about his destiny with a shocking ending. There are also allies and enemies in the game and they all play a role in the story.
- There is a very nice central park as the openworld in this game. You can drive cars around but some areas requires you to walk in. This is nt a walk in the park, i think this is a pun :D There are monsters cruising around just like you.
- In this apocalyptic survival horror, you will need a weapon obviously. You only have one handgun but you can utilize it with other inventory objects. Inventory plays a very big role in this game. For example there are explosive bottles and you can throw them on to the enemy and shoot it in the air to blow it up. You have a lighter and you can use it with mosquito spray to creeate fire like a dragon. You can create a molotov with a piece of colth and an explosive bottle. Even more, you can wrap it with a bandage to make it stick on a surface or enemy. You can use your knife to penetrate the blood bags and create a path to a trap. Because some creatures are blood thirsty. And there are other inventory items and possibilities as creative as these. You will find items in the trashes or cars or in buildings or jsut in the middle of nowhere.
- There is a healing mechanism in this game. If you take a critical hit, you will start beleeding. You should stop beleeding with bandage. If you get hurt, you can heal your wounds with a medical spray. Use and store it wisely.
- The enemies in this game have a weakness. They show a specific fissure-like wounds and those places can be set on fire. So yeah you are basicaly burning zombies :) This is the efficient way of killing them. Your X-Ray vision is required to progress through the game and it gets enhanced as you kill evil roots of evilness. You will now what i mean if you play the game.
- Fire is a usefull element. You will need fire extinguishers to extinguish fires.
- There are 2 different cameras. First and third person views.
- There are nice riddles in the game. You have to be creative to solve them.
- The game is chapter based. There are 8 chapters with severals checkpoints. The good thing is that you can play or skip any chapters at any time. Disclaimer: If you're the kind of person who doesn't like visual novels and thinks that they shouldn't be on Steam for whatever reason, you can leave now. If, instead, you're interested in this sort of thing or is willing to try something different out, read on.
Now, with that out of the way, WOW is Analogue good. Probably one of the best things I've tried out on Steam recently! It's about you, a space investigator, attempting to find out what happened to a ruined spaceship (the Mugunghwa). A simple premise, but the execution is amazing.
To start off, let's talk about the presentation. The entire story is told through old logs written by the ship's inhabitants, as well as conversations with its AIs (*Hyun-ae and *Mute), and all of this is seen through a single computer interface. Again, it's simple, but it works perfectly while also being quite unusual, so I really liked it. It does a very good job at delivering the plot and setting by simultaneously giving you a lot of information while also allowing your imagination to put everything together by itself.
And speaking of the setting, that's where Analogue truly shines! First off, it's based on Korean culture, which is... not something that you see very often (if at all), so it's refreshing to have something like this. Second, I really appreciate the research that was put into it. As the author explains in the bibliography, society aboard the Mugunghwa was based on a certain period of Korean history, and knowing that things like this actually DID happen at some point in history adds so much more weight to the story, as well as having the secondary benefit of making it educative without feeling forced.
But what about the story, huh? There's no easy way of explaining it properly, but it's a wild ride. The horrible things detailed in some of the logs really leave an impression on you (sup Block 1), but you also have things such as *Hyun-ae dressing up in a maid outfit and being adorable or *Mute being tsundere, and the contrast between the serious and easygoing parts causes both to be even more impactful. In addition, though the narrative is mostly direct, it still sometimes leaves little hints about certain things here and there, so that you can put everything together in your head before seeing it explained in a log or something, and it's great.
Other things to talk about... the art, while not the best, is still pretty good, and does its job well. Same goes for the music, pretty much. And I really enjoyed that one puzzle involving the reactor and a command-line interface.
But of course, Analogue is not without faults, and I find that most of those can be found in its technical side. It's annoying how you need to wait a second for buttons to work after you change pages, and there are some problems involving event flags, such as the one involving decrypting Block 3... but really, those things are pretty much insignificant in the grand scheme of things, not managing to be anything more than annoyances.
Bottom line: if you don't mind reading a lot and is interested in learning something about Korean history, definitely give Analogue a try. I certainly didn't expect it to be as good as it turned out to be.

RimWorld is the kind of game that you can sink days into, some would argue that you can sink weeks into. You make your own story (or in this case, your colony's story), you get attached to your characters - even the ones you recruit a bit more forcefully - and you get sad when they will eventually die.
RimWorld is a management game, you manage a group of survivors (or just one - depends on what start you choose) and with them you build a colony. You can either build it so that you can have a foothold for your main mission or just so you can own a plot of land on the planet (or more).
You can build, craft, fight and conquer. Your colonists do everything for you as per the tasks you assign them. They can hunt for food, cook it so that they don't starve to death, chop down trees and use the wood to make walls, doors, bed, furniture, you can research tech that you use to unlock more ways to expand your colony such as having the ability to make farms, craft stone blocks (or other types of stone), make weapons, make turrets, power, etc.
Its fun, from the starting position you choose all the way up until you have that dream colony or loose all your colonists to the various disasters that the AI throws at you.
Its a very long game, but because of that you'll definately get your money's worth.

There's also an easier mode without perma-death, so you can have a super chill, casual run going as well as your more conventional or hardcore roguelike runs. As someone who is pretty bad at all games, I like this feature.
Overall, I say this is a good game that has the potential to turn into a great game.

The game really isn't worth 25-29 dollars on Steam. I honestly expected more use of the CryEngine rather than just volumetric effects and light rays through window shutters.
The engine looked beautiful at first, but then I noticed that it wasn't gritty and destructive like I expected it to be for a WWII game. It looks like a Crysis port but lost in time and ended up in World War II due to the colour of the trees and the sky.
I partially enjoy the storyline, it opens up stories about the characters in the game but only briefly. I don't understand why the protagonist is an American fighting in Poland against Nazi Germany, he mentions at the beginning that his mother was Polish but I wouldn't think of that as reason to fight for the country, especially since Poland became completely occupied in WWII at the beginning. There is also the problem of it throwing you right into the action, you start off at the very beginning defending a blockade on a street in Poland, with the tutorial teaching you the controls of how to shoot and move around.
As mentioned before, I expected the engine to be used much more extensively like other titles previously on it, especially when it's the third generation of such a game engine, you would expect so. There is an option in the advanced settings for the physics to be changed from low, medium and high, but that doesn't make a big difference at all since the majority of the areas that you go into are static objects, and that also includes wooden crates and barrels which were moveable in the Crysis franchise so that was a big disappointment. The engine does use the light rays through window shutters and glass reflections which looks rather beautiful, but it's a detail that goes heavily missed due to the constant rushing around and shooting, it is only really noticed when walking down corridors on the sides of buildings.
The AI isn't very good. If you walk straight into an enemy you can completely stop them from shooting by standing right infront of their gun while they are just standing there waiting to shoot you. Some people say they can be quite difficult as they flank you and force you back a bit into previous areas of the level, which I haven't encountered at all. I have found that you can counter this situation simply by killing them as they are moving towards you. A lot of the time you find yourself sneaking towards new sets of enemies and then turning it into an instant bloodbath that also seems to end in a matter of seconds. They have some unique things not seen in other FPS games, like taking enemy soldiers hostage, holding a knife to their throat and a pistol in the other hand to use them as temporary cover, however that disappears quickly as your hostage's friends decide to willy nilly blow the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of their body rather than think of the loss of a comrade if they did so.
There are explosions, yes, but they are very odd. At the beginning of the game, I sneaked into a small plaza with three men doing shooting practise on a wall with a target on it. Just on their left of them I could see a giant box of TNT or something similar with wires and fuses hanging out, and decided that I could eliminate 3 of the 9 men in the situation by shooting at the box of explosives a couple of times. The box was literally 2 centimetres away from the nearest enemy, and when I shot at the box it took only one bullet to set them off, and the explosive was like as if the entire thing was soaked in water and all the explosives were duds. It was the tiniest explosion I have ever seen in a videogame. The three men simply turned around away from the explosion and start blazing rounds at me rather than look at the exploded box and think of as to why it exploded in the first place.
I have an i5 3570k, 8GB of RAM and an overclocked ASUS GTX 560 Ti with 1 GB of memory. When I started the game, I was getting an average of 40 FPS and further into the game I decided to lower the settings a bit, so I turned down post processing and shading, but it looked exactly the same like as if I never turned down the settings, and yet I got 80 FPS after doing so.
I wouldn't say the game is non-linear as the description suggests, you have two playing styles in the beginning of every situation which turns into just one full on combat situation with bullets whizzing past your head. You can sneak and kill probably 3-4 people silently but then someone will always notice the dead bodies even if you put them into a place where they can't find them and you have to go loud to get through the area. Oh, did I mention you can drag bodies around after you kill someone? You place them over your shoulder and you pull out your pistol with your other hand to shoot people. Although I ran into a bug where my hand holding the pistol was just holding it up to the sky like as if I was trying to avoid friendly fire and I couldn't fire it at all which was useless. I also ran into another bug where I picked up a Kar-98, a semi rifle which requires you to click out the casing of the bullet everytime you fire, but I ended up with a fully automatic sub-machine gun that was nowhere to be seen.
If I was to rate this game out of 10, I would give it a 3.

This casual reverse tower defense game has a very cute aesthetic with simple, yet harder to master, gameplay which has the potential to entertain you for a couple hours.  Even more if you're the "hardcore" type that has the intrinsic need to complete every challenge and gather every collectible.
The whole game revolves around creating a route for your zombies to mindlessly follow to collect brains and turn every human enemy into a zombie ally, even if that means having to place them into strategically thought out suicidal situations. Different zombie types are introduced at the beginning of certain zones with different abilities to help you complete the zone. Clicking on a zombie to pause them in their tracks adds to the strategy needed to navigate the field as gun wielding humans scan and guard a predetermined area or path. If a zombie falls within their field of view, things can get deadly for the cute zombies and if it was unplanned, it means you failed to think quickly and effectively... most of the time.
It doesn't come without its own faults though. There are some basic physics interactions for certain objects that your zombie has to plow through to get to a human. This is a neat effect but this is where the minor frustrations begin. Zombies may get stuck attempting to navigate around one of these objects as they attempt to clear a path to continue on their mission. Instead they may find themselves simply kicking or pushing it continuously in front of them before they either get stuck or take a while to find a way around the object. There were also a few times where it was difficult to draw a valid path past some areas due to the size of the opening, but they were few and far between. For a game that relies heavily on this concept, it would be best to fix the zombie pathing issues to make this a solid game.
The minor frustrations can be overlooked due to the length that it takes to complete each level. They are quick and fun, so if it fails to go as planned the first few times, resetting the level is an instant click away.

Controls are different from other games. You move by right-clicking objects in space to travel there, and otherwise have very little control over your ship. While this can be described as an exploration game, it is mainly trade and battle. Dont expect to visit random places in this game, as you can only visit premade locations.

Tangledeep is a turn-based, rogue-like, 16bit dungeon crawling RPG, and even in early-access is a great game, with hundreds of hours of replayablity. The game places a massive emphasis on 'health management', because none of the classes/characters have any reliable healing abilities, so your health declines after every battle and eventually will run out, and the only want to heal yourself in the game is from food (which is pretty rare), flasks (which are pretty rare also) and the healer in the town (which costs gold). So if you run out of gold and can't kill anymore mobs because your hp is too low, then you're dead. So the game is pretty punishing if you can't minimize the damage you take with every encounter. Another thing that I really like about the game is the small amount of armor/gear that you can equip (only 4 at once), which means you have to be very selective with what your characters wears. Overall even in early-access, you can get hundreds of hours of fun gameplay out of it and there's still so many good things that can be added to the game, but the base game is already good and enjoyable.

Plight of the Zombie is a well designed puzzle game that represents the second foray onto Steam following the mixed reaction to the free to play Firefly Online Cortex which was released in January, 2015. That game was designed to be a short term solution until their much awaited Firefly Online was released. Unfortunately that game has not come out and shows no signs of being released anytime soon as there has been a significant number of delays at this point and fans of the television show have grown tired and frustrated with the developer’s efforts on that game.
However, that is not this game – this particular focus is on Plight of the Zombie. It’s actually a pretty solid puzzle game. You need to engineer a route for your zombies around the map in order for them to eat the brains that are scattered around the screen and create new zombies by attacking the humans. Sounds easy, right? Well it is to a certain extent. Those pesky humans hunting you down will pick apart the weakness of your character and eat you for lunch if you’re not careful.
There are 60 action packed levels for you to solve and the beauty of the game lies in the fact that just as one mechanic is seemingly growing old and you complete one set of levels you get to get a new zombie to star in the next set. For example you start off with Craig who is pretty much your weak generic zombie. He’s really a tutorial mode dude. He’s there to teach you the mechanics. Then you move onto Charlie Chunker whose a big fat zombie who can take a lot of damage before he’s shot to death. His issue, however, is that he cannot fit into small spaces so in order to advance throughout some levels you’re going to have to get a Craig like zombie who can do the work that Charlie cannot.
By successfully completing levels you’re going to get zombie coins as well as brains. The brains just tell you how well you have done on a level using the gold-silver-bronze system. The coins, however, are the interesting part. There’s a zombie shop in the game where you can buy cosmetic upgrades. These just change the appearance of your zombies but I have to say that it’s a pretty sweet touch to the game.
The game functions, looks and plays as well as I would hope for. I enjoy the graphics and the cool soundtrack as well. But I am left just a little bit disappointed. Regulars will already know my stance on puzzle games and achievements. They go hand in hand. This is no exception. I’d love for the devs to truly embrace Steam. Please add achievements into your game and consider the Steam Trading Card program as well. Achievements would work wonders in this game. They’ve got the cosmetics store, etc. and thus there are a number of different layers of achievements that should be added. How about some for items purchased from the store, for equipping certain objects onto specific characters on top of those of level completion, etc. It would be a relatively quick process that would add enormous value to the game.
Plight of the Zombie is an already pretty rock solid puzzle game that could be made better quite easily by simply embracing the Steam platform. I do hope that the developers give Steam users an extrinsic award for playing their game. Even without the achievements I would consider the game to be a fairly easy one to recommend for fans of puzzle games.

Plight of the Zombies is a fairly casual strategy/puzzle game.  This game isn't you're typical zombie game, instead of mowing down droves of mindless brain gobblers, this one see's you in the shoes of the hungry zombie.  Going about his business, eating brains, turning human's into zombies and trying to find love.. (OK the whole part about love isn't true, but if that's you're thing, I'd suggest Warm Bodies).  The game is broken down into 6 main stages, with each of those stages having 10 different puzzles to solve.   To finish the stages you need to turn all the human's into zombies, and also collect the brains, many of which are timed, if the timer run's out they disappear.   Trying to prevent you from finishing the puzzles are a slew of different enemies, unarmed human's, shotgun wielders, handgun, etc etc etc..
Plight of the Zombies isn't the type of game you'll find yourself wanting to play for 10 hours a day, but it can be a nice time killer when you have an extra few minutes to kill and don't want to get into a deep game.  The early puzzles are fairly simplistic, but the further along you get, the more complex and challenging they get.  Often times you're left having to employ three, four sometimes even five zombies to complete a task.   The game is a good casual game for people to play now, then put down for a few days and pick up to play without missing a beat.  It's pretty solid in every department, the only issue I found with the game was the pathing of your zombies, it happened more times than I'd have liked to see, but occasionally my zombie would clip into an obstacle they clearly should have walked around, this would cause them to endlessly walk in place until I altered their course.
This game is recommended to anyone who enjoy's playing the anti-hero, if you would rather destroy the world rather than save it, this one is for you.  It's also for people who like fun, casual experiences that don't require hundreds of hours to learn.  It's a very pick up and play type game.  I'd say this can be enjoyed by gamer's of all ages, kids will enjoy the simplistic nature and goofy zombies, adults will enjoy the complex challenge of trying to complete the stages in the fastest time possible.  Would also be nice to see some achievements added in the near future, but certainly aren't neccesary.

Firstly,I can't belive how good this game is and secondly,that It's free! I got 40 minutes in and then had to go to work. Trust me,If I didn't have to stop playing it,I wouldn't have. I haven't played a game in ages that has captivated me quite like Estranged did,and have just been waiting for one to come along. It's left me feeling like I just have to leave a review for it.

LAMBDA REVIEWS Analogue: A Hate Story
Score: 7/10
========================================
Analogue: A Hate Story is a wonderful look at society in collapse - how man falls and how he behaves in times of desperation. Through the eyes of the impotent and the weak in a society, Love teaches about the corruption inherent in absolute power and the evils of paternalism.
Much like Margaret Atwood (especially in her "The Handmaid's Tale"), Love here very obviously takes a side, but unlike Atwood, Love exercises subtlety in her approach and refrains from meandering tracts meant to score political points against straw men. In Atwood's work, the message might as well have been duct-taped to an anvil and dropped on the reader's head, but here, the effect is just as shocking, but nowhere near as heavy-handed.
The art and sound are also excellent, more than enough to serve their purpose in delivering the story.
Watch out, this one's got a wicked bite.

If you don't like long reviews, I'll just claim that this game is simply awesome.
If you want to know why I wrote that, I'll explain.
The game sets an unknown character -the player- is sent to a long-lost space ship, the Mugunghwa, to discover what happened there. On the Mugunghwa you find two AI's in charge of the logs of the ship. The gameplay is pretty simple, read the logs, show them to the AI's so they can help you find more, and repeat until you are satisfied. Maybe you can get one of the AI's back home, maybe not, or maybe both.
But what makes this so amazing is the backstory behind the Mugunghwa, its people and its tragic conclusion. Saying anything about that would be considered spoiler, so if you want to know what happened, either buy this, try the demo to catch a glimpse, or get spoiled somewhere else, I'm not talking anymore about the heartbreaking story.
Only found a pair of problems with this game. First, sometimes it's possible to get "stuck", specially during the meltdown sequence. That's not neccesarily bad, but can get frustrating. The other problem comes with the specs. Even if my computer can move this, sometimes it lags a little bit. It doesn't affect the gameplay, but can be annoying from time to time.
So overall, this game is simply pure love, 9/10 on my opinion. It's entertaining, enjoyable and fun, yet it can make you sad, or even have people lose hope in mankind. How's that possible? You might know by playing.

This product  took me be surprise, so I just had to review it. And I say product because this doesn't necessarily qualify as a game. I was on the fence with this for a while because I wanted to expand my gaming genre horizons a little bit and decided that a visual novel would be a pretty big expansion. I downloaded the demo, tried to rush a little gameplay in before bed, and was surprised at the fact that there was none. I finally picked it back up on another day, when I could actually read without worrying about the time and actually got into the text. I was hooked instantly.
I want to use the new Steam Review Feature, so I'll make a quick overview of the visual novel here.
----------PROS
Nice Sy-fy setting
Unique form of storytelling (I haven't seen it presented this way very much)
Pleasant art-style
Deep subjects
Interactivity
Multiple endings
Korean culture
----------CONS
Lots of reading
Minimalistic artwork
Short Storylines
Korean Culture
I can't think of anything really bad about Analogue: A Hate Story, just know that it isn't a game. It's called a visual novel because there is a lot of reading. If you do not enjoy reading you probably would not enjoy A Hate Story. Another potential problem is that it has more "mature" topic matter. Nothing EXTREME, but it would most likely bore children since it has deeper subjects like ethnicity and sexuality. I haven't finished all the endings or found all the files yet, but so far I've only found 3 pages that might cause a problem. The worst in here is the word breast so far, and I don't think anything is going to get any worse.
I don't like how each ending can be played in one sitting, but there are multiple endings so you could at least squeeze a few more playthroughs out of it.
The product features Korean, mostly only in the names. It won't be a problem though, because Analogue: A Hate Story goes as far as to give you a little cheat sheet so you know how to pronounce all those names. The downside is, the names are really confusing at first but that only helps make the story more submersive later on. If I remeber correctly, it's got full Korean support, so that's a plus too. If anyone is trying to learn Korean this is definitely something they should look into.
The interactivity is hard to explain. One thing over people seem to have problems with is visual novels with only the words and pictures and scenes. This isn't the case, and you'll need to do a lot of clicking and typing to complete stuff. (Keep in mind that that's all you do gameplay wise.)

It's got an anime/manga artstyle, but it's not intrusive and it shouldn't scare you away if that kind of stuff isn't your thing. There could have been better artstyles, but the manga one conveys the message well. It conveys the story better than a more realistic approach would for me, and it keeps in line with most visual novel styles that I know about.
When I started it up and actually read everything, I wasn't expecting anything too good, but I kept reading and got interested in the plot. When the demo ended I bought the game instantly and kept playing. If you aren't sure about this product and haven't tried the demo, I highly recommend it.
It just blew me away personally, and it made me want more. I'm definitely going to try to read everything in this and the sequel. The best part is, it sparked my interest in the Koreas and Korean, and I'm wanting to try to learn more about it.
Well, I'm tired and should be in bed as of the time of this review being written. I hope I could at least help someone.
RECAP
This will be good for people who are new to the visual novel genre or want to try to get into it.
This is good for people who enjoy reading.
This will be good for someone who wants to think about the deeper meanings of things like politics or ethics.
This will be good for people who want to get into Korean and Korean culture.
This will be good for people who enjoy space-agey novels and such.

It's a decent indie visual novel (on steam, yay), which means that it isn't really a game, more like an interactive story with 2 girls being the main focus of the dialogue and progression.
You will get to play a "detective" role to find out what happened to a crashed colony ship that departed Earth years ago, this ship was maintained by 2 female A.I. entities that survived the crash and will tell you about it.
As common with a VN you can unlock several endings and dialogues with the girls, some of which are interesting to read that touch themes such as feminism, solitude and broken family ties.
My main gripe with the story progression is that it's not all well explained, the only way to know about certain events is by reading log files and you need to pay attention to family trees and relations between characters.
I recommend it whether you like visual novels or not, the story shouldn't be boring and it's a short and simple different experience

What can be said about EVE?
The game is more then a game.  EVE confronts you with the absolute freedom to do anything you want, in space.  This scares a lot of players as there is no path to follow, you create your own path.  The new version of the tutorial is far better then it was ages ago when I started the game and shows off many of the systems the game offers to play in.  The stories you've heard of this game about massive wars, huge corp espionage, and massive back-stabbing are all true.  The game doesn't punish you for much and even then it is usually just a small decrease in your security rating.  Gang teams do roam the "safe" space areas and will kill you just for giggles.  The learning curve of this game is not hard, the hard part is learning to play a game where consequences are real.  Your ship got destroyed?  It is gone forever, there is no save point to go back to. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off another player, they may call in friends to grief you, or worse yet blacklist you across their alliance.  Jumped into wormhole space and forgot to bookmark the exit?  Lol, drift forever until you decide to self-destruct your ship.
What then draws people into this game?  The fact the you do impact the overall universe, even if just in the smallest way.  You choose to mine your days away?  Your new influx of minerals can push down the market costs.  Start taking transport jobs?  You could be delivering the weapons/equipment an alliance needs to turn the tide of battle in a region of space.  Became a pirate?  Live on the edge and enjoy the rush of kills and looking over your shoulder.
The game is amazing.  I play it for a few months each year because it is a blast to play.  I can only do small chuncks of it because I become too involved in it.  If you give EVE a chance, it will do the same to you.

If you enjoy Roguelikes, this will be up your alley.  If you don't, there is an "Adventure Mode" that removes some of the brutality of traditional roguelike mechanics, so you can still give it a shot and not worry about things like permadeath, if that's more your style.  Tangledeep is grid-based with a variety of job classes, each with it's own playstyle.  Monster collection with a Corral system, upgrading items by entering the levels held within them and beating them, and plenty of NPCs and various other items being added frequently.  The developer is also the main composer, but has brought in others whose names you may recognize as the project progresses.
Tangledeep has been consistently updated since the end of the Kickstarter campaign and that has continued through it's Early Access release on Steam.  Jobs are being added, areas expanded, etc.  It has the consistent updating required to make Early Access more than just testing, but also fun.  I've been having a blast with this game!  My hours played do not reflect the builds I played prior to it's Steam version.

If you liked the Portal games,  definitely check this one out. Since people are bound to compare to the portal games I'll lay some stuff out.
1. The main mechanic is shifting between 4 different dimensions to solve puzzles. This was almost as fun as thinking with portals.
2. In the game, your uncle talks while you solve puzzles. Big drawback: he's not very entertaining. At all. Seriously, this was just terrible writing. Only slightly better than complete silence.
3. You're required to do some platforming at some parts. I've read about some people getting aneurysms over this, and while I never had too much trouble making jumps, I can see why people would gripe.
Other things:
+ I really did like the cartoony art style.
+ The barfing cloning devices and cat that follows you around were always welcome sights.
- Level design was just lazy. When going between rooms, you'll pass clones of the same corridors over and over.
- In the last third of the game, there were maybe 2 or 3 areas that I'm sure plenty of people will get annoyed over. Not because they're hard to figure out, but tough to execute.
This game will exercise your brain with puzzles that are not too challenging but definitely fun. It's not the perfection that Portal 2 is, but it'll help scratch that puzzle itch.

There is so much to say about this game. Aside from the obvious (gorgeous old school pixel art and music that sounds direclty out of any given 90's JRPG,) Tangledeep feels like a long lost game from my childhood.
First and foremost, this is very much a real roguelike - but only if you want it to be. You can play it as a regular RPG if you desire, but it's clearly meant to appeal to roguelike fans. If you want meta-progression, it's there, but it's in no way necessary. If you don't want permadeath, you can play without it.
The crux of the game is a standard tower ascension dungeon crawl. You pick a starting job (class), and you're on your merry way. There are quests to help you progress, and the flexible job system lets you design any kind of character you can think of within the span of skills available to you. You may switch jobs at any given point, provided you have the necessary gold (or a special item.) All the skills you spent JP (the resource you use to buy skills) on will be kept when you switch jobs. You could, if you really wanted, learn one skill per job and just keep switching. Highly inefficient, but still possible.
The weapons classes in the game (i.e. sword, axe, bow, staff, etc...) all have a unique feature to them. For example, swords have an increased parry chance, and the ability to riposte upon parry, while axes hit all adjacent enemies. You can have four weapons equipped at once, which lends flexibility to each job. Some jobs clearly prefer certain weapon classes, of course; the Hunter works best with bows, while the Brigand works best with daggers, but these aren't hard rules (though some skills do require specific weapon types.)
There is no hunger clock. You *can* grind - though the usefulness of grinding diminishes heavily very quickly. Of note, your ability to heal is finite. You carry a flask which heals based on a percentage of your max health, and has a limited number of charges. You can refill these at fountains scattered throughout the dungeon, but these fountains are also finite. You can also heal through food and an NPC in town, but you will eventually run short on food if you mess around too much, and the NPC in town charges higher and higher prices to heal with each subsequent heal. So if you grind too long, you will probably lose the war of attrition.
The dev is amazing. This game is updated very frequently, each update bringing quality of life changes and bug fixes, and often times some content. I'm serious when I say it's updated *VERY* frequently. Like 4-5 times a week. The dev is friendly and communicative and fixes bugs pretty much right after they're caught. He is open to suggestions and seems to enjoy communicating with the players.
I keep forgetting this game is Early Access. It has a TON of content already, and quite a bit more on the way. There are currently 9 jobs, but 3 more are slated to be released before 1.0. There are so many ways to approach a win here, and that number will only increase. This is well worth the $15.
True modern roguelikes are uncommon, but this game fits the bill. Perhaps the most extreme purists won't see this as a true roguelike, but if you are playing on hardcore, I fail to see how it is anything but. I highly, HIGHLY recommend this game.

Where to begin? First off, when the storage page promises a ''truly modern'' fps game, this is NOT what I expected. Lets go through some of the pros and cons of this game, based on the couple of hours that I, at the time of writing this, have forced myself through.
The pros:
-The game looks good during gameplay. The enviroment as well as the characters looks smooth.
-The voice acting is good during gameplay. The yells of both allies and enemies are clear and sound somewhat ''realistic''.
-The game is interesting. Personally being a fan of history, especially the ww2 era, I find the story behind the game very interesting.
The cons: PRACTICALLY EVERYTHING ELSE!
-The game is glitchy: enemies see you through walls, appear out of nowhere and do all kinds of random things, which not only makes the experience total crap, but also makes the game unplayable.
-The controls of the character are wierd. Trying to navigate through a ruined city with a character that apparently suffers from cerebral palsy while trying to shoot enemies and figure out what the hell you're supposed to do is pretty painful.
-The bugs in this game are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥: If you aim down the sights of a gun, you can crouch and stand back up, right? Well, in this game that works with everything but snipers; with snipers you can crouch while aiming, but can't stand back up. There are buildings that you can walk in just normal, but if you crouch and try to stand back up, you can't. The detection system in this game is also just stupid. If enemies notice you (Which can also happen if you throw too many rocks btw. I know, right?) they will alert others of your presence. That's cool even if it happens a little wierd (the enemy notices you and everyone IMMEDIATELY knows where you are), but in this game some the enemies don't know what's going on and just run around and then suddenly realize where you are when everyone else is dead. This has caused me to run after enemies countles times, because the enemy is determinate to get to where-ever is was when the others noticed me. So annoying.
-The gun animations: If you shoot at an enemy and your character starts to put another bullet into the gun or pull the bolt of the rifle, you can't do ANYTHING. You can barely walk forwards, which is somewhat annoying when you have a gazillion enemies shooting at you.
-The objectives: Half the time you just end up running around wondering WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ you're supposed to do. The game gives you the main objectives and the ''secondary missions'', but you don't get any info as to what you're supposed to ACTUALLY do. The first time you encounter a tank, the game says you either need a bazooka or two grenades. Well, I only have one grenade, sooo, where's the bazooka? Who knows? You have to play this annoying game of hide and seek with 90% of the things you're supposed to pick up. All I'm wondering is WHY? Why, for the love of god, isn't there any indication as to where you are actually supposed to go?????
That's all I can come up with right now. Bottom line is, don't buy this game unless the developers do some serious fixing with the game. This game is the cheap mix of Sniper Elite and Far Cry, both of which I would recommend over this.

Easily the best Telltale game I've played by far.
Sure, the Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones were all fantastic but it didn't really feel like your choices mattered much in the long run. And yet in this you can let key characters die which will drastically change the outcome, would you rather let an old friend that betrays you die or spare them to get 9 million in the end? Or maybe let one of your best friends die as payback for her betraying you? These are just 2 examples of choices that really do have consequences.
While there is more talking than action, this feels like a true Borderlands game and ties in with the previous titles fantastically, bringing in old favourites or introducing new, incredible characters. The game perfectly blends, action, comedy, and humour together, almost effortlessly. You'll go from laughing to crying at the most unexpected times.
The voice acting and animation, everything about this game is near perfect, I don't recall many instances of the frame rate dropping like in previous Telltale games. As for as the voice acting, it's one hell of a cast: consisting of some truly stellar voice actors like Patrick Warburton, Troy Baker, Nolan North, and Laura Bailey. Telltale couldn't have picked a finer crew.
Finally, the references in this game are just amazing, especially the Power Rangers one towards the end of the final episode.

Analogue is heartfelt and well written, and while it has a few flaws, it's one of my favorite games ever. The story is delivered in two ways, conversations with the AI's, *Hyun-ae and *Mute, and text logs written by people aboard the now empty spaceship. The two AI are both very human characters, and despite the art style, aren't cliche anime girls. The text logs are all believable, and manage to bring people you never see or hear to life. It would be hard to describe the plot without spoiling things, but it talks about misogyny really well, showing both the individual and the large scale effects of it.
The biggest issue with this game is that some of the logs and minor characters feel like filler, meaning you'll probably just skim a lot of it. This, combined with the confusing (to a westerner like me) Korean names, can make events a little hard to keep track of. But the rest of the game is more than good enough to compensate.

Visually, Interstellar Marines is beautiful; blurring and lighting effects are gorgeous. The audio is great as well, with lots of environment sounds to listen to. I don't have a good rig, but I get around 20 frames on 100 ping. Not bad. As far as gameplay goes, that game's not bad... generally. I mean, there are some nice features like running reloads that always come in handy. Movement feels pretty fluid, though there's no proning, which can be annoying.
Immersion is very well done, with an actual animation for attaching a weapon's suppressor. You can see your helmet, and can raise and lower it, which I love. You just
like you're an Interstellar Marine in space; it's awesome. I once played a game where we were in a large cargo bay, and happened to pass a large window looking in space. Pausing to look through the window, I saw earth. Standing there, looking through the window at our slowly orbiting planet, I was just in awe. It felt so real, like I was actually in space looking down on plant earth. On the dark side of earth, I could even see the millions of pinpricks of light the showed populated areas. I probably stood there for a full minute looking an earth and space, before my squadmates got my attention again.
Now, for weapons. There are but three weapons available as of now, an assault rifle, a combat shotgun, and a submachine gun. They're all fun weapons and are visually gorgeous, but... there's only three of them. The assault rifle is basically a designated marksman weapon, because it has an unremoveable 4x optic. The combat shot does meager damage, about the same as the SMG near as I can tell, and that combined with semi-automatic fire makes it an unpopular weapon. This can be remedied by buffing the damage a bit, which ought to be done anyway, because it's a combat shotgun, The SMG is fine. Using automatic on the assault rifle and SMG is unrealistically innaccurate. Maybe things are different in the 22nd century, but you aim goes all over the place, and you really have to work the mouse while firing to land your shots.
The multiplayer is good, but I personally enjoyed the co-op; a four man team advancing through an abandoned space station fending off attacks by defective robots. It's pretty rad.
In the end? IM is a pretty fun game. Things can get a bit repetetive, but in general there's a lot of enjoyment to be had in outer space in the 22nd century. I've had the game for a few days, so I don't know what update frequency is like, though I've heard it's not stellar (pun intended). I hope to be proven wrong.

This game reminds me a lot of The Handmaid's Tale. If that statement intrigues you, then you can probably safely ignore the rest of what I have to say.
Analogue has a lot more story than most games. It's also more brutal than most game stories are, which makes the cute art and presentation all the more dissonant. This may have been intentional, to contrast with the overt and at times graphic themes of women's rights suppression and child abuse, but it could also be interpreted as a somewhat cynical marketing gesture. For all of the motivation the story gives the player, the player's ability to influence events is extremely limited; you're basically playing a data recovery simulation while answering yes/no questions to abused women. I did not feel empowered by the game to make a palpable difference in the game world, and I can't recommend it.

I've played EVE for months (non-steam), and think it's a nice and deep game. The player-driven economy is incredible (though more to observe than participate in, at this point), exploration and 1vX pvp are very fun.
The difficulty/learning curve is exaggerated greatly in most places (if I have to see that stupid learning curve picture one more time...), the game isn't hard to grasp, it's mostly just poorly explained, and there is a lot of research to be done. If you know how to use a search-engine to answer your questions, the game becomes rather straight-forward.
If you plan on joining a nullsec corp and get into fleet pvp asap (which you can do on your first day), I think subscribing to the game is probably worth it. For all other aspirations, while it's true that you can do wormhole exploration in week 1 (I know, I did it), realise that it will take months of passive training (= maintaining active sub) to train up the skills needed to become even remotely competitive in a field. For instance, even if all you want to do is 1v1 pvp in frigates, you will need a lot of gunnery skills researched to even be able to use T2 guns and ammo, not to mention the passives like tracking speed, etc, which you will need to compete with people who have been playing the game for years.
tl;dr: if you know how to help yourself, and if you come to the game with the knowledge that it is a time investment, I can absolutely recommend EVE Online.
