I'll just say this before my review so that you have it in mind. My pc is well under-specced for this game and I have always given each patch a small bit of playtime before temporarily stopping. The lag is killing my brainwaves haha
PROS:
1) The world is very open. This, itself, gives the player alot of freedom, though, I still dont see many people that leave the starting zones.
2) This game is based mostly off of crafting. Actually this is a pro and a con, but for now, the pro part of it is that you can craft everything you would ever need if you have the patience and skill for it.
3) Lots of skills, 87 different skills if I am correct. That means you can pretty much always have something to do and its solely up to you how you do it.
4) Unlike most mmos where you have to grind for money, this game practically gives it away through quests, loot, and putting for crafted goods on the Auction House. For someone who plays a few hours a week, I can make about 15k in one sitting because of it.
5) Player Housing. There are 3 forms of this but one of the ways to use this to your advantage is building a nation and a player built city for just your friends.
CONS:
1) Prepare to learn the command "/unstick". You will practically get stuck on every little crevice due to some bugs that haven't been resolved.
2) Back to the crafting issue. This is very tedious and near quantum mechanics level of difficulty. Thankfully, the auction house can have pieces to help with this issue.
3) There is still massive amounts of lag in towns and in some fields. It has been improving but its not quite at a level where its acceptable
4) There is absolutely no direction after the tutorial. It plops you in the main game and basically makes you figure out what to do next.
5) The tutorial is extremely long and rather boring. The first time I did it, I managed it with only minor loss to my patience. The second time, I passed out from exhaustion thanks to crafting haha.
While there are many pros and cons left to this game, it does the game alot of injustice to point it all out. I would highly recommend this game, but would probably also recommend waiting for it to hit beta first. The game has a patch about once a month or every few months so small things are constantly being updated. Before you buy this game, check out some reviews on youtube to get a gist on what to expect.

Havent  been able to play much but here are some first impressions. I would not recomend this game to 90% of people. Right  now its ugly, janky, buggy, crashes a lot , and  a bit  like  trying to learn quantum physics  in kindergarten.  but those 10% of  people who enjoy that kind  of stuff, this is the game  for you.
Pros
Crafting- Oh my god crafting feels  good (although probably a bit to over complicated) You can craft pretty much everything you will ever need.
The world- Its massive with lots of  places to explore.
The community- So long as you are  asking  simple questions you will get fairly reasonable answers.
Pets! - Want to create a better  Monster? try genetic engeneering. More  of a nature  loving sort? Tame a wild beast. Killer robots  more your  speed? yup got those too! Plus side is you can probably buy them from someone who has already figured it  out.
Cons
Combat- is abysmal and  boring. Its tab combat. boring. Even the "action" mode  is just tab combat with clicking instead  of button presses ( IE you click your mouse to use your  auto attack on whatever  monster you have tab targeted.)
Overly Complicated- So depth is a great thing, complexity can be  a great thing, But having a graduation from simple to learn grating up to hard to master  would be  a better  way to do some  of the stuff in this game. As it is, not very new player friendly.

First off I want to say that I like this game, it has a very solid rule system behind its gameplay that's almost in depth enough to be a pen and paper RPG.
However charging for it at this point is just embarrassing for the devs and mildly insulting for players. Between getting stuck on the edge of a handrail while jumping(go into stealth or change stance to crouch), to getting the first person scope overlay stuck on your screen all the way out to distant third person(go back to character select), to hostile raiders running
the giant tree for cover and firing out of it at you(retreat out of range so they charge out of their perma shield). Add in words that are plain out wrong (ofs where ifs should be ect.) this game just isn't at a point functionally where I'd really feel good paying more then $10 for it.
That being said, I love the
skill/crafting/gathering system. It took me a couple hours to get my head around it, but as your knowledge of specific plants/recipes and you applicable skill increase you get better quality materials and make better items and equipment out of it. This is
as simple as it sounds, gather water and log trees then purify the water using the logs as a heat source, then breakdown logs with distilled water and some logs for the heat source to just to make glue. Combat is broken down into 4 melee, 6 ranged, 3 armor classes, plus tactical knowledges, multiple healing types, plenty of different pet-like things, driving and vehicle repair, stealth and awareness.
It's massive and I love it and it has so much promise, they need to pay a horde of english students to edit all the flavor and information text, preferably drop the entry price or make it a full demo until it's solidly in beta (I know devs, it hurts not getting the money but you'll get more good interest out of free then why did I pay $20)

Third review of this game, this time after 6 more months of stalled development (again); now over 2 years since the last patch and with abysmally low player count. I've been around this game in some form for almost 4 years now and have reviewed it 6 months ago and almost another 2 years before that, both time as a "recommend".
The IF Studio team didn't have what it takes to handle a situation like this one, both from a technical and a PR standpoint. I also believe they didn't properly assess the workload involved before getting into that deal, and didn't pour enough resources into reviving the game.
I no longer believe this game can be brought to its potential given the current circumstances and its history. Right now, all I'm expecting is (if we're lucky) a couple weak patches, bringing incremental changes, before the game completely dies off due to lack of resources by sometimes in the next year or two, tops.
It's kinda sad, but given that, I can't recommend this game as a promising mmorpg sandbox in early access and alpha, as I once did. If that's what you're looking for, look elsewhere.
In it's current state however, I think for the right price, it can be worth the hours of entertainment for some folks, but as long as you're ready to put up with a sub-par game quality-wise and no real hope to be anything else, ever.
Good luck.

Analogue: A Hate Story is an interactive novel where you have to find out why a spaceship filled with colonists is now floating in space devoid of life. (The name is a play on a previous game, Digital: A Love Story.) As you read the various logs, you also discuss them with the ship's two AIs to get the full picture.
(This is all from the early part of the story to avoid spoilers. If you don't want to see story, skip this paragraph.) The story that unravels revolves around a sick young girl in a culture much like modern Korea who is placed in a stasis pod in hopes that future technology can cure her. She is instead woken up far in the future where culture has actually regressed several centuries, and not only can they not cure her, but they instantly arrange a marriage against her will to gain status for the family.
This is a very sad story, but powerful and worth reading. It's not for kids, though.
There's not a ton of gameplay here to judge. The music is pretty nice, and the soundtrack isn't a bad purchase. Ultimately, the value of this game hangs entirely on its story, and if you're not interested in reading it, then this game has nothing for you. If you're okay with delving into the story for a few hours, then you may find a lot to enjoy. It's definitely worth getting on sale if it sounds interesting to you.

Unassuming, and understated; at first glance, it appears as though Rimworld is a generic colony management game. It's an understandable opinion, with it's cutesy graphics, and clean, almost clinical interface, it's easy to mistake the game for something a child would play. However, you decide to take the plunge, and buy the game.
When the main menu loads, you're greeted with one of the game's highpoints - it's soundtrack. An acoustic guitar riff, gentle and soothing, set against a background of stars, and a distant Rimworld planet. It almost begs to give you a relaxed, ethereal experience. But that, that was just a ruse.
After choosing your colonist(s), and starting location, you are cast down onto the planet's surface, amidst smoke, wreckage, and supplies. As you begin ticking through the tutorial steps, it finally sets in - this is not going to be easy. The game has a slight learning curve to get over, without a doubt, learning what needs to be built first, what your initial priorities should be, and such. By the time the tutorial steps are over, you're given enough information to set out on your own - a woefully naive, yet eager, settler.
The game's difficulty settings provide a large amount of variety to keep things fresh. Three "story tellers" provide different difficulty ramps, as well as provides a slew of sub-difficulty settings that affect the ingame event system, to add even more randomness to things. Needless to say, the game does not lack options. Not doing well in the game? Try choosing Phoebe Chillax as your story teller, set to "Base Builder" difficulty - attacks will be very rare, and events will be far less brutal. Experienced, and ready for hard action? Go hardcore with Randy Random on Extreme, and get a brutally hard curve with lots of random game events.
As noted before, the soundtrack of the game does not disappoint. Laced with acoustic instruments and soft synthetic beats, it feels like it would be right at home on the set of Firefly, The Expanse, or even Deadwood. It's a great accompaniment to the game's sound design, which showcases well balanced soundFX across the board.
Visually, the game is on par with other colony management style games, such as Prison Architect. Nothing super detailed, but more than enough to get the job done. The sprites are drawn in a cutesy, simplistic style, and are clean, and easy to read, even when zoomed out. Nothing award-winning here, but certainly a cut above others in the genre, I'd say.
The character backgrounds, and their interactions, are what makes this game for me. Each colonist comes with a rich background of life events, which dictate their skillset and behavior towards others. A child thief who grew up to be a pirate king might have amazing shooting skills, but they might be terrible at socializing and unable to haul things. Conversely, you might have a lovable art teacher who is great with animals, but they are anti-violence and will not fight. All of these story and personality traits change every time you play, and it offers the most diverse, and entertaining experience I've had in a game, in a long time.
The ultimate goal of the game is to build a new star ship, and leave the planet. However, most people tend to play the game as a survival challenge, and see how long they can last against the odds (how I like to play). Either way, it's going to be a long game, and a tough challenge. On top of that, there are a lot of mid-game things to deal with, such as forming trade caravans, forming peace treaties with rival factions, and a slew of other things that get explained throughout the tutorial.
It's a game you need to invest some time into, to get good at. You're not going to master Rimworld in 10 hours, or 50, even. I have over 640hrs into the game, and I still have times where I'll die in a few days to some random series of events. Later down the road, if you get bored with the vanilla game, the Steam workshop also has a HUGE amount of mods (1000+) to expand the game even further. The game will always be a challenge, but will always be rewarding. It's well worth the price, and the time investment.

Coming after the complete mess that was Puzzle Quest: Galactrix, Puzzle Quest 2 returns to the tried-and-tested Puzzle Quest formula we know and love with some enhancements to the gameplay and a streamlined story/quest mode. It's a good game (I wouldn't have played it for as long as I did if it wasn't) but leaves some things to be desired.
First things first: the game is *incredibly* slow compared to its predecessor, both in character movement on the map screen and within the gameplay itself. And whilst the story of the original didn't set any new records in originality, Puzzle Quest 2's story is both completely unrelated to the first and so boring that I just skipped it entirely. They have also stripped out large chunks of the sidegames in the first game (castle building, mount training, item creation, etc) and replaced them with laughably easy "unlock doors" and "disarm traps" minigames.
The addition of the new weapon system makes things interesting, and opens up a new strategy to the game. But towards the end of the game I found this just made the game a cycle of building up weapon points, and unleashing them on the enemy - ending the fight within a few turns of doing so and reducing fights to a monotonous routine. The armor/blocking mechanic is also interesting at first, but to be honest it just makes the game slower.
That all said though, it's still a good game. Three-in-a-row game mechanics are simple and addictive, and I don't feel that the time I spent playing the game was wasted, but I don't see myself replaying it any time soon due to its slow nature (compared to the first game that I completed at least five times.)
If you like three-in-a-row games then you'll like this. But I would recommend the first Puzzle Quest a lot more than its sequel.

Is the game fun to play? YES. It strikes a good balance of story and interaction along with that thing Dragon Ball fans have been craving in a game [CHARACTER CREATION].
Creation is a little limited in my opinion and the choices you make during creation only have a small and limited effect on eventual character outcome. I have come to realise endgame you can end up being forced into certain build types to be able to compete with high level players and beat the later missions. Those builds are almost all entirely based around blast supers and there is little to no emphasis on the actual fighting. Even the beefiest of characters have to rely on long range attacks to get anywhere. But all in all you do get some nice options and if you really don't give a toss about ranking you can do what you want. One thing to note is that when you make your first character you have to complete the main story before you can make any more characters.

The paralell quests were a nice distraction doing various different battles, even siding with villains etc. They do however become the ultimate ballache later on when you have to farm them forever in the hopes of an item dropping (especially Dragon Balls which become ridiculous when you have 6 and the drop rate plummets). That said when the servers are stable you can have fun hammering these quests with friends or strangers. The online system is quick and easy to jump into for both the pve and pvp stuff.
The graphics were ace. I don't like the gloss applied to everything personally but I can honestly say it doesn't really affect anything at all. Nothing feels out of place, there aren't any environment issues (that I've encountered) and the whole thing maintains a steady 60FPS even on my dated cart (GTX640).
It's not perfect. It feels like it's lacking something, it feels incomplete.
But it's Dragon Ball and it's not Battle of Z (a complete an utter dog♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of a game abortion) which is awesome.
I'd give it overall an 8/10 as a Dragon Ball fan BUT, I'd only get this on sale. It's asking price and the combined cost of DLC is a bit ridiculous in my humble opinion (and it's a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥take that the game has been on sale but the DLC hasn't unless bought as part of the Bundle Edition).

I know I have a lot of hours on this game here, but it is NOTHING compared to the 4+ years I dedicated to this game on the Nexon client. It was my second MMORPG (as I count Fusionfall as one), and a lovely one at that. First, a few cons.
Cons:
- Disconnects: I haven't seen these as a problem very recently, but I did have issues in the past of random disconnects. However, what MMO does not have those?
- Overwhelming: This game has a LOT going on, and can be overwhelming to new MMO players. Try to find veteran players willing to help out, or maybe see if a friend knew about the game. I personally love helping new players out!
- Story: It is compelling, but....I honestly don't remember most of what happened. The lore is really cool, as it is based on Irish mythology. But...it got more confusing as time wore on.
Pros:
- Huge open world with so many places to explore! 3 continents, along with other small off-map areas to unlock, and even special event areas.
- NOT PAY TO WIN- I WILL FIGHT THIS!!!!!! I played for a long time, and no, it is not pay to win. Over all of my time playing, I have put $5 into this game, which was for one small thing. However, I have gotten TONS of pets, LOTS of great outfits, amazing weapons, and even some pons (special currency) all from events!!! Heck, I got one of my pets from part of the story ( and she is my favorite! )! You can still get lots of skills, great gear, and a fun time, without putting any money in it.
- Customization: While the base customization is very small (though event-earned pons can expand it a bit), there are tons of outfits and accessories you can get! As you get better at earning gold, they become easier to get a hold of, so it takes a little patience. Also, there are many modest outfits for those who are sick of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ MMO costumes.
- Gorgeous: The music is AMAZING AHHHHH and if you liek the anime style, the characters are all well designed, even if a little too angular.
- COMBAT/CLASSES: My favorite aspect of the game is that you are not limited to a specific class and skillset! You can focus on a class, but you can learn all the skills you want! Some skills are only for certain races (elf, giant, and human), but only few. For instance, my elf is mage-focused, but is also extremely versed as a fighter and a bard, with tons of other skills on the side! You also can easily assign skills to hotkeys in a way that fits your fighting style and strategy, or according to a certain monster's weaknesses!
All in all, it's a big game! With lots of cool things to explore! Sure, the story slips my mind, but the combat and the open world are worth it. If you find yourself interested, but a little confused, hit me up! :D

Estranged: Act 1 is a new Half Life 2 modification by Alan Edwardes. You play a lone fisherman who is stranded on a mysterious island during a violent storm, all radio communications being sent out are being blocked by a looping curfew message from the mysterious Arque Corp. (Fun fact: Earlier in development it was Omnicorp)
And frankly, I'm happy to see another new, interesting Half Life 2 mod, as we haven't had one in a while, and many famous ones have been broken by Valve's updates, case and point: Black Snow. The most recent one I can think of is actually the full release of Underhell. So this is a nice new mod for fans like me. However, it does have a few problems.
Thankfully, it does have a fair amount of custom content, models and textures, along with new weapons. (However, the pistol is mainly a re-skin of the HL2 pistol, and the hammer being a crowbar replacement, albeit with a slightly slower swing speed. Except for the SMG, which is simply the stock HL2 model.) But the game itself is fairly simple. Easy puzzles and so-so gunplay. While I don't want to spoil any more of the game than I have already have.
The game has some pretty good voice acting in it, but sadly you don't get to see many characters for too long. The first character you you encounter in the game you only interact with for about five minutes, then he gives you a gun and sends you on your way. And the others you don't get any real background on, which I hope is changed in future acts.
Overall, the game is really nothing special, it is still enjoyable to play and I would recommend giving it a try.

An interesting 1st person puzzle platformer, in which the main mechanic consists in switching between 4 dimensions which affect your surroundings. For example: you can make objects lighter to transport them/throw them, make them heavier to break through glass or indestructible.
I recommend it simply for the puzzles and the satisfaction it gives to complete a section when you've discovered an entirely new mechanic a dimension proposes, just by yourself. Honestly, there's a lot more into play than in Portal 1 and almost as much as Portal 2, and if you liked those two games, there's a lot of content to entertain you for a while in this game.
However, I believe this game has a major flaw: its ending. No spoilers will be given here, but honestly, there is a great, inmensely great build-up while progressing through the final stages of the game. I was genuinely curious as to what was going to happen in the very last puzzle, and started imagining what it could be; but... Nothing. A rather abrupt ending, virtually no final puzzle, and... in retrospect, the puzzles right before the ending weren't even that much of a challenge either. I would have expected their difficulty/completxity to be something much greater, but... meh. I was really disappointed. And I mean, really, disappointed.
Nonetheless, it's still a good game, and I really recommend it for those who want to enjoy the challenge and the gimmicks that this game can offer.

I've been always both frustrated and fascinated by DOTA 2. There are times when I flame, rage, laugh, cry (not really), and be shocked about the gameplay, patches, metagame, bugs, and balance and garbage (pls mr lizard) fixes. Still, I am amazed at how it turned out to be!
Back when DOTA 2 has started, it was beneath the shadows of a larger behemoth that is the League of Legends (LoL ) waaay back. Since LoL was very predominant than DOTA 2, there are few players back then. I was somewhat part of the early Alpha Release and mostly Closed Beta, and it was mostly ridden with bugs, but it was fixed as long as many people complained of it. Still, DOTA 2 was like a toddler back then, with tournaments giving prizes worth just hundreds of bucks, with some reaching thousands of dollars.
Some, like me, felt like DOTA 2 will never prosper, because LoL was in full flight back then. Generally, computers can play LoL because it uses less resources, whereas DOTA 2 requires you to have a more powerful PC than those regular office desktops, which is commonplace to where I live.
Much like the tournaments in LoL and the Majors in CS:GO, DOTA 2 has tournaments of its own, however it's still small compared to the former games, respectively. But it was a start, that a new competitive scene is blooming, albeit a small one.
But then, The International happened. Then it changed.
Now, DOTA 2 boasts the biggest prizepool ever in eSports. The fact that most of the prizepool has been crowdfunded by the staunch DOTA 2 Community gives the fact that people are really supportive of the DOTA 2 Competitive scene.
With the Majors on the rise along with The International, DOTA 2 will become bigger than ever before.
But before that, one must look at the professional players. Some are enthusiasts who wanted to show the world that they are the bestest DOTA 2 Professional team. Others wanted to earn popularity make statuses of themselves. Few wanted the prize money to make a living. But they didn't came and participated just for the money, but they came to achieve what is at stake: the Aegis of Immortality. It is in the Aegis of Immortality that their name will be engraved for all eternity, as long as DOTA 2 is still alive. It is the proof that they struggled through thick and thin, just to be at the top.
Blood (though not really), sweat, money, and tears are shed and wasted just to participate in one of the biggest tournament ever to happen on DOTA 2, rather, to the eSports Scene.
Teams will fight to the bitter end, and one team will emerge victorious. That's how you fight in The International.

Did you enjoy playing Galaxies between launch and the CU? Do you like complex crafting systems (the good kind)? Do you like the freedom to level 1 or 2 things or Everything if you want on one character?
The Repopulation might be for you, then.
Use any weapon, or heal.
Tame wild animals, or make your own to fight with and / or for you.
Completely customize the way your character looks on creation, and afterward in-game if you didn't pick the right things. Think about the Saints Row Series - make a normal-looking or goofy character if you want.
Entertain and buff yourself and other characters in rest zones like pubs in and outside. Not near a town? You can pop open a tent and do the same with your group.
Not interested in being a good guy? Stealth your way around and pick pocket / steal from people and shops. Become an assassin with rogue-like abilities - backstab with one or two knives for massive damage. (From my experience, starting out along this path is a little tricky in the current state 7/29/15). There are several skill lines that are beneficial - Stealth, Assassination, Bladed Weapons, Thievery, etc.
Want to build your own robots, vehicles, and other advanced items? You may want to consider joining a nation (guild). Crafting is complex for most advanced items and you may want friendly teams of people gathering to accelerate the process.
The game is early access, which means many things haven't been refined to perfection, and there are still some features on the "To Do / To Add" list. In its current state, I can still recommend this game to all those interested in it. Be warned; there is a guaranteed wipe slated for the launch of the game. There are only rumours of other wipes between now and then, but no official word on any.
There are GMs that occasionally do testing with players ingame to hunt down bugs and troubleshoot various things. Watch General chat for opportunities like these.
On live streams (Twitch) you'll be able to get info on new features, ask about development, etc. As of the one that was done a few days ago, I had the opportunity to ask about Space Exploration ("Will we be Repopulating other planets at some point?"). It was confirmed that this is something they want in the game; Space Exploration and Space Combat.

Remember the first time you parachuted into occupied (virtual) Normandy, France in the dead of night? Took out those German patrols stealthy-like? Created a distraction so your comrades-in-arms could take the beachhead and secure a landing site? Or remember being packed in an LCU (VIRTUAL), sea water and vomit sloshing beneath you; the Atlantic tossing you about like a plaything before your ship slammed into the beach? The ramp lowered, bullets chewed your men up around you; imposing, gray, gloomy skies contrasted that red, roiling surf? I sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥do. The developers of “Enemy Front” also remember. They remember and they want you to TOO.
It's been years since we've gotten a great WWII shooter. DAMN OUR HUBRIS. “Developers, we are SICK of killing Nazis. Come on, let's see something new,” we cried. “Okay, how about Nazi zombies?” they replied. And we were content for a time. But we wanted more. So they decided to drown the market in Tom Clancy Russian/Arab/Chinese right-wing wet dream masturbatory aid for the last SEVEN years. It's gotten more boring than WWII ever was. Because history is tangible. It happened. It happened to our grandparents. We can read books and watch documentaries and visit sites. It's real. It's powerful. Pretend future conflicts just aren't the same. They aren't bad, no! Just different. They don't have the same staying power. Remember my first paragraph? Bet you all remembered each of those moments vividly as I described them. Okay, now reflect on some of the latest modern shooter moments. OH♥♥♥♥♥♥ REMEMBER THAT TIME YOU GOT NUKED? Yep. That was pretty heavy. WHAT ABOUT THE GHILLIE SUIT CHERNOBYL LEVEL?!? Oh yeah, that was excellent! Got anything else? No? Okay.
So I hope I've made my position in this debate clear. Now this WWII shooter might not be the savior we're looking for, but it's a fine first effort. The story is interesting, but Citizen Kane this is not. The characters are interesting but one note, underdeveloped, and underutilized. But this is to be expected from the genre. This isn't why we play WWII shooters though, is it? No. We play them to kick Nazi butt. So what little suffers from the weaker story elements the gameplay salvages.
You can approach a level in one of two ways: either come in Captain America style, rocking Nazi faces with your raw and unrelenting patriotism, or you can hit them Sam Fisher stealth style. This duality is very rewarding. The gunplay is great. I can feel the jolts up my arm; I feel the impact of each bullet, whether it's striking flesh or cover. I feel totally immersed. I'm a grimy, grizzled, Nazi-blood-hungry warrior – I'm not playing a video game in my underwear, hungry for day old pizza. The AI is serviceable. I'm playing on expert difficulty. They tend to rush in, unfortunately. Sometimes they display tactics, but on at least a few occasions I've taken a shot in an open area and fallen back, watching them funnel one by one into my death corridor. But otherwise they're competent – just don't expect “Brothers in Arms” tactics. The graphics are excellent, especially considering this is also a PS3 and Xbox 360 release. The ruined cities feel alive, buzzing and burning. The countryside is verdent and beautiful, still scarred by the brutality of war. And the sounds, last but not least, the sounds. Bullets whiz and ping, Germans shriek and shout orders, bombardments are heavy. The score is a little repetitive but it certainly is soaring and epic, fitting for the setting. If the gameplay makes this immersive, then the sound design is the icing on the cake.
A few gripes worth mentioning. I'm a resistance fighter. Thank God the Germans just left open ammo crates lying around everywhere otherwise, I don't know, I might have had to drop my weapon, change things up! And I'm tired of every European out of WWII speaking near perfect English. I wouldn't have minded subtitles; French speaking French, Polish speaking Polish. Finally, the game touts open worldness as a feature and pressures you to explore. I wish there were some collectables... propoganda leaflets and art, love notes and correspondence. History. An unfortunate missed opportunity.
So for my fellow history buffs and historical war enthusiasts AND EVEN A FEW OF YOU MODERN FANATICS, I think you'll have a good time with this game. It has serious nostalgia potential. You will likely smile and reflect on your time with this game when you're finally finished playing. For thirty bucks this is well worth your time. This is almost AAA quality. You owe it to yourself to give it a try.
Now go liberate (VIRTUAL) Europe.

Borderlands is an action-RPG / first person shooter. It features cooperative-play, phat loot(tm), and vehicles. This is a game designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible. In this regard, it's a success.
But what do I think of it? Well... eh. I mean, I like Borderlands well enough... I guess. When it comes to this game, the best statements I can muster come off as half-hearted and wishy-washy. I've always been a fan of loot-driven games, but there has to be some sort of hook beyond the basic qualities. It doesn't have to be something particularly clever, but it has to make the game stand out. I think Borderlands lacks this quality, but it's still an alright way to spend a weekend of four.
Oh wait. You're probably expecting an explanation of what this "quality" is supposed to be aren't you? When it comes to videogames, originality can only go so far. Oft-times, we just have to accept the fact that not every game we play is going to be completely unique and excellent. Sometimes we end up buying games because they look interesting, are in a genre we enjoy, or our friends are playing them. Borderlands is a perfect example.
To me, the words perfect and mediocre, are two sides of the same coin. Today's perfection is tomorrow's mediocrity. What was once the gold-standard, has now become the base-line. Borderlands has everything it needs to accomplish its goal of being a competent FPS Lootemup, and nothing more. The shooting mechanics aren't anything brilliant, the controls are acceptable, and the story/writing serve their purpose. The skill-tree system is neat, but only in a "that makes sense" sort of way. The build you create isn't really important, because the same two or three abilities tend to dominate every encounter.
The guns, the aspect that should set this game apart from the pack, are merely okay. One commonality among loot-based games (especially more recent ones), is that very few character-builds actually use their weapon. By that I mean the sword, polearm, or otherwise is merely a stat-boosting piece of equipment. Usually, the player just uses their skills in order to kill enemies, instead of swinging a large piece of metal around. Practically the sole method of killing in Borderlands is through the usage of guns. Unfortunately, 98% of them are useless. This is especially true of the "gimmick" guns dropped by bosses. More often than not, you're going with the standard weapons, just because they're actually effective. In other words, instead of swinging the boring swords, you have to fire the boring guns. The inability to create an identity through play-style is the #1 reason why this game fails to stand out.
A game like Borderlands could have really benefitted from more intricate level-designs, as well as a greater level of depth in terms of controls. I'm thinking that the developers could have come up with all sorts of crazy manuevers to pull off. Sliding, air-dashes, back-flips, shoulder-charges, some parkour stunts, you get the idea. Not all of these moves would have to be in the game, but even a couple of them would have lended more dynamism to the combat. This would also make the maps more fun to explore, well... if there was more to them besides wide-open spaces to catch a ride(tm) through, or the bog-standard "rooms filled of cover" that's in every other FPS.
The RPG elements, while appreciated, sometimes make the game feel too much like an MMO. I know it's just a guideline, but when everything has a level suggestion next to it, the atmosphere is lost. While I always enjoy the immediate pleasures of leveling up and finding better gear, the world-building gets pushed away. Didn't TellTale make a Borderlands game that addresses this very concern? Hm... Perhaps I should look into it.
When a game makes an attempt to stand out, it can instead become flawed. The developer tried something different, and either it was a bad idea to begin with, or they didn't quite get it right. Borderlands doesn't take these risks. It's a perfectly mediocre product that delivers enough incentivization to keep gamers playing, it doesn't strive to do any more than that. I don't think that makes this game worthy of praise, but I still enjoyed it well enough... I guess.

It amazes me how many people are ignoring basic critical game play mechanics because they want a star wars clone SO BAD.
This game doesn't have a solid leg to stand on. Crafting & City Housing could've been, but they're just as broken as every other aspect of this game. The backers are hostile towards anyone who mentions this. The devs respond with, "Dx 11 & hero engine update will fix everything". No, it will not. Two patches focused on suckering new players in and keeping backers on top of the economy. Zero attention paid to broken mechanics. Next patch won't focus on any of them either.
Map - Completely fubared. Pass 4-5 zones and you're crashing. Teleport = 50% chance of crash. Got a buddy with you? Not anymore, he's invisible to you. Ridiculous amount of holes in the map. Some areas are so bad you get stuck in them. Teleporting out just moves you to another area and brings the bugs with you, if you dodged the teleport crash. This is by far the most broken and frustrating part of the game.
Crafting - This is probably the strongest aspect of the repopulation. Still has it's bugs, and it's meaningless if you can't get around to collect resources without back to back crashes, loading freezes, etc.
Combat - Clunky, unresponsive, half the time your fittings aren't working and there's no point fighting anything. Buffs are equally screwed up. Most of your time will be spent running away from a fight because of some bs mechanic not working or the NPC bugging out. We see these problems a lot in alphas, we just usually see some sort of progress on fixing them.
PVP - Nobody PVPs because combat is garbage. There isn't even an incentive to pvp. A lot of people come in wanting to test pvp and end up jumping threw a lot of hoops just to be able to pvp. Three second fight and... we're done.
City Sieges - Doesn't exist. This is how I got sucked in. Fake video with fake city fight. I figured if they were at this point in the alpha it had to be pretty solid, right? Nope. Cities are so broken they should be overhauled before even thinking about sieges.
Sandbox - You can't have a sandbox if everyone is shoehorned into what works vs what they want to play.
In short, EVERYTHING feels half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥with a "it'll get fixed later" attitude. This is a small team, big game, and it's alpha, I get it. But how many times are you going to use that excuse? How long has it been in alpha? Who's going to fix it later? Why would you continue building a house on an unstable/broken foundation? Fix something, anything.
The backers own the game. They own the cities. They own the economy. They demand new content and get it. And if you try to question the devs about critical bugs not being addressed you will get mobbed by them. The game is perfectly stable and ready for release in their opinion. (your 20 bucks will feel wasted, and 60 bucks for a game this broken is just beyond nuts.)
I think people want a good scifi mmorpg, this just isn't it. This one calls itself an alpha, says they're ready for beta, patches like it's open, but feels like a first year alpha. This team's "direction" coupled with hostile backers conning people into buying the game has turned this into a "Stay the F away" for me. I've seen nothing to indicate things will get better.

Puzzle Quest 2 is incredibly tedious, stripping out any pretense of a story, so you just clear out floor after floor of mobs, with nothing to break up the monotony. They've removed all side activities, like conquering castles, taming mounts, crafting items. Instead of equipment conferring interesting abilities, all it does now is raise a generic Defense stat (except for the weapon, of course). You meet sidekick characters that are immediately forgotten the second they join your party and never speak again.
Yes, they moderately improved the match-3 aspect by removing pointless gold and experience and replacing them with purple mana and action points, but that's literally the only improvement. Across the board, every other change they made is a detriment to the game. THE ART IS TERRIBLE.
Puzzle Quest: Challenge of the Warlords is a much, much better game. It had a simple but fun fantasy plot, solid sidekick characters, a neat (if unbalanced) mix of equipment, and decent enough art. The match-3 gameplay honestly isn't that different between the two, so even if that's your focus, I still recommend the first game due to its much higher quality and variety.
Puzzle Quest 2 is a bad game that wastes your time.

I haven't played the first or second game in the series, but this was a refreshing experience for me. A very fun, action-packed game with many, many characters to offer - each with impressive and broad movesets that feel awesome to pull off. Furthermore, it's stunning, the anime style was beautifully implemented into this 3D game. I've played for roughly 20 hours, finishing the story mode, and most characters I've yet to unlock, so there's plenty to do. I have but a few issues with the game that I've got to address. Sometimes it's a real pain when crewmates are about to flee from battle and you have to run all the way across the map to help them. Special attacks can get pretty repetitive, it would be nice to have more - even two per character would make a big difference. Missions generally can get kind of repetitive when there are just too many foes. Boss fights don't stand out enough as they work nearly the same as any other fight. It'd be cool to have some cinematic quick time events or more of a God of War approach to the boss fights. For replay value, I think a versus mode would really help the game. It's kind of a shame that you can't put two or more characters in a fight outside of Legend, Free or Dream Log. Also the sountrack, while of good quality, is too repetitive. Too much of the same melody. That's about it. I haven't explored the game in it's entirety but these are my impressions at the moment. I would highly recommend the game, lots of fun.

Day of Defeat Source, the so called, engine port of the original Day of Defeat. When I first launched this game I was greeted with a 2 sided menu with an impresive and epic theme which got me hyped for the first server I was going to join and have a remastered version of the game I once played years ago but when I sent client info and chose my faction, I had realized that this game was more than a simple engine upgrade, it was a remake. Everything was different from the classes, balance, and factions.
- Faction and Class Balance: They got rid of the British and most of the classes for the Wheremacht and Americans limiting them down to 6 for the 2 factions. You could say this was done to balance the game a bit more but all it did was break the balance even more. For the US, the rocketeir class's secondary weapon,The M2 Carbine (which was the primary weapon of Staff Sargent from the Original), outmatches the rifleman and assult's primaries and not to mention that the rocket launcher is a 1 hit kill weapon.
-Maps: Mechanicaly the maps are reskins of the original which actually play fine and meet graphical expectations of the time of release, but they also look heavily unpolished to where I found multiple void holes in a number of the defualt maps.
-Sound Design: Outside of the epic intro theme, the voice acting is passable and sound ok but it's nothing close to being considered impresive in comparison to Valve's other games such as TF2, Portal, or Dota 2. for weapons sounds, they actually fit well with the guns they are given to but this leads to a larger problem that mainly lies in server hosting. If you go onto certain servers that have a certain setting enabled/disabled, you will not be able to hear the weapon sounds made by other players  which nearly kills the experience since ive seen this issue occur on several servers.
-The Community: DoD Source is one of those games where you get a lot of older folk playing it and the servers belong to clans what have existed in Valve gaming since the release of Steam. The downside is that those folk who come on the servers are very few in number to where you wil either find yourself playing a game with only 3 people or a server filled with bots. The map making community from what I've seen has produced some maps ive come to like but I havent seen anything that is complete garbage or a game developer masterpeice.
-The Shooting: The gimic that Day of Defeat has behind its shooting mechanics is very simple. The more you fire your weapon the more your crosshair will want to jump upward. The way you would maintain accuracy is to either fire in bursts, move your mouse downward as you fire, fire from the feet upward to ensure all your bullets hit. It's very simple and it would seem very easy to execute but there is one major flaw in the system and that is the hitboxes. The hitboxes are the worst thing I have ever seen any game I have ever played, I have come behind a stationary bot and sprayed into him with my mp40 and I see bloodmarks all across his body but he then turns around and the bot kills me in 1 hit with his rifle. You might suggest I use my melee instead but there is a bigger issue in the melee system. you can only, and I mean ONLY deal damage when you are aiming at their head with your knife/spade and another thing is if you go for a backstab, there is no way you can do to someone who is moving because the game will force you into a 2 second animation when you backstab and it will cancel if you move at all or if the target is too far away so you are better off just trying to use you grenades in any given senario. The grenades in day of defeat as a franchise has always been ♥♥♥♥ed, they are 1 hit kill, have a large radius, and you are given around 5 per life so the game turns into nothing but a game of throwing bombs at eachother like ISIS on a Tuesday.
-The Conclusion: If you like WW2 shooters that takes place in the American German Theatre. I would advise you pick up a game like Day of Infamy or the original Day of Defeat.

Borderlands is an action-RPG / first person shooter. It features cooperative-play, phat loot(tm), and vehicles. This is a game designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible. In this regard, it's a success.
But what do I think of it? Well... eh. I mean, I like Borderlands well enough... I guess. When it comes to this game, the best statements I can muster come off as half-hearted and wishy-washy. I've always been a fan of loot-driven games, but there has to be some sort of hook beyond the basic qualities. It doesn't have to be something particularly clever, but it has to make the game stand out. I think Borderlands lacks this quality, but it's still an alright way to spend a weekend of four.
Oh wait. You're probably expecting an explanation of what this "quality" is supposed to be aren't you? When it comes to videogames, originality can only go so far. Oft-times, we just have to accept the fact that not every game we play is going to be completely unique and excellent. Sometimes we end up buying games because they look interesting, are in a genre we enjoy, or our friends are playing them. Borderlands is a perfect example.
To me, the words perfect and mediocre, are two sides of the same coin. Today's perfection is tomorrow's mediocrity. What was once the gold-standard, has now become the base-line. Borderlands has everything it needs to accomplish its goal of being a competent FPS Lootemup, and nothing more. The shooting mechanics aren't anything brilliant, the controls are acceptable, and the story/writing serve their purpose. The skill-tree system is neat, but only in a "that makes sense" sort of way. The build you create isn't really important, because the same two or three abilities tend to dominate every encounter.
The guns, the aspect that should set this game apart from the pack, are merely okay. One commonality among loot-based games (especially more recent ones), is that very few character-builds actually use their weapon. By that I mean the sword, polearm, or otherwise is merely a stat-boosting piece of equipment. Usually, the player just uses their skills in order to kill enemies, instead of swinging a large piece of metal around. Practically the sole method of killing in Borderlands is through the usage of guns. Unfortunately, 98% of them are useless. This is especially true of the "gimmick" guns dropped by bosses. More often than not, you're going with the standard weapons, just because they're actually effective. In other words, instead of swinging the boring swords, you have to fire the boring guns. The inability to create an identity through play-style is the #1 reason why this game fails to stand out.
A game like Borderlands could have really benefitted from more intricate level-designs, as well as a greater level of depth in terms of controls. I'm thinking that the developers could have come up with all sorts of crazy manuevers to pull off. Sliding, air-dashes, back-flips, shoulder-charges, some parkour stunts, you get the idea. Not all of these moves would have to be in the game, but even a couple of them would have lended more dynamism to the combat. This would also make the maps more fun to explore, well... if there was more to them besides wide-open spaces to catch a ride(tm) through, or the bog-standard "rooms filled of cover" that's in every other FPS.
The RPG elements, while appreciated, sometimes make the game feel too much like an MMO. I know it's just a guideline, but when everything has a level suggestion next to it, the atmosphere is lost. While I always enjoy the immediate pleasures of leveling up and finding better gear, the world-building gets pushed away. Didn't TellTale make a Borderlands game that addresses this very concern? Hm... Perhaps I should look into it.
When a game makes an attempt to stand out, it can instead become flawed. The developer tried something different, and either it was a bad idea to begin with, or they didn't quite get it right. Borderlands doesn't take these risks. It's a perfectly mediocre product that delivers enough incentivization to keep gamers playing, it doesn't strive to do any more than that. I don't think that makes this game worthy of praise, but I still enjoyed it well enough... I guess.

As a fan of Dragon Ball Z, this is the sort of game I have been waiting for a long time. You can also replay secondary quests with any of the characters you have previously defeated,  Want three Siabamen going up against Frieza?  You got it.  Want to team up with Vegeta and Nappa and beat the snot out of Krillin?  You've got that too,  THe huge cast of characters, in addition to completely new ones makes this game well worth the money paid for it.
The only drawback I can really complain about is the limitations of online play.  The fact that one cannot directly chat with other players is saddening.  Instead they give you some predetermined phrases that you get to choose from.  I've been trying to do some co-op battles with other players but there never seems to be any sort of interest in that, as there are barely any ever "rooms" available to join,
If you are a fan of Dragon Ball Z, get this game.  It's well worth it and training your own character in the DBZ Universe is a friggin' blast.

So i bought this game, played plenty of it, or rather still do at around 40 hours barely having anything finished. (Quiet alot to do in here espicially since there are 64 characters in this.) But i notice alot of complaints about little to nothing worth of reason.
Those i notice most:
1. Mouse/Keyboard controls. Lolwut? There are not even mouse controls, and i S-Rank half this♥♥♥♥♥♥with keyboard controls i dont see a problem here.
2. Graphics. Havent we talked about this trillions of times since past COD that grafics have no impact on your gameplay experience? There are plenty of high graphic games that are complete trash :D. No seriously tho this is from a Anime, you cant expect Ultra high quality grafics from something that is supposed to have those comic grafics with them. Not like those 3 or 4 extra lines in their facial expression does anything.
3. Missing Customes: To be fair. They never said any about that, you actually get a activation key you can enter on their homepage for those.
As for the crashes and bugs, i never experienced any and my Computer about 3 years old and of medium quality. And i run this game on max settings.
Enough of that, now about the game:
While i only watched about 100 episodes of this extremly long running Anime (Which is at over 700 Episodes right now) I can fairly say it got alot of fanservice, In dreamlog you can have all the 64 characters in the core game fight against each other for whatever reason in a lore-friendly/unfriendly fashion which sometimes trigger special ingame-sideconversation, which has no deep impact tho. And like you would expect from a Dynasty Warriors spin off almost every character got alot of flashy and stylish attacks. Complete eyecandy for the friends of this Anime.
As said im not a anime fan but i still enjoy this because you can aswell be just a Dynasty Warriors fan to play through it, unlike other spin offs the story is actually well developed by plenty of cutscenes and inbetween comic segments which are partially animated. Good touch, and they did a good job having it 1:1 with the anime.
As for the gameplay. Sufficient Graphics, The animation of the characters are very good.. including the breastphysics of those for some reason well endowed ladies which i do not recall having a chest like that in the anime... but hell why not. And the voice acting sounds reasonable to the translation given in text.. which i may be wrong about since this game offers no english audio. Never bothered me however.
The sound is.. eeh.. its easy to notice that some tracks are about 10~15seconds loops, least it tries to mix up the many clips during the mission objectives.
So thats all the positive things.. so whats bad to tell about the game eh?
Its rightfully called 'Overpriced' for a originally portable title, And they expect you to pay for big bucks for story DLCs ontop of that, which is sorta a let down but BandaiNamco never really cared about their customers wishes and wallets aslong the money went into theirs. What you get in this game is 64 Playable Characters, a Story mode that covers about 150~200 episodes of the anime (Without DLCs, im not sure how many they cover precisley) And a Dreamlog mode which covers no story aspect beside the last fight with *Spoiler* which is the pre-last island on it. Which can keep you busy for maybe 40h~60h in total depending how quickly you bumrush the game.
On another note there are characters which are not very well balanced, Appears that most of the female characters are too gimmicky to show any efficiency compared to most of the male characters.. not to flame any feminism but i found myself avoiding to pick females despite of the treasure events. Its also easy to notice the further you go through the store the more powerful do the characters get, which is fine. But eventually they become walking nukes spitting AoEs everywhere without much of a effort.
Lastly is the usually repeated problem of the games repetitive nature, which seemed to have gotten no solution whatsoever regardless of how long this franchise and their spinoffs go already. There feels to be no real attempt of changing that even in this one.
So, my verdict?
Wait for a sale. It's a fair game for about 25$ But its not worth a triple A price. Espicially since it was closely released along with Phantom Pain where you can see the 'pain'ful difference of quality of a AAA Game and a repetitive Copy/Paste game that has been reskinned.
Makes this game overall NOT a bad game. Gets my thumbs up.

If you are a fan of the genre, PQ2 is a welcome addition, however it is not as strong as PQ1 in my opinion.
Firstly, avoid the iOS and Android version of this game; it has awful monetization requirements.
Puzzle Quest 2 is much more dungeon-focused than its predecessor. While this still makes for a good game, it pales in comparison to the original Puzzle Quest. The maps are not as interesting and there certainly is not as much to do. The introduction of mini-games to determine quality and quantity of loot gets tedious; fast. The game looks just as polished as its predecessor.
In this Puzzle Quest, you cannot have your own castle or ride mounts or capture enemies to learn their abilities. This definitely takes away from the replayability of the game. Being able to learn any ability from any enemy really added a level of depth that, when missing, makes PQ2 feel barren.
Overall, this game is not bad, but I do feel the developers tried changing too much with their game and took it in a direction that is less welcoming to people who wish to replay it.

This 'game' is often described as a visual/interactive novel, which I find fairly accurate.  It's written by a Canadian author named Christine Love and puts you in the role of an investigator sifting through the logs of a long-missing colony spaceship that's recently reappeared.
Journals, transcripts, letters - primary document-type stuff for those of you who paid attention in history class - provide fragmented glimpses that slowly come together to make a full picture from many different sides.  You're not alone; the ship's two AI constructs guide you through and connect you to the world with their experiences and opinions - and connect with you via your own opinions.
When I started noticing the parallels to a certain historical topic (I'll put exactly what as a comment; mild spoilers), I was indeed reminded of a particular year of history class in school, and the further I delved into the records, the more I fell in love with and was horrified by their backwards portrayal of future and past.
Don't be fooled by the appearance of the characters - this is a mature story that deals with some heavy topics.  It's got multiple endings by way of interaction with the vessel's two AIs, which represent opposite opinions on some of the story's central themes.  You don't need to like science fiction or history - all you need is to not be afraid to read.

It was a pain to start up. Performance was managable, but every time I clicked something, the screen flashed white for a millisecond. Any time something attempted to load, the game's resolution either broke or the screen flashed black and white fast enough to give your Jewish grandmother a seizure just by being within 5 kilometers, and since I'm American I don't even know how far that is. The game only gives you an "options" button after you finish Chapter 1, so you'll have to deal with hearing aids for the rest of your life after the music blew your ear drums so effectively that your neighbors filed a noise complaint thinking that you started an invisible outdoor rock band. Once you gain around 10.5 achievements just by standing still and finding out that chickens lay eggs (no, really, your character celebrates after discovering this), you can sift through all of the on-screen menus to find the settings button buried under tabs after tabs after tabs. Hold your horses, though, chicken-molester, because if you try to actually change any of the settings - even screen brightness - you're disconnected from the server and told that you can't start or exit the game until your 30 seconds of probation are up. After waiting through your tedious 30 seconds, you realize that the warning doesn't actually count for you. You have to end the game through task manager and open it up again in order to log in. Now, while my ugly little elf-boy with asymmetrical facial features may be able to follow a cursor (although not being able to spell WASD) may be creepily intimate with your constant bewildered gaze, it's not enough for me to keep this game installed. To those that play this game religiously - since there are those in every game - I would both like to learn computer skills and patience from you, but I also would not want to shake your hand.

Quantum Conundrum is a family friendly, less narratively interesting first person puzzler with unique and fun puzzle devices. My biggest complaint would be a couple puzzles toward the end of the game that are just miserable and lazy. The rest of it is fun and engaging if only for short bursts. This isn't a bad thing for a typical puzzle game but feels odd for a game which feels like it will grip you like Portal did, and never does.
The game is often compared to Portal, a better game, to Conundrum's detriment, but it has earned the comparison. It attempts a snarky, dark humored irreverent and unkind narrator.  It has both seemingly deliberate "puzzle rooms" and behind the scenes type puzzle sections, very similar to what Portal offered. The lead designer was one of the original Portal creators and I'm assuming she figured the formula was flawless. Well... It's not flawless but it is pretty darn good.  If you're a game designer, consider playing it just to see how cleverly the dimensional swap mechanics can be used for physics gameplay.

If you miss SWG, this is the game for you.  If you love open-world sandbox games, this is the game for you.
Its Alpha.  Things are amiss.  Because its Alpha.  But there is still an incredibly rich experience to be had even at this early phase.  The Alpha community is generous, helpful and knowledgable.    Are there glitches, bugs, random CTDs and errors than require you to wait for a midnight server reset to unstick your character?  Yep.  It's Alpha.  These things happen.
There isn't a lot of hand-holding.  In fact, a lot of critical documentation has yet to be implemented, but give the game a day or so to grow on you.  I'm a SWG day one vet and have quite a bit of exposure to sandbox games.  I was still mystified by many of the game's aspects.  Three days in, I had figured most of it out.
Fair warning: the crafting system is incredibly deep and complex.  This isn't going to be like Galaxies where you can be self-sufficient after leveling a couple of Alts to Master.
I have a couple of beginners 'tips:  There's an NPC doctor in the hospital who wants parasites that can be looted while mining or logging.  Grab the 10cr used logging saw and used mining drill and have at it.  Rise and repeat all the way to your fist vehicle.  Price are about 2K for a decent cycle.  Or buy a Light Assault Mech and get killed by a vulture.  I take that back, don't by the Light Mech.  Just buy a cycle.
Anytime you get an Engagement Mission....head out and do it.  The rewards will be worthwhile.
Don't start fights you can't finish....specifically with any NPC mob that has "Medic" in their name.  Serioulsy OP atm.
8/10 currently.  I can't give it 10/10 because it's not quite finished and polished (because Alpha).  Entirely worth the 20 bucks for the basic level backer's pack and Alpha access.

I recently bought this on steam for £15, it truly is SWG 2.
I've been really impressed with the level of customization, especially with player cities.
The crafting system is complex. There is a grading system in place. 50 grade levels with F0 - A9 that applies to components, ingredients and the actual items crafted. There is a big learning curve with the crafting system and it is designed so you are dependent on other crafting professions for certain high level components.
There is the normal AH, accessible from anywhere that also allows you to place work order for others to fill (think EVE).
The levelling system isn't straight forward, it is similar to SWG (from what I can remember) but not exactly the same. You pick up a weapon and the beginner skills, and you level it by using the weapon. When you reach a certain level you unlock an ability, but you do not get the ability yet. There are two ways to attain the ability, one is to spend training points which are given to you for completing missions. Mission completion can also give reward you directly with a choice of ability. It's a little hard to explain.
Another element of the skill/levelling system is Skill Imprinting points. All sorts of in game actions can reward you with SI points, which you can then invest in the relevant skills to give your level a boost.
There are two main factions warring with each other, and you can create your own third faction and align them with either main faction. I've not had a chance to play with this feature yet but as far as I know you can change your alignment at any time.
Combat seems pretty good to me but needs a little work. You can roll like in GW2 and there are a lot of combat classes such as Rifles, Automatic weapons, grenades, aerosol, bladed weapons, unarmed, blunt weapons, martial arts, axe, handguns, probably a few more and you can dual wield some of them. And shields.
There are healing abilities that require a healing scanner in the main hand, so any class can heal but it requires swapping out your weapon.
Anyone can play the entertainer class that dances and tells stories to give buffs. You can only do this in a "rest" zone, which comes in the shape of inner city bars or player placed tents when out in the wild. You can tame animals with animal handling or buy them from a genetic engineer, use robots made by robotics, go fishing, logging, foraging or mining. Place harvesters, get into hacking or diplomacy. Culinary arts can make food buffs, stims made by pharmacists. There are stylists, interior decorators, disguises, stealth, traps and quite a number more that I've not mentioned such as armour/weapons crafting etc.
I know that every time a new game comes out, someone makes a huge post listing all the great features it has and tries to get people hyped. We're all a bit above that kind of hype train nonsense now but I hope that the info I've given is of some help.

There is so much I could tell you about this game, all of which is positive, I have no beef with this game, none at all, I love this game so much.
This game is fantastic, without a doubt, it allows you to control the lives of two amazing characters as well as interact with some awesome companions. All the characters have great chemistry, they all just work so well together, Sasha and Fiona (This sisters) and Rhys and Vaugn (The Hyperions). My favorite this about this is how well the characters get along, i could talk about this forever. Now i should mention, Spoilers here, so if you wanna skip spoilers, just skip to the next paragraph :), The choices you make can change the outcome of ending, for example, if you are a good guy all the way throughout, and even turn down the offer Handsome Jack makes Rhys in chapter 4, will depend on how the characters like you, more specifcally Sasha, like, like like, if you know what i am saying. There isn't any romance however there is a little flirtation interactions with Rhys and Sasha which I really like and I really hope to see more of these characters in the next Borderlands game. Now, there are some other characters you meet, such as Loader Bot, one of my favorites because he is so loyal and he has his funny moments as well as a very strong friendship with Gortys who is also adorable and I could'nt get enough of her, she is so funny. Now the spoiler bits are over.
Now, for most of the story, you hear the Story from a captured Rhys and Fiona as they are being help captive by a Mysterious person; you do later discover who it is, and it is a real shocker, believe me I was trying to guess who is was all the way through with what little evidence I had such as the body build as well as the voice. Going through the story of Rhys and Fiona, i loved it so much, although there was some moments that was very emotional, and that's coming from someone who tries to stay emotionally distant. With episode 5 you play as present day Fiona and Rhys, after discovering who The Stranger is and battle something (Won't say what, that's for you to discover).
Now, if someone put a gun to my head and said "Say something bad about it! NOW!" Then there is one thing that I wanted from this...I wanted the story to continue, i wanted more, more and more, these characters facinated me to the point where I was reading up on them on the Wikia reading every little thing about them. When Borderlands 3 comes out, I want these characters, I want them either as playable characters or incredibly important, i want the game to be about them as well as the Borderlands 2 games, and if it doesn't, I want a stand-alone game, like this, about these characters either in this, 'Choice's Matter' style of game or like the Borderlands games. I want these characters either way.
I would recommend this to anyone and everyone, its to awesome of a game to miss, if you have £19 lying around, doing nothing, get this.

I can't adequately explain how many hours of my life I've lost to Puzzle Quest and its sequel here. One of the few games I'm tempted to replay, except when I start another round I know I'll certainly lose several more hours to its clutches. You don't play for the story - rather, the story is alright, sure - you play for the gameplay.
It's basically everything people enjoy about Bejeweled and its genre, except with actual character designs and a supernatural old time setting. This installment has a narrator to make you feel especially epic and important, even though you're just playing a puzzle gem-swapping game. But if you're the type of person (like me) who frequently wastes time on gem-swapping games anyway, this is the top of the line for 'em. It'll make you regret wasting time with the others, when you could've been battling epic monsters and spell-casting and matching exploding skulls instead of staring at a shiny screen.

Frankly, there are two questions you need to ask yourself about this game:
Do you like One Piece? Do you like Warriors games?
If you answered yes to both of these questions, you will not be disappointed.
If you answered no to both, well, give this one a miss.
If you answered yes to one, or "I don't know" - there are a few things to know.
Pirate Warriors 3 follows the Warriors tradition of expanding upon existing games - you do not need Pirate Warriors 1 or 2, as Pirate Warriors 3 will cover the story from the beginning.
The story, of course, is the storyline of the One Piece series - if you have read the manga or watched the anime you will be at an advantage in some instances, as the battles you undertake are indeed based on the series' events, and prior knowledge can help you know who your character should be targeting for certain bonuses. Essentially, you tend to be rewarded for following the events of the series "correctly."
It must be noted, of course, that the story presented in the game is abridged - if you want to experience the One Piece story in its entirety, you should opt for the anime or manga.
As for how it stacks up as a Warriors game, it's the standard formula with some tweaks - as is standard for Warriors spin-offs.
This time, we have the basic standard/strong attack combos, Musou-style specials, camera-targeting, a dodge-dash, an unorthodox "unique attack"on a separate button - seems to be a ranged attack, and the 'big' feature of Pirate Warriors, the crew system. Crew members will join up with your character and charge a meter not unlike the rage gauge or similar  in previous Warriors games, when full you can activate the crew assist, which functions much the same as the rage state did - boosting your abilities in various ways, while also bringing the crew member in to fight beside you. While active, you can also use a powered up Musou special attack, teaming up with your crewmate. This gets stronger as you play, as after using this crew assist, you will form a team with that crewmate, at which point you can switch your crew assist member, and build the gauge anew - which is where it gets interesting! With the new crew member, building the gauge again and executing the crew assist will form a team with THAT member - the previous member will stay part of your team, and thus your crew assist grows in strength, with both joining in for the Crew Musou special attack. You can have a team of up to four for your crew assist - the sheer devastation caused by a team of this size is really something to behold.
If you like the spectacle of wiping out large crowds in your Warriors games, you will have a lot of fun with this!
There is definitely less focus on capturing terrirory compared to other Warriors games - most of the time, capturing a territory removes it from play, stopping enemy spawns but not providing any benefits to your own forces. This fits with the theme, obviously, since the Pirates are a small band of rogue agents only sometimes assisting other forces.
If you've never played a Warriors game and aren't a One Piece fan, I would suggest cutting your teeth elsewhere, but as it stands, this is a really solid Warriors installment! Lots to do, lots to unlock, definitely a title to keep you invested for a long time!
Highly recommended for the right audience!

This is by far my favorite game in the Puzzle Quest series.  If you're looking for a change from the twitch gameplay of FPS and Action RPG games, this one offers a very chill experience.  The game is absolutely huge too, and there are no shortage of fights, treasures, and traps to discover.  The RPG elements are surprisingly deep for what is essentially a game of Bejeweled.  I really enjoyed the equipment and upgrade system, as well as the large amount of spells you can use for battles.  It sets up a surprising amount of strategy for battles.
As great as this game is, there are also some issues, though nothing that ruins the experience.  The AI is pretty much infalliable, especially if you leave a 4 or 5 match on the board accidentally.  It will always match it, without fail.  Regardless of how good you are, you will sometimes miss these bonus matches - and the AI always makes you pay immediately.  Second, some of the fights seem to drag quite a bit later in the game.. some of the trash monsters seem to cling to life for quite some time.  They're still very easy fights, but it shouldn't take 15+ minutes for a glorious hero to take down a random skeleton.  (Though it should be noted that I play a templar, and they're not meant to be damage machines)  Lastly, the board seems to Mana Drain a little more often than it should.  I understand there's a very random aspect to this game, but the AI should be able to compensate for this when deciding what the next gems will be.  I've had some fights mana drain 3 or 4 times in a few minutes, and that really draws out the battles.
Again, these problems are very minor, and I would still give this game a 9/10.  It's simply great addictive fun.

When you open this game, you play it until it's done--roughly 3 hours later. You'll likely feel some regret, too, regarding ill-made decisions made from ignorance as an unseen timer counts down, giving good reason for replaying.
You only do a few things throughout the three hours; most of it's spent reading historical logs on a space ship that suffered a catastrophic event (as well as a loss of species fitness!) leaving its ignorant crew wiped out in an instant.  You also chat with two lovable AIs and input a couple computer commands as you search for the truth, which you may or may not get your first time through.

Its a wonderful game that involved me more emotionally than most other games I've played, which spend hours on getting you to be invested in your character and building an involving plot. Perhaps the strongest indication of the quality of its narrative is that your only declared goal is to get in, download, and get out, but within minutes I had ceased to care about that entirely and spent hours past what I needed to accomplish that. While many game spend their entire time trying to hook you into their central plots, Analogue effortlessly drew me into its narrative and I was not content to leave until I had thoroughly probed the depths of the Mugunghwa uncovered her story. Only then did I, could I choose to leave and I did so completely satisfied.

Well guys, will tell you this game IN REVERSE.
The ending was horrid. Not only do you NOT get to see the professor (outside of pictures throughout the house that is), when you get to the end - and start to free him, the game abruptly ENDS! OK, that said. this game is FKN AMAZING! First off, do not play it right after you finish the PORTAL series. You'll be greatly disappointed, as you will spend a lot of your time comparing the two.  PORTAL is more of LOGIC based puzzles and QC is more PHYSICS based.
You have four dimension, you are introduced to one at a time, and are in control of throughout the game. Each one is used to help solve each room you traverse through, as yo make your way down to save your uncle (who, at the beginning got stuck in a different dimension)
FLUFFY: makes things light, allowing you to pick up just about any item not nailed down
SLOW: More like slo-motion on crack! Its REALLY slow. helps slow things down
HEAVY: makes things extreamly heavy - mostly used to solve puzzles that need excessive weight - like switches(these require weirght that the safes cannot produce)
REVERSE GRAVITY: reverses gravity - here you really learn about physics..
Music is very nice. and does a good job as background music, as it does not distract your attention. John De Lance was amazing as the voice of the profesor which his cutting sarcasm that makes think throughout the game - what is his real motive.

On the face of it, this game could offer everything a fan of sandbox games wants. Yes the crafting is complicated and has huge depth and the game doesnt hold your hand.
But deep down, in an attempt to add deep crafting, they have forgot to add any ease of use. For example, to craft a gun, you need to craft X amount of components, and those components need Y amount of items. And to figure out where to get these items from, you have to navigate an over complicated badly written in-game database, which tells you what node is needed to harvest. Once you know the node, you then have to scan while in the respective zone in order to find their location.
The animation of characters and monsters is something from early 2005, the movements are sharp and at times 'spikey'. Ability visuals are uninspiring currently and its impossible to tell any visual difference. The graphics as a whole are nothing special either and yet they use a lot of system power. This all may change as there was talk of them using a newer more up to date engine in a future patch.
The audio is almost pointless, and the sound effects are uninspiring and just a general laser pewpew for almost every gun..
There is little community (at least on EU servers) and the ones i have come across have been verbally hostile/rude, which impacts a sandbox game much more than a theme park, as you require other players assistance to progress (crafting, farming, forming pvp groups etc).
The blog states the release is Q4 2015 which concerns me as i see this game still as a very early alpha test.
Deep down, the ambition is amazing, SWG + UO is the inspiration behind the game, but they have bitten off way more they can chew.
